About the Authors
Piyali Ghosh  is an Assistant Professor with School of Management Studies, Motilal Nehru National 
Institute of Technology (MNNIT) Allahabad. She has earned her PhD from MNNIT Allahabad, MBA 
from University of Allahabad and MA (Economics) from CSJM University, Kanpur. Dr. Ghosh has 
earlier been associated as member of faculty with Birla Institute of Technology and Science (BITS) 
Pilani and Institute of Management Technology (IMT) Ghaziabad, and has been teaching courses 
on Industrial Relations & Labour Legislations, Human Resource Management, Business Ethics & 
Corporate Governance and Managerial Economics. Her research interest lies in Industrial Relations, 
Training & Development and Employee Engagement. Dr. Ghosh has worked on an international 
project on women entrepreneurs spanning several countries and is presently working as a principal 
investigator in a project on housing for urban homeless poor funded by HSMI-HUDCO, New Delhi. 
She has co-authored a book on Managerial Economics , has more than 20 research papers published in 
national and international journals and has presented over 10 research papers in various conferences.
Shefali Nandan is an MBA with specialization in Human Resource Management (HRM) from 
Lucknow University, Lucknow and earned her PhD in the area of HRM from Dr. Hari Singh Gour 
Central University, Sagar, Madhya Pradesh. She also holds a Master’s degree in Chemistry and has 
qualified UGC-NET. With a teaching experience spanning over thirteen years, Dr. Nandan is currently 
teaching Business Management at School of Management Studies, Motilal Nehru National Institute 
of Technology Allahabad. Her teaching areas include Industrial Relations & Labour Legislations, 
Human Resource Management, Organisational Behaviour, Change Management and Cross-Cultural 
Management. Earlier, she has taught postgraduate and undergraduate courses in Business Management 
at Dr. Hari Singh Gour University, Sagar, for more than four years. She has 45 national and international 
publications to her credit. She has worked on an international project on women entrepreneurs that 
covered 18 countries and is currently working as co-principal investigator in a project on Investment 
Patterns of Urban Poor  funded by Indian Council for Social Science Research. Dr. Nandan has been 
a resource person for training at various organizations including Jawaharlal Nehru Police Academy, 
Sagar. Her research is primarily focused on labour issues, performance appraisal and human resource 
development. Other areas of her work include corporate change management, women entrepreneurship, 
gender issues and other issues of social interest.

Foreword
Growth of industries is very essential for the economic development of a nation. Industries can flourish 
only when there is a healthy relationship between management and workers — the two most impor-
tant components of any organization. Today, the relationship between management and workers has 
undergone a huge change due to factors like globalization, extensive use of technology, revolution in 
information and communication technology and changes in the nature of jobs. Outsourcing has become 
very popular and composition of workforce is changing. It is therefore essential to understand indus-
trial relations from a new perspective in this changed scenario. It is essential for a practising manager 
and for a future manager to comprehend various dimensions of management-workers relations along 
with various labour legislations governing and regulating this relationship to find optimum and lawful 
solutions to problems related to workers.
Industrial Relations and Labour Laws  by Dr. Piyali Ghosh and Dr. Shefali Nandan takes a com-
prehensive view of various aspects of industrial relations and discusses labour legislations in a lucid 
manner. The book covers issues that are relevant in current scenario. Each chapter is well planned that 
begins with its objectives and builds on the topic with the help of researches in the area. The layout 
of the chapters has been designed creatively, where ‘Spotlight’ in the chapters highlight important 
concepts and definitions, while ‘Reflection’ connects it with previous chapters.
The section on industrial relations has very deftly integrated current problems and issues related to 
management-workers relations in today’s business environment with traditional concepts. It explains the 
changes that have taken place in various aspects of industrial relations over a period of time. Labour 
Legislations have been discussed with proper introduction to each legislation and using a simple lan-
guage, including recent amendments. The real-life cases and caselets in each chapter help the readers 
understand the nuances of the topics.
The book will address the needs of not only students and professionals in the field but may also 
prove to be of interest to anyone who wishes to understand the subject. I congratulate the authors for 
making an excellent effort in bringing a clear understanding of the subject through this book and wish 
them all the best in their endeavours.
(S. K. Khare)
Former General Manager (Employee Relations)
Indian Oil Corporation Limited
Marketing Division, Head Office, Mumbai
IR&LL_Prelims.indd   6 3/3/2015   11:36:41 AM

Preface
The subject of industrial relations basically deals with the relationship between management and 
workers in an organizational set-up. With the current dynamic business environment  and organiza-
tions witnessing fast changes since the past few decades, the concept of industrial relations could not 
remain insulated. Labour-management relations are gaining new hues; labour legislations are getting 
amended in tandem with the times, and new legislations are getting enacted. It is in this backdrop that 
the title Industrial Relations and Labour Laws  has been designed and developed.
The blueprint of this title had been drawn in our minds a few years back and this book is an out-
come of our thought process, analysis and interpretation of the subject. Through our experience of 
teaching industrial relations and labour legislations as a part of the curriculum of MBA programme, 
we have come across a general perception that the concept of industrial relations is changing shades 
and shapes with factors like growth of the service sector, emergence of new kinds of jobs, changes 
in the structure and functions of trade unions, and use of new technologies. Thus, today there is a 
need to look at the relationship between management and workers with a new perspective. It is this 
fresh standpoint that is the focal point of this title. It prepares the students of business management, 
practicing managers and professionals to understand the various dimensions of the issues that lead to  
friction between labour and management in the current scenario and help them find solutions to the 
problems governing labour-management relations.
While designing the structure of the book and critically analysing  some of the existing titles on this 
subject, we realised that the book  should be neither too bulky, nor too concise, without compromising 
on the quality of the content. At a time when the country has been witnessing violent strife between 
workers and management in big industrial houses like Maruti Suzuki, Jet Airways and Hyundai Motors, 
we have included real-life cases from such industries, to help readers connect with theory and also to 
keep them abreast with the recent changes in the industrial relations scenario of the nation. We have 
endevoured to maintain a balance between the usage of academic citations, latest available data and 
examples from real life.
The book is divided into two sections: Section I covers industrial relations and Section II covers 
labour legislations. The section on industrial relations, spanning from Chapter 1 to Chapter 13, cov-
ers aspects like trade unions, collective bargaining, industrial discipline, dispute settlement, industrial 
safety and health, and international perspective on industrial relations. An additional feature is that 
pertinent recommendations of the Second National Commission on Labour have been included at 
appropriate places in the chapters.
Section II covers labour legislations in India and runs from Chapter 14 to Chapter 26. All major 
labour legislations have been included in this section. It has been observed that students of business 
management, especially, may not find interest in the legal jargons that usually are indispensable part  
of Acts. Care has, therefore, been taken to explain all the Acts in simple and lucid language. Keeping 
pace with the recent developments in the legislative framework of the country, ‘The Sexual Harassment 
of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013’ has also been included 
as an Appendix.
A special feature of this book is “Case Corner” containing real-life legal cases and business situa-
tions that have been given at appropriate places in each chapter. Another aspect is ‘Spotlight’ in each 
IR&LL_Prelims.indd   7 3/3/2015   11:36:41 AM

chapter that highlights the important concepts in the chapter. ‘Reflection’ is a connecting link with 
concepts discussed in earlier chapters. Other learning aids include desired knowledge competencies 
at the beginning of each chapter, end-of-chapter summaries and case studies, discussion questions and 
exercises, glossary, and an extensive list of references for further study.
To sum up, the aim of this book is to provide a rich repository of both theoretical concepts and their 
practical application. Emphasis has been laid on critical thinking and creative analysis of situations 
related to labour-management dynamics. This book will benefit students of business management, 
human resource management, personnel management, industrial relations and law. The book will also 
act as a reference for practicing managers and consultants, and as an invaluable guide for UGC-NET 
aspirants. We sincerely hope that the book will be highly useful to all the readers and would contribute 
to increasing their understanding of the subject.
Piyali Ghosh
Shefali Nandan

Acknowledgements
Writing a book of this magnitude is an enormous task which requires contribution of many helping 
hands. First of all, we are grateful to Almighty for giving us the inspiration to commence on this 
journey and the strength to complete it.
As a subject Industrial Relations and Labour Laws has earned many opinions. Some find it inter-
esting, though a lot many see it as difficult more because it delves into the intricate realms of human 
behaviour at work. This book is designed to unlock the doors to the challenging yet fascinating world 
of industrial relations. It was close to two years in writing, but cumulatively around ten years in the 
making. We are thankful to students, practitioners and all others whose need for a comprehensive re-
pository on Industrial Relations and Labour Laws provided us with the motivation to write this book.
We express our heartfelt gratitude to Dr. Geetika, Professor and Head, School of Management 
Studies, Motilal Nehru National Institute of Technology Allahabad, for her constant guidance and 
support in our endeavour. Her insights on the subject have gone a long way in adding value to every 
chapter. This book would not have taken its present form without the inputs from our other colleagues 
who helped in improving the contents of the book. We appreciate their valuable suggestions. Students 
are a teacher’s best critics. We are thankful to all our students as queries of these young minds drove 
us to explore new dimensions of the topics covered in the book.
Our sincere thanks go to Shri S. K. Khare, former General Manager (Employee Relations), Indian 
Oil Corporation Limited, for agreeing to write the Foreword and for being so enthusiastic about our 
work. We are grateful to all the copyright holders, organizations and individuals for their permission 
to use their works in the book. Each source of our cases and examples has been acknowledged at the 
point of usage. We owe much to by Shri Abhijit Majumdar, Faculty, Indian Institute of Coal Manage-
ment, Ranchi, who extended support in allowing access to the rich repository of labour-related journals 
in the library of the Institute. His profound practical knowledge of disciplinary proceedings in public 
sector enterprises has also assisted in shaping several issues in the book. 
We cannot thank our families enough for supporting and encouraging us in every possible way 
and makings things convenient for us so that we could fully concentrate on our task of book writing. 
We acknowledge the contribution of the reviewers in the form of invaluable comments and sug-
gestions that proved to be instrumental in enhancing the value of the book. We are indebted to all 
others who have directly and indirectly helped us in bringing the book to its present form. Finally, we 
thank the publishing team whose support, efforts, diligence and pains taken round the clock helped 
the book see light of the day. 
We hope our readers discover how interesting Industrial Relations and Labour Laws can be.
Piyali Ghosh
Shefali Nandan

Industrial Relations: An Overview
Desired Knowledge Competencies
cTo describe the concept and evolution of industrial relations.
cTo discuss the theoretical perspectives in industrial relations.
cTo identify the impact of globalisation and technology on industrial relations.
CONCEPT OF INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS 
An industry has two main components: management (including the owner or the capitalist) and labour. 
The concept of industrial relations may be said to have come into being with the need to manage the 
relations between labour and management in industry. This need emerges because on one side there 
is management (on behalf of the capitalist) that invests money and procures various inputs with the 
objective of reaping profits, while on other side, there is labour that toils hard for the production of 
goods and services and gets compensation in return. Their objectives may sometimes clash with each 
other and such a situation may prove to be detrimental to the interests of not just the two parties 
involved but that of the community as a whole. However, if they work in harmony, the outcome of 
the efforts of labour and management may contribute to the development of the economy and would 
benefit the entire community. 
The concept of industrial relations is characterised as collectivist and pluralist in nature. It has been 
traditionally viewed as the relationship between employers and their representatives and workers and 
their representatives, emerging out of work. However, the modern approach to industrial relations 
includes not only relationships between workers, between workers and employers, and between em-
ployers and employers, but also various processes involved in these relationships, such as organising 
of workers, workers’ participation in decision making, dispute settlement, collective bargaining, etc. 
Yoder (cited in Singh and Kumar, 2011, p. 5) defined industrial relations as the “relationship between 
management and employees, or among employees and their organisations, that characterise or grow out 
of employment.” Many scholars have viewed industrial relations in a narrow sense and have focused on 
specific aspects of this relationship. Flanders (1970, p. 86), a British industrial relations scholar, defined 
industrial relations as “a study of the institutions of job regulation.” Hyman (1975, p. 12) considered 
“struggle for power” as an inherent feature of industrial relations and proposed industrial relations as

1.4 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
“the study of processes of control over work relations”, with focus on collective actions of workers’ 
organisations. Johri (1969) (as cited in Monappa, 1999, p. 8) defines industrial relations as “the relation 
between an employer and employee in the course of running of an industry and may project itself to 
spheres which may transgress to the areas of quality control, marketing, price fixation, and disposition 
of profits among others.” According to Singh (1968, p. 9), industrial relations “involve a study of the 
State, the legal system, the workers’ and employers’ organisations at the institutional level; and of the 
patterns of industrial organisation (including management), capital structure (including technology), 
compensation of the labour force, and the study of market forces—all at the economic level.”
The economic, political, social and technological environment of a country affects its industrial 
relations framework. Work and workplaces are affected by norms, rules, and regulations created by 
various institutions and organisations (e.g., organisations of employers and government agencies). The 
institutions which devise and implement this network of rules are an important component in the study 
of industrial relations (Bray and Wailes, 1997). Thus industrial relations cannot be separated from the 
institutional framework, which is mainly made up of government agencies responsible for creating 
policies and rules governing industry and labour. The involvement of government agencies gives rise 
to tripartite nature of industrial relations, with labour, management and the State as the three actors.
In India, industrial disputes on wages, employment conditions, work-
ing conditions, retrenchment, lay-off, production, etc. may be resolved 
through bipartite processes with involvement of both workers and man-
agement. But when it is not possible to resolve disputes at this level, the 
State intervenes, and then it takes a tripartite form. The rationale for State 
intervention is to achieve cooperation and social justice (e.g., prevention 
of exploitation of sweated and child labour). The State also acts as a 
regulatory body for industrial relations in India.
Taking the above definitions and concepts into consideration, we may define industrial relations 
as a means by which the various interests involved in the labour market are accommodated, primarily 
for the purpose of regulating employment relationships.
INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS AND THE CONSTITUTION OF INDIA
The Constitution of India provides the basic guidelines for creating the 
industrial relations system of the country. The Fundamental Rights and 
the Directive Principles of State Policy in the Constitution act as the basis 
for labour policy. Any policy, rule or law, under any circumstances, cannot 
violate the Fundamental Rights. In fact, these rights have been ensured 
through various labour legislations and include: the right to equality (Ar-
ticle 14), prohibition of discrimination (Article 15), the rights to freedom 
of speech and association (Article 19), the rights to life and personal liberty (Article 21), prohibition 
of traffic in human beings and forced labour (Article 23), and prohibition of employment of children 
in factories, etc. (Article 24).
The Directive Principles of State Policy enshrined in the Constitution act as guidelines for the State 
in creating such industrial relations system in the country as provides equity, justice and welfare for 
workers. These guidelines require that the State should aim to: secure a social order for the promotion 
of welfare of people (Article 38); direct its policies towards securing adequate means of livelihood for 
all citizens through various means including equal pay for equal work, protection of health and strength Spotlight

HISTOR Y OF INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS IN INDIA
We will study the evolution of industrial relations in India by dividing it into two phases: pre- 
Independence phase and post-Independence phase.
Pre-Independence Phase
The history of industrial relations in India can be traced back to the time of emergence of industries. 
Though the Industrial Revolution in Europe had begun during the eighteenth century and by the nine-
teenth century industries were well established, in India beginning of modern industries was during the 
mid-nineteenth century. Indigo plantations, established in 1831, may be said to be the first industry in 
India. Later, a cotton mill was established in 1851 in Bombay (now Mumbai) and jute manufacturing 
was started in 1855 in Calcutta (now Kolkata).
During the early phase of industrialisation there was a clear divide between capitalists and labour. 
Capitalists or employers were in a commanding position; their sole concern was to earn and maximise 
profits. Workers were treated merely as tools of production. They subsisted on meager wages, had 
long working hours, and lived in poor conditions; there were hardly any laws to protect them. To get 
rid of such poor working and living conditions, workers gradually begun to organise themselves and 
protest against the atrocities inflicted upon them by the employers. This laid the seeds of trade union-
ism. The year 1860 marked the beginning of labour unrest in India to protest against the oppression 
of indigo cultivators in Bengal, followed by instances of labour unrest observed in Nagpur (in 1877), 
Bombay and Surat. However, due to unequal distribution of power between labour and employers, the 
former had to suffer for protesting, by way of dismissals, victimisation, etc.
Enactment of the Factories Act, 1881 was an important milestone in 
the evolution of industrial relations, as it ushered in a force that awakened 
workers. Several workers’ organisations had begun to take form by this 
time, and in 1890, the first workers’ association, named Bombay Mill 
Hands Association, was established with the efforts of N.M. Lokhande. 
After this several other associations were formed, though it was not easy for these organisations to 
get legal recognition. The Trade Unions Act that came into existence in 1926 contained provisions 
for registration of trade unions.
Meanwhile, certain developments at international level too had an impact upon workers and employ-
ers. The World War I (1914-1918) resulted in price rise, which enabled employers to generate profits. 
However since wages remained the same, workers had to face a situation of economic distress. Labour 
unrest increased and a number of strikes took place, prominent amongst which were the strikes of 
workers of Textile Labour Association Ahmedabad in 1917, led by Mahatma Gandhi and the strikes at 
Madras (now Chennai) by workers of Buckingham and Carnatic Mills in 1910 and 1921. Formation of 
the International Labour Organisation (ILO) in 1919 gave a boost to the labour movement. Around this Spotlight

1.6 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
time another significant development took place in the form of establishment of the All India Trade 
Union Congress in 1920. A number of labour legislations were enacted, including the Workmen’s (now 
Employees’) Compensation Act, 1923 and the Trade Unions Act, 1926. The Economic Depression 
in 1929 worsened the condition of workers, as a result of which labour unrest grew and there were a 
number of strikes and lock-outs deteriorating labour-management relations. Government’s intervention 
during this time to control labour unrest was the  beginning of the tripartite nature of industrial relations.
The Second World War (1939–1945) again resulted in price rise, profits for capitalists, and poor 
living conditions for labour. Since the establishment of tripartite consultative machinery in 1942, the 
principle of tripartite structure of industrial relations was gradually evolved and refined, that shaped 
the industrial relations machinery in India. Many developments took place in the years that followed 
the World War II. The Indian National Trade Union Congress was formed in 1947. A number of leg-
islations were enacted during this phase, including the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 
1946, and the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
Post-Independence Phase
Immediately after Independence the emphasis of the Government of India was to contain labour unrest 
and increase industrialisation for growth and generation of employment. A Tripartite Conference was 
convened in 1947 in which the Industrial Truce Resolution was adopted. It required management and 
labour to agree to maintain industrial peace and prevent any work stoppages during the next 3 years 
to promote industrial growth. The Labour Relations Bill of 1950 introduced the concept of collective 
bargaining. Though the Bill could not be passed, nonetheless, it initiated a thought process towards 
non-legal bipartite approach of solving industrial disputes. 
Emphasis was laid on industrial peace in the First Five Year Plan 
(1951-1956), which had set targets for all round development of the na-
tion. The Plan also mentioned about methods of settling disputes between 
labour and management through tripartite bodies, the need for a grievance 
procedure and the importance of works committees. The Second Five 
Year Plan (1956-1961) evolved norms, codes and methods for achieving harmony and discipline in 
industry. It spelt out the need for union recognition and to end unresolved disputes through voluntary 
arbitration, rather than compulsory adjudication. Schemes for workers’ 
participation in management were evolved during this period, including 
Joint Management Councils in 1958. The Indian Labour Conference held 
in 1957 emphasised on maintaining discipline in industry and the Code 
of Discipline was evolved in 1958. The Workers’ Education Scheme was 
also initiated in 1958 to support industrialisation.
In the Third Five Year Plan (1961-1966), specifically during Chinese aggression on India, the 
Industrial Truce Resolution was adopted in 1962, in which labour and management resolved to settle 
disputes peacefully and pledged to increase production. Central Wage Boards, Safety Councils and 
the Model Grievance Procedure were initiated during this period. An important event during this Plan 
was the appointment of the First National Commission on Labour that took a comprehensive view of 
industrial relations in the country in its report. The first half of the decade of 1970s, during the Fourth 
Five Year Plan (1969-1974), saw a lot of industrial strife. Political interference in trade unions had 
increased by this time. Efforts for maintaining industrial peace initiated in the early years of Indepen-
dence proved to be inadequate. The Government declared Emergency in 1975 to control the ongoing 
volatile economic conditions in the country and to maintain peace. Right to strike was suspended during 
the emergency period. The subsequent Five Year Plans made some brief mention of issues related to Spotlight

We have touched on government policies on labour and the Five Year Plans in detail in Chapter 10.
Notable changes in the industrial relations scenario in the country took place with the adoption 
of the New Industrial Policy of 1991, that aimed at liberalisation of the economy. The policy put the 
responsibility on the Government to equip workers with adequate skills in order to deal with techno-
logical changes. It considered workers as equal partners in economic growth and emphasised upon 
training and workers’ participation in management. 
In the changed business scenario, trade unions have taken up varied functions and have adopted a 
participative approach, shifting from the traditional militant approach. We have analysed such traditional 
and new functions of trade unions in Chapter 3.
THEORETICAL PERSPECTIVES 
Several theories and perspectives have been proposed to understand the concept of industrial relations 
and the rationale behind the beliefs and actions of labour and management. We will discuss some of 
the prominent ones in this section.
Systems Model
The Systems Model proposed by Dunlop in the 1950s views industrial relations system as consisting 
of three actors: management, workers and their formal and informal organisations, and government 
agencies. These actors function in an environment that is made up of technology, labour, markets, and 
various power equations in the society. Dunlop believed that all the three constituent actors, at least 
to some extent, are affected by environmental factors. Within this environment all these actors interact 
to work and to determine the rules that help in running the industrial relations system.
The three unique factors in Dunlop’s model are: external environmental 
forces acting upon the labour-management relationship; specific char-
acteristics in labour-management-government interactions; rules arising 
out of and at the same time governing existing employment relationships 
between the three actors; and a shared understanding of rules that gives 
stability to the entire system.
Dunlop viewed the above-mentioned arrangement of industrial rela-
tions as a system, wherein the components are interacting and interde-
pendent, while freely giving and receiving information from the external environment for dealing with 
certain issues and are together responsible for certain outputs. Thus industrial relations may be viewed 
as a social sub-system operating within environmental constraints.
Unitary Perspective
The essence of the Unitary Perspective is that the enterprise is a social 
system or a unitary organisation made up of management and workers, 
both having the common objectives of achieving high efficiency and 
high profits that would ultimately benefit all, and hence there exists no 
conflict. Management adopts a leadership role and holds the responsibil-
ity to design such policies as are beneficial to workers, management and 
all the other stakeholders. It must also work to promote loyalty amongst 
employees.Spotlight

1.8 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
According to this theory, all the actions and ideas of management and the State are right and rational, 
while the actions and beliefs of workers that are conflicting with management and the State are irra-
tional. In fact, even trade unions are an outcome of imperfections in common understanding of shared 
interests between workers and management. The main characteristics of the Unitary Perspective are:
rManagement is the main authority in an organisation and there is no conflict of interest between 
management and trade unions.
rBoth the parties must work together to achieve their common objectives. 
rTrade unions are not essential for the well-being of workers or for managing conflicts. 
The unitarist view sees employer-employee relations as essentially harmonious, punctuated only 
by occasions of temporary and illegitimate conflicts. Conflict is thus an anomaly and a dysfunctional 
aspect of working that disturbs harmony and hence could be eliminated.
However, this theory fails to recognise that power is unequally distributed between workers and 
management in an organisation and that this inequality in itself may generate conflict. It views conflict 
as a negative force rather than as an opportunity to achieve harmony. Further, it adopts a normative 
approach as it believes in the common interest of all stakeholders but does not propose ways to identify 
these common interests.
Pluralist Theory
Conceptually the Pluralist Theory of Flanders is the opposite of the Uni-
tary Theory. According to this approach, an organisation is the sub-system 
of a social system, and is made up of two divergent groups, viz., man-
agement and trade unions, each having its own interests and perception 
of the social structure. However, these two interconnected groups have 
a common objective of the maintenance and growth of the organisation 
by making use of the process of bargaining. Any conflict that arises 
between the groups is over distribution of profits, and is natural and inevitable. The Pluralist Theory 
views conflict between workers and management as difficult to reconcile and that conflict itself is 
not wrong. The focus should be on ‘how to handle it’ rather than ‘how to avoid it’. State intervention 
may be required if the conflict cannot be handled by workers and management. Thus, the pluralistic 
perspective takes the view that the potential for conflict is inherent in the employment relationship, 
but is manageable and can be contained by an appropriate network of rules and regulations. Pluralist 
perspective emphasises the use of various conflict resolution techniques that involve the parties in 
conflict and other stakeholders.
One of the main drawbacks of the Pluralist Theory is its over-emphasis on rules and procedures. 
Though rules and laws can be made to resolve conflicts, they cannot adapt to changing conditions at 
workplace (Gennard and Judge, 2002). In fact, rules need to be reviewed and changed from time to 
time in order to be effective. Also, the focus of this theory is too much on workers’ interests, and that 
can jeopardise the effectiveness of collective bargaining processes.
Radical Perspective
The Radical Perspective is inspired by the Marxist view on capitalism. It considers work and working 
conditions in an organisation as exploitative to workers. Class conflict exists in society and conflict 
between labour and management is simply a part of it. The followers of Radical Perspective consider 
organisations as representing the oppressive nature of the general societal structure. Conflict is unavoidable 
in organisations as management represents the interests of capitalists who want to maximise profit at the Spotlight
The Pluralist Perspective views

an organisation due to the pres-

cost of workers. Even the modern practices of improving employee-management relations like employee 
empowerment or gain-sharing, are viewed as solely motivated by the objective of benefiting management.
Followers of Radical Perspective view industrial relations in terms of an enduring structural conflict 
between employers and those who sell their labour to the employers. Temporary accommodations to 
this conflict, according to radicals, do little more than controlling employees in their exploited position 
and secure the stability of a system that continues to favour employers.
TRADE UNIONISM
Trade unionism refers to the whole gamut of activities related to trade unions, including their structure 
and functions. Very often the terms ‘labour movement’ and ‘trade union movement’ are used synony-
mously, but it may be understood here that the former has a wider connotation. Trade union movement 
may be seen as a sub-set of labour movement, and is largely a by-product of industrialisation. According 
to Tannenbaum (1951), trade unionism is a natural outcome and an inherent feature of a capitalistic 
society, while labour movement refers to awakening of labour class for their rights as workers and as 
human beings. To secure their rights, workers found it convenient and useful to organise themselves 
and fight as a body rather than demanding their rights individually, which would have less impact on 
employers. Gradually these organisations got consolidated and started fighting for their legal status. 
This struggle of workers to associate and get recognition for their organisations is referred to as the 
trade union movement. Unions represent workers and adopt various means like strikes, gheraos, etc.,
to pressurise employers. Traditionally, the role of trade unions was considered to fight for workers’ 
rights, but with changing times they have witnessed a number of changes in their roles. We will talk 
about various aspects of trade unions in India in Chapters 3 and 4.
OR GANISATION OF INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS IN INDIA
The framework for industrial relations in India is formed by a number of labour legislations in the 
country that contain obligations and duties for both employers and workers. Under the Constitution of 
India, labour is a subject in the Concurrent List, which empowers both the Central and State Govern-
ments to enact legislations subject to certain matters being reserved for the Centre.

1.10 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Industrial relations in India revolve around three actors: employers, 
workers and their trade unions, and the State. This three-pronged (or tri-
partite) structure tries to balance the power equation between management 
and workers. According to Brandes (1976, p. 6, as cited in Wad, 1996, p. 
16), tripartite structure helps in managing “a continuing tug of war between big labour and big business 
with government seeking to prevent either side from gaining predominance”. Many tripartite bodies 
have been set up in India for joint consultation between the representatives of government, employers 
and workers. These bodies, such as the Indian Labour Conference (ILC), the Standing Labour Com-
mittee (SLC), and Industrial Committees provide a forum to discuss and resolve the issues related to 
labour. We have covered tripartism as a statutory measure for resolving industrial disputes and various 
tripartite bodies in India in chapters 8 and 10.
The role of the State is protective for labour, the weaker partner in industrial relations. The Gov-
ernment is not only a policy maker; it is also an employer in public sector enterprises. It initiates and 
ensures proper implementation and administration of policies and legislations for workers’ welfare, 
social security, health and safety. Chapter 10 also features an elaborate discussion on the role of State, 
Labour policies in the Five Year Plans, and provisions and welfare measures for women and child 
labour. In view of the large proportion of workforce employed in the unorganised sector, the Govern-
ment of India has been making efforts to provide social security to workers in this sector too. Various 
aspects of labour welfare and social security have been dealt with in Chapter 10, while the concept of 
industrial health and safety has been explored in detail in Chapter 13.
There are certain bipartite arrangements like collective bargaining (covered in Chapter 5) for 
managing relations between workers and management. The emphasis of bipartite methods is on set-
tling any dispute between management and workers through mutual dialogue and on failure at this 
level tripartite methods of resolving disputes may be resorted to. The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947
has provisions for such methods of settling disputes with the intervention of the Government. These 
include conciliation officer, board of conciliation, voluntary arbitration, and compulsory arbitration. 
There are Labour Courts, Industrial Tribunals, and National Tribunals in which compulsory arbitration 
proceedings take place. Various dimensions of disputes in industry and dispute settlement have been 
dealt with in chapters 7 and 8 respectively. 
Industrial discipline is very essential for maintaining peace and harmony in industry. Various methods 
are available for disciplining employees. There is a procedure for initiating enquiry against employees. 
The principle of natural justice must be adhered to in the process of initiating and conducting enquiry. 
Grievance settlement mechanisms exist in organisations for settling grievances at individual level. In 
fact, the First National Commission on Labour had even proposed a Model Grievance Procedure. The 
concepts of discipline, grievance and grievance handling have been covered in Chapter 6.
The Government of India has sought to involve workers in decision making through various 
schemes for workers’ participation. Works Committees, Joint Management Councils, Joint Consulta-
tive Committees, shop councils and joint councils are methods that have evolved from time to time for 
achieving effective workers’ participation in management. We will elaborate on workers’ participation 
in management and related aspects in Chapter 11.
Labour Administration Machinery
In India the Ministry of Labour & Employment controls labour-related issues. The Ministry has four 
attached offices, namely, Office of the Directorate General of Employment and Training, New Delhi; 
Office of the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central), New Delhi; Labour Bureau, Chandigarh and 
Shimla; and Directorate General of Factory Advice Service and Labour Institutes, Mumbai. Besides Spotlight

NATIONAL COMMISSIONS ON LABOUR
Two National Commissions on Labour have been established in the 
country so far to review various labour-related issues and give recom-
mendations. The first Commission was set up to study the industrial 
relations scenario in the country when the industrialisation process had 
been initiated by the Government for economic development. The Second 
Commission on Labour was set when the process of economic liberalisa-
tion had been initiated. Let us give a brief overview of both the Commissions in this section.
First National Commission on Labour (1969)
The First National Commission on Labour was set up on 24 December, 1966 under the Chairmanship 
of Justice PB Gajendragadkar. The Commission studied and analysed the industrial relations in India 
and its various dimensions for the first time both in the organised and unorganised sectors. It submit-
ted its report in August, 1969. The issues covered in the report included labour welfare, wages, wage 
policy, bonus, social security, workers’ training and education, workers’ and employers’ organisations, 
and industrial relations machinery.
Recommendations of the First National Commission on Labour resulted in amendment of certain 
labour laws, including the Workmen’s (now Employees’) Compensation Act, 1923 (like removal of 
wage ceiling for coverage); the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (mainly in respect of unfair labour 
practices); the Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948 (in terms of enhancement in the wage limit for 
exemption from payment of employees’ contribution); the Factories Act, 1948 (like making penalties 
more stringent for violation of safety requirements and provision of welfare facilities); and the Em-
ployees’ Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 (namely enhancement in the rate 
of contribution and making default of dues a cognizable offence). 
The Commission’s recommendations have been instrumental in enactment of certain laws, like the 
Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970; the Limestone and Dolomite Mines Labour 
Welfare Fund Act, 1972; the Iron Ore, Manganese Ore and Chrome Ore Mines Labour Welfare Fund 
Act, 1976; the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976; and the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) 
Act, 1986.
The recommendations of the Commission have also brought about certain changes in government 
policies and programmes in some areas like wage policy and minimum wages, vocational training, 
labour statistics and research, and workers’ education.
Second National Commission on Labour (2002)
As specified earlier, vast changes took place in the economy due to 
the policy of liberalisation-privatisation-globalisation adopted by the 
Government of India in 1991. With the opening up of the economy, the 
business environment suddenly became very dynamic. In view of the Spotlight

changes taking place in the industrial relations scenario, the Government felt the need to set up another 
National Commission on Labour. Thus, the Second National Commission on Labour was established 
in 1999 under the chairmanship of Ravindra Varma. The Commission submitted its report to the Gov-
ernment in 2002, in which it made a comprehensive analysis of issues related to labour by taking into 
consideration the impact of globalisation, need for change in the existing labour laws, dynamics of 
the Indian labour system, progress of industrial development after Independence, etc. The Commis-
sion gave recommendations related to review of laws, social security measures, women workers and 
child labour, wages, skill development, labour administration, unorganised sector, etc. To ensure the 
welfare of workers in the unorganised sector, it proposed an umbrella legislation for social security of 
workers in this sector. The Ministry of Labour & Employment drafted the Unorganised Sector Workers 
Bill, 2004, which, inter alia , envisages provisions for safety, social security, and health and welfare 
matters. The recommendations of the Second National Commission on various labour-related issues 
feature in the respective chapters of the book.
INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS IN MODERN ERA
The industrial relations system in India has undergone a sea change in the post-liberalisation phase. The 
last two decades have witnessed notable transformation in the way business is done. Physical boundaries 
between nations are no longer an obstruction for business; multinational organisations are emerging in 
large numbers and are continuously expanding; concern of employers towards the rights and interests 
of workers is increasing; and workers are much more aware of their surrounding environment and are 
awakened towards their rights as compared to the pre-Independence period. New management systems 
are emerging that are designing novel ways of managing worker-management relations. 
Initially the scope of industrial relations was limited, more or less, to procuring and securing work-
ers’ rights by trade unions. Now this scope has expanded to all those aspects of work-related activities 
that require interactions between workers and management. Workers, through their representatives, 
participate in decision making in the enterprise to find ways to enhance firm performance and to 
discuss discipline-related issues, training of workers, etc. Thus workers have come a long way from 
olden times when they were treated merely as a tool for production to a time when they have a voice 
in decision making on issues that affect them.
Changing nature of business has also given rise to new issues for col-
lective bargaining. Business organisations are now hiring employees on 
contract basis as expenses incurred on such workers are lesser as com-
pared to permanent employees. Due to this, job security has emerged as an 
important issue in collective bargaining besides wages, work conditions, 
etc. The various dimensions of labour and employment in the present 
scenario have been covered in Chapter 2.
Impact of Globalisation
Globalisation is the process of interconnecting people across the world on various dimensions including 
cultural, economic, political, technological and environmental  aspects (Greenberg and Baron, 2008). It 
has become a defining characteristic feature of the world as we see it in the twenty-first century. The 
process of globalisation influences not only macro-level economic policies, but also arrangements at 
enterprise-level. It has brought a remarkable shift in the traditional system of industrial relations and 
has changed the dimensions of the relationship between management and workers. The boundaries of Spotlight

of work-related activities that 
require interaction between 
workers and management.

Industrial Relations: An Overview 1.13
doing business, initially limited within a country, have now expanded across nations, bringing about 
economic interdependence between countries. In addition, as pointed out by Michael Camdessus, ex-
Managing Director of International Monetary Fund, increased competition in market has resulted in 
change in products traded, with a shift to more skill-intensive products in developing countries and 
less skill-intensive products in developed countries (Camdessus, 1996).
To support these changes there have been a number of modifications in work arrangements in or-
ganisations so that they can sustain themselves. This has had a considerable impact on the employer-
employee relationship and has also altered the roles played by trade unions. Camdessus (1996) has 
summarised the situation as “……really traumatic when workers through lack of the ability or means 
to learn new skills, or because they are too old to change, lose their jobs. Trade unions have a role to 
play to help workers re-train, ensure that social entitlements are fulfilled and are maintained at an 
adequate level…”
Globalisation has resulted in multinational corporations (MNCs) 
establishing their operations in other countries where locals are hired. 
Cross-cultural issues are bound to emerge in such a scenario, adding a 
new dimension to existing worker-management relations. Labour migra-
tion is another related aspect, which needs to be dealt by employers today. 
With increasing job opportunities, workers’ migration is taking place 
not just within a country from village to cities, but from one country to another, for improved living 
standards.
Enterprises have been seeking ways to optimise their operations in order to strengthen their com-
petitiveness by reducing costs on labour and other resources. This has been done by identifying the 
core strengths and functions to maintain competitiveness and subcontracting peripheral functions to 
external organisations, downsizing, and adopting technology to substitute labour. Besides, companies 
are joining hands through mergers and joint ventures to get strategic advantages. Such situations have 
created a volatile environment for employment.
The economic liberalisation programme in India has encouraged MNCs from developed nations 
to enter India with sophisticated technology. There has been a steady growth of the tertiary sector 
in recent years, which has created new employment opportunities; at the same time shrinkage of the 
primary sector has also been witnessed. MNCs have been detrimental to the growth of indigenous 
products and have been responsible for displacement of people engaged in traditional sectors. The 
reports of a large number of suicides by weavers in Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, etc. are a testimony 
to this phenomenon (Report of the Second National Commission on Labour, 2002).
The relationship between labour and management has seen a lot of changes in such a scenario. 
MNCs based in economically developed industrialised countries are opening up operations in resource-
rich developing countries, where they get cheap labour. This situation has created changes in various 
aspects of labour standards in different industries and regions as trade unions take a comparative view 
of existing wages, welfare and other related issues that affect industrial relations. Keeping in mind 
the need to understand industrial relations in other countries in a networked economy today, we have 
included certain dimensions of industrial relations in other countries in Chapter 12.
Industrial Relations and Technological Change
Besides the various outcomes of globalisation that have affected industrial relations as talked about 
in the previous section, technological change has been an important aspect that has had a significant 
impact on labour-management relations. New technology is adopted by organisations for various Spotlight

reasons like cost-cutting, achieving better product quality, time saving, efficiency and gaining competi-
tive advantage. Whatever the objective may be, adoption of technology affects wide-ranging aspects in 
an organisation, including human resource, employment, job profiles, work arrangements, employee 
attitude, training and industrial relations (Kanawaty, Gladstone, Prokopenko and Rodgers , 1989).
With intensifying competition in markets, product/service quality has become a deciding factor in 
increasing customer base and ultimately decides profits generated by an organisation. Customers always 
demand quality at lesser price. ‘Benchmarking’ and quality standards (like ISO, BIS, 6 Sigma, etc.) 
are increasingly being adopted. Demand in the market fluctuates and enterprises need to be very re-
sponsive and flexible while catering to the needs of customers in terms of product quality and prices. 
Adoption of better technology can ensure quality and reduce costs. Production processes and schedules 
need to be adapted according to the demand. With the integration of modern production technology 
and information technology (IT), enterprises are trying to handle the vagaries of market with flexibil-
ity in their operation schedules. With integrated computerised systems, it has become possible to 
coordinate operations in different units located across countries to manage supply and demand in the 
market. Work methods like kanban (an approach for incremental process improvement) and ‘just-in-
time’ are being adopted in companies to maintain efficiency and to respond to customer needs in time.
What needs to be noted is that whatever change is brought about in 
production technology, it ultimately goes down to workers, as they have 
to learn and adapt to new ways of working. It generates apprehensions 
in them regarding job security, economic benefits, change in habits, 
redundancy and skill obsolescence. These apprehensions are not un-
founded. Workers have to learn new skills, build new capabilities, and 
need to be trained to operate new machines. Embracing new technolo-
gies has increased the demand for skilled employees. Thus employee training and retraining issues 
arise with technological advancements. Many private sector organisations in India are responding 
by taking initiatives to enhance the skill-level of their workforce. Fear about job security may affect 
management-worker relations and may also result in labour unrest. Management needs to handle such 
situations deftly; workers may be made partners through their representatives in bringing about such 
changes in an enterprise.Spotlight

Industrial Relations: An Overview 1.15
Use of information technology has changed the way business is done, and the modes of interaction 
with employees, customers, suppliers and stakeholders. IT has also resulted in increased awareness of 
workers regarding labour laws, their rights, working conditions in other enterprises in the same industry 
and other industries, and so on. IT facilitates them to interact and discuss issues with worker leaders 
in other regions of the country and the world. In other words, information technology has helped in 
widening the vista for workers and in opening up their minds for their broader roles in an enterprise.
Concerns of cost cutting have forced enterprises to seek novel ways of operations, of which 
outsourcing has become very popular. Systems of contracting and sub-contracting have altered the 
traditional systems of production and the established pattern of employer-worker relationship, reducing 
the need for workers in enterprises. There has been an increasing trend in the number of informal workers. 
These changes have influenced trade union membership and have adversely affected their bargaining 
power.
INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS AND HRM/HRD
Human Resource Management (HRM) is a process that helps in proper utilisation of the existing 
workforce in an organisation and creation of such work conditions and systems as can result in better 
employee efficiency. According to Cascio and Aguinis (2005, p. 4), “HRM is concerned with manag-
ing of staff, retention, development, adjustment, and change in order to achieve both individual and 
organisational objectives.” Limited to enterprise-level, the focus of HRM is to carry out organisational 
functions of recruitment, selection, maintenance and separation with effectiveness and efficiency so 
as to achieve organisational objectives and motivate employees. HRM may be considered to be indi-
vidualistic in approach. 
Human Resource Development (HRD), on the other hand, may be seen as a sub-set of HRM. Werner 
and Desimone (2006, p. 15) define HRD as “a set of systematic and planned activities designed by an 
organisation to provide its members with the opportunities to learn necessary skills to meet current 
and future job demand.” Rao (1985) believes that the process of HRD helps employees in identifying 
and using their potentials for self and/or organisational development, and develops such organisational 
culture as supports team work and collaborations among sub-units which contributes to the professional 
wellbeing and motivation of employees. Thus, the process of HRD is developmental in orientation with 
the objective to improve and enhance employee capability and competence through their development, entities, to upgrade in-house training facilities and also to provide training to potential employees 
to make them job-ready.
In early 2008, the Government formed the “Coordinated Action on Skill Development” with a 
3-tier institutional structure consisting of: Prime Minister’s National Council, the National Skill 
Development Coordination Board (NSDCB), and the National Skill Development Corporation 
(NSDC), with the objective of creating skilled workforce. The Prime Minister’s National Council 
on Skill Development has a vision to create 500 million skilled people by 2022 through skill 
systems.
(Adapted from: FICCI (n.d). Skill Development: Sector Profile. Retrieved from www.ficci.com /sector/74/ 
Project_docs/ SectorProfile.pdf on 1/2/2014.)

1.16 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
in order to gain competitive advantage. The focus of every aspect of HRD is on developing a skilled 
and superior workforce through continuous learning so that the organisation can satisfy its customers.
Industrial relations, though concerned with employer-worker relations, may be seen to be different 
from HRM/HRD in several ways. It has a wider scope than HRM as its objective is to achieve improved 
relations between workers and management at various levels, starting from unit-level, through enterprise-
level, regional-level, and finally at the national-level. Industrial relations issues may have involvement 
of workers across the industry, for example strike by workers of a unit may be joined by workers of 
other units/enterprises too in the form of sympathetic strike. Further, industrial relations is inherently 
collectivist in nature as it considers management and workers as two bodies distinct in every aspect of 
their relation. Another difference is that while industrial relations is tripartite in character, though some 
of its processes are bipartite too (e.g., collective bargaining), HRM/HRD lacks any such feature and 
simply involves devising of policies to maintain an efficient workforce in an organisation so as to 
ultimately get competitive advantage. Moreover, HRM/HRD policies are designed by the management 
and changed from time to time; industrial relations issues, on the contrary, are mostly governed by 
labour laws that cannot be modified by management or workers while regulating their relations.
Despite these differences, industrial relations and HRM/HRD cannot 
be seen as totally different concepts. Both address employee-related con-
cerns, though industrial relations as an area is construed to be dealing with 
labour/blue-collar employees and HRM/HRD is concerned with white-
collar/managerial staff. Issues like employee welfare policies, grievance 
handling and training of workers are of common concern to HRM/HRD 
and industrial relations. In the modern industrial scenario, improving 
quality of work life of employees is also seen as a common concern. As 
mentioned above, HRM/HRD helps in maintaining, utilising and developing available skilled workforce 
that also involves motivating workers through rewards and other methods. This helps in maintaining 
harmonious work relations. It has been already explained that the scope of industrial relations today 
has expanded to all aspects of interactions between workers and employers that include HR functions 
like performance appraisal, recruitment and selection, compensation, training, etc. Thus industrial rela-
tions and HRM/HRD may be integrated for general development, motivation and welfare of workers 
and for achieving harmonious employee-management relations.
PRINCIPLES OF LABOUR LEGISLATIONS
Out of the two main players in industry, i.e., labour and management, labour has always been the 
weaker one. The factory system had certain evils attached to it that affected the already weak labour. 
The need for labour laws emerged from the need to manage the “problems relating to human rela-
tions arising out of large scale development of factory system which has emerged in consequence of 
industrial revolution” (Mishra, 1999, p. 2). The sole concern of employers was to increase production 
and productivity without any focus on improving the condition of workers, who were largely illiterate 
and poor and unaware of their rights. To support their families they had to accept whatever meager 
wages were offered. The State had no interference in the relation of employer and labour. Gradually 
when conditions worsened too much, the government was forced to intervene to improve the condi-
tion of workers.
The labour laws of independent India derive their origin and guidelines from the Constitution of India 
and from the beliefs and ideologies of leaders of the struggle for Independence. The Indian Constitution 
guarantees social equality and social justice to all the citizens. These are the two basic principles on Spotlight

Industrial Relations: An Overview 1.17
which labour laws are based. According to Mishra (1999), social justice 
implies two things: first, fair distribution of profits between owner and 
workers in an industrial enterprise and second, providing safe and healthy 
work conditions to workers. According to Article 38 of the Constitution, 
“the State shall strive to promote the welfare of the people by securing 
and protecting as effectively as it may, social order in which justice, social economic and political, shall 
inform all the institutions of the national life.” Social equity refers to equality between different social 
groups such as rich and poor; male and female, and young, old and children, religious groups, people 
belonging to different castes, etc. There must be no discrimination in terms of opportunity, wage distribu-
tion, benefits, etc., between different social groups. Article 39 enshrines such principles of social equity.
Labour legislations have also been significantly influenced by the Conventions and Recommen-
dations of the ILO, recommendations of the National Commissions on Labour, and deliberations of 
various sessions of the Indian Labour Conference and the International Labour Conference. These 
legislations aim at maintaining harmony and discipline in industry so as to promote the growth of the 
national economy. Though they have been enacted to protect workers, workers have their share of 
obligations too in maintaining peaceful working conditions in industry. Labour legislations in India 
may be broadly classified into the following five categories:
rRegulatory legislations (e.g., the Trade Unions Act, 1926 and the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947)
rWage-related legislations ( e.g., the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 and the Minimum Wages 
Act, 1948)
rWelfare legislations (e.g., the Factories Act, 1948, the Plantation Labour Act, 1951 and the 
Mines Act, 1952)
rProtective legislations (e.g., the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 and the Child 
Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986)
rSocial security legislations ( e.g., the Employees’ Compensation Act, 1923, the Employees’ State 
Insurance Act, 1948 and the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961)
Chapters 14 to 26 exhaustively cover some of the important labour legislations.
Summary
rThe concept of industrial relations may be said to have emerged with the need to manage the 
relations between labour and management in industry. It has traditionally been viewed as the 
relationship between employers or their representatives on one side and workers and their rep-
resentatives on the other, emerging due to work.
rThe Constitution of India provides the basic guidelines for creating the industrial relations sys-
tem. The Fundamental Rights and the Directive Principles of State Policy in the Constitution 
act as the basis for labour policy.
rThe history of industrial relations can be traced back to the time of emergence of industries 
in India. Enactment of the Factories Act, 1881 was an important milestone in the evolution of 
industrial relations, as it worked as a catalyst that awakened workers. Several workers’ organisa-
tions had begun to take form by this time.
rWorld War I and World War II resulted in price rises due to which employers generated profits, 
and workers faced situations of economic distress. This led to increase in labour unrest and 
strikes. Formation of ILO in 1919 gave a boost to labour movement.
rA lot of emphasis was laid on industrial peace during the First Five Year Plan (1951-1956). 
The first half of the decade of 1970s, during the Fourth Five Year Plan (1969-1974), saw a lot 
of industrial strife.Spotlight

1.18 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
rDunlop viewed industrial relations as a system consisting of three actors: management, workers 
and the government, that functions in an environment made up of technology, labour, markets, 
and various power equations in the society.
rThe Unitary Theory views work enterprise as a social system made up of management and 
workers with common objectives and no conflict. The Pluralist Perspective views an organisa-
tion as made up of groups of people with divergent objectives and hence considers that conflict 
is natural. Radical Perspective is inspired by the Marxist view about capitalism that considers 
conditions and work in organisations as exploitative to workers.
rIndustrial relations system in India is tripartite in nature. The First National Commission on 
Labour was set up in 1966 which, for the first time, studied and analysed the industrial relations 
in the country. The Second National Commission on Labour was set up in 1999, which analysed 
the industrial relations in India in the era of globalisation. 
rThe concepts of HRM/HRD and Industrial Relations may be integrated to create an efficient 
and motivated workforce working in a harmonious environment.
rThe era of globalisation and liberalisation has had a deep impact on labour in India as it has 
resulted in increased competition, quality consciousness, cost awareness, downsizing and tech-
nological changes. It has also generated the need for skill-development in workers.
rTwo important principles of labour legislations in India are social equity and social justice. 
Labour legislations may be broadly divided into five categories: regulatory legislations, wage 
related legislations, welfare legislations, protective legislations, and social security legislations.

      TUDY
Labour Problems at Toyota-Kirloskar
Background In 1997, the Toyota Motor Corporation of Japan had entered into collaboration with 
the Kirloskar Group in India and established its motorcar manufacturing unit, Toyota Kirloskar Motors 
Limited (TKML) at Bangalore, Karnataka with a capital investment of Rs. 7 billion. Initially both Toyota 
and Kirloskar held equal shares, but the share of Toyota increased in steps to 99:1 in 2003, resulting 
in a complete takeover by Toyota Motors. The total strength of the workforce in the production line 
in TKML was 1,819, encompassing both regular and contract workers. TKML is the main assembling 
unit while Toyota Kirloskar Auto Parts Ltd. (TKAPL) and Toyota Techno Park are the manufacturing 
units of auto parts. The employees’ unions in TKML and TKAPL have played an important role in the 
labour affairs. Union interventions were successful in improving the work conditions, introduction of 
good attendance allowance and policy issues relating of labour welfare. Bargaining through the union 
has been instrumental in wage revision and introduction of mediclaim and shift allowance.
There were a large number of contract workers at TKML and TKAPL and hence job security had 
emerged as an important issue. These contract workers, due to reasons like uncertainty of employment, 
were not organised. This lack of organisation had sign ificant repercussions on wages, working conditions 
and labour relations in terms of differentials between regular and contract workers. Workload, harassments 
and stressful conditions were also found to be higher for contract workers. The TKML followed ‘kanban’ 
or ‘just-in-time’ and other methods in production that are known to create higher levels of workload 
and stress. Performance appraisal system at TKML was very subjective and resulted in discriminatory 
management practices. All these factors were generating dissatisfaction amongst the workers.
The Struggle
The unrest in Toyota Kirloskar started with the discriminatory and unfair labour practices of the man-
agement in terms of salary revision, irrational disciplinary actions and non-confirmation of trainee team 
members. In 2001, TKML announced a hike of Rs. 300 for team members in response to a long-standing 
demand of the workers for salary revision. This nominal increase was unacceptable to the employees 
and they protested. The management finally agreed to discuss the issue with some representatives of 
the employees and solved the problem temporarily, but a majority of the employees were not satisfied 
with the decision of the management, and they decided collectively to continue with their protest. 
IR&LL_Ch_01.indd   20 1/1/2008   4:47:59 AM

Industrial Relations: An Overview 1.21
The management applied pressure tactics by starting disciplinary action against the leaders and sus-
pended three workers, accusing them of non-performance and instigating violence. Workers continued 
their protest. In order to destabilise the collective action of the workers and to prevent the formation 
of an employees’ union, the management suggested constituting an association by the name Team 
Member Association (TMA) in the unit. Despite differences of opinion amongst workers, the TMA 
was formed with 15 elected members. In the meantime, a team member, who was very active in the 
struggle, was terminated for non-performance. Disciplinary action against the workers continued. The 
workers sought explanations through the TMA from the management for the suspension of workers. 
But the management refused to entertain the TMA as a body for bargaining and negotiation; it con-
sidered the functions of the TMA to be restricted to issues of workers’ safety and welfare. This led to 
another strike, which continued for 12 days. 
Repeated disciplinary actions by the management and the incapability of the TMA to counter them 
prompted the workers to register the TMA as a trade union. The employees’ union in TKML, affiliated 
to Centre of Indian Trade Unions (CITU), was formally registered in July, 2001. The workers organ-
ised themselves under the banner of Toyota Kirloskar Motors Employees’ Trade Union and submitted 
a charter of demands to the management, that included revoking of the decision of suspensions and 
terminations. Some of the demands of the employees’ union were settled in a tripartite meeting or-
ganised by the Assistant Commissioner of Labour, Bangalore. However, the demand of revoking the 
suspensions and dismissals was not settled in the meeting. The termination of workers continued. On 
termination of service of a trainee, the union began a fresh agitation and as a result jobs of two of the 
office bearers of the union were terminated. The workers immediately went on strike that lasted for 
52 days with the demand to re-appoint the two union leaders. It was at this juncture that the Govern-
ment of Karnataka categorically included Toyota Kirloskar in the Public Utility Services (PUS) and 
redefined the norms of PUS by amending the First Schedule of the Industrial Dispute Act, 1947, in 
2001. The strike was therefore called off.
The management started suspending union leaders selectively on the charge of non-performance. 
This triggered off fresh agitation and several union members were suspended on different pretexts, 
beginning from January, 2004. Two charters of demand presented by the union in a gap of few months 
were turned down by the management, which accepted only the wage revision demand in the first 
charter. Strike notice was served by the union. Protests continued outside the premises of the com-
pany and grew in proportion. At this stage, the Minister for Labour, Government of Karnataka held 
a discussion with the union members and management for resolving the issue. The management did 
not revoke the suspension of the workers. Discussions with the Deputy Labour Commissioner also did 
not bring any result. The strike, which had started on 6th January 2006, subsequent to the suspension 
of three employees for ‘severe misconduct’, was a part of the long struggle of the workers against the 
practices of victimisation in the unit.

Relations in Transnational Corporations, Labour File, Vol. 4 No. 1, pp. 34-37. Retrieved from www. labourfile.
org/ArticleMore.aspx?id=268 on 1/2/2014.)

INTR ODUCTION
Labour is the physical or mental effort of human beings that undertakes any production process; it 
is known as the primary factor of production. As a corollary, labour force is an inseparable aspect of 
the economy of a nation. Ever since industries came up, there have been efforts to understand work 
and workers in order to improve efficiency and increase productivity. Changes in social, economic, 
political and technological environments of a nation bring about changes in the nature of its workforce. 
This chapter provides a basis for understanding the structure, composition and trends of the labour 
force of India.
According to the definition adopted by the 66th Round of National
Sample Survey (2009-2010), labour force comprises persons who are 
either ‘working’ (or employed) or are ‘seeking or available for work’ (or 
unemployed). As defined by the Manual on Labour Statistics (I) 2012, 
brought out by the Central Statistics Office, Ministry of Statistics and 
Programme Implementation, Government of India, labour force covers the 
current economically active population consisting of the employed and the unemployed. The Manual 
further explains the economically active population as including all persons of both the sexes who 
provide labour for the production of economic goods and services during a specified time-reference 
period as defined by the United Nations system of national accounts and balances. These persons must 
also fulfill the requirements for inclusion among those who are either employed or unemployed. The 
Manual also discusses the term ‘employed’ as defined by the International Labour Organisation (ILO), Spotlight

comprising the employed and

2.2 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
as encompassing all persons above a specific age, who during a specified brief period, either 1 week 
or 1 day, were in the following categories: 
a. Paid Employment
(i) at work: persons who, during the reference period, have performed some work for wage or salary, 
in cash or in kind;
(ii) with a job but not at work: persons who, having already worked in their present job, were tempo-
rarily not at work during the reference period and had a formal attachment to their job.
b. Self-Employed
(i) at work: persons who, during the reference period, have performed some work for profit or fam-
ily gain, in cash or in kind;
(ii) with an enterprise but not at work: persons with an enterprise, which may be a business enter-
prise, a farm or a service undertaking, who were temporarily not at work during the reference 
period for any specific reason.
The term “some work” used here may be interpreted as work for at least an hour.
Workers in India can be broadly divided into 3 categories: self-
employed, casual wage labour, and regular salaried/wage employees 
(Ministry of Labour & Employment, 2010). These categories may be 
explained as follows:
a. Regular Salaried/Wage Employees
These are individuals who work in farm or non-farm enterprises of others (both household and non-
household) on full time or part time basis and receive salary/wage on a regular basis, which could be 
either time wage or piece wage or even salary. This category also includes paid apprentices.
b. Casual Wage Labour
A person who is casually engaged in others’ farm or non-farm enterprises (both household and non-
household) is casual wage labour. Wages are received according to the terms of the daily or periodic 
work contract.
c. Self-Employed
Persons who run their own farm or non-farm enterprises or are engaged in any profession or trade 
independently on their own account or with 1 or a few partners are said to be self-employed. There 
are 3 categories of self-employed persons, as follows:
(i)Own-account Workers:  These are self-employed persons who run their enterprises on their own 
account or with 1 or a few partners and, who by and large, do not hire any labour.
(ii)Employers:  Employers are self-employed persons who operate on their own account or with 1 or 
a few partners and who, by and large, run their enterprise by hiring labour.
(iii) Helpers in Household Enterprises:  These are self-employed persons (mostly family members) 
who are engaged in their household enterprises, working full time or part time, assisting a related 
person living in the same household in running the enterprise. They do not receive any regular 
salary or wage in return for the work performed.Spotlight
