Indian Labour Force 2.3
Let us take a quick look at some more terms to understand the dynamics of labour force in India. 
These are measures used by the National Sample Survey Office (NSSO), Ministry of Statistics and 
Programme Implementation to collect data on employment, and include: Usual Status, Current Weekly 
Status and Current Daily Status, which may be understood as follows:
a. Usual Status (US)
Usual Status reflects the status of a person as belonging to the labour 
force, if he/she had been either working or looking for work during the 
major part of the 365 days preceding a survey by the NSSO. Usual Sta-
tus is divided into 2 categories: Principal Status and Subsidiary Status. 
Principal Status (PS), also called Usual Principal Status (UPS), is the 
activity accounting for majority of a person’s time over the year, and such workers are called principal 
status workers. Subsidiary Status (SS) refers to any activity other than the principal activity undertaken 
on a short-term basis, and such workers are called subsidiary status workers. These categories taken 
together constitute total employment on the basis of Usual Principal and Subsidiary Status (UPSS), 
or Usual Status.
b. Current Weekly Status (CWS)
Current Weekly Status is the activity status of a person during a period of 7 days preceding the date 
of a survey conducted by NSSO. A person is considered as a worker if he has been involved in an 
economic activity at least for 1 hour on any day of the reference week.
c. Current Daily Status (CDS)
Current Daily Status is determined on the basis of a person’s activity status on each day of the refer-
ence week. A person is taken to be employed for the full day if he/she has worked for 4 hours or 
more during the day.
GR OWTH AND SIZE OF INDIAN LABOUR FOR CE
Demographic profile of a country has an important bearing on the structure of its labour force. Ac-
cording to the 1991 Census of India, the economically active population stood at 285.9 million and 
the estimated labour force had grown by more than 65 million since 1981. The findings of the ‘Key 
Indicators of Employment and Unemployment in India 2011-12’ released by the NSSO, based on the 
data collected in its 68th Round (2011-2012), reveal that according to the Status (PS+SS), the workforce 
at national level has increased from 459.0 million as on 1st January 2010 (NSS 66th Round), to 472.9 
million as on 1stJanuary, 2012 (NSS 68th Round), indicating a growth of about 13.9 million. Further, 
the Report to People on Employment, 2010 has made a projection of growth of the labour force to 
574 million in 2014-2015. As per the projections of the 2011 Census report, the ongoing demographic 
changes in the country are likely to contribute to increasing size of the labour force. There is a projected 
increase in the proportion of population in the working age group (15-59 years) from approximately 
58 per cent in 2001 to more than 64 per cent by 2021 (Ministry of Labour & Employment, 2010). The
period from the first half of the last decade, i.e., 1999-2000 to 2004-2005, has witnessed an employ-
ment growth of 2.9 per cent per annum, with a significant growth in employment for women both in 
rural and urban areas.Spotlight

SECTORAL DISTRIBUTION AND MAJOR OCCUPATIONS IN INDIA
Indian economy can be divided into 3 major sectors: primary (including agriculture), secondary (in-
cluding manufacturing), and tertiary (including services). As an impact of globalisation, and with 
growing industrialisation in the country, the share of tertiary sector in the economy has been continu-
ously increasing over the years from about 49 per cent in 1991 to about 62 per in 2006-2007 (Paul 
et al., 2009) and has remained at the highest among all the 3 sectors. Growth in agricultural and in-
dustrial sectors had registered a sharp decline in 2008-09 over the previous year. Though the growth 
of these sectors has improved by 2010-2011, still it has been less than that of the tertiary sector 
(Ministry of Labour & Employment, 2011).
From 2009-2010 to 2011-2012 employment in the tertiary sector, in general, has increased, while it 
showed a decrease in agriculture. According to the ‘Key Indicators of Employment, 2011-12’, among 
the workers in Usual Status, about 49 per cent is enagaged in the agricul-
tural sector, 24 per cent in the secondary sector and the rest 27 per cent 
in the tertiary sector. Table 2.4 shows the data on sectoral distribution of 
workers in India across different years. In 2009-2010, the contribution 
of agriculture to total employment had declined by approximately 5 per 
cent as compared to that in 2004-2005. Although the share of agriculture 
in India’s GDP has come down, 49 per cent of the workforce, majority of which are wage labourers, 
still continues to depend on this sector (NSSO Survey 2011-2012).
There was a marginal decline in the share of the manufacturing sector in 2009-2010 as compared 
to that in 2004-2005. The service sector (including hotels, restaurants and trade, and public admin-
istration and community services) registered a marginal increase in share in 2009-2010, though the 
share of the service sector in total employment has increased from less than 20 per cent in 1993-1994 Spotlight

Indian Labour Force 2.7
Organised Sector/Regular Employment
The organised or formal sector in India basically consists of public sector enterprises and private sec-
tor organisations. This sector employs less than 10 per cent of India’s workforce. According to the 
estimates of the Ministry of Labour & Employment (2010), around two-
thirds of the total organised sector employment was in the public sector 
and the rest in private sector, largely corporate manufacturing and a va-
riety of services. Regular employment (or organised sector employment) 
in India has grown at a slower rate in comparison to total employment, 
implying faster growth of employment in the unorganised sector. This is 
evident from the findings of various surveys.
The 2001 Census showed that the organised sector comprised just 7 per cent of the workforce. There 
has been no significant change in the proportion of regular employed, for both males and females, 
over the years. However, a change in this trend was observed and there was a marginal increase in 
the proportion of regular employment from 14 per cent in 1999-2000 to 15.6 per cent in 2009-2010. 
One of the possible reasons for this increase, as put by Kundu and Mohanan (2009), may be the need 
of the emerging sectors to meet global competition. 
Unorganised Sector Employment
The term ‘informal sector’ was first used by the International Labour Organisation in 1972, to denote 
a wide range of small and unregistered economic activities. At the 15th International Conference of 
Labour Statisticians (January 1993), the informal sector was considered to be the one that “may be 
broadly characterised as consisting of units engaged in the production of goods or services with the 
primary objective of generating employment and incomes to the persons concerned. These units typi-
cally operate at a low level of organisation, with little or no division between labour and capital as 
factors of production and on a small scale. Labour relations, where they exist, are based mostly on 
casual employment, kinship or personal and social relations rather than contractual arrangements with 
formal guarantees” (Kolli, n.d., p. 4).
In India, the Report on Conditions of Work and Promotion of Livelihoods in the Unorganised Sector, 
2007, published by the National Commission for Enterprises in the Unorganised Sector (NCEUS), has 
defined unorganised workers as those who work in the households or unorganised enterprises without 
any security of employment or social security provided by employers. The NCEUS (2007) has also 
provided a structure to the informal sector in India, by classifying the workforce into the following 
segments:
(a) Unorganised non-agricultural workers 
(i) Wage workers in non-agricultural sector
(ii) Self-employed workers in non-agricultural sector
(iii) Women workers in non-agricultural sector
(b) Other disadvantaged workers (migrant, child, and bonded labour) 
(c) Agricultural workers
(i) Agricultural labourers
(ii) Farmers
The unorganised sector (often referred to as the informal sector) plays 
a pivotal role in the economy of India, by providing employment to a high 
proportion of socially and economically underprivileged sections of the Spotlight

society. The NSS 62nd Round indicated that workers in unorganised informal enterprises constituted 92.4 
per cent of all workers. According to another estimate, informal employment accounted for 95.5 per 
cent of total employment in 2004-2005, with 1.5 per cent each in public and private corporate sectors 
(National Statistical Commission, 2012). The growth in employment in the Indian economy is largely 
due to increase in the informal sector, irrespective of whether the employment is in the organised or 
unorganised sector. For example, the growth in employment of 61 million (from 362 million to 423 
million) has been of informal employment in the organised sector (NCEUS, 2007).
Another prominent trend has been that of increased casualisation in work. Casual wage labour 
forms a part of the unorganised sector. These workers lack social security benefits, and do not even 
have a regular job contract. Studies indicate that sub-contracting arrangement of work in the unorgan-
ised sector is increasingly becoming popular as it ensures longer hours of work without higher pay. 
This is an outcome of globalisation and capital-centric growth policies (Bhaduri and Patkar, 2009) .
Agriculture is the main sector where the majority of casual labour is absorbed, followed by the 
manufacturing and service sectors respectively. At the national-level, the largest proportion of casual 
labour is involved in growing of food grain crops, followed by general constructions activities.
The informal workforce in India faces a host of problems. It has low rate of education, and low 
awareness, and a majority of it works under poor working conditions. There is no job security or social 
security. The most vulnerable sections of the society belong to this sector. 
‘Inclusive growth’ has remained an agenda of the Government of India 
since quite some time. To attain the objective of inclusive growth there has 
been a perceived need for improving the quality of work life and raising 
the level of living standard of workers, particularly those who occupy 
a pivotal position in the overall growth process of the country. In this 
regard the Unorganised Sector Workers’ Social Security Bill, 2007 aims 
at providing social security to unorganised sector workers. The Rashtriya 
Swasthya Bima Yojna  is another social security measure introduced by the 
Government for these workers in the recent years, which provides health insurance cover to workers 
below the poverty line in any empanelled hospital in the country.
CHARACTERISTICS OF INDIAN LABOUR
India’s vast labour force has its own unique features. It is diverse in terms of religion, caste, gender, 
culture, education level, skill level, area of working (rural and urban), and so on. These features have not 
only affected its growth and development, but have also affected the overall industrial relations scenario 
in the country. Certain important characteristics of Indian labour force are discussed in this section.
Caste System
Caste has been the one of the most significant discriminating factors in 
the Indian labour market. The country has a deep rooted caste system that 
influences not only the day-to-day activities of people, but also affects the 
occupations they choose. Medhora (1965) pointed out that the Indian caste 
system has been so pervasive in every aspect of life of people that it deter-
mines not just access to opportunities and choice of economic activities of 
a person, but also his social status. In olden times, the Indian society was Spotlight

Exhibit 2.1 Discrimination in the Indian Private Sector
A field experiment was carried out to seek evidence on discrimination in Indian job market. The 
study analysed responses to job applications sent to private sector firms to ascertain the effect of 
caste and religious backgrounds in the process of job market selection. 3 responses were sent to 
each call–as an upper caste Hindu, as a Dalit, and as a Muslim. The identities were differentiated 
only by the names on the applications, which otherwise were similar in all other respects. The 
companies chosen were securities and investment companies; pharmaceutical and medical sales; 
computer sales, support and IT services; manufacturing; accounting firms, automobiles sales and 
financing; marketing and mass media; agriculture sales; construction and banking. The study found 
that job applicants with a Dalit or Muslim name were less likely to have a positive application 
outcome than equally qualified persons with a high caste Hindu name.

2.10 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Education Level
There is a low literacy rate in the labour force in India and spreading even basic education is still a 
challenging task. NSSO (2007) reveals a direct link between level of education and regular employ-
ment, indicating that as the level of education rises, the percentage of regular employment increases. 
The all-India school drop-out rates have been reported as 27 per cent, 40.6 per cent, and 49.3 per cent 
in the year 2010-2011 for classes I-V , I-VIII, and I-X respectively (Amirtham and Kundupuzhakkal, 
2013). The school drop-outs usually join the pool of unorganised labour, and this in turn explains the 
large size of unorganised sector in India.
Gender
Let us now take a look at the gender dimension of labour force in India. In 
general, women’s participation in the labour market has been typically low 
in India. According to the Annual Report to the People on Employment 
(2010), bulk of employment in India is concentrated in the agricultural 
sector. In rural areas, agriculture constitutes up to 68 per cent of the 
total employment, engaging approximately 81 per cent female workers 
and 66 per cent male workers. Employment growth rate and labour force growth rate of females are 
lower than that of males. According to the Second Annual Employment and Unemployment Survey 
2011-2012, conducted by the Labour Bureau, Ministry of Labour & Employment, the Female Work 
Participation Rate (FWPR) is estimated to be 23.6 per cent at all-India level under the UPS approach, 
as compared to the Male WPR of 75.1 per cent. There has also been a long term downward trend 
in the FWPR for rural areas, with the downslide more pronounced in the case of UPS workers. The 
proportion of UPS workers among rural females consistently fell between 1983 and 2009-2010, except 
in 2004-2005. Another interesting observation is that out of the 3 employment categories of workers 
recorded by the NSS, a higher proportion of female workforce is always in the self-employed group. 
Also, rural female workforce comprises a large proportion of unpaid workers, consistently above 40 
per cent since the period 1993-1994 to 2007-2008, with an all time high of 48 per cent in 2004-2005. 
The share of paid or income-earning self-employed has been around 15 per cent. Another striking 
feature is that casual labour accounts for the majority of the paid female workforce in rural areas 
(Mazumdar and Neetha, 2011).
If we look at the compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of labour force during the period 
2004-2005 to 2009-2010, it is higher for urban persons than for rural persons for all workers, but  
there has been a decrease in CAGR of female workers, both in rural and urban areas, the decrease 
being higher in rural areas (Table 2.7). Total female employment had declined by about 1 million in 
urban areas and by nearly 19 million in rural areas. Subsidiary status workers, that comprise usually 
the most vulnerable section of workforce, showed a prominent decline in employment. It may be 
concluded from the available data that a large proportion of the decline in total employment during 
2004-2005 to 2009-2010 is accounted for by the decline in the subsidiary status employment of women 
workers.Spotlight

The main reasons that have been pointed out for the low participation of women in the labour 
force are that wage rates of women are lower than that of men in many occupations and that women 
are denied of many occupations though they are capable of working with same competence as men 
(Planning Commission, 2008). Other reasons include failure to recognise many of the women-centric 
work (such as cooking, collection of fuel and fodder, house and utensils cleaning, etc.) as economic 
activities, social and family compulsions, and patriarchal nature of the society. Despite this, it must 
be noted that women’s participation in labour market has significantly increased in recent years, par-
ticularly in urban areas (Ministry of Labour & Employment, 2011).
Liberalisation has brought a lot of changes in the Indian economy, that have had a significant 
impact upon the state of women’s employment. These changes include increasing informalisation of 
the economy; sub-contracting and outsourcing to developing countries; and growth of export-oriented 
manufacturing (Nihila, 1999; Neetha, 2002). As observed by Ghosh (2004), a term that is now being 
used to characterise the labour force that is required for these jobs is ‘feminisation’. The principal 
characteristics of feminisation are: a move towards casualisation of labour, shift to part-time or piece-
rate contracts, and higher freedom of hire and fire. Under these situations women seem to be the 
preferred choice for employers since they are available at lower wages and are easier to ‘manage’.
It is interesting to note that though the percentage of regular female employees is relatively low as 
compared to males in both rural and urban India, it has been increasing over the years. As per the An-
nual Employment Review (2010), published by Director General of Employment and Training, Ministry 
of Labour & Employment, there has been an increase in women’s employment in the organised sector 
from 4.93 million in March 2004 to 5.53 million in March 2009. This could partly be due to increase in 
demand for domestic workers, who are categorised as regularly employed (Paul et al., 2009). However, 
the percentage of regular male workers showed no significant change from 1999-2000 (17.2 per cent) 
to 2009-2010 (17.7 per cent), as shown by NSSO survey (Ministry of Labour & Employment, 2011).

2.12 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Migratory Character
In recent years, with increased mobility of population, the study of migration characteristics has as-
sumed significant importance. Any movement which involves change of residence from one village 
or town to another village or town is known as migration. Historically speaking, migration as a new 
source of employment appeared after the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) had 
sharply increased crude oil prices in 1974. The Middle East oil-exporting countries begun huge de-
velopment programmes based on their large oil revenues and hence required skilled and unskilled 
labour. Many workers from India migrated to these Gulf countries during that period in search of 
lucrative jobs. In recent times, there has been a widespread migration of labour from villages to towns 
as well. Globalisation may be seen as the prime reason for this trend. New job opportunities lure the 
youth to move to towns. Farmers, especially from the upper caste, who constitute the bulk of the 
agricultural community, are the worst hit. While the family members from the lower communities, 
including women and children, engage themselves in agricultural activities, the upper caste women 
keep away from such activities as these are considered below their dig-
nity. Therefore such farmers are forced to migrate to cities to earn their 
living. Migration is not just taking place from rural to urban areas, or of 
skilled workers to Gulf countries; there has been migration of profession-
als to emerging sectors like Information Technology (IT), and of doctors, 
engineers and scientists to other developed countries for better career 
opportunities and higher earnings.Spotlight
Migration refers to any move-
ment which involves change of 
residence from one village or 
town to another village or town.
Exhibit 2.2 Problems of Labour Migration
Migration of labour to towns in the State of Bihar has created problems for farmers who were on 
the threshold of a bumper paddy crop after a spell of drought for 2 years. Lack of labour made 
harvesting a daunting task. The ever-increasing trend of labour migration is mainly an offshoot 
of rich cash offered to the migrants and also the lucrative commission and perks earned by the 
brokers, who act as a conduit between the labour and the employers from other States. These 
touts, a good number of them who are mostly unemployed youths from the villages, earn nothing 
less than `50,000 to `0.2 million every year.
Bihar Institute of Economic Studies reveals that migration among the Musahar community 
was alarming. It attributes the reason to the poor performance of the Mahatma Gandhi National 
Rural Employment Guarantee Act that had promised employment to workers. Roughly 4 lakh 
labour, comprising nearly 5 per cent of the district’s total population, have migrated to States 
like Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana and West Bengal. While majority of them prefers to work 
in brick kilns, only a small minority is into harvesting work in these States.
(Adapted from: Sinha, S. B. (2011). Labour migration leaves farmers high and dry. Retrieved from www.

Absenteeism and Labour Turnover
Absenteeism and labour turnover are common problems in Indian industries . Absenteeism rate amongst 
workers in an industry is an indicator of the level of their job satisfaction, morale and commitment to 
IR&LL_Ch_02.indd   12 1/1/2008   4:48:12 AM

Indian Labour Force 2.13
job. It directly affects the productivity of the individual worker as well 
as the entire industry. There are multiple implications of high levels of 
absenteeism on an organisation, besides decrease in productivity. These 
include reduction in quantity of output and decrease in quality of product 
or service that may result in loss of customer base and ultimately affect 
profits adversely. Reasons for high level of labour turnover could be poor 
human resource policies of the organisation, dissatisfaction with salary/
wage, long working hours, low career growth opportunities, better opportunities offered by competi-
tors, and personal variables like family responsibilities, particularly in case of women.
There has been a consistent increase in the rate of absenteeism of workers. The Annual Survey of 
Industries (2009-2010) reports that the rate of absenteeism at all-India level has increased to 8.75 per 
cent during 2009 from 8.65 per cent during 2008 (Ministry of Labour & Employment, 2013). In 2007 
it was 8.34 per cent and was still lower at 7.99 per cent in 2006 (Ministry of Labour & Employment, 
2012 ). The highest absenteeism rate amongst the directly employed regular workers during 2009 was 
reported in the industry group ‘Manufacture of Tobacco Products’ (15.64 per cent) and the lowest in 
‘Water Collection, Treatment and Supply’ (1.59 per cent). At all-India level, 66.85 per cent factories 
had reported labour turnover in their units during 2009, the highest being 96.43 per cent in the indus-
try group ‘Manufacture of Man-made Fibres’, followed by 94.74 percent in ‘Mining and Quarrying’ 
(Ministry of Labour & Employment, 2013).
Move towards Informalisation
From the discussion in the previous sections it is clear that there is a shift towards forced informalisa-
tion of labour in the Indian economy. This move has been necessitated by the changing economic and 
global business scenario. It is becoming tough for the workers, new and old, to get secure employment. 
Informal jobs are increasing even in the organised sector. Those with full time regular jobs are forced to 
move to part-time or casual, low-paid jobs in the unorganised sector. This can be seen from the growing 
trend in outsourcing of manufacturing from the large scale sector to the small and medium sector. This 
is also one of the reasons for the de-industrialisation of most of the industrial centers. Big companies 
hire casual labour or outsource their requirements of materials, etc. Operating at the level of small 
scale industries is advantageous to big companies as most of the laws for protecting employment are 
not enforced in these industries. Another advantage is that these industries are exempted from paying 
taxes for the first 5 years. This trend may be seen as an outcome of liberalisation, which has resulted 
in increased competition at all levels and organisations are forced to make such strategies as would 
help them reduce costs and increase profits. The overall effect is the growth of the informal sector.
Child Labour
Considered as a vulnerable group in the Indian labour market, child
labour, according to the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 
1986, constitutes the work done by children below 14 years of age. States 
like Andhra Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Karnataka, Orissa, West Bengal, 
Madhya Pradesh and Delhi and are having relatively higher concentra-
tion of child labour. Giri (2005) has identified the causes and impact of child labour. While the causes 
include poverty, illiteracy, lack of education, lack of unionism, migrated population and large family 
size, the impact of child labour on human resource development was found in the form of exploitation, 
low earnings of workers, and low career options.Spotlight

2.14 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Elimination of child labour has been a policy concern for the Government of India not only from 
the perspective of development of children, but also for maintaining labour standards. The Govern-
ment has launched several direct and indirect measures to control this problem. The National Policy 
on Child Labour was formulated in 1987, aiming to eradicate child labour and protect all children 
from exploitation.
Exhibit 2.3 Child Labour in Glass Industry
The district of Firozabad is known for its glass industry. The products of the glass industry 
broadly include glass bangles, glass hardware, products for science laboratories, automobiles, 
domestic purposes, etc. Glass manufacturing takes place in hazardous conditions. Temperature as 
high as 1400°C to 1600°C is used during the manufacturing process which increases the ambient 
temperature up to 50oC in manufacturing sheds.
A large number of children are engaged in various processes of glass works. These children 
are as young as 5-6 years. Maximum number belongs to the age group of 8-12 followed by 13-
16. The operations which involve majority of child labour are carried out in the informal sector 
outside the factory at household levels and godowns. These processes include Jhalai  (straightening 
of bangles), Jurai (joining), Murai  (designing by use of forceps), Katai  (designing by grinders), 
polishing, Chaklai  (sorting), packaging in small cardboard boxes and transporting the bangles 
from the place of one process to another. Children are preferred as they have no bargaining power, 
and are more active, agile and disciplined. Poverty of the family pushes them into this work. The 
working conditions cause injury to health and often result in physical disabilities.
(Adapted from: Chandra, A. (2009). Child Labor– A Study from Anthropological Perspective with Special 
Reference to Glass Industry, Firozabad, Anthropologist, Vol. 11 No. 1, pp. 15-20.)
EMPLOYMENT IN EMER GING SECTORS
The Indian economy has witnessed phenomenal changes ever since liberalisation was introduced 
more than 2 decades ago. The developments that have taken place as a result have given a boost to 
the economy and have consequently affected the labour market in a significant manner. Increased 
exports from India have led to an increase in employment opportunities in the export-oriented sectors. 
Some of the high employment potential sectors include IT, IT Enabled Services, engineering goods, 
gems and jewellery, hospitality and health care, automobile, mining, readymade garments, textiles 
and handicrafts. Expansion and dealings across borders have provided an impetus for introduction of 
modern technologies that provides a reason for skill enhancement of the Indian workforce. Certain new 
sectors are also emerging that are providing good employment opportunities. As observed earlier in the 
chapter, the service sector is growing in size; many of the above mentioned emerging sectors belong 
to the service sector. According to the Ministry of Labour & Employment (2010), a large number of 
people are employed in the retail sector, which includes both the organised and unorganised labour 
market (7.1 per cent). The second largest labour market comprises the construction industry (5.9 per 
cent). This sector is male dominated (7.7 per cent) and pro-urban in terms of employment, employing 
nearly 8.7 per cent of the urban and 5 per cent of the rural workers.

LABOUR ADMINISTRATION MACHINER Y
The ILO Convention No. 150 has defined labour administration as “public administration activities 
in the field of national labour policy” (Labour Administration, n.d.). The government of any nation 
applies international labour standards through its national laws and policies. It is therefore essential 
that a country maintains a robust and active labour administration system or machinery that holds 
the responsibility for formulating and implementing labour policies. Casale and Sivananthiran (2010) 
propose that labour administration system encompasses all public  administration bodies responsible 
for and/or engaged in labour administration, which may include ministries, departments of ministries,  
public  agencies (state level, regional, or local agencies), or any other form of decentralised adminis-
tration, and any institutional framework for the coordination of the activities of such bodies, and for 
consultation with and participation by employers and workers and their organisations.
Looking at the history of labour administration in India we find that during the late nineteenth 
century, matters pertaining to labour administration were enforced through Magistrates. There were 
only a few laws in existence to regulate labour conditions (e.g., Fatal Accidents Act, 1855; Workmen’s 
Breach of Contract Act, 1859; Employers and Workmen (Disputes) Act, 1860, etc.). Labour adminis-
tration was done on a temporary and casual basis as there was no fixed policy on labour issues. The 
Government of India Act, 1919, for the first time, gave some shape to labour administration and defined 
in some detail the distribution of legislative and administrative powers between the central and pro-
vincial governments. Generally, the Central Government could enact labour laws relating to mines, 
railways, major ports, seamen, and international and inter-provincial 
emigration, and the provincial governments could deliberate on labour 
matters pertaining to factories, plantations, public works, inland vessels, 
labour disputes, labour welfare, and housing, but under the control of the 
Central Government.
Today, India has a fixed system of labour administration with a well-defined structure. Labour falls 
in the Concurrent List of the Constitution of India. This means that both the Central Government and 
the State governments have the power to make laws on this subject. Machinery for administering 
labour issues exists both at the central and State levels.
Labour Administration Machinery of the Central Government
The highest authority with respect to labour issues lies with the Ministry
of Labour & Employment, while the Secretary, Ministry of Labour & 
Employment, holds the executive authority. The Ministry has 4 attached 
offices and 10 subordinate offices, in addition to 4 autonomous organisa-
tions, several adjudication bodies and 1 arbitration body. Apart from the 
Ministry of Labour & Employment, Ministries specialised for certain 
industrial sectors (for example the Ministry of Power and the Ministry of Mines) cover aspects of 
labour administration such as safety and specific aspects of social security and labour welfare, with 
respect to defined groups of workers.
The Chief Labour Commissioner (CLC) at the Central level controls the implementation of provi-
sions of labour legislations. The organisation of the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central), known as 
the Central Industrial Relations Machinery (CIRM), was set up in April 1945, as an outcome of the 
recommendation of the Royal Commission on Labour in India. It was entrusted with the responsibil-
ity of preventing and settling industrial disputes, enforcing labour laws and promoting the welfare of Spotlight

list of the Constitution of India.

the responsibility to enforce the Industrial Disputes Act, 1948, the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, and 
rules made in respect of mines, railways, air transport services and docks, wharves and jetties in ma-
jor ports, Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946, the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, the 
Maternity Benefit Act, 1961, the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965, the Contract Labour (Regulation and 
Abolition) Act, 1970, the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976, the 
Inter-state Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) (RE&CS) 
Act,1979, the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986, the Labour Laws (Exemption 
from Furnishing  Returns and Maintaining Registers by Certain Establishments) Act, 1988, the Indian 
Railway Act, 1989, the Building and Other Construction Workers (RE&CS) Act, 1996, Chapter VI-A 
of the Indian Railway Act, 1989, Hours of Employment Regulations for Railway Employees, 1961 
(now known as Railway Servants (Hours of Work and Period of Rest) Rules, 2005 w.e.f. 28.02.2005),

for organisations where the Central Government is the appropriate government ( www.clc.gov.in ). The 
CLC is responsible for enforcing labour legislation with respect to wages, remuneration, child labour, 
contract labour, migrant labour, working time, industrial disputes, and maternity benefits in the indus-
tries and establishments for which the Central Government is the appropriate Government.
Each State in India has a Labour Minister who heads the Department 
of Labour of that State. The Secretary of the Department has the executive 
authority. Though many agencies and government departments such as 
Chambers of Commerce, Factory and Mines Inspectorate, Social Insur-
ance Directorate, and the Department of Human Resource Development 
and Education are involved in labour administration, but it is primarily 
the responsibility of the Department of Labour to formulate, develop and 
execute labour policies.
Labour Commissioner at State-level has the responsibility of ensuring the proper implementation 
of the provisions specified in labour legislations. The Labour Commissioner has multiple responsi-
bilities that include inspection of factories, conciliation, and hearing of various review applications 
of aggrieved parties under various labour laws. The Commissioner may act as appropriate Govern-
ment for granting sanction for prosecution, besides functioning as a competent authority for issuing 
orders under various provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and other labour legislations. At 
State-level below the Labour Commissioner are the Joint Labour Commissioner, the Assistant Labour 
Commissioner, and other officers.
Department(s) Responsible for Labour Inspection
The Directorate General, Factory Advice Service and Labour Institutes 
(DGFASLI) and the Chief Labour Commissioner are attached offices 
of the Ministry of Labour & Employment. The CLC is responsible for 
enforcing labour legislations related to working conditions, as discussed 
above, whereas the DGFASLI is responsible for carrying out inspections 
related to occupational safety and health issues.
At State-level, the Inspectorates of Factories, under the control of State Labour Departments, enforce 
the Factories Act, 1948 in their respective States. The Directorate General of Mines Safety conducts 
safety and health inspections with respect to safety and health regulations in mines and oilfields.

respect of labour. There are also special inspectorates in some States covering particular industries, 
for example, the Plantation Inspectorate in Kerala. Labour Inspectors may conduct inspections on re-
ceiving a complaint or in cases where it is deemed necessary to ensure the safety of workers. Powers 
of Inspectors are limited to filing complaints in the courts of law but Inspectors can issue a prohibi-
tion order in such conditions at places like construction sites, mines etc., where there is a danger to 
life—safety and health of the workers or of the public— until measures have been taken to remove the 
cause of the danger to the Inspectors’ satisfaction. Inspectors may consult the trade unions or workers’ 
representatives during inspections.
The Director General of Inspection in the Central sphere is authorised to exercise the powers of 
an Inspector as well as a quasi-judicial authority, and holds the power to impose fines on offending 
employers.
Some Central laws are enforced by the Central Government and others by the State governments. 
Nature of the establishment or sector decides whether it will be governed by Central or State Govern-
ment. For example, factories, boilers and electricity fall under concurrent legislative powers, whereas 
railways, highways, major ports, mines and oilfields come under the competency of the Union.
Local Divisions
For the purpose of effective labour administration, there are 18 regions across the country, each headed 
by a Regional Labour Commissioner. The DGFASLI has both its headquarters and the Central Labour 
Institute in Mumbai and 4 Regional Labour Institutes at Chennai, Kanpur, Kolkata and Faridabad. It 
works in coordination with its Central and Regional Labour Institutes. The activities of DGFASLI 
include mainly framing policies and plans, and executing the programmes pertaining to safety, health 
and welfare of workers in industries and docks; it a lso maintains liaison with national and international 
agencies for its activities.
Summary
rLabour force includes the current economically active population comprising the employed and 
unemployed.
rWorkers can be broadly divided into 3 categories—self-employed, casual wage labour and 
regular salaried/wage employees. At the national-level majority of the workers belong to self-
employed category.
rCertain measures used by the National Sample Survey Office to collect data on employment are: 
Usual Status, Current Weekly Status and Current Daily Status.
rMajority of workforce in rural areas is employed in the primary sector, while majority in urban 
areas is employed in the tertiary sector.
rThe organised sector employs less than 10 per cent of India’s workforce. Regular employment 
or organised sector employment in India has grown at a slower rate in comparison to total 
employment. 
rIndian economy is showing a trend of movement towards informalisation as a result of changing 
economic and global business scenario. Informal employment accounts for major proportion 
of total employment. There has been faster growth of employment in the unorganised sector.
rMigration of labour from rural to urban areas is a common feature. Migration of professionals 
to countries abroad is also taking place in search of better career and earning opportunities.

rWorkforce is India is highly variegated. Heterogeneity exists mainly with respect to gender, area 
of working (rural/urban), skill and caste. Indian labour force is characterised by low education 
level and shows a tendency towards absenteeism and turnover.
rWomen have a low participation rate in the labour force. Many socio-cultural factors are respon-
sible for this situation. There is also a prevalence of child labour in India.
rLabour falls in the Concurrent List of the Indian Constitution.

      TUDY
Indian Migrants to the Gulf Countries
Indian migrants have been working in the Gulf countries, mostly at low positions in oil companies, 
since the time oil was discovered there in the 1930s, and the their number gradually increased till the 
1970s. After a sudden rise in price of oil in 1973, t here was a huge demand for workers in these 
countries due to infrastructural development activities being taken up there. A large numbers of mi-
grant workers from Asia were found going to the 6 Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries of 
Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, and the UAE. India and Pakistan provided most 
of the unskilled labour. Gradually the migrants from India further increased and Indian migrants 
became the largest in number. Later, after the Kuwait war of 1990–1991, Indians even replaced 
non-national Arabs in the Gulf, like the Jordanians, Yemenis, Palestinians and Egyptians. By 2006, 
Indian migrant population to the Gulf had crossed 3.5 million.
After the mid 1970s, in order to control the rapid growth of migrants, the GCC countries 
imposed a number of restrictions such as: foreign nationals cannot own any business or land 
and they can have business only in partnership with the locals. It gradually became difficult for 
the workers even to take families with them. Though the demand for professionals has gradually 
increased in these countries, yet a large chunk of migrants comprises semi-skilled or unskilled 
workers. These workers, who are employed as housemaids, cooks, gardeners, cleaners etc., have 
been reported to be working and living in wretched conditions. They live in cramped rooms with 
no facilities for kitchen or toilet. They have to bear unfriendly weather conditions and hardly get 
any opportunity for socialisation. Female workers working as housemaids even face sexual abuse. 
There is no protection of any local labour law for them. Long separation from their families and 
adverse living conditions break them emotionally and physically.
Back home, these workers face exploitation on another front. These unskilled and semi-skilled 
workers work under short contracts (rarely exceeding 2 years). They come back home after their 
contract ends and search for a new job contract begins. Many recruitment and placement agen-
cies, in collusion with potential employers, take advantage of illiterate workers who are hardly 
aware of laws and their rights and so have to suffer in many ways. These agents and employers 
deduct money from the wages of the workers in the name of various types of fees and withhold 
their passport. They provide them with inadequate medical and other facilities at work, and even 
use them for carrying smuggled goods.
A large proportion of the migrant workers come from the south Indian States of Kerala, Tamil 
Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka, other States being Maharashtra, Punjab and Rajasthan. It 
was estimated that by 2005 1 out of every 3 or 4 Indians living in Gulf was from Kerala. Towards 
the end of 1990s, it was believed that migration had improved the condition of poor families in 
Kerala and appeared to be one factor that seemed to have done better than agricultural reforms, 
trade union activities, and welfare legislations. This was one aspect of the situation. Very soon the 
side effects of migration in the State of Kerala had begun to be felt. One was increase in unem-
ployment rate due to rise in education and the other was migration of workers from other States 
to Kerala to replace the workers who had emigrated. Education rate increased seemingly because 
the youth of Kerala watched other emigrated workers. They too, like other emigrants, wanted to 
IR&LL_Ch_02.indd   21 1/1/2008   4:48:13 AM

2.22 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
get jobs in Gulf countries and earn a lot of money to lead a happy life. To realise this dream they 
were motivated to get educated, more so, when secondary education was made compulsory for 
migrants in many Gulf countries. 
The emigrated Indian workers to the Gulf countries have had an impact upon the economy 
of the country. They have been sending huge remittances to their homes in India. This has been 
one of the significant aspects of their migration. In the mid 1970s, remittances from the migrated 
Indians to the developed countries had increased, but later on, its share gradually decreased as 
they were joined by their families. Remittances from Gulf continued to increase and reached to 
US $21,700 million in 2004. In 1999-2000, it contributed 3 per cent to the GDP. In the middle 
of 1991, when India faced a serious balance of payment crisis, remittances from migrants to the 
Gulf countries played an important role in bringing the country out of the crisis.
The phenomenon of worker migration has been perceived to have resulted in both gains and 
losses. Married men who left their families and went away, leaving the household responsibility 
to their wives, made many women expert in ‘home management’. The children of these work-
ers can get better education and facilities. But the flip side is that it also resulted into social and 
psychological problems, for example, a feeling of loneliness experienced by the family members 
of these workers who moved to unknown destinations in foreign countries for the sake of giving 
good social status and a better life to their family back home.
(Adapted from: Khadria, B.  India: Skilled Migration to Developed Countries, Labour Migration to the Gulf.

INTR ODUCTION
Trade unions are an inseparable part of the industrial relations system of any nation, having their 
own sets of objectives or goals to achieve, and each having its own strategy, based on its ideology, to 
reach those goals. Unions are an instrument for promoting the cause of the working class; they allow 
workers to demand their rights and voice their grievances in a legitimate manner.
There is an interesting treatise on the causes that had fuelled the labour movement and hence con-
tributed to the birth of trade unions. Hoxie (1921) proposes that unions are an outcome of common 
interpretation by workers of social situations in which they lived, and the aims, policies and methods 
of unions acted as a remedy to these conditions. Perlman (1928) attributes the birth of trade unionism 
to job consciousness and scarcity of employment. Tannenbaum (1951) suggests that while machine 
was the cause, labour movement was the result.
Evidences suggest that seeds of trade unionism were sown with the beginning of industrialisation, 
to be more specific, the Industrial Revolution. Industrialisation brings with itself 2 diametrically oppo-
site phenomena: on one hand, workers pick up the necessary skills that lead to enhanced productivity, 
and on the other hand, automation reduces the labour needed for a given level of output, thus throw-
ing workers out of employment. Thus industrialisation casts insecurity in the minds of workers due 
to fear of obsolescence and loss of employment. Following the age-old adage that unity is strength, 3
Trade Unions: 
Concept, Evolution and Functions
IR&LL_Ch_03.indd   1 1/1/2008   4:48:25 AM

3.2 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
workers as a consequence of such insecurity demand more wages and 
better working conditions through their collective actions. Thus a trade 
union is born. To sum up, the growth of unions across the world can be 
traced back to the growth of industrial organisations. Though the concept 
of unions had originated in the context of blue-collar manual workers, it has eventually extended to 
cover white-collar employees also, including supervisors and managers.
According to the International Labour Organisation (ILO), trade unionism is a means for workers 
to liberate themselves from poverty and social exclusion; they provide a forum to workers to express 
their views. Trade unions are supposed to play an important role in maintaining harmonious relations 
between management and labour. Their purpose is to make an attempt to provide a dignified life to 
workers, while fulfilling their obligations towards management. In situations in which interests of 
workers and management clash, trade unions play a crucial role in negotiating with the management 
to maintain industrial peace and harmony. 
The following sections cover the concept of trade unionism, objectives, types and functions of 
unions, and the various methods they adopt to achieve their objectives. We have also deliberated upon 
eminent theories of trade unionism. Separate sections have been devoted to the history and evolution 
of trade unionism and structure of unions in India.
DEFINITIONS OF TRADE UNIONS
Trade unions have been defined by several authors and institutions at dif-
ferent points of time. Sidney and Beatrice Webb (1920, p. 1) define trade 
union as “a continuous association of wage earners for the purpose of 
maintaining or improving the conditions of their working lives”. Dankert 
(1948, p. 1) proposed that “a trade union is a continuing organisation of 
employees established for the purpose of protecting or improving, through 
collective action, the economic and social status of its members”. Cole
(1955, p. 13) defines a trade union as “an association of workers in one 
or more professions carried on mainly for the purpose of protecting and 
advancing the members’ economic interest in connection with their daily 
work”. According to Yoder (1974, p. 159), a trade union is “a continuing, long-term association of 
employees formed and maintained for the specific purpose of advancing and protecting the interests of 
members in their working relationships”. The International Labour Organisation defines a trade union 
as an organisation of employees, usually associated beyond the confines of 1 enterprise, established 
for protecting or improving, through collective action, the economic and social status of its members. 
According to Section 2(h) of the Trade Unions Act, 1926, a trade union can be defined as “any 
combination, whether temporary or permanent, formed primarily for the purpose of regulating the 
relations between workmen and employers, or between workmen and workmen, or between employ-
ers and employers, or for imposing restrictive conditions on the conduct of any trade or business, and 
includes any federation of two or more trade unions”.
Stated in simple terms, trade unions are voluntary associations formed by employees to safeguard 
their interests through collective actions. Combining the various definitions, we get the following 
characteristics of a trade union:
rIt is an association of workers or employers.
rIt is voluntary in nature; hence an employee has a choice to join or not to join a union.Spotlight

OBJECTIVES OF TRADE UNIONS
Trade unions were primarily formed for protecting the interests of workers.
The aims and objectives of major trade unions in India are seen to vary according to their political 
ideologies (Ratnam, 2006). Nevertheless, the broad objectives of unions are:
rEnsuring Rights to Workers: An important objective of unions is to ensure rights to workers. 
Trade unions had actually emerged for this purpose, since a single worker may not be effec-
tive to demand for better terms and conditions of work from management; bargaining power 
is greater as a group or association. Towards this end, unions also offer legal representation to 
their members. They oppose any such policy or action of management, or even the government, 
that is perceived as a potential threat to workers’ interests and rights.Spotlight

Exhibit 3.1 Furore over New Manufacturing Policy
The Center of Indian Trade Unions (CITU) has strongly opposed the new National Manufactur-
ing Policy approved by the Union Cabinet, and has termed it as an attempt by the Government 
to give backdoor entry to the so-called labour reform of ‘hire and fire’ that is being pressed by 
business houses through the creation of new manufacturing zones. The Center believes that “the 
National Manufacturing Policy will create new islands of lawlessness with bountiful concessions to 
business houses and absolute jungle raj in implementation of labour laws of the land”. It said that 
the Government cannot unilaterally change the labour laws legislated by the Parliament through 
executive policy or order, and announced that it would oppose any such action.
CITU pointed out that the new policy would also be discriminatory against those industries 
which do not operate from these special zones, whereas those manufacturing in these zones would 
take undue advantage of the concessions offered by the Government. It has also laid down that 
this is a kind of disregard shown by the Government to the basic norm of industrial democracy, 
and that the Government must consult with central trade unions before taking any decision on 
such labour-related issues.
(Adapted from: www.thehindu.com/business/Industry/article2577119.ece accessed on 23/10/2014.)
rSecuring Economic Interests of Workers: Trade unions were formed to save workers from 
oppression. Getting fair wages/remuneration is a right of workers. Unions continuously strive to 
ensure that workers are getting wages according to the going-rate. Besides wages, they safeguard 
other economic interests of workers, like bonus and compensation for accidents.

REASONS FOR JOINING UNION
We have mentioned earlier that trade unions are voluntary associations and therefore it is not manda-
tory for a worker to join a union. This brings us to a pertinent question: why would a worker join a 
trade union? Right from the beginning of the trade union movement, it has been very evident that 
workers tend to collude when they have a demand from, or a grievance against their employer. Trade 
IR&LL_Ch_03.indd   4 1/1/2008   4:48:26 AM

Trade Unions: Concept, Evolution and Functions 3.5
union has always been a platform to workers to promote their interests; workers could not have attained 
much success if they dealt with such issues individually.
Waddington and Whitson (1997) classify the reasons for joining trade 
unions as individual benefits and collective reasons. Individual benefits in-
clude training and education, industrial benefits and professional services 
like free legal advice and financial services. Collective reasons comprise 
mutual support, improved wages and working conditions, peer-group 
pressure and belief in union organisation.
A worker’s decision to join a union can be ascertained purely on 
the basis of cost-benefit analysis of such a decision. While costs may 
include membership fee (monetary) and time devoted to union activities 
(non-monetary), benefits of unionisation may include safeguard against 
victimisation by management (Mills, 1994; Modi, Singhal and Singh, 
1995); facilitation of redress of grievances (Modi, Singhal and Singh, 
1995); sense of security; greater bargaining power; and power of repre-
sentation. As pointed out by Schnabel (2003), it is the balance of costs and benefits combined with 
the expectations about the degree to which the union would be able to realise the collective, social 
and ideological motives that would determine the actual membership decision.
The various reasons that may be instrumental behind a worker joining a trade union may be as 
follows:
rGreater Bargaining Power:  A worker possesses very little bargaining power as an individual. 
Pursuing an issue as a cohesive group instead of an individual would have greater prospects of 
being heard and addressed to. Workers can, as members of a union, participate in matters that 
affect their lives through collective bargaining agreements between union and management.
rSense of Security: Workers as individuals may feel exposed to the 
whims and fancies of top management decisions. However, union 
membership instills a sense of security among them to safeguard 
from uncertainties in income and other hazards.
rOther Reasons: Other reasons behind joining a union may be 
negotiation for wages and working conditions, protection from 
unforeseen exigencies like accidents and illness, etc. Gratification of social and psychological 
needs and “social pressure” (Mills, 1994; Modi, Singhal and Singh, 1995) may also be other 
rationale for joining union.
Following the model proposed by Schuler and Youngblood (1986), there are 3 separate conditions 
that influence an employee’s decision to join a union, namely: dissatisfaction, lack of power and union 
instrumentality. These are explained here briefly.
rSatisfaction of Employee: Satisfaction of an employee at work is contingent upon 2 types of 
contracts: employment contract (pertaining to conditions of employment like wages, hours of 
work, etc.) and psychological contract (consisting of unspecified expectations of the employee 
about reasonable working conditions, nature of supervision, empowerment, etc.). An employee’s 
level of satisfaction would be determined by the degree to which the organisation fulfils these 
contracts.
rPowerlessness: Contrary to what seems to be obvious from the above discussion, an employee 
would not join union when he perceives dissatisfaction. In fact, when he is dissatisfied, an Spotlight

3.6 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
employee would first try to resolve the reason by himself. Now, the degree of success of such 
an individual attempt would depend on 2 features of the job: essentiality andexclusivity .
Essentiality refers to how important or critical the job is to the overall success of the or-
ganisation, while exclusivity refers to how difficult it is to replace an employee (Schuler and 
Youngblood, 1986). If an employee has greater degree of essential-
ity and exclusivity, he would be in a commanding position and 
would be likely able to force his employer to improve the situation. 
Low essentiality and exclusivity would render an individual’s at-
tempt as unsuccessful. In other words, an employee would not be 
able to remove his cause(s) of dissatisfaction if he is not exclusive 
and can be substituted easily, and in such a case he is in a state of 
powerlessness. It is under such circumstances that the employee 
would wish to overcome his dissatisfaction through other means, 
including joining a union, which may address the reason(s) behind dissatisfaction through a 
common forum.
rInstrumentality: Instrumentality refers to the degree to which an effort would lead to desired 
outcomes. In this context, we may explain instrumentality to be a calculative or utilitarian re-
lationship with unions based on a cognitive assessment of the costs and benefits pertaining to 
union representation (Newton and Shore, 1992). According to Brett (1980), workers feel bound 
to their unions simply because of the rewards that these unions secure for them. A worker may 
thus determine if a union is instrumental in removing his dissatisfaction. For this, he may compare 
the costs and benefits of union membership; if the benefits outweigh costs, the employee would 
join the union. However, in many cases an employee may not be able to ascertain such benefits 
and costs, and opt for joining union without any such evaluation and comparison.
TYPES OF TRADE UNIONS
Trade unions differ in their purposes, membership pattern of workers and level of operation. Let us 
talk about the different types of unions on these bases in this section.
Classification on the Basis of Purpose
Following the philosophy of Hoxie, unions may be classified on the basis 
of their purposes and functions, as follows:
rReformist Unions: These are the unions that seek to improve 
the existing economic and social conditions of workers, without 
attempting to uproot or drastically change the existing system. 
Examples are unions associated with the American Federation of 
Labour (AFL) and the Congress for Industrial Organisation (CIO) 
in USA. Hoxie’s business unionism and friendly or uplift unionism belong to this category.
rRevolutionary Unions:  These are the unions that seek to destroy and abolish the existing eco-
nomic and social order by means of some kind of force, with an objective of improving the status 
of workers. The means adopted by these unions may be revolution or exercise of political strength.
Thus a revolutionary union may be either anarchist union  or political union .Spotlight

Trade Unions: Concept, Evolution and Functions 3.7
rPredatory Unions:  These stick to no particular means and adopt any method to fulfill their pur-
pose. They may be of 2 types: hold up-union , formed by combination of employee and employer, 
both not abiding by any principles, concerned with their own benefit, without any concern for 
outsiders; and guerilla unions , that work against employers, and are controlled by a ‘boss’. They 
use violence and other secret methods to achieve their objectives.
Classification on the Basis of Membership Pattern
Trade union members may all belong to the same trade/craft or different crafts; they may also be 
blue-collar or white-collar employees. Thus on the basis the types of membership, trade unions may 
be classified as: occupational or craft unions, industrial unions, general unions, and blue-collar and 
white-collar unions.
rOccupational/Craft Unions:  The earliest form of trade unions found were craft unions , which 
comprised members from the same craft or trade. It is obvious that such unions operated purely 
for the interests of the members of the specific craft. Further, since the membership of such 
unions is open only to those belonging to a particular craft, craft unions may be quite small in 
size. These unions are found in modern times also, such as pilots’ associations, etc. In India, 
the Singareni Collieries Engineering Workers Union, affiliated to the Hind Mazdoor Sabha, and 
the Navigators Union of Air India are examples of craft unions.
rIndustrial Unions: Size of craft unions was small, since they were restricted to a single craft or 
trade. Eventually with increase in work complexities, such unions begun to collude amongst 
themselves, and thus emerged industrial unions. The focus area of such unions is broader, as 
they are no longer limited to the interests of a particular craft; they aim to represent all employ-
ees in a specific industry, regardless of their type of work. An industrial union would comprise 
all workers in an industry with different skill sets, namely, skilled, semi-skilled, and unskilled, 
engaged in a particular industry or enterprise. The United Automobile Workers (UAW) is an 
industrial union in USA, representing skilled craft workers, assembly line workers and unskilled 
workers in all of the major American automobile companies. The Textile Labour Association 
Ahmedabad is one of the most famous industrial unions in India. The Steel Employees Trade 
Union (SETU) (affiliated to CITU) is another example.
rGeneral Unions : With their origin in the early nineteenth century in Great Britain, general unions
are for skilled and unskilled workers performing different jobs in different industries, employ-
ments or crafts, while industrial unions are for different workers in 
thesame  industry. GMB and the Transport and General Workers’ 
Union (TGWU) are examples of general unions in Great Britain. 
Jamshedpur Labour Union and the National Union of Municipal 
and General Workers are examples of general unions in India.
rBlue-Collar and White-Collar (Managerial) Unions : A further 
classification of unions can be made within this category, on the 
basis of the level of employees as members of a union. For this 
we would first need to explain the concept of blue and white-collar 
workers
Blue-collar workers are those who are at the operative level, 
employed at the production floor, or in maintenance shops; they 
are paid on piece-rate or time-rate basis. Unions representing such 
workers are regarded as blue-collar unions . White-collar employees, Spotlight

on the contrary, do not work on the shop floor; they are non-manual workers who are paid on 
a monthly basis. Unions representing such workers are regarded as white-collar unions . White-
collar employees are distinct from their blue-collar counterparts in aspects like educational 
background, higher social status and occupational position. As such their unions are usually 
regarded as “guilds” or “associations” or “officers’ associations”, possibly to distinguish them 
from workers’ unions. The primary objective of formation of such associations is similar to that 
of trade unions, i.e., to protect the interests of officers. We find ample evidence in the history 
of Indian trade unionism that white-collar employees were initially shy of unionising at the be-
ginning; they have eventually formed strong unions. Examples of such unions are the All India 
Bank Officers’ Association and the Airports Authority Officers’ Association (India), a recognised 
multi-cadre association of the Airports Authority of India (AAI).
Classification on the Basis of Level of Operation
The organisational pattern of a trade union federation is usually a 3-tier 
structure, comprising enterprise-level unions, industry-level unions and 
national-level federations. 
rPlant-level Unions : A plant-level union  is, as is suggestive from the 
name, is a union that operates at the factory or plant level.
rIndustry-level Unions:  An industry-level union  operates at the 
industry-level, comprising several factories or enterprises.
rRegional-level Federations: These are organisations of all the constituent unions in a particular 
State or region. 
rNational Federations:  These are national-level bodies to which plant-level unions, local-level 
unions and regional-level unions may get affiliated.
Apart from these, there may be another type of unions, namely, agricultural unions , comprising
agricultural workers. The Khet Mazdoor Union of AITUC, Bharatiya Khet Mazdoor Union (BKMU), 
and All India Agricultural Workers Union (AIAWU) are examples of agricultural unions operating 
in India.
STRUCTURE OF TRADE UNIONS IN INDIA
Structure of a trade union refers to the organisation of the union and the 
pattern of linkages of various units within that union. The level of opera-
tion of unions, as discussed in the previous section, also forms the basis 
for understanding the structure of trade unions. The organisational pattern 
of a trade union federation in India is usually a 4 tier structure, comprising 
plant (or enterprise)-level unions, local-level federations, regional-level 
federations and national-level federations, as depicted in Figure 3.1.
rPlant-level Unions: Operating at the factory or plant level, plant
(or enterprise)-level unions  comprise the first tier in the structure. A single plant may have 
several such unions, as the Trade Unions Act, 1926 allows any 7 workers to come together to 
form a union. Enterprise-level unions can be of 2 kinds: those having affiliation with national-
level federations, and those that are independent (i.e., without any affiliation). The Rourkela 
Shramik Sangh, the recognised trade union body of the Rourkela Steel Plant, is an example of 
plant-level unions.Spotlight

rLocal-level Federations: Plant-level unions in a particular craft or industry at the local-level may 
constitute a local-level federation . This is the second tier from below, and is above the plant-level 
unions. The local federation holds together the local, plant-level unions in a particular craft or 
industry. Such a federation may be independent, or affiliated to either some regional-level or 
national-level federation.
rRegional-level Federations:  Federations of all the constituent unions in a particular State or 
region forms regional-level federations . Such federations are a vital component in the structure 
of unionism in a vast country like India where language, customs, religion, geography and impact 
of political factors vary from region to region. These federations may have 2 types of members: 
affiliating plant-level unions and affiliating local federations. Many regional political parties may 
have their own trade union wings. Telugu Desam in Andhra Pradesh and Trinamul Congress in 
West Bengal are 2 such examples of regional political parties.
rNational Federations:  Constituting the highest level in the 4 tier structure of trade unions in 
India, national federations  are the central or apex  organisations that act as coordinating bod-
ies, to which plant-level unions, local unions or regional-level unions may get affiliated. These 
federations may have their own regional or State-level coordinating bodies to which plant-level 
unions may get affiliated. Examples of such organisations in India are the Indian National Trade 
Union Congress (INTUC) and All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC). Detailed structure and 
working of certain national-level federations have been taken up in the next chapter.

Marxian Class Conflict Theory
Karl Marx was the founder of communism. According to him, trade 
unions are an outcome of the capitalist system, and are an important in-
strument in the struggle between workers (proletariat) and capitalist class 
(bourgeoisie). He believed that capitalism results in 3 outcomes which aid 
in the growth of labour movement, namely tendency of accumulation of 
wealth with capitalists; tendency for depression of wages and resultant 
problems of workers; and inevitability of economic crises. Therefore the 
labour class must continue its struggle to abolish capitalism.
In his Communist Manifesto,  Marx stated that competition divides 
the interests of workers, but the cause of maintaining wages gives them 
a common reason to unite and present resistance against capitalists. 
Unions must organise workers to eliminate competition among themselves for employment. They 
should generate awakening amongst workers to abolish the wage system as a whole, and contribute 
to the decay of capitalism. 
Marx was of the opinion that unions facilitate workers to get gainful employment, and hence per-
form the function of protecting their wages; however, they must not restrict themselves to fulfillment 
of these narrow objectives. He proposed that trade unions must provide orientation towards changing 
the social structure and propounded revolutionary and radical means to bring about this change. 
Perceiving that outside guidance and support is necessary for the working class, Marx defined a 
role for intellectuals to imbue social and political awakening in the working class. He suggested that 
trade unions by themselves cannot do anything beyond economic struggle; therefore they must be 
ready to accept guidance from outside, in order to get permanent gains and establish a socialist state.
Webb’s Theory of Industrial Democracy
Sidney and Beatrice Webb, authors of the title Industrial Democracy 
published in 1897, were leaders in the Labour Party in Great Britain. They 
witnessed trade unions emerging not from any particular institution, but 
from every opportunity for the meeting together of wage earners of the 
same occupation. According to the Webbs, the chain of supply involves 
the worker, employer, wholesaler, retailer and customer. The pressure 
created by the customer due to comparative prices in the market increases 
at every link in the chain, which finally accumulates at the employer’s 
level, who is eventually forced to lower the costs of production by reduc-
ing wages and other inputs. Thus, the ultimate sufferers are the workers, 
and to protect their interests, they unionise. Therefore market pressures and competition lead to the 
formation of trade unions.
Unions sought to establish ‘Common Rules’ which refer to efforts in making firms pay workers at 
least a minimum wage and provide certain minimum working conditions in terms of working hours, 
safety measures, leaves, etc.Spotlight

Trade Unions: Concept, Evolution and Functions 3.11
The Webbs rejected the Marxist concept of a ‘classless society’: Though both opposed the capitalist 
system, but unlike Marx, the Webbs advocated peaceful means to establish a socialist society. They 
believed that trade unionism was neither a temporary function which arose as an outcome of industrial 
development, nor a means to overthrow capitalism. They proposed that unions were the prime agents 
of industrial democracy in bringing equality between employers and workers in terms of bargaining 
power, by giving voice to workers.
Unions do not just exist to give economic benefits to their members; a larger purpose of their 
existence is to reconstruct the society by replacing capitalism with a form of socialism and have a 
permanent function to fulfill in the democratic State.
Cole’s Theory of Union Control of Industry
G. D. H. Cole is celebrated in the history of industrial relations for his work The World of Labour ,
published in 1913. His approach to trade unionism is somewhere between those of the Webbs and 
Marx. Cole believed that unionism exists to carry on class struggle. He has suggested that the control 
of industry should be in the hands of the true producers, namely, workers, in partnership with the 
State. This is in sharp contrast to revolutionary methods proposed by Marx.
Hoxie’s Theory of Functional Classification of Unionism
Robert F. Hoxie is amongst the earliest to have argued that trade union-
ism has evolved differently across socio-psychological factors. Economic 
factors, according to him, are not the only reason for the growth of trade 
unionism. He proposed that workers with similar thinking and economic 
conditions tend to develop similar interpretations of problems and solu-
tions, and this is the outcome of group psychology. Further, Hoxie pro-
vided a different approach of understanding the concept of trade unions 
by classifying unionism on the basis of functions, as follows:
rBusiness Union: Also regarded as bread-and-butter unionism ,
business unions working on this ideology are concerned with improving wages and working 
conditions, rather than changing political and social situations in which workers live. Thus these 
unions are trade-conscious rather than class-conscious. They stress on immediate goals and dis-
play an instrumental orientation. Such unions accept the capitalistic system and wage structures, 
rather than questioning them, and in that they are conservative in nature. The means they adopt 
to seek their goals are collective bargaining and industrial action (like strikes).
rFriendly or Uplift Union: The primary aim of unions following this principle is to contribute 
towards better life of workers by elevating their moral, intellectual and social life. Thus these 
unions are trade-conscious, and they advocate methods like cooperative enterprises, profit-sharing, 
etc. They use collective bargaining and political actions as means to achieve their objectives.
rRevolutionary Union:  These unions adopting revolutionary methods belong to this category of 
unionism. They are class-conscious. They follow the dictums of Marx and reject private ownership 
of productive resources and wage system. They are radical in approach, and use a combination of 
industrial and political actions to achieve their objectives. The ultimate aim of such unions is to 
replace the capitalistic system with a socialistic system. Hoxie has divided revolutionary union-
ism into 2 categories on the basis of objectives and methods of unions: one adopting socialistic
approach (unionism),  with focus on socialist ideologies, and the other adopting quasi-anarchy 
approach (unionism)  that practices means like strikes, sabotage and violence.Spotlight

3.12 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
rPredatory Unionism: The unions belonging to this category are leader-based, instead of member-
based; they do not follow any ideology, and adopt any method to secure better wages and benefits 
for members. These unions may even join hands with employers for mutual benefit. They may 
be either trade-conscious or class-conscious.
rDependent Unionism:  In this type of unionism the unions are dependent on the support of 
workers and other labour groups. They are usually of 2 types: company unions  (that depend 
entirely on employer), and label unions  (that depend upon the label imprinted on the products 
made by the union members and such products find a ready market among unionists and union 
sympathisers).
Hoxie believed that trade unions may not exactly be like any 1 of the 4 he has proposed. The meth-
ods and objectives of a trade union are dependent upon the beliefs of the competing groups within 
the union. He was also of the opinion that though the effect of trade unionism is ultimately bringing 
democracy in industry, but systems within trade unions hardly depict any democracy.
Tannenbaum’s Sociological Theory
Frank Tannenbaum, a professor with the Columbia University, USA, 
proposed the Sociological Theory of trade unionism. The Industrial 
Revolution had disrupted the older way of life and also put the life of 
workers into threat. Workers became totally dependent on machines and 
employers made them feel insecure. They responded by self-defence 
through trade unions. According to Tannenbaum, “the initial organiser 
of the trade union movement is the shop, the factory, the mine, and the 
industry. The agitator or the labour leader merely announces the already 
existing fact.” Thus the emergence of trade unions was spontaneous, and 
in fact, inherent in the growth of capitalism; he proposed that machine 
is the cause, and labour movement is the result. The employer acted as a 
catalyst in the process of organising workers into a self-conscious group, and trade unionism emerged 
as a means to restore the organic life and dignity that workers enjoyed before the advent of capitalism.
According to Tannenbaum, unions have become very powerful bodies that try to gain monopoly 
over labour supply to industry. They tend to bargain with employers over wages and those firms that 
cannot pay wages are driven out. He also believed that unions cannot remain isolated and they gradu-
ally begin to perform the functions of the management, because every activity of management affects 
workers in some way or the other.
Tannenbaum was of the opinion that trade unionism did not challenge capitalism; rather it civilised 
capitalism and integrated workers through collective bargaining. The real essence of the trade union 
movement could be appreciated only by seeing the role it has played in the lives of workers in the 
transition from a simple society to a complex industrial and urban economy.
Commons’ Environmental Theory
John R. Commons was a professor of Economics at the University of Wisconsin, USA. His ap-
proach to trade unionism was based on environmental factors, and hence his theory is regarded as the 
“Environmental Theory of Labour Movement”. Factors like free land, market expansion and resultant 
competition, and immigration with influx of races, nationalities and languages, according to Commons, Spotlight
