Commons believed that unionism is a protective device for workers who had to be shielded from the 
harshness of the market. Collective bargaining was an instrument of class struggle, and Commons 
proposed that ultimately there would be partnership between employers and employees.
Perlman’s Theory of Scarcity Consciousness
Perlman, an economist at the University of Wisconsin, USA, was an 
associate of Commons. He had extensively studied trade unionism in 
USA and authored the title A History of Trade Unionism in United States 
in 1922, in which he argued that scarcity consciousness , expressed by 
sharing job opportunities, had motivated American unionism. Perlman’s 
theory attributes the emergence of trade unionism to the “scarcity 
consciousness” of workers, which implies “economic pessimism of the 
manual group”. He was of the opinion that scarcity of opportunities 
was a universal psychology, typical among manual workers. Scarcity 
consciousness emerged because of the fact that the economic position of 
workers could not be improved beyond an ordinary standard of living, and 
this gave rise to job-conscious unionism, wherein unions controlled job opportunities. Based on studies 
conducted in 4 countries, namely, USA, UK, Germany and France, Perlman proposed 3 factors that 
controlled union activities: first, the resistance power of capitalism; second, the role of intellectuals; 
andthird,  the degree of maturity of trade unions. Unions established certain job rights, which they 
would then ration amongst the members through various regulations related to employment conditions, 
like working hours, seniority, etc.
In his path-breaking monograph, Theory of the Labour Movement  (1928), Perlman proposed that 
unions and collective bargaining are the essential components of a democratic society. Workers must 
organise unions and engage in class struggle against their employers. According to Perlman, work-
ers lacked cohesiveness and class-consciousness. Neither did they join unions to further the cause of 
the labour class, nor were they willing to make sacrifices to make the unions a strong organisation. 
Unions therefore capitalised on the self interests of certain workers and attempted to maintain an intact 
organisation of workers by focusing on their economic needs.
Unions accept the legitimacy of capitalism, though they aim to limit its excesses, and they must 
strive to establish job rights for workers. Perlman proposed a pragmatic approach to be adopted by 
unions in improving the economic condition of workers through social and economic reforms. He 
believed that intellectuals and non-manualists (outsiders) undermined the approach of trade unions. 
They attempted to impose their beliefs on labour movement and believed that the condition of the 
labour class could only be remedied if it adopted their ideologies.
Kerr and Associates’ Protest Theory
Kerr, Dunlop, Harbison and Myers used the term ‘labour organisation’ for trade unions. They observed 
that labour studies have been conducted mostly in Western capitalist countries, and hence were of 
the opinion that to understand the actual nature of labour organisations, one must not be restricted 
to the views proposed on the basis of such studies. These thinkers believed that the protest of the 
labour class against industrialisation is a universal phenomenon, as industrialisation puts a universal 
demand and a change is required in the relationship of worker and his work and that with the cultural Spotlight

environment. Kerr and associates proposed that a new recruit dislikes 
discipline and perceives that the compensation received is commensurate 
with his efforts or his needs. The dynamic industrial system is unable 
to provide him with security. He then protests against this system in the 
form of turnover, sabotage, absenteeism, etc. Unionism is an organised 
form of such protests against the ills of the system, as a natural aspect 
of industrialisation.
Kerr and associates suggested that leadership of the industrialisation 
process is taken by one of the following 5 ideal types:
rDynastic Elite:  Under this leadership, unions undertake social func-
tions at plant-level and indulge in political activities challenging 
the workers. Usually such unions are class-conscious and adopt 
revolutionary means to achieve their objectives.
rMiddle Class:  Unions undertake regulation of management at the local-level under this leader-
ship, along with independent political activities that do not challenge employers. Such unions 
embrace reformist approach.
rRevolutionary Intellectuals:  The main function of unions in this type of leadership is to act 
as an instrument to educate and lead workers with an objective of improving production and 
political activities .Such unions are affiliated to centralised federations.
rColonial Administrators:  Such unions are anti-colonial and are led by nationalists and inde-
pendent leaders. They fight for independence and thus are a part of independence movement.
rNationalist Elite:  Nationalist in nature, these unions are led by nationalist leaders. They try to 
achieve a balance between economic development and protection of workers’ interests.
Simons’ Theory of Monopolistic, Anti-Democratic Trade Unionism
The contribution of Simons in theories of trade unionism can be linked to his seminal work on the theory 
of order. As a pronounced adherent of democracy as the ideal form of government, (1945/48) Simons 
describes democracy as “government by discussion” and depicts consensus as the key prerequisite 
for the orderly functioning of the democratic process. According to his theory, the general framework 
within which private individuals are free to transact is to be designed in a manner which maximally 
destroys the power concentration in the economy (in all fields of economic policy) and in government 
itself (by federalism, decentralisation and the rule of law). Simons (1944/48) denounced trade unionism 
on the ground that it is monopoly founded on violence, and also claimed that “monopoly power has 
no use, save abuse”.
Mahatma Gandhi’s Trusteeship Theory
Mahatma Gandhi believed in the philosophy of Sarvodoaya , which attempts to establish class harmony. 
He proposed that trade unions are not just meant for carrying on the struggle for wages and working 
conditions, but they must act like reformist organisations built with the belief that labour and capital 
must exist in harmony, instead of opposing each other. Unions must uplift workers and help in their 
all-round development, including teaching supplementary occupations, in order to reduce uncertainties 
during periods of hardship.Spotlight

Trade Unions: Concept, Evolution and Functions 3.15
According to Gandhian thought, social order is based on social neces-
sity and not on personal greed. Resources are to be shared by everybody 
and wealth is for those who generate it. Thus one who controls resourc-
es is not the owner, but the trustee. The concept of trusteeship implies 
stewardship without ownership, and therefore it presumes that a capital-
ist is a trustee for those on whom he depends for the making, retention 
and enhancement of his capital. Gandhi proposed that a capitalist should 
keep minimum wealth for himself and give the rest to the trust for the 
greatest good of all. 
Gandhi did not advocate workers’ participation in politics because they are not awakened enough 
for the purpose and also because political leaders may exploit and use them for their own interests.
Gandhi differs from Marx in the sense that the latter believed in destruction of the exploitative 
social order, but Gandhi talks of a constructive order based on reformation of such exploiters. While 
Marx advocated a violent method, Gandhi adopted non-violent means, though he did not oppose 
peaceful strikes. According to Gandhi, strikes should be used as the last resort, when all peaceful 
negotiations, conciliation and arbitration are exhausted. He believed that respect for mutual rights and 
responsibilities can settle all disputes. Gandhi added the concept of social trusteeship to socialism and 
State-regulated trusteeship, and proposed that ahimsa  or non-violence, peaceful conduct of relations 
and positive cooperation can lead us to the correct path of industrial relations.
HISTOR Y AND EVOLUTION OF TRADE UNIONS IN INDIA
The trade union movement in India can be traced back to the period when industrialisation begun in 
the country in the 1850s, with the establishment of cotton mills in Bombay (now Mumbai) (1851) and 
jute mills in Calcutta (now Kolkata) (1855) (Singh, 1965). Consequently, this may be considered as 
the period for emergence of the working class in India. However, the factory system created a lot of 
problems for workers. Emphasis was on increasing production, with little or no concern for workers; 
they lived and worked in poor conditions at meager wages, which lead to widespread discontentment. 
This situation itself provided an impetus to the development of a system 
that would mitigate the problems of workers. 
The early years of the labour movement were fraught with difficulties. 
Strike committees, naming themselves as trade unions, would demand 
the privileges of unions, without any means of discharging responsibili-
ties thereof. With such turbulent years in the beginning, unions have tra-
versed a long journey so far, and the country has seen a steady rise in the 
number of unions, with increase in their membership base, as also their 
funds.
We have divided the span of more than 16 decades of trade union 
movement in India into 3 phases: pre-World War I, post-World War I, and 
post-Independence. The objective of this section is to trace the origin and 
development of trade union movement in India. We have also portrayed 
the characteristics of the labour movement and the factors which were 
instrumental behind the growth of this movement in each of these phases.Spotlight

3.16 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Pre-World War I
Industrialisation in India in the 1850s during British rule had ushered in benefits for capitalists, but 
resulted in acute misery of workers, who were made to work hard for long hours under poor condi-
tions. 1860 marked the beginning of labour unrest in India, to protest against the oppression of indigo 
cultivators in Bengal. In 1875 Sarobji Shapurji made a protest in Bombay against poor working condi-
tions of workers (Giri, 1959). The first Factory Commission was appointed in 1875, and to improve the 
situation of workers in India, the British government passed the Factories Act in 1881. However, this 
Act was inadequate to address the issues of women and child labour; this eventually led to the next 
Factory Commission in 1884. In 1885, the Indian National Congress was born with A. O. Hume as 
its president. Its leaders took up the cause of the working class. This gave a strong impetus to labour 
movement in India. In the year 1890, N. M. Lokhande sponsored the first labour organisation in India, 
the Bombay Mill Hands Association, as its president. However, the Association was not a trade union 
in its true sense, as it had no existence as an organised body, and no formal roll of members or funds 
or rules to support its structure and functioning.
A number of workers’ associations were formed during this period. Some of the important ones 
are: the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants in India and Burma (1897), the Printers Union, 
Calcutta (1905), the Bombay Postal Union (1907) and the Kamgar Hityardhak Sabha and Service 
League (1910). These organisations or associations were not trade unions in the real sense, as they 
did not have any specific aims and objectives, and they worked primarily for the welfare of workers. 
The post-1890 period was also marked by several strikes. The most notable ones are the 2 strikes in 
Bombay in 1894, the first big strike of mill workers of Ahmedabad in 1895, and the strike in jute 
industries at Calcutta in 1896. It may be mentioned here that in 1911 the Factories Act was passed to 
regulate the working conditions in industrial set-ups at that time. 
The most notable features of the trade union movement in this phase are that the movement was 
essentially led by social reformers and not by workers, and that the unions which were operational in 
this phase were not unions in the true sense.
Post-World War I
Several authors have classified this period as the era of formation of modern trade unionism. Social, 
economic and political changes were taking place around the world during World War I (1914–1918). 
These developments gave further impetus to the growth of the trade union movement in India. Move-
ment for independence from British rule and labour movement were going on side by side, both get-
ting support and boost from each other. Masses were awakening and becoming aware of the political 
conditions in the country. With a sharp rise in the prices of essential commodities and a “wage lag” 
(Sinha, Sinha and Shekhar, 2006), condition of workers was going worse. The Russian Revolution of 
1917 also greatly influenced the labour movement in India. The stage was all set for the emergence 
of trade unions that could voice their demands through militant activities. The first organised trade 
union in India, the Madras Labour Union, primarily an association of textile workers, was formed 
in 1918 by B. P. Wadia. Meanwhile, the International Labour Organisation was formed in 1919 with 
India as the founder member, and the Textile Labour Association Ahmedabad was formed in 1920 
under the leadership of Anusuya Ben Sarabhai and Shanker Lal Banker. Other notable unions that 
came up in this period were the Indian Seamen’s Union, Calcutta Clerks’ Union and All India Postal 
and RMS Association.
Rising prices, without a commensurate increase in wages, despite the huge profits made by em-
ployers, fuelled a new awakening in this phase. Growth of trade unions was accompanied by a large 
IR&LL_Ch_03.indd   16 1/1/2008   4:48:26 AM

Trade Unions: Concept, Evolution and Functions 3.17
number of strikes, beginning in 1918 and continuing up to 1920, mainly as a protest to the largely 
deteriorating condition of workers. Several unions were formed after this, including the All India 
Trade Union Congress (1920) and the Railway Men’s Federation, recognised by the Railway Board, 
(1922). Similarly, the All India Union of Postal and Telegraph Employees was also formed, and it got 
recognition from the Director General of Posts and Telegraphs.
Labour uprisings were taking place in many parts of the world. Due to the resultant pressure created, 
coupled with interventions by the ILO, several industrial legislations were passed during this period. 
The agitation for legislation for trade unions had begun under N. M Joshi, also called the “Father of 
Trade Union Movement” in India. The Trade Unions Act was finally passed in the year 1926. This was 
an important milestone in the evolution of trade unions, as the Act gave legitimate status to unions, 
and association of workers was made a lawful activity. This was followed by the Trade Disputes Act, 
1929, which provided for ad hoc  Conciliation Board and Court of Enquiry for the settlement of trade 
disputes. Meanwhile, a split took place in AITUC, namely, leftist and rightist. The All India Trade 
Union Federation, a wing of the AITUC, was formed in 1929. Efforts were made to unify the split 
sections of AITUC in the interest of the labour movement. Another split in 1931 led to the formation 
of All India Red Trade Union Congress.
The Great Depression during this period greatly affected the already suffering workers. There were 
mass retrenchments, lay-offs and wage-cuts. A large number of strikes took place to resist this. The 
maximum unrest was witnessed in Bombay (Verma, 1987). In 1935, the All India Red Trade Union 
Congress merged itself with AITUC; further in 1938, an agreement was made between the National 
Trade Union Federation (NTUF) and AITUC, and consequently NTUF affiliated itself with AITUC. 
The year 1938 saw the most important State enactment, namely, the Bombay Industrial Disputes Act, 
1938, providing for setting up of an Industrial Court, and prohibiting strikes and lock-outs under 
certain conditions. The Act laid down compulsory recognition of unions by an employer, and gave 
the right to workers to get their cases represented either through a representative union, or where no 
representative union existed in the industry or center or unit, through elected representatives of work-
ers, or through the Government Labour Officer. However, the scope of the Act was limited only to 
certain industries in the province.
The Second World War broke out in 1939, bringing with itself the same kind of chaos as the First 
World War. India, like many other parts of the world, was going through economic and political 
turmoil. In November, 1941, the second split took place in AITUC when the radicals left the party 
and the Indian Federation of Labour (IFL) was formed with M. N. Roy as the General Secretary. The 
Federation aimed to mobilise the support of the working class for ensuring uninterrupted production 
services in industries. By the time the World War II came to an end, the Indian trade union arena had 
2 major central federations: AITUC, under the control of the Indian Communist Party, and IFL, under 
the domination of the Radical Democratic Party.
The year 1946 saw another milestone in labour relations, with the enactment of the Industrial Em-
ployment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946. The objective of the Act was to bring uniformity in the condi-
tion of employment of workmen in industrial establishments, and thus minimise instances of industrial 
conflicts. The Act requires employers in industrial establishments wherein 100 or more workmen are 
employed, or were employed on any day of the preceding 12 months, to define with sufficient preci-
sion the conditions of employment under them, and to make the said conditions known to workmen 
employed by them. Another important State-level enactment that was passed was the Bombay Industrial 
Relations Act, 1946, aimed at regulating the relation of employers and employees, making provision 
for settlement of industrial disputes. Meanwhile, the end of the Second World War marked a new phase 
of misery to the working class, with unemployment, shortage of consumer goods and soaring prices. 
IR&LL_Ch_03.indd   17 1/1/2008   4:48:26 AM

3.18 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
The obvious consequence was large scale strikes. The most notable one was the strike of the All India 
Postmen and Lower Grade Staff Union in 1946, which went on for more than 3 weeks.
Post-Independence
India became independent on 15 August 1947. A significant development in this period was the First 
Pay Commission, appointed in May 1946, to mainly address the demand for revision of salaries of 
Government servants in the face of rising prices. Following Bhattacherjee (1999), we divide the post-
Independence phase further into the following phases: Phase I (1947 to mid-1960s), Phase II (mid-1960s 
to 1979), Phase III (1980 to 1991) and Phase IV (1991 to 2000), and extend it to Phase V (2000 and 
beyond). Let us describe each of these phases briefly here.
rPhase I (1947 to mid-1960s): This phase corresponds to an era of State planning and setting of 
up of public sector enterprises to provide employment to people. The State played an important 
role and intervened in issues like determination of wages and working conditions. The period 
1946-47 was marked by increase in the number of industrial disputes, which led to the enact-
ment of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. This Act introduced compulsory adjudication on a 
permanent basis. Another important landmark in the trade union movement was the establishment 
of INTUC in May 1947, with Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel as its first president. Eventually INTUC 
became the most dominant of all central federations in terms of membership, and in 1948, the 
Government of India recognised it as the most representative among central federations. Thus 
INTUC got the right to nominate workers’ delegations to the ILO.
Meanwhile socialists belonging to the AITUC moved out and formed the Hind Mazdoor 
Panchayat (HMP) in 1948, which later became the Hind Mazdoor Sabha (HMS). In 1949, the 
United Trade Union Congress (UTUC) was formed under the leadership of Mrinal Kanti Bose, 
a Marxist, with the objective to create a classless society and non-political unionism. Hence by 
1949, there were 4 central federations carrying the baton of the trade union movement in India: 
AITUC as the senior-most union, INTUC, HMS and UTUC. In 1954, Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh 
(BMS) was formed under the aegis of the Jan Sangh Party, presently known as the Bharatiya 
Janata Party. The year 1960 saw several amendments in the Trade Unions Act, 1926, including 
minimum membership subscription; further amendments were incorporated in 1964. By 1965, 
a splinter group of socialists, headed by George Fernandes, formed the second Hind Mazdoor 
Panchayat.
rPhase II (mid-1960s to 1979) : This period was marked by economic stagnation and political 
turmoil. Employment slowed down, inter-union rivalries increased and there was widespread 
industrial conflict. The split in the communist movement divided AITUC, leading to the forma-
tion of the Center of Indian Trade Unions (CITU) in 1970 by the Marxist Communist Party. 
UTUC was also split into 2 along ideological lines, the splinter group calling itself UTUC (Lenin 
Sarani). The Hind Mazdoor Sabha and the Center of Indian Trade Unions emerged as important 
trade unions during this phase, which also saw the emergence of women in trade unions when 
the Self Employed Women’s Association (SEWA), the trade union of women in the unorganised 
sector, was formed in 1972, under the guidance of Ms Ela Bhatt. In the same year, 3 central 
trade union organisations, namely, HMS, INTUC and AITUC agreed to establish a National 
Council of Central Trade Union Organisations to enhance understanding and cooperation in the 
activities of the central unions, to promote the interests of the working class and to further the 
trade union movement.
IR&LL_Ch_03.indd   18 1/1/2008   4:48:26 AM

Trade Unions: Concept, Evolution and Functions 3.19
During the late 1970s, there was a major change in the growth of independent employees’ 
unions and economic unionism, mainly in the new capital intensive industries. Datta Samant rose 
as an influential trade union leader in this period. His approach was revolutionary. He resorted 
to long strikes, sometimes overreaching economic demands, bypassing legalistic struggle and 
by significantly using violence against opponent workers and trade union centers.
rPhase III (1980 to 1991) : This corresponds to a period of segmented and uneven economic 
development, witnessing the phenomenon of decentralised bargaining and independent trade 
unionism. Inter-State and inter-regional variations in the nature of labour-management became 
very obvious. The Trade Unions (Amendment) Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha in 1982. 
It proposed to make several amendments in the Act, like a minimum qualifying membership of 
10 per cent of workmen (subject to a minimum of 10) employed in an establishment where a 
trade union is proposed to function, with a view to reduce multiplicity of unions.
rPhase IV (1991 to 2000): This was the transition phase between traditional and modern meth-
ods of trade unionism. Economic reforms in India were introduced in 1991, which had a great 
impact on the way businesses are run, and ultimately affected workers and unions. The advent 
of globalisation in India required the replacement of rigid and stabilised systems with more 
flexible ones, open to changes. The roles and functions of trade unions had to be adapted with 
the new requirements, like workers’ training for adoption of new technology and issues related 
to the V oluntary Retirement Schemes. Regional trade union organisations affiliated to regional 
political parties such as DMK, AIADMK and MDMK in Tamil Nadu and the Shiv Sena in Ma-
harashtra also emerged during this phase. The year 1999 saw a consensus among leading trade 
union federations like BMS, AITUC, CITU and INTUC to provide protection to the domestic 
industries, strengthening of public sector units by revival and amendment of labour legislations. 
(Adapted from: Economic Times, New Delhi, 14/2/1999.)
rPhase V (2000 and beyond): The recent phase is characterised by political instability, with no 
single party being able to emerge as the majority. The coalition government, with a number of 
political parties, is forced to follow a combination of ideologies that appeases every party in the 
coalition. The Trade Unions Act, 1926 underwent several amendments in 2001, which became 
effective on and from 9th January 2002. As per such amendments, no trade union of workmen 
shall be registered unless at least 10 per cent or 100, whichever is less, subject to a minimum of 
7 workmen engaged or employed in the establishment or industry with which it is connected, are 
the members of such trade union on the date of making of application for registration. Further, a 
registered trade union of workmen shall at all times continue to have not less than 10 per cent or 
100 of the workmen, whichever is less, subject to a minimum of 7 persons engaged or employed 
in the establishment or industry with which it is connected, as its members.
It is in this phase that the Government opened up the economy for Foreign Direct Investments. 
Further, the World Trade Organisation (WTO) rules and policies on trade liberalisation (for instance, 
implementation of product patents regime from 1st January 2005) had their own impact on business. 
Besides increasing the percentage of their shareholding, several foreign companies acquired Indian 
companies by buying controlling interests. Thus Coca Cola bought Parle Drinks, while Hindustan 
Lever took over Tata Oil Co. Ltd. At the same time, a number of Indian-owned companies went 
into the hands of foreign investors.
It would be rather iterative to say that workers are naturally the ones who are directly affected by 
such changes. The employment scenario has changed dramatically in this phase, with a shift from 
formal to informal sector, which has had an impact on the membership status of trade unions. This 
phase has also seen the onset of the economic recession beginning in the year 2007. Large scale 
IR&LL_Ch_03.indd   19 1/1/2008   4:48:26 AM

3.20 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
lay-offs and retrenchments have taken place, and unions are being vigilant for any injustice being 
caused to employees, and are found to oppose it vehemently. A good example of this is the mass 
retrenchment of Jet Airways staff that had to be repealed due to strike by the union of its employees. 
Trade unions are also adopting pragmatic practices to keep pace with changes in technology, and are 
hence getting involved into supportive and developmental roles, thus moving ahead of their tradi-
tional militant role. This phase is also witnessing increased participation of women in trade unions.
FUNCTIONS OF TRADE UNIONS
Trade unions were seen as a ‘military school’ for class war by Engels (Hyman, 1971). Traditionally 
the role of unions has been to safeguard economic interests, secure better conditions of work and life, 
fight against exploitation and arbitrariness by management, and to ensure fairness and equity in em-
ployment contexts. During the long history of the trade union movement many positive changes have 
taken place in workers’ conditions. Several legislations have been passed in order to ensure a better 
life to workers. Working class itself has become better educated. Today due to developments in the 
Information and Communication Technology, workers have become better informed and are aware of 
the forces that impact their industry. They are directly involved with the economic system of production, 
and over the years they have come to a position where they can influence not only the employment 
conditions and policies of an organisation, but also labour policies at national-level. Unions have seen a 
quantum change in their roles and functions; they have been performing a plethora of functions, some 
of which have been more prominent than others at different phases of their evolution. Ewing (2005) 
has identified that over the course of time trade unions have developed 5 principal functions: service, 
representation, regulatory, governmental and public administration, with more emphasis being placed 
recently on service, governmental and public administration functions.
Since many important central trade unions are wings of political parties, they are bound to be affected 
by the ideology of their respective parties. For instance, some unions that are influenced by Leftist prin-
ciples aim at changing the capitalist system as a whole. However, irrespective of their political affiliation, 
the generic functions of unions in the current scenario may be categorised as primary and new functions.
Primary Functions
Scholars and practitioners have been debating since long over what are the 
primary functions of a trade union. While it is commonly comprehended 
that the primary function of a union is to protect the economic interest of 
workers (Hoxie, 1921; Perlman, 1928), many are of the opinion that the 
most basic function of a union is to build up its own organisation, and to 
give weight to its collective actions; once this function is accomplished, 
other functions follow.
Considering the fundamentals of unionism, there is an unequal dis-
tribution of wealth and power in all organisations. The basic function of 
unions is thus to reduce this inequality. According to the First National Commission on Labour (1969), 
the principal function of a union is to promote and protect the interests of its members in all aspects 
of their working life, including improvement in their civic environment. Extant research reveals the 
following as the primary functions of trade unions: 
rTo secure fair wages for workers; unions ensure that they are not exploited in any way, particu-
larly in economic terms.Spotlight
The primary function of a union 
is to promote and protect the 
interests of its members in all 
aspects of their working life, 
including improvement in their 
civic environment ( First National 
Commission on Labour, 1969 )

rTo offer responsive cooperation in improving levels of production, productivity, discipline and 
high standards of quality.

(Freeman and Medoff, 1984).
rTo enlarge opportunities for promotion and training. 
rTo promote integration of workers’ interests with their industries. 
rTo cooperate in and facilitate technological advancement by broadening workers’ understanding 
of underlying issues.
Exhibit 3.3 Demand for Welfare Board for IT Sector Employees
Majority of the employees in the Information Technology (IT) sector in Kerala are unorganised and 
therefore subjected to exploitation. Many of them are forced to work for over 12 hours a day for 
low wages. Government agencies such as the Kerala State IT Mission, Keltron, Information Kerala 
Mission, Akshaya and IT@School are alleged to be functioning as commission agents to enter into 
contracts for getting the work done by low-paid workers in the small-scale IT units. The Association 
of IT Employees (AITE) believes that exploitation in the private sector is now being extended to the 
Government IT sector. It has hence urged the Kerela Government to set up a welfare board for those 
working in this sector. It has also asked the Government to announce minimum wages for employees 
in the IT and allied sectors. The Association is trying to pressurise the Government to provide job 
security for IT workers under the Government agencies such as the IT Mission and Information Kerala 
Mission; strengthening of e-governance; and expansion of e-district programmes to the entire State.
(Adapted from: www.thehindu.com/todays-paper/tp-national/tp-kerala/article2590509.ece accessed on 
2/10/2014.)
New Functions
The last few decades have witnessed a lot of turbulence in the global busi-
ness environment in the form of redefined national boundaries, influence 
of WTO in national business laws, policy matters, economic recession and 
so on. This has resulted in changes in employment patterns and emergence 
of new sectors in the economy. Such changes have had a direct impact 
on the way trade unions are functioning. Rapid advancements in technol-
ogy and successive revisions in pay have undoubtedly improved workers’ 
conditions within the organised sector, but mostly at the cost of loss of 
control over jobs (Ratnam, 2006). Except for SEWA, little success has 
been noted in organising workers in the small-scale enterprises, as well as in other segments of the 
informal sector. All such factors have necessitated a paradigm shift in the roles of trade unions; from 
predominantly bargaining institutions, they have become specialised agencies, representing the voice 
and interests of labour. They have redefined their roles and functions to match with new issues facing 
the workers, management and organisations.
In addition to their traditional bargaining activities, unions now have a newly acquired voice and 
representative function. Many of them are trying to increase their value by providing a variety of ser-
vices to their members, as well as to the community to which they belong. Such services range from Spotlight

dEducation
dTraining

dSocial work

providing legal and financial advice to improving skills of workers (Ghosh, Nandan and Gupta, 2009). 
These new functions of unions, also called ancillary functions (Monappa, 2000), can be categorised 
into the following groups: 
rCommunication : Many large unions publish newsletters and/or magazines, with the main aim of 
clarifying their policy or stance on certain principal issues, as well as to pass on information about 
their activities. For example, The Indian Worker  is a fortnightly bilingual publication of INTUC.
rWelfare Activities : A number of trade unions are engaged in various welfare activities, such as pro-
viding housing and schooling facilities for the wards of workers establishing cooperative societies 
for promoting thrift among workers and providing consumer items at discounted prices. Unions 
are also playing an instrumental role in advocating against social evils like child labour, and in 
counseling employees on various matters. This apart, unions are being catalytic in promotion of 
cultural and recreational activities. The Textile Labour Association Ahmedabad has ventured to 
organise self-employed women in SEWA and has even started banking activities for this purpose.
rEducation: Education makes workers aware of their surrounding environment. Unions strive to 
launch educational programmes for workers to enhance their knowledge of the work environment 
and to inform them about issues regarding their rights and responsibilities, about procedures and 
systems that exist in the workplace for redressing grievances, and similar issues.
rTraining of Workers:  Trade unions also provide training to workers in order to enhance their 
efficiency and effectiveness. This function has gained greater relevance in the current scenario 
when changes in technology are taking place very fast and obsolescence of skills is a routine 
phenomenon. For example, unions in India and Bahrain have joined hands to tackle exploitation 
of workers from Kerala and to make them aware of their rights when they land in Bahrain and 
other Gulf countries in search of employment opportunities. The General Federation of Bahrain 
Trade Unions Bahrain’s main trade union body, and INTUC have come together to push for a 
pre-departure training programme for workers before they leave Kerala .
(Adapted from: www.financialexpress.com/news/india-bahrain-trade-unions-join-hands-to-protect-workers/891310/ 
accessed on 23/10/2014.)
Exhibit 3.4 R ourkela Shramik Sangh: Towards Skill Enhancement
The Rourkela Shramik Sangh (RSS), the recognised trade union body of Rourkela Steel Plant 
(RSP), has put forth its demand to the management of the Steel Authority of India Ltd. to send 
workers abroad for enhancement of their technical skills. This would equip them to better under-
stand the need for maintaining the quality of work in the ongoing expansion and modernisation 
process of RSP.
(Adapted from: Economic Times, 24 August, 2010.)
rResearch: Union negotiators require updated information to be collected systematically and 
analysed meticulously at the bargaining table. They also need to backup their wage demands 
with knowledge of the industry, of productivity, and of comparative industry practices. Many 
unions conduct their own research to this effect, laying emphasis on practical problems, espe-
cially day-to-day affairs at work. The Indian Labour Research Center is the research wing of 
the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh, and is actively engaged in such research.

Exhibit 3.5 Union Participation in Managing Change
A number of labour leaders had established the Center for Workers Management (CWM) with 
the understanding that a change of culture in the labour movement as well as at management 
level is required in order to ease the strain in management-labour relations. A visionary plan was 
developed by CWM to bring about a change in the role of trade unions in a scenario in which 
privatisation is taking place. This was implemented in a limited number of large private enter-
prises, and about 30 firms responded to this initiative. Kamani Tubes Ltd. at Mumbai and Kamani 
Metals Ltd. (with plants in Mumbai and Bangalore) were the first to get involved in this plan. 
The Supreme Court had ruled in favour of the labour movement initiative of transforming Ka-
mani Tubes that had gone bankrupt due to mismanagement, into a workers’ cooperative. Workers 
then raised a considerable sum of money to build a new financial asset structure. Leadership, rather 
than management, was provided by CWM in defending the enterprise’s interests with respect to 
commercial banks, supervisory boards imposed by the Government of India, and courts of law. 
Though, due to the economic situation 1990 onwards and various other problems like weak 
management, this attempt could not be successful, nonetheless, it provided an example of shift 
in the role of trade unions from militant orientation to development orientation.
(Adapted from: www.ilo-mirror.library.cornell.edu/public/english/bureau/inst/papers/1999/dp100/ accessed 
on 25/10/2014.)
METHODS OF ACHIEVING OBJECTIVES
The history of trade union movement bears evidence to myriads of methods adopted by unions to 
achieve their objectives. Such means may be peaceful or equipped with agitation and revolution, de-
pending upon the ideologies followed by the trade unions. The Webbs propose the following methods 
adopted by unions: collective bargaining, mutual insurance andlegal enactments . Pressure tactics 
including strikes, picketing, gherao  and boycott are also often used to achieve the objectives.
rMutual Insurance:  Unions have since long tried to provide insur-
ance and other benefits to their members, which act as a security 
against casualties and also contribute to improvement in the condi-
tions of workers. This method implies that in exchange of fees that 
members pay, unions render certain services to them. It involves 
creation of a common fund to which every member is required to 
contribute, and the fund thus created is to be used for schemes for 
mutual benefit. Such benefits would enable unions to prevent work-
ers from accepting employment on terms and conditions injurious 
to the trade (Ironside and Seifert, 1995).
The Webbs referred to the method of mutual insurance adopted by trade unions as acting as a 
“friendly society”, that would provide insurance and other forms of assistance to members. Trade Spotlight

of workers.

3.24 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
unions in Great Britain and USA are known to have provided mutual insurance to their members. 
British unions in the nineteenth century provided their members with insurance against unem-
ployment, sickness, accidents, pensions for retired members and funeral expenses. The method 
of mutual insurance in Great Britain predominantly involved craft unions. Unions in USA have 
also provided benefits to their members from out of their funds, to meet economic uncertainties.
Mutual insurance is not a primary purpose of trade unions, neither does it have any actuarial 
basis or legal standing; in fact, this function can be performed better by other social and private 
bodies. But for union purposes, reserve funds are valuable because such funds enable the union 
of workmen to acquire wealth that binds them into a cohesive body.
Webb and Webb (1920) were of the opinion that unions adopted insurance policies primarily 
to strengthen the working-class organisation . They proposed the following advantages of mutual 
insurance (Boyer, 1988): 
jInsurance benefits motivated hesitant recruits to join unions.
jThese benefits were a powerful instrument for maintaining discipline among the members, 
and for enforcing on all the decisions of the majority.
jIt results into commitment and loyalty towards the union, as members who had contributed 
to the benefit fund for several years would not want to be separated from the union as that 
would imply the forfeiture of old age and funeral benefits.
jUnemployment benefits adopted by unions helped in preventing unemployed members from 
accepting employment with wages below standard rate.
jThese funds were a moral influence in negotiating with employers, thus enhancing bargain-
ing power of the union.
The amount and number of benefits that can be provided by any trade union as a part of mutual 
insurance would essentially depend upon the funds of the union created through contribution by 
its members. This method is not very popular in India because of weak financial condition of 
unions and lack of sufficient advancement of trade unions as compared to countries like UK and 
USA. However, certain big unions like the Textile Labour Association Ahmedabad and Rashtriya 
Mill Mazdoor Sangh, Bombay have undertaken welfare measures for members.
Mutual insurance policies have undoubtedly attracted young workers to unions, observed Boyer 
(1988); despite their large scale acceptance, these policies gradually waned out, and unions in 
capitalist countries have shifted their focus to collective bargaining.
rCollective Bargaining: Collective bargaining came to be adopted 
as a method for achieving trade union objectives after unions re-
ceived legal recognition and came to be recognised as legitimate 
representatives of workers. It is a method by which unions protect, 
safeguard and improve the conditions of the lives of their members. 
Under this method, trade union representatives bargain with the 
employer over terms and conditions of employment like wages, 
hours of work, incentives, working conditions, etc. An individual 
worker is not as influential and effective as a group in negotiating 
the terms and conditions of work. Due to this reason, collective bargaining came to be recognised 
as a useful method adopted by unions to achieve their objectives. Union representatives bargain 
with the employer and enter into an agreement, which is known as a collective agreement; such 
an agreement may deal with a single issue, or may include multiple issues. Negotiations may 
be conducted at different levels: they could be at local or plant level, where union representa-Spotlight
Collective bargaining is a meth-
od by which unions protect, 
safeguard and improve the 
conditions of the lives of their 
members, by bargaining with 
employers over terms and con-
ditions of employment.
IR&LL_Ch_03.indd   24 1/1/2008   4:48:27 AM

Trade Unions: Concept, Evolution and Functions 3.25
tives negotiate with the management at factory or unit level, or at regional or national level. 
Though bargaining with a single employer is commonly found, employers may also unite for 
the purpose of bargaining.
Collective bargaining as a method has succeeded in introducing an element of industrial 
democracy; it enables workers to participate in the decision making process on the issues influ-
encing them in industry, which was earlier the sole prerogative of the employers.
Collective bargaining has succeeded in the field of industries and labour management, par-
ticularly in countries like USA and UK, where trade unionism is very well developed. In Indian 
scenario, trade unions are mostly affiliated to political parties, and hence are controlled by such 
parties, regarded as “outsiders”. It is the presence of such outsiders that influences the process 
of bargaining, and often contributes to the failure of the collective bargaining process.
Failure to reach an agreement through collective bargaining may result in the adoption of 
other means like strike or lock-out. We shall be dealing with collective bargaining as a process 
in further detail in Chapter 5.
rLegal Enactments/Political Actions: Legal enactments and politi-
cal actions also help trade unions achieve their objectives. Unions 
send their representatives to legislatures to present the views and 
concerns of workers and convince the political leaders to enact laws 
for securing better working and living conditions. Once enacted, 
these laws define the legal rights of workers, and the industry has 
to abide by such laws.
How is legal enactment or political action different from mutual 
insurance and collective bargaining? As the Webbs opined, mutual insurance allows unions to 
aid needy members directly, and collective bargaining focusses on negotiating with employers 
on issues pertaining to workers, while legal enactments emphasise on securing laws that would 
mandate general and specific work regulations at all levels of the government. Thus the impact of 
legal enactments is on the working class in general, while that of both mutual insurance and col-
lective bargaining is restricted to the members or employees of a particular plant, industry or craft.
Labour laws on dispute settlement, labour welfare, social security, wages, working condi-
tions, employment of women and children, etc. have contributed immensely to ensuring rights 
to workers and improving their conditions. The International Labour Organisation has played an 
important role in influencing enactment of labour laws; workers’ representatives are sent to ILO 
to participate in various meetings of the body along with government representatives.
Affiliation to political parties dates back to the early history of trade unionism; political con-
nections help unions gain power and influence. Since the time of their inception, trade unions 
in India have sought to affiliate themselves to one political party or the other. AITUC, the first 
trade union of India, is affiliated to the Communist Party of India; INTUC is associated with 
the Indian National Congress.
rDirect Action: When unions fail to achieve their objectives through 
any of the means discussed above, they resort to direct action, which 
refers to exerting pressure on employers by resorting to tactics like 
strikes, boycott, blockade, etc. Before we take up some of these 
tactics in brief, let us specify here that direct action leads to loss 
of productivity, and involves not only the employer and workers, 
but also suppliers, consumers and other stakeholders; hence this method must be avoided and 
used only as the last resort.Spotlight

3.26 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Strike refers to collective withdrawal from work by the members of a union. It is a powerful 
weapon in the hands of a union to get its demands accepted. Picketing is an action taken by 
union members to prevent employees from attending work after a strike has been called. Boycott 
refers to the rejection by workers of specific products or services provided by the employer. 
Gherao  (literal meaning: confinement) is the confinement of managerial personnel within a 
small space, till the management is compelled to give a more favourable decision. Blockade
refers to obstruction of products, etc. at a certain point by workers, though it does not involve 
any stoppage or reduction in production. We shall be telling more about all these tactics in the 
chapter on industrial disputes.
Other means of direct action may include mass subordination, demonstration, postering, etc.
RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE NATIONAL COMMISSIONS ON 
LABOUR
The First National Commission on Labour (1969) had encouraged the formation of national federations, 
as these would be more effective at collective bargaining forums and also as agencies to which educa-
tional and research activities for the benefit of workers in the concerned industries could be entrusted.
According to the recommendations of the Second National Commission on Labour (2002), federa-
tions of trade unions, as also central organisations of trade unions and federations in India should be 
covered within the definition of trade unions, and be subject to the same discipline as a primary trade 
union. The same dispensation shall apply to employer’s organisations, as also employees’ organisations. 
Further, the Commission was not in favour of craft-based or caste-based organisations of workers or 
employees or employers.
Summary
rTrade unions are association of workers (or employers) formed on a continuous basis; they are 
a means to provide workers a medium to express their demands and views.
rThe main objective of unions is to ensure workers’ rights, safeguard economic interests, partici-
pate in management, make provision for welfare of workers and their families and contribute 
to national development.
rThe various reasons that may influence a worker in joining union are: greater bargaining power, 
sense of security, gratification of social and psychological needs, negotiation for wages and 
working conditions, protection from unforeseen exigencies like accidents and illness, etc.
rTrade unions can be classified on the basis of their purposes, membership pattern of workers 
and level of operation.
rNotable theories proposed to explain the approaches and functioning of trade unions are: Marxian 
Class Conflict Theory, Webb’s Theory of Industrial Democracy, Cole’s Theory of Union Control 
of Industry, Hoxie’s Theory of Functional Classification of Unionism, Tannenbaum’s Sociological 
Theory, Common’s Environmental Theory, Perlman’s Theory of Scarcity Consciousness, Kerr and 
Associates’ Protest Theory, Simon’s Theory of Monopolistic, Anti-Democratic Trade Unionism 
and Mahatma Gandhi’s Trusteeship Theory.
rEvolution of trade unionism in India can broadly be divided into 3 phases: pre-World War I, 
post-World War I and post-Independence. The post-Independence phase may be further studied 
under 5 distinct periods.

Role of Unions: Traditional and Beyond
National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC) Limited, a ‘Navratna’ public sector unit and the larg-
est power generating company of India, was incorporated in the year 1975. NTPC’s core business is 
engineering and operation of power generating plants. With a strong employee base, NTPC has won 
several distinctions of being one of the best employers in India.
Trade Unions at NTPC, Unchahar
There are around 1,200 employees at the Unchahar Power Station (hereon also referred to as Plant 
or Power Station), in the State of Uttar Pradesh, of which 693 are in workmen grade. The role of 
trade unions assumes critical significance in the success of the Power Station. At the apex level, 
union-management relations at NTPC are governed through the National Bipartite Committee (NBC) 
consisting of 4 Central Trade Union Organisation (CTUO) nominees, viz., AITUC, BMS, CITU and 
INTUC, with representatives of unions from various projects/stations on one side, and management 
representatives on the other. Following are the major unions at the Plant. 
(i) NTPC Power Karamchari Sangh: Affiliated to CITU and inspired by CPI (Marxist), the 
Sangh follows Communist philosophy. It negotiates with the management on the workers’ inter-
ests and problems. With its inception at the Unchahar Station in the year 1992, the Sangh now 
boasts of 310 members as per the last elections held. It is animated by the goal of organising 
IR&LL_Ch_03.indd   29 1/1/2008   4:48:27 AM

3.30 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
workers to further their interests in economic, social and political matters. The methods adopted 
by this union are legislation, demonstrations, agitations and intensification of the class struggle. 
(ii) NTPC Employees’ Union:  Affiliated to INTUC, the Employees’ Union has adopted the ide-
ologies of the Congress Party, and negotiates with the management at the plant-level. There are 
140 members in the Union as per the last elections held. The main objectives of the Employees’ 
Union are: to secure greater participation of workers in the management of the enterprise; to im-
prove the conditions at work; and to provide various social security measures. The means adopted 
for the furtherance of these objectives are peaceful, through the process of law and negotiations. 
(iii) NTPC Mazdoor Sangh: The NTPC Mazdoor Sangh is affiliated to the Bharatiya Mazdoor 
Sangh, and has adopted the principles of the Bharatiya Janta Party. It also negotiates with the 
management at plant-level. The methods employed by the Mazdoor Sangh are legitimate, peace-
ful and democratic.
(iv) NTPC Electric Employees’ Union (EEU): Affiliated to INTUC, EEU has adopted its consti-
tution from the philosophies of Congress. It is in the minority since it got less than 10 per cent 
votes in the last elections held, and hence it does not negotiate with the management at a large 
level. Purpose of formation of this union was to organise those workmen/employees of electricity 
organisations of Uttar Pradesh, namely, the UP Power Corporation, NTPC Unchahar Electricity 
Production Departments, and The Cooperative Electric Society Ltd., who do not fall under ex-
ecutive and supervisory categories. 
Other recognised unions of the Plant are Feroze Gandhi Urja Thermal Power Plant (FGUTPP) 
Pariyojna Karamchari Sangh (Independent), FGUTPP Pravidhik Karamchari Sangh (Independent), 
UP Vidyut Mazdoor Sangh (affiliated to Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh) and NTPC Shramik Sangh (affili-
ated to UTUC). Unions that are not recognised include the UP Vidyut Panchayat and NTPC Workers’ 
Association.
Role of Trade Unions at NTPC, Unchahar
Trade unions at NTPC not only act as machinery to voice employee grievances and problems before 
the management, but they also have a fair involvement in welfare measures for workers. They actively 
participate in discussions with the management at different levels regarding safety, work conditions 
and various other worker-related issues. Meetings are held from time to time, in which management 
and union representatives discuss and try to resolve several issues, the primary among which are issues 
pertaining to labour welfare. Welfare activities of the workers at Unchahar Power Station are divided 
into 2 broad categories: plant welfare and township welfare.
Plant Welfare Under this category, there is a provision for facilities of canteen, drinking water and 
restrooms for employees.
Township Welfare The Plant has welfare bodies like Union Working Committees, Employee Welfare 
Association and Township Advisory Development Committee, which look into the affairs of township 
welfare. Aspects related to entertainment like cable TV facilities, reading rooms, music halls, sports 
and theatres are being taken care of by the representative trade union. Besides, there are facilities like 
activity center for children, and Sports Council which organises various sports events like cricket, 
football, table tennis, etc. for the employees. There are 3 schools in the township, the infrastructure 
of which is provided by NTPC. All other expenses of the schools are met by their tuition fee. There 
are different clubs and associations that organise various events and celebrations. Different types of 
programmes on aspects like technical skills, safety and information management systems are organised 
by the Employee Development Center for the employees (including workers).

Desired Knowledge Competencies
cTo develop an understanding of the objectives, ideologies and other aspects of Central Trade Union 
Organisations in India.
cTo review trade union membership in India and its recent trends.
cTo identify the problems encountered by unions and the contemporary issues of trade unionism in 
India.

INTR ODUCTION
In the years following India’s Independence there has been an increase in the total number of trade
unions and their federations. Membership of unions has also increased over time. However, union 
activities have been more or less confined to the organised sector, more so in public sector enterprises, 
from which over 70 per cent of union membership is drawn.
The process of liberalisation and globalisation has ushered in a series of structural changes in the 
Indian economy. Perhaps the most notable of such changes are disinvestment of the public sector and 
introduction of new work practices like outsourcing and contractual employment. The past decade has 
also witnessed the emergence and expansion of new sectors including retail, Information Technology 
(IT) and business process management (BPM). These are human capital-intensive sectors comprising 
knowledge workers, who have a unique style of working and are generally averse to joining unions. All 
these factors have resulted in marginalisation of the labour movement as a whole and have eventually 
contributed to the weakening of trade unions.
In this chapter we will talk about the objectives and ideologies of notable Central Trade Union 
Organisations (CTUOs) in India, besides touching upon the issue of trade union membership. Many 
social, political, legal and economic factors are found to affect the functioning of unions leading to a 
IR&LL_Ch_04.indd   1 1/1/2008   4:48:39 AM

4.2 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
number of problems related to multiplicity of unions, leadership, finances, etc. This chapter makes a 
critical analysis of such problems faced by unions. Certain other contemporary issues like member-
ship of women in trade unions and the impact of globalisation on unions have also been covered in 
a separate section.
CENTRAL TRADE UNION OR GANISATIONS IN INDIA
Before we talk about the Central Trade Union Organisations in details, let us briefly explain the concept 
of recognition of a union as a CTUO. The criteria laid down by the Ministry of Labour & Employment, 
Government of India for trade unions to be recognised as CTUOs are as follows:
rTheir affiliates must be spread over at least 4 States and in 4 industries, and
rThey must have a minimum of 5 lakh (i.e., 0.5 million) members.
The strength of a CTUO is taken to be the combined membership of all registered unions affiliated 
to that CTUO. Once recognised, the Government gives a CTUO representation in various fora like 
the International Labour Organisation (ILO), international and national conferences, development 
councils, tripartite bodies, committees, etc. on the basis of the results of General Verification. We 
shall be explaining the concept of General Verification subsequently in the chapter in context of union 
membership.
In this section we shall be discussing some of the important CTUOs in terms of their objectives, 
membership patterns and other details. The Self Employed Women’s Association has also been included 
mainly because it has established itself as a successful association of women workers, in spite of being 
relatively younger than the other CTUOs.
All India Trade Union Congress
The All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC), the first trade union in India, was founded in the year 
1920 at Bombay (now Mumbai), with Lala Lajpat Rai as its first president. Up to 1945, Congress-
men, socialists and communists worked under the flag of AITUC; subsequently the union split up on 
account of difference in political ideologies. Since then, it has been associated with the Communist 
Party of India. AITUC has been a key player in the labour movement and has also played a crucial 
role in India’s struggle for freedom.
Objectives AITUC aims to achieve the following objectives by peaceful and legitimate means:
rTo establish a socialist state in India.
rTo socialise and nationalise the means of production, distribution and exchange as far as possible.
rTo improve the economic and social conditions of workers.
rTo protect and further the interests, rights and privileges of workers in matters related to 
employment.
rTo safeguard and promote workers’ right to freedom of speech, freedom of press, freedom of 
association, freedom of assembly, right to strike and right to work.
rTo abolish political/economic practices based on caste, creed, community, race or religion, and 
to fight against all forms of social oppression and injustice.
rTo oppose all forms of atrocities and harassment against women at workplace.

Trade Unions in India: V arious Issues 4.3
Membership Any union seeking affiliation to AITUC must, on 
application, pay an annual contribution and special levies, as per rules. 
The membership of AITUC is about 3.6 million. The unions affiliated 
to it are from the organised sector like textile, engineering, coal, steel, road transport and electricity 
board, as well as from the unorganised sector, such as beedi , construction and head-load workers, 
anganwadi , local bodies and handloom. Recently a number of agricultural workers’ unions have 
affiliated themselves to AITUC.
Structure The structure of AITUC comprises affiliated unions, a general council including office 
bearers, working committee of the general council and State bodies.
Hind Mazdoor Sabha
The Hind Mazdoor Sabha (HMS) was founded in Calcutta (now Kolkata) during a trade union confer-
ence from 24thto 26th December 1948, with R.S. Ruikar as the first president. The key factor behind 
the emergence of this union was the realisation that the trade union movement must be freed from 
misuse of unions by political parties in meeting their own interests. Affiliated to the International Trade 
Union Confederation (ITUC)—which represents 175 million workers in 
153 countries and territories and has 308 national affiliates—the HMS has 
been functioning as an independent and democratic trade union centre, 
free from the pulls and pressures of political parties, employers and the 
government. However, HMS may not be construed to be apolitical; it 
denounces the concept of a market-driven economy and privatisation as 
a one-stop solution to the problems in the economy.
Objectives As per the philosophy of this union, free market is solely profit-oriented and has no 
social concerns. For a country’s balanced development with equity, the state should play a regulatory 
role. In this pursuit, following are the broad objectives of HMS:
rTo ensure all-round development of workers and their families. For this HMS encourages and assists 
unions affiliated to it to take up non-traditional activities which address social evils like child la-
bour and generates awareness on issues like gender equality, environment protection, adult literacy, 
etc.
rTo make endeavours towards having a single unified trade union movement.
rTo promote industrial democracy, workers’ education and cooperative movement.
rTo build the trade union movement as an effective instrument of the country’s socio-economic 
transformation with social justice.
Membership As per the findings of the General Verification conducted by the Ministry of Labour 
& Employment, with year 2000 as the year of reckoning, HMS had a membership of 3,342,213 in 
2002 (13 per cent of the total trade union membership in the country). It has members from a cross 
section of industries like textiles, iron and steel and coal mining, spread over 23 States.
Structure HMS has affiliates at State-level from various industries, which in turn have affiliations 
from regional and plant-level unions. The office has an elected president at the top, followed by vice 
presidents, general secretaries and chief advisors.Spotlight

4.4 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Indian National Trade Union Congress
The Indian National Trade Union Congress (INTUC) is the trade union wing of the Indian National 
Congress. It came into existence on 3rd May 1948, after a resolution to this effect was passed by the 
central board of the Hindustan Mazdoor Sevak Sangh on 17th November 1947. Many attribute the birth 
of INTUC as a historic necessity to voice the genuine demands of the working class, keeping in view 
national interest as well.
INTUC is guided by Gandhian Sarvodaya philosophy, and is associated 
with ILO since 1949. It is inspired by the idea of transforming its 
beliefs with changing times, which can enable it to tackle the problems 
and contemporary issues related to workers. These include: promoting 
egalitarianism in the society; community welfare; maintaining and 
strengthening links with the unions of other countries having the same 
employer, as in the case of multinational firms; focus on improving the 
working conditions and the general quality of life for workers; and training 
and research for workers.
Objectives The objectives of INTUC are:
rTo establish an order of the society that promotes all-round growth and development of its 
individual members and eliminates exploitation and inequality.
rTo organise the society in such manner as to ensure full employment and the best utilisation of 
its manpower and other resources.
rTo secure increasing association of workers in the administration of industry and their full 
participation in its control.
rTo promote the social, civic and political interests of the working class.
rTo place industry under national ownership and control in suitable form in order to realise the 
aforesaid objectives in the quickest time. 
Membership Any registered trade union may seek affiliation to INTUC. Each affiliated union has 
to pay to the union the prescribed annual affiliation fee per member on the basis of membership on 
its rolls on the close of the preceding year, subject to a minimum of `100. The Working Committee 
may grant concession in the rate of affiliation fee in respect of unions functioning in beedi,  fisheries, 
agriculture and such other industries in the unorganised sector. As per the provisional statistics of the 
Ministry of Labour & Employment, the membership figure of INTUC stood at 3.9 million in 2002.
Structure The union has a president at the top, followed by the general secretary and treasurer. 
There are affiliated State branches, each having its own president.
Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh
The Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh (BMS) was founded on 23rd July 1955 under the leadership of 
Dattopantji Thengdi. BMS was not the result of any split in the existing 
trade union organisations, unlike in the cases of almost all other unions. 
Hence it had the formidable responsibility of building its organisational 
structure from the grassroot level.
BMS does not believe in class concept and is non-political in nature. 
The grounded philosophy of this union is that a trade union can exert Reflection

influence on management and policies of government only when it adopts the principle of non-political 
trade unionism. With its productivity-orientation, BMS rejects the idea of State control and proposes 
the restriction of State control to inevitable sectors like defence. However, the union strongly supports 
public accountability of each individual. It denounces coercive methods and adheres to constructive 
approach in all its struggles; in this context the philosophy of BMS is strikingly different from that 
of class struggle proposed by Marx.
Objectives The aims and objectives of the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh are:
rTo establish such order of the society in which there shall be security of, among other things, 
full employment and maximum production; economic democracy, development of autonomous 
industrial communities, and provision of work with living wage to every individual.
rTo enable workers in realising the above objectives by assisting them in organising themselves 
in trade unions; directing and coordinating the activities of affiliated unions and bringing unity 
in the trade union movement.
rTo secure and preserve for the workers their legitimate rights, including the right to strike as the 
last resort for redressing grievances; good conditions of living, a living wage and due share in 
the profits in their respective industries as partners; and enforcement, amendment and enactment 
of new labour legislations.
rTo inculcate in workers a sense of responsibility towards their industry and nation. 
rTo educate workers through seminars, lectures, training programmes, etc. 
rTo bring out publications in the interest of workers and to encourage labour research. BMS has 
established the Bharatiya Shram-Shodh Mandal , a research-based institution in 1980 to promote 
objective studies based on impartial examination of facts and developments in the industrial field. 
rTo contribute to ameliorate the social, economic, cultural, civic and general conditions of the 
workers and bring about welfare of their families.
BMS has set up the ‘ Paryavaran Manch ’ in 1995 to pragmatise the activities of trade unions, earlier 
limited to issues related to wages, bonus etc. It is also engaged in multiple activities directed towards 
the upliftment of the working class. The non-political ideology of BMS has now gained currency and 
is finding acceptance even at international levels.
Membership As of the year 2002, the total membership of BMS stood at 2,15,797, and the union 
claims to have presence in all the States of India, with more than 5,000 affiliate unions in all the 44 
industries classified by the Ministry of Labour & Employment.
Structure BMS has a president, vice presidents, general secretary, a few other secretaries, 
department in-charges (each looking after various departments of the union office like media, external 
affairs, etc.), zonal organising secretaries (where each zone comprises several States) and in-charges 
of federation groups formed by grouping together federations from different industries (for example, 
railway, defence and postal federations form 1 group).
Self-Employed Women’s Association
The Self Employed Women’s Association (SEWA) is a registered trade 
union of about a million women workers in the informal sector. It was 
founded in 1972 by Ela Bhatt, a lawyer and union organiser. SEWA grew 
out of the Textile Labour Association Ahmedabad, India’s oldest and Spotlight

a living through their own labour or small businesses. Established with the purpose of assisting women 
belonging to households of mill workers and with its focus on training and welfare activities, SEWA 
has now stretched its wings, and today it is a national union with members from nine States—Gujarat,

Structure Each of the State-level unions of SEWA is its affiliate. The union is governed by a 
2 tier level of elected representation. The members of each trade elect their representatives in the ratio 
of 1 representative per 100 members. These representatives then form the trade council (Pratinidhi 
Mandal) . In addition, and parallel to the trade council, are the trade committees (Dhandha Samiti)
in each trade. A trade committee has no fixed number of members; the number usually varies from 
15 to 50. Members of trade councils are members of their respective trade committees as well. The 
organiser of a trade group is the Member Secretary of the trade committee of that group. Besides, each 
State-level union has representation in SEWA through the national council.
UNIONISATION OF WORKERS AND UNION MEMBERSHIP
Trade unionism in India has experienced a steady growth with support from both society and 
government. The number of registered trade unions and membership of unions both have increased 
steadily after Independence, except for a few periods. The most authentic source of the number of 
unionised workers in India is the General Verification of membership of 
trade unions affiliated to CTUOs, and is an exercise undertaken by the 
Chief Labour Commissioner (CLC) (Central), on the directions of the 
Ministry of Labour & Employment. The purpose of such verification is 
to determine the representation of CTUOs in various national and 
international councils, committees, conferences etc. General Verification 
of CTUOs was earlier conducted in 1980, followed by another in 1989, Spotlight

Though the number of registered trade unions has increased from 1989 to 2002, the percentage of 
unions submitting returns has decreased, and in 2002 it was merely 11.4 per cent of the total number 
of trade unions. The total membership, excluding Agricultural and Rural Workers (A&RW), of all 
CTUOs has increased in absolute terms from 10,541,932 in 1989 to 17,131,529 in 2002, registering an 
increase of 62.51 per cent at an average annual growth rate of 3.74 per cent. It may be noted here that 
agricultural unions may or may not be included during the General Verification. In 2002, the data on 
A&RW has been presented as an industrial-sector category and has been considered while calculating 
the membership of CTUOs. Consequently the total number of members of a CTUO now includes the 
members that a union might have among A&RW.
Overall, trade union membership does not show any fixed pattern in terms of increase or decrease. 
For example, the pattern of growth of trade unions from the year 1991 to 2008 shows that there has 
been a continuous rise in the number of unions from 1991 to 2007, except in 2004, when there was a 
slight decrease, and then a decrease in 2008. The percentage of unions submitting returns decreased 
to 9.7 in 2003, from 11.4 in 2002 and then to 7.0 per cent in 2004 (Table 4.2). This could also be due 
to the fact that membership is calculated only for those trade unions that are submitting returns and 
total membership calculated is dependent upon membership of these unions only. The membership of 
trade unions increased from 5.42 million in 2000 to 9.57 million in 2008, though there was a notable 
fall in 2003, 2004 and 2007 over the previous years. Average membership per union has also shown 
a remarkable decrease in 2002, 2003, 2004 and 2008. This decrease may be attributed factors like 
changing employment patterns, growth of service sector and rise in informalisation of labour in the 
country. Other reasons could be fragmentation of major unions and rise of independent unions at 
unit-level.
