PR OBLEMS OF TRADE UNIONS IN INDIA
Unions in India are too fragmented; they split up due to various reasons. Earlier unions were affiliated 
to different political parties each having its own ideology. Consequently the splits in unions tended to 
be on ideological grounds. However, more recently, leadership issues have become the main reasons 
for their fragmentation, thus weakening unions. Adoption of downsizing strategies by decentralising 
production and by sub-contracting various operations to small businesses have led to reduction in the 
growth of jobs in the organised sector and a consequent increase in the share of the informal sector 
in industrial employment. Regular workers are being replaced by contract workers to reduce wage 
costs so that business firms could compete in the market. This has accentuated the process of weaken-
ing of trade unions (Datt, 2008), as majority of union membership comes from the organised sector. 
Other issues that weaken the structure and functioning of trade unions include declining membership, 
poor finances, influence of politics, dominance of outside leadership, multiple subscriptions of union 
membership and inter and intra union rivalries arising out of multiplicity of unions (Das, 1999), both 
at macro and firm levels. Moreover, intense competition within the product market and instability of 
the labour market have made the job of unions very difficult. In this section we will analyse some of 
the glaring problems of trade unions in India.
Recognition of Trade Unions
Existence of a strong and recognised trade union is an essential ingredient for industrial peace. A 
serious flaw in the legislations related to trade unions in India is the absence of any recognition pro-
cess for unions. The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 does mention the term “recognised unions”, but it 
does not prescribe any procedure for recognition. The Trade Unions Act, 1926 also does not address 
this issue. Except for Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Rajasthan and West 
Bengal, there are no State enactments regarding the recognition of trade unions. Lack of any central 
enactment may result in employers ignoring or even by-passing representative unions while entering 
into various agreements or settlements, to the disadvantage of majority of workers. This undermines 
the collective bargaining rights of workers and eventually threatens industrial peace (Menon, 2010).
IR&LL_Ch_04.indd   10 1/1/2008   4:48:40 AM

Trade Unions in India: V arious Issues 4.11
There have been many instances of strikes by workers on the issue of recognition. In the year 
2010, more than 7,000 workers of Foxconn, a Taiwan-based manufacturer of electronics components, 
went on a strike in the city of Sriperambudur. These workers were demanding the recognition of their 
union, Thozilalar Sangam (FITS), affiliated with the Stalinist Communist Party of India (Marxist) 
by the management, for all labour-related discussions. Foxconn management, with the full support 
of the Tamil Nadu Government responded with police attacks against the striking workers, including 
repeated mass detentions, which led to the arrest of more than 300 workers (Kumar and Kumar, 2010).
Exhibit 4.1 Strike at Maruti Suzuki’s Manesar Plant
Around 2,000 young workers at Maruti Suzuki’s Manesar facility in Haryana went on a wildcat 
sit-down strike from 4th to 17th June 2010. The motive was to put pressure on the management, 
demanding recognition for a new union, the Maruti Suzuki Employees Union (MSEU), mainly 
consisting workers at the Manesar plant. According to the striking workers, the existing Maruti 
Udyog Kamgar Union (MUKU) which is mainly dominated by those working at Maruti’s Gur-
gaon plant was not able to represent the workers at Manesar. There was no notice of the strike 
to the management; workers stopped production completely and stayed inside the factory for 
nearly a fortnight.
The Manesar plant produces cars like the A-Star, Dzire and SX4. The strike postponed the pro-
duction of 13,200 cars and caused a loss of about `6 billion (US$133 million/100 million Euros). 
Maruti Suzuki’s sales figures for June dropped by 23 per cent; this incidentally was the sharpest 
fall in the past 2 and a half years. In July, the management announced to shift a production-line 
back from Manesar to Gurgaon plant. Workers continued the strike despite the police stationed 
within the factory premises and ignoring the official declaration by the Haryana Government on 
10th June that the strike was illegal.
(Adapted from: www.gurgaonworkersnews.wordpress.com/gurgaonworkersnews-no-941/ accessed on 
30/3/2014.)
Leadership
Trade union leadership is an important issue that seeks serious attention. Most of the unions have 
affiliation with political parties and union leaders are often used as means by these parties to their 
political ends. These leaders may be internal or even external and they usually work on honorary 
basis. An external leader is one who is not a full time employee of the organisation, and hence does 
not emerge from amongst the workers. Such a leader may be working for than 1 union and may find 
little time for each.
There are advantages and disadvantages with both the types of leader-
ship. An external leader has better knowledge of the trends and practices 
in other organisations in the industry, and therefore may prove to be more 
effective on the bargaining table. If he is a politician or a person with 
strong political links, especially with the ruling party, then he may be able 
to provide some advantages either in terms of policy or of implementa-
tion of administrative actions. On the other hand, his involvement with Spotlight
An external leader is not a full 
time employee of the organisa-
tion, and hence does not emerge 
from amongst the workers.
IR&LL_Ch_04.indd   11 1/1/2008   4:48:40 AM

4.12 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
plant-level problems would be much less, as he is not on the shop floor to understand the intricate 
issues applicable to a particular plant. Since an external leader does not belong to the organisation, 
he lacks the required depth of understanding of working of the unit. In contrast, internal leaders have 
first-hand experience of day-to-day problems faced by workers, and are available and more easily 
accessible to workers.
Multiplicity of Unions and Inter-Union Rivalry
The provision in the Trade Unions Act, 1926 that 7 or more workers can form a trade union has 
resulted in multiplicity of trade unions at every level. Another reason behind union multiplicity is 
affiliation with rival political parties. As put up by Mathur and Mathur (1957, p. 201), “The clay of 
unionism is possibly effervescent industrial labourers, but the sculptors chiseling it into shape have 
certainly been members of political parties.” Every union tries to impress upon the workers that it 
is their true representative, and in an attempt to increase membership and gain power, each tries to 
lure the members of other unions. In such a scenario, instead of working in the interest of workers, 
union leaders tend to indulge in a different power play. Thus there may be inter-union rivalry which 
ultimately weakens the trade union movement as a whole, reducing the bargaining power of workers 
in securing their rights. Another problem that arises out of multiplicity of unions at plant-level is that 
the management may face problems in identifying which one would be the representative union of 
workers for the purpose of collective bargaining. Rift amongst unions themselves may put workers at 
disadvantage when it comes to pressuring the management to meet their demands.
Declining Membership
Growth in membership of trade unions in India has not been in the same proportion as the growth of 
employment. With shift of employment to the unorganised sector and employment in the organised 
sector being almost stagnant, union membership has been severely affected. Sub-contracting has 
emerged as a typical employment practice, whereby workers are no longer in any employment rela-
tionship, rather they are involved in a contractual relationship. This is also contributing to declining 
membership in trade unions.
Exhibit 4.2 Increasing Informalisation of Labour
With the recent move towards forced informalisation of labour, new entrants to the labour market 
cannot hope to get secured employment. Those with permanent jobs are being pushed into insecure, 
low-paid jobs in the unorganised sector. This can be seen from the growing trend in outsourcing 
of manufacturing from the large-scale sector to the small and medium sector. For example, there 
has been a gradual shrinking of employment and production in the Hindustan Unilever Limited 
(HUL) factory at Sewri in Mumbai, leading ultimately to the total closure of the factory. Despite 
this, HUL products are increasing manifold. This is so because the conglomerate has shifted its 
production from large factories to small-scale industries located in industrial estates in different 
parts of the country.
(Adapted from: Bhowmik, S.K. (n.d.). Labour Rights Deficits in the Service Sector, (Commentary - The State 
of Labour) Labour File, Vol. 6, No. 1, pp. 24-26.)
IR&LL_Ch_04.indd   12 1/1/2008   4:48:40 AM

Trade Unions in India: V arious Issues 4.13
The new pattern of unionisation points towards a shift from organisation of workers in a region 
or industry to the emergence of independent unions at the enterprise-level. These unions are mainly 
concerned with enterprise-level issues, with no forum to link them with national federations that could 
secure for them a voice at national policy-making levels. Also, with increasing demand for skilled 
workers, especially in the IT sector, a new class of managers and skilled workers is being recruited in 
business firms with lucrative compensation packages and offers for frequent promotions on performance 
or merit basis. These workers place individual interest at a higher level than group interest; they do not 
prefer to be members of trade unions; rather they form their own associations to seek larger benefits.
Low Finances
Trade unions need to perform a variety of functions in the process of rendering services and fulfilling 
their goals. As such, a sound financial position is an essential ingredient for their effective function-
ing. However trade unions in India are plagued with the problem of a weak financial base. According 
to the statistics of the Ministry of Labour & Employment, the total income including previous year’s 
closing balance of trade unions had decreased from `1,387 million in 2000 to `1,105 million in 2007; 
total expenditure had decreased from `594 million to `430 million during the same period.
There are several factors contributing to the financial problems faced by unions. The primary source 
of finance for unions is member subscription fee. Since members are mostly poor workers who live 
on meager wages/salary, this fee is deliberately kept low, though the amount of fee varies across unions. 
There is another very interesting aspect that is responsible for low finances of Indian trade unions. 
Multiplicity of unions is resulting in a competitive situation, where each union tries to keep its mem-
bership fee low in order to increase its membership. The situation becomes more precarious when 
many a times there are defaulters who would not pay their fees timely. Due to low finances, trade 
unions not only find it difficult to meet their expenses, but also have to face other kinds of problems. 
For example, the Trade Unions Act, 1926 allows for half of the office bearers of any union as outsid-
ers. However, a feeble financial structure incapacitates a union from supporting its staff. This leads to 
increased dependence of these unions on national-level trade unions to which they are affiliated, which 
are in turn affiliated to political parties; thus indirectly they get controlled by political parties. Unions 
may even get dependent on management for finances; this may result in co-optation. Under this situ-
ation unions cannot raise their voice and fight against management for issues related to workers. Thus 
the entire purpose of their existence may get defeated.
Keeping in perspective the costs imperative in collection of member-
ship fees, including the time spent thereby and the reluctance on the part 
of workers to pay the fee, no matter how small the amount may be, many 
organisations have adopted the check-off system.  Under this system, sub-
scription dues of a worker are directly deducted from his/her pay by the 
employer, before disbursement. Thus the amount of union subscription 
deducted is given directly to that union in favour of which the member 
worker has given written consent for deduction of subscription. The 
check-off method finds application in General Verification by which the 
management verifies the membership of a union on the basis of subscriptions given by the workers to 
the different unions operating in the organisation.Spotlight

of the member worker, and pay-

CONTEMPORAR Y ISSUES
Changes taking place in the internal and external business environment have a direct or indirect im-
pact on trade unions. Increased literacy level, dual career families, greater participation of women in 
workforce, shifting demographics, escalating aspirations of the working class and many other factors 
are contributing to transformations in the composition, beliefs and functioning of unions. Economic 
slowdown also has had a great influence on the role of unions, as it usually results in decreased pro-
duction levels, retrenchment and mass lay-offs. In addition, removal of trade barriers and opening up 
of the Indian economy for foreign companies has also directly affected unions. Another issue that asks 
for attention is the role of women in unions today. The increasing participation of women in trade 
unions and the impact of globalisation on unions have been discussed in the following sub-sections.
Women in Trade Unions
Characterised by low level of unionisation, India has one of the lowest trade union densities in the entire 
Asia-Pacific region, and more alarmingly, this density is on the decline. In this context, participation 
of women in unions is an issue that cannot be overlooked. While women are known to have actively 
participated in many union activities and struggles, their growth within unions, however, does not have 
many instances to cite. Sectors like textiles and engineering that were spearheads in the trade union 
movement in India were essentially male-dominated. As a corollary, women’s role in the movement 
was also not much significant, and hence does not fetch many illustrations. In the 1960s, Anusuiya 
Ben was the union leader of Calico Mills. Later, Ela Ben organised women in the unorganised sector 
to form SEWA. In a similar manner, Jaya Arunachalam organised women working in the unorganised 
sector in 4 Indian southern States under the Working Women’s Forum.
A striking characteristic of the current phase of the labour movement in India is the increasing 
participation of women in trade unions. As evident from Table 4.2, female membership of trade 
unions submitting returns saw nearly 4 times increase from just 0.5 million in 1991 to 2.1 million in 
2008, though this growth rate has not been uniform. Later, both 2009 and 2010 have witnessed fall 
in women’s membership, though not significant. The trends are encouraging as far as participation 
of women in the workforce and their involvement in unions is concerned. Yet the bitter reality is that 
women’s membership is still low. When compared, it can be seen that male membership in 1991 
stood at around 5.5 million and at 3.1 million in 2010 with no fixed pattern of increase or decrease.
Let us explore some of the reasons behind such low female participation in union activities. Studies 
are suggestive that women are predominantly (as high as 96 per cent) engaged in the informal sector, 
where wages and working conditions are lower than the formal sector and there is no clear employer-
employee relationship. Thus many of the segments like agriculture and domestic work in cities, where 
women usually outnumber men, are not covered by most of the legislations in the country. Unionisa-
tion of men in its own is low in the informal sector; hence the status of unionisation of women is still 
lower. There are very little or no women workers in some geographical regions and certain industries. 
Among all industries, agriculture, hunting and forest industry had the highest proportion (57.07 per cent) 
of women workers, whereas the lowest proportion (1.99 per cent) of women was found in wholesale 
and retail, repair of motor vehicles, motorcycles and personal and household goods in the year 2003. 
In 2004 the least (2.14 per cent) representation of women was in the electricity, gas and water supply 
industry, while fishing industry registered the highest proportion (56.36 per cent) of women members 
(Statistical Profile of Women Labour, 2009-2011).
IR&LL_Ch_04.indd   14 1/1/2008   4:48:40 AM

Trade Unions in India: V arious Issues 4.15
Sometimes restrictions on work timings and nature of work (for example, night shifts or work in-
volving hazardous conditions) do not allow for employment of women workers in many jobs. Perhaps 
the best example would be underground mines, wherein women workers are banned from working. 
Such restrictions and bans have further affected the employment rate of women.
Martens and Mitter (1994) point out that the lack of interest in unionism among women workers is 
not as a result of any inherent characteristics of women, but because of the culture of mainstream trade 
unions that does not sufficiently address the needs and problems of working women, like child care, 
sexual harassment, etc. As a consequence, women either remain unorganised or mobilise themselves 
in informal associations. Of the very few who join unions, even a fewer participate actively in union 
activities. Some other reasons behind the under-representation of women in unions are as follows:
rFamily responsibilities:  The Indian society expects a woman to fulfill family responsibilities 
even if she is employed. Childcare is considered to be the sole responsibility of the mother. Such 
commitments pose hindrances to any woman who has to thus balance her work and family and it 
becomes difficult for her to find time for union activities. “The fact that some jobs can only be 
done outside employees’ normal working hours (settling individual problems, inter-professional 
meetings, etc.) means that trade union activity encroaches on the time generally set aside for per-
sonal life” (Mario, 2002, p. 231), and round-the-clock availability may not be feasible for women.
rSocio-cultural inhibitions:  Social taboos and cultural inhibitions in the Indian sub-continent 
inhibit a woman from assuming a public profile as a representative of any union. There is 
patriarchal control within unions that restricts women from moving into roles of authority 
(Ramaswamy, 1998). Similarly engagement in union activities in a male-dominated ambience 
is also looked down upon.
rMale dominated culture of unions:  ILO (2000) has identified male-dominated culture of 
unions as a barrier to increase in women’s membership. The functioning of unions is in tune 
with masculine ways. The timings at which union meetings are arranged are usually beyond 
normal working hours, and such meetings may even continue till late hours, which makes it all 
the more difficult for women union members to attend. Further, male member workers often use 
union jargons, and discussions are loaded with sexist language (Ratnam and Jain, 2002), where 
women member may feel ‘out of the place’.
rEmergence of new jobs : Women are particularly affected by the growth in new types of jobs. 
Many multinational corporations have evolved a vendor system of sub-contracting for their pro-
duction. Depending on the nature of work, some of these vendors either employ women workers 
in large numbers or give out work to home-based workers mostly through contractors (Jhabwala 
and Sinha, 2002). This is likely to reduce the access of women to trade union activities.
rLack of physical infrastructure : Union offices often lack proper physical infrastructure (includ-
ing childcare facility and rest rooms), which may be inconvenient for women members to attend 
meetings and other activities at the office premises. Further, women may be constrained by lack 
of safe and affordable transportation facilities from union office to home.
rOther reasons : As compared with men, women have lesser access to formal education and 
training, which hinders their gaining confidence to shoulder responsibilities and assume leader-
ship roles in unions.
Studies indicate that India has taken a lead in organising women in the unorganised sector through 
various modes that include trade unions, cooperatives and self-help groups (ILO, 1994; Datt, 1997). 
Almost all major central trade unions have established internal cells or subcommittees for working 
women, directed at taking up the specific problems of women members; but there is still a long way 
to go.
IR&LL_Ch_04.indd   15 1/1/2008   4:48:40 AM

4.16 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Globalisation and Trade Unionism
The era of economic liberalisation in India was initiated in the year 1991 during the Prime Minis-
tership of P.V . Narasimha Rao. One of the obvious outcomes of this policy was increase in market 
competition for the domestic firms, which were now required to compete not only with other domestic 
players, but also with international firms in terms of quality, price and technology. Firms thus adopted 
cost-cutting in order to compete in the market by resorting to practices like downsizing, outsourcing 
and replacing regular employees with contract employees to save expenses on workforce. Large scale 
retrenchments were taking place. Since public sector organisations could not retrench employees, some 
of them reduced fresh recruitments and introduced the scheme of voluntary retirement, also known as 
the Golden Handshake Scheme; examples of such organisations include State Bank of India and the 
Indian Telephone Industries. As a result of such initiatives, there has been a huge decline in public 
sector employment, which led to reduction in employment in the organised sector. Privatisation of 
State enterprises by the process of disinvestment has further contributed to decline in employment. The 
consequences on workers were many, and perhaps the most serious one was decline in job security.
The phased economic liberalisation process has touched every aspect of the economy. With in-
creasing demands for more skilled workers, especially in the IT sector, a new class of managers and 
skilled workers called knowledge workers are now in demand. For these highly paid workers, being 
members of trade unions is not important. They have needs different from traditional factory workers 
and to promote their interests they form their own associations. In recent years, workers of various 
industries have chosen to form their own independent unions which are not affiliated to any political 
party and these function as independent bodies. Examples include the National Co-ordination Com-
mittee of Electricity Employees and Engineers, and unions formed in banks, insurance companies and 
financial institutions.
This new environment has had a far reaching impact on trade unions and has weakened their power. 
It has also added new responsibilities and crafted out new roles for unions, which must now review 
their old objectives and policies, redefine their functions to embrace the changes, and prepare workers 
to meet the challenges of the changed business environment. The new functions of trade unions have 
already been reviewed in detail in Chapter 3.
EMPLOYERS’ OR GANISATIONS
Employers and their organisations are an important component of the industrial relations system of 
any modern society, though these organisations have not been very successful in seeking as wide at-
tention as have workers and their organisations have (Alexander, 1972). Employers’ organisations are 
a formal body of employers, from the same or from different sectors, set up with the objective to 
champion and further the interest of employers, represent them at various fora, and advise them to 
improve the conditions of conducting trade and maintaining harmonious industrial relations.
The earliest employers’ organisation in India was set up during British rule; it was the first chamber 
of commerce, known as the Calcutta Chamber of Commerce, started by 
an English businessman in 1833 at Kolkata. About half a century later, 
Indians organised a chamber of their own and the first Indian Chamber 
of Commerce, named the Native Merchants’ Chamber of Coconada, was 
set up at Coconada, Andhra Pradesh, in 1885. After 2 years the Bengal 
National Chamber of Commerce and Industry was established at Kolkata Spotlight
Some notable employers’ or-
ganisations in India are: ASSO-
CHAM, FICCI, EFI, CII, AIOE, 
AIMO and NASSCOM.

Trade Unions in India: V arious Issues 4.17
(Alexander, 1972). Post-Independence, India saw the emergence of employers’ associations primarily 
in industries like jute, textile and engineering in response to labour enactments (Ratnam and Verma, 
2011). In fact, there has been a significant growth in these organisations after Independence.
Employers’ organisations are different from trade unions, as the latter are made up of workers. On 
the contrary, employers’ organisations comprise individual companies though they fall within the pur-
view of the definition of trade unions as given in the Trade Unions Act, 1926. They may be registered 
under any of these 3 legislations: Indian Societies Registration Act, 1860; Trade Unions Act, 1926; 
and Indian Companies Act, 1956.
The Council of Indian Employers (CIE) is the umbrella organisation for Indian employers. It was 
formed when the Employers’ Federation of India (EFI) (established in 1933) was amalgamated with 
the All India Organisation of Employers (AIOE) in 1956. CIE was joined by the Standing Conference 
of Public Enterprises (SCOPE) in 1973. The Council of Indian Employers is not registered under any 
Act of the country, but all its 3 constituents are registered individually under some Act or the other. 
CIE is fully recognised by the Government of India and other national and international bodies and 
apex employers’ associations dealing with labour and social policy issues. EFI represents Indian em-
ployers at ILO in Geneva and at the International Organisation of Employers (IOE)— a world body of 
employers in Geneva— the largest representative organisation of the private sector all over the world 
with 157 national employers’ organisations across 44 countries.
Some of the most notable employers’ organisations in India are the Associated Chambers of Com-
merce (ASSOCHAM), the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI), the 
Employers’ Federation of India (EFI), the Confederation of Indian Industries (CII), the All India 
Organisation of Employers (AIOE), the All India Manufacturers’ Organisation (AIMO) and the 
National Association of Software and Services Companies (NASSCOM). We would be talking about 
only 4 of these organisations here in detail, namely, ASSOCHAM, FICCI, EFI and NASSCOM.
Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry of India
The Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry of India, India's 
apex industry body, was established in 1920 by promoter chambers, 
representing all regions of India. It has membership of over 0.2 million 
companies and professionals across the country. ASSOCHAM repre-
sents the interests of industry and trade. It establishes an interface with 
the Government on policy issues and interacts with other international 
organisations. ASSOCHAM is represented in all national and local bodies. It acts as a voice of the 
industry and conveys its stance and opinions relating to various issues including public-private part-
nerships for economic development.
ASSOCHAM members represent trade (national and international), industry (domestic and inter-
national), professionals (e.g., chartered accountants, lawyers and consultants), trade and industry as-
sociations and other chambers of commerce. The services it provides to its members include offering 
expert advice, analysis of legislations, organising workshops, seminars for generating awareness and 
facilitating interaction, etc.
The objectives of ASSOCHAM are to promote trade by representing industry at various national 
and international fora; enhancing competitiveness; and disseminating information about national and 
international policies.Spotlight

4.18 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry
The Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry is the larg-
est and oldest apex business organisation in India. It was founded by G.D. 
Birla and Purushottam Das Thakurdas in 1927. It is a non-government, 
not-for-profit organisation. FICCI has membership from various sectors 
including manufacturing, gems and jewellery, chemical, mining, power 
and retail. These members are from the corporate sector, both private and public, including small and 
medium enterprises and MNCs. FICCI enjoys an indirect membership of over 2,50,000 companies 
from various regional chambers of commerce and has tie-ups with over 200 industry associations and 
chambers across the globe.
FICCI has the vision of being the thought leader for industry; to be an advocate for policy change; 
and to take steps for ensuring effective implementation. Its main objectives are: to enhance efficiency 
of Indian industry; to promote global competitiveness of its members; and to expand business oppor-
tunities both in domestic and foreign markets. It strives to achieve these objectives through a range of 
activities that include: providing help in arbitration, advising on economic affairs, conducting research 
on economic issues, carrying out consumer research, assisting in technology commercialisation, offering 
B2B solutions, maintaining relations with customers and generating awareness for maintaining quality 
of products and services.
Employers’ Federation of India
The Employers’ Federation of India was established in 1933, as an associ-
ation of autonomous organisations of industries in India, with the purpose 
of defending, promoting and championing the interests of employers. EFI 
is an apex body of employers’ organisations and industries that plays an 
important role in matters concerning labour, human resource management, 
industrial relations and other related issues. It was initially registered under the Indian Companies 
Act, 1956. Later it was unregistered and registered again in 1963 under the Trade Unions Act, 1926.
The Federation represents employers’ concerns and views at various tripartite fora of the Ministry 
of Labour & Employment, such as the Standing Labour Committee, Indian Labour Conference and 
other industry committees and sub-committees at State and national levels. It is a key constituent of 
CIE, along with AIOE and SCOPE. EFI represents Indian employers at the international level as a 
member of the Confederation of Asia-Pacific Employers and IOE.
The principal goals and objectives of the Employers’ Federation of India include regulating and 
maintaining harmonious relations between employers and workers; promoting and protecting the le-
gitimate interests of employers; collecting and disseminating information affecting employers; sup-
porting employment generation; helping accelerate labour reforms; and improving policies to enhance 
competitiveness.

RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE SECOND NATIONAL COMMISSION 
ON LABOUR
The following are some of the important recommendations of the Second National Commission on 
Labour (2002) regarding trade unions:
rOnly that union which has at least 10 per cent members amongst the workers of a unit should 
have the right to represent individual workers. To meet this requirement, Section 36 of the In-
dustrial Disputes Act, 1947 must be amended accordingly.
rA worker who is not a member of any trade union will have to pay an amount equal to the union 
subscription rate, which may be credited to a statutory welfare fund.
rCentral organisation of trade unions and federations should be covered within the definition of 
trade union.
rCraft-based or caste-based unions shall not be allowed to be registered.
rCheck-off system must be made compulsory for an establishment employing 300 or more workers.
rRecognition of any union should be on the basis of check-off system. A trade union with 66 per 
cent support must be accepted as the single negotiating agent, and if none of the unions has 66 
per cent support, then unions that have the support of more than 25 per cent should be given 
proportionate representation.
rRecognition once granted should be valid for a period of 4 years.
rOrganisation of the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central) should be responsible for verifying 
the membership of unions affiliated to Central Trade Union Organisations for the purpose of 
giving representation in national and international conferences and committees, as also of unions 
for the purpose of recognition under the Code of Discipline.

Women Workers in the Indian Garment Industry: A Long Road Ahead
Working Conditions The garment industry in India, particularly in the export sector, has very 
poor conditions of work, typical of the informal and unorganised sector. Manufacturing of garments 
for export is spread all over the country, though it is mostly concentrated in urban areas. The industry 
mainly consists of 2 types of units: independent, small proprietary units at one end, and sub-contracting 
units at the other. A large proportion of end jobs are also given out to home-based workers. The methods 
of production and work organisation are heterogeneous. The production process is broken down into 
separate functions that are performed in different locations and managed by different parties such as 
export agents, contractors and sub-contractors. In general, core processes such as design, cutting and 
IR&LL_Ch_04.indd   22 1/1/2008   4:48:40 AM

Trade Unions in India: V arious Issues 4.23
sampling are centralised, while other jobs like sewing, button stitching, thread cutting, embroidery and 
washing are sub-contracted. Extensive sub-contracting has deeply fragmented the industry, leaving the 
workers with no permanent linkages. Most of the fabricators (i.e., workshops) are unregistered small 
units without any legal backing. Since work is seasonal, production units are usually dismantled when 
there is no work. These units are located in crowded areas and working conditions are poor with little 
lighting and insufficient ventilation.
There is a large number of women workers in these garment manufacturing units. They have quite a 
heterogeneous profile; very few of the women who work in large fabricators are technically trained and 
literate and are employed in specialised jobs. Most of the women are unskilled—working as checkers 
and helpers—and not listed in the records. Division of labour continues to be affected by customs and 
traditions and seems to be benefitted little by technology. Women’s work contains a large component 
of piece-rated work and some of skilled work ‘here and there’ within a framework of employment 
which itself is casual and informal. A large number of women in the industry are invisible as home-
based workers, getting work from the contractors and sub-contractors, often having little interaction 
with the principal employer. With the exception of large units, wages are piece-rated. Studies reveal 
that women get lower wages than men even when they do similar work. Although policy prescribes 
that all garment units must be registered and conform to legislative prescriptions, reality reveals large-
scale evasion. There is a huge feeling of job insecurity due to the constant fear of closure of units. Any 
attempt to organise the workers results in units being closed down and relocated elsewhere. Frequent 
closures also result in worker mobility that is horizontal and not vertical.
Trade Unions and Women While women suffer as casual and marginal workers with low 
skills and poor wages in production processes of the garment manufacturing units, the perception 
that management and even unions have about women’s work is not very encouraging. The general 
discernment is that apart from their nimble fingers, women’s expertise does not lie in the skilled 
operations in spinning, carding, weaving, designing and cutting in this industry. Trade unions do not 
seem to have made appreciable efforts and have not been forthcoming in taking up the issue of women’s 
employment or their rights. Their major focus has instead been on problems relating to wages, fringe 
benefits and production.
Women themselves have come forward with their issues at individual, departmental and even plant-
levels to protect their employment. While these women leaders have been active in their respective 
departments, few have even been a part of the wider trade union movement and decision-making pro-
cesses. Yet, the performance of women workers in trade unions of the garment industry has been far 
from satisfactory. The burden of household responsibilities and the culture of the wider society do not 
encourage women to be active in unions. Their small number is another reason for this condition. More 
importantly, women in this industry are mainly engaged as reelers and cone winders, and hence they 
do not have the clout that spinners or weavers have either with the management or with trade unions.
Most union leaders admit that the task of organising women workers in garments, handlooms and 
power looms is in itself arduous. Statistics about women’s employment levels are sometimes men-
tioned in the charter of demands that trade unions put up to employers, but are rarely discussed in the 
bargaining forums. The small number of women workers seems to be of little concern for the unions, 
but a few organisations such as SEWA in Ahmedabad and Annapurna Mahila Mandal in Mumbai have 
organised women who have been displaced, and have turned them into home-based and self-employed 
workers. Especially SEWA has organised women in several trades and has been making relentless 
efforts for appropriate legislation for self-employed and home-based women workers. It has given 
considerable thrust to worker education programmes to educate their members on their rights. Such

efforts, however, have continued to remain mere innovative experiments, and are too few in number 
to meet the challenges of the numerous workers. The need of the hour is to combine the organising

in the existing conditions.

Trade Unions in India: V arious Issues 4.25
Annexure I: Criteria of Recognition of Trade Unions under Code of Discipline
The Code of Discipline (or ‘Code’) comprises guidelines aimed at maintaining harmony in industry in 
India; it came into effect in 1958 and is voluntary in nature. The process of recognition of trade unions 
has been prescribed in the Code, though it is not binding upon the companies to adopt it.
Where there is more than 1 union, the union claiming recognition in an establishment should have 
been functioning for at least a year after registration, but where there is only 1 union, this condition 
would not apply. The membership of the union should cover at least 15 per cent of the workers in the 
establishment concerned. Only those workers who have paid their subscriptions for at least 3 months 
during the period of 6 months immediately preceding the reckoning would be counted as members. 
A union may claim to be recognised as a representative union for an industry in a local area if it has 
membership of at least 25 per cent of the workers of that industry in that area. When a union has been 
recognised, there should be no change in its position for a period of 2 years. Where there are several 
unions in an industry or establishment, the one with the largest membership should be recognised.
A representative union for an industry in an area should have the right to represent the workers in 
all the establishments of the industry. If a union of workers in a particular establishment has a member-
ship of 50 per cent or more workers of that establishment, it should have the right to deal with matters 
of purely local interest, for instance, handling of grievances pertaining to its own members. All other 
workers who are not members of that union might either operate through the representative union for 
the industry or seek redress directly. In the case of trade union federations which are not affiliated to 
any of the central organisations of labour (i.e, CTUOs), the question of recognition would have to be 
best dealt with separately. Only that union which observes the Code of Discipline would be entitled 
to recognition.

Collective Bargaining
Desired Knowledge Competencies
cTo discuss the concept and significance of collective bargaining.
cTo explain the process of bargaining and the levels at which collective bargaining takes place.
cTo analyse the hindrances in collective bargaining in India.
cTo identify the essentials of a successful process of collective bargaining in India.
INTR ODUCTION
Workers and employers in any industrial relations system have devised several tools to manage con-
flicts between them and thus maintain harmonious relations with each other. The process of collec-
tive bargaining is one such tool that strives at arriving at peaceful settlement of any dispute existing 
between the two parties. There can be numerous issues of dispute between workers and management, 
including conditions of work, wages, hours of work, and so on. We have covered disputes and their 
underlying causes in Chapter 7. Workers, either at individual level, or as a group, may have demands 
from the management, which, if not fulfilled, may brew disputes. Instead of each individual worker 
negotiating with the management to get his/her demands fulfilled, it was found that if negotiation is 
done in a collective manner, it can be beneficial for both workers and management, and the impact 
would be much deeper and wider. Trade unions take up such issues on behalf of their members and 
negotiate with management. Thus there is collective interest involved in negotiations.
The concept of collective bargaining had originated with the emergence of trade unions. When 
there were no trade unions, workers were at disadvantage as an individual worker had no power to 
influence the employer to listen to the problems and accede to the demands. Nonetheless, the rise of 
trade unionism changed the scenario, as workers were now able to put forth their problems in a col-
lective manner. This was the genesis of collective bargaining. The term ‘collective bargaining’ was 
first used by the economic theorist Beatrice Webb in Britain in 1891 to describe the process in which 
representatives of a group of workers conduct the bargaining of the sale of their labour on behalf of the 
whole group of workers ( www.eurofound.europa.eu ). This concept was first used in USA by Gompers.
IR&LL_Ch_05.indd   1 1/1/2008   4:48:52 AM

5.2 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
The beginning of collective negotiations in India may be traced back to the period of 1920s, when, 
with the interventions of Mahatma Gandhi, efforts were being made to reach an agreement between 
the textile workers of Textile Labour Association Ahmedabad and management to settle disputes in 
textile mills in Ahmedabad. With the growth of trade unionism and passing of the Trade Unions Act, 
1926, workers’ associations got a legal status in the form of registered trade unions, which could now 
formally bargain with employers. Later, when the Constitution of India was formed, it granted freedom 
of association as a fundamental right through Article 19(c). Freedom of association ensures that work-
ers and employers can form associations that can represent workers to negotiate labour-management 
relations. Before the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 came into existence, collective bargaining was 
practiced only in rare cases, but with the passing of the Act, the practice of collective bargaining got a 
fillip. Initially statutory status was given only to settlements that were arrived in conciliation proceed-
ings and were binding in nature. However, by an amendment to the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 in 
the year 1956, bilateral agreements between workmen or their trade unions and employers also got 
statutory recognition and enforceability. Some of the pioneering collective agreements that took place 
at that time were the agreements related to bonus between TISCO and Tata Workers’ Union in 1956, 
between Indian Tea Association and Indian Tea Planters’ Association representing the management 
and Hind Mazdoor Sabha and Indian National Trade Union Congress representing the workers in 
1956 and between Bata Shoe Company Ltd., Calcutta and Bata Mazdoor Union (beginning in 1948 
and contracted from time to time).
CONCEPT AND DEFINITION OF COLLECTIVE BAR GAINING
The term collective bargaining is made up of two terms: ‘collective’, indicating an activity by a group 
of people and ‘bargaining’, indicating negotiation. Putting them together, we may simply say that col-
lective bargaining involves a negotiation between groups to arrive at a common agreement. It denotes 
participation of workers and management in the process of reconciliation of their conflicting interests 
through peaceful negotiations. The process denotes industrial democracy, in which workers voice their 
interests, demand their rights and participate at an equal platform with the management in arriving at an 
agreement. Collective bargaining is the first step in finding a peaceful solution to the problems existing 
between labour and management. So, it may be seen as a technique to maintain industrial harmony.
Ever since the concept came into existence, collective bargaining has been defined by many research-
ers. We shall be referring to some of these definitions in order to analyse the nature of the process.
The International Labour Organisation (ILO) Right to Organise and Collective Bargaining Conven-
tion (No. 98), 1949 describes collective bargaining as “voluntary negotiation between employers or 
employers’ organisations and workers’ organisations, with a view to the 
regulation of terms and conditions of employment by collective agree-
ments” (Silva, 1996). According to another definition (International La-
bour Office, 1960, p. 3), collective bargaining stands for “the negotiations 
about working conditions and terms of employment between an em-
ployer, or a group of employers, or one or more employers’ organisations, 
on the one hand, and one or more representative workers’ organisation 
on the other with a view to reaching agreement.”
Some authors describe collective bargaining in terms of the steps involved in it. For example, ac-
cording to Beach (1979, p. 96), collective bargaining “involves the process of union organisation of 
employees; negotiation administration, and interpretation of collective agreements, covering wages, 
hours of work, and other conditions of employment; engaging in concerted economic action and dispute Spotlight

working conditions or terms and 
conditions of employment.

Collective Bargaining 5.3
Exhibit 5.1 Collective Bargaining and Industrial Jurisprudence
Collective bargaining in India has been a subject matter of industrial adjudication since long, 
and has been defined by law courts at different points of time.
InKarnal Leather Karamchari Sangathan vs. Liberty Footwear Co. [(1989) 4 SCC 448] the 
Supreme Court had observed that, “Collective bargaining is a technique by which dispute as to 
conditions of employment is resolved amicably by agreement rather than coercion.” Accord-
ing to the Apex Court, collective bargaining forms the basis to bring about social justice in the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
InBharat Iron Works vs. Bhagubhai Balubhai Patel and Others (1976 SCR (2) 280) it was 
held that “Collective bargaining, being the order of the day in the democratic, social welfare 
State, legitimate trade union activities, which must shun all kinds of physical threats, coercion or 
violence, must march with a spirit of tolerance, understanding, and grace in dealings on the part 
of the employer. Such activities can flow in healthy channel only on mutual cooperation between 
the employer and the employees and cannot be considered as irksome by the management in 
the best interests of its business. Dialogues with representatives of a union help strike a delicate 
balance in adjustments and settlement of various contentious claims and issues.”
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/77506/ accessed on 10/1/2014; Collective Bargaining Process 
in India: A Critique. Retrieved from www.articles base.com/organisational-articles/collective-bargaining-
process-in-india-a-critique-539870.html on 10/1/2014.)settlement procedures.” Dunlop (1958) focused on the issues involved in the process while defining 
collective bargaining as a system which sets, modifies and administers workplace rules; a procedure 
to determine the amount of compensation and distribution of economic benefits for employees; a 
method of resolving disputes during the pendency of an agreement, and also determining if strike or 
lock-out should be resorted to after the expiry of an agreement. Perlman (1936) believes that collec-
tive bargaining is not just meant to demand wage raise, improvement in working conditions and terms 
of employment, or to establish democracy at workplace. It serves a bigger purpose. It is a technique 
through which the weaker and lower class of the society exerts pressure and demands for itself more 
of ‘social sovereignty’, welfare, security and liberty.
We may thus define collective bargaining as a voluntary and formal process of negotiation between 
one or more organisation(s) of workers and the organisation of the employer regarding work, working 
conditions or terms and conditions of employment, and thereby also serves as a means of establishing 
industrial democracy.
From the above discussion we can conclude that collective bargaining has the following charac-
teristics:
rIt is a process . There are several sequential steps or phases in collective bargaining, beginning 
with presentation of a list of demands, followed by negotiations and signing of a collective 
agreement, which leads to administration of the contract.
rIt is a bipartite  process involving 2 parties. Negotiations take place between workers and their 
employers. 
rIt is a collective  activity. Groups of workers and employer(s) are involved in this process, and 
both parties act collectively.
IR&LL_Ch_05.indd   3 1/1/2008   4:48:52 AM

5.4 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
rNegotiations  form the basis of collective bargaining. The process involves mutual ‘give and take’ 
between labour and management through discussions that may result in compromising and ac-
commodating situations for the other party.
rCollective bargaining is a formal  process by which employers and unions of workers decide to 
resolve their conflicts and disputes.
rThe process aims at establishing industrial democracy  as it provides workers a forum to demand 
their rights.
rThe underlying objective of collective bargaining is always to resolve the issues between labour 
and management through a dialogue, and to come to an agreement rather than strike, lock-out or 
other methods of coercion that disrupt industrial harmony. Thus it helps in promoting industrial
peace .
rCooperation  and understanding between management and labour are the basic requirements for 
the success of collective bargaining.
SIGNIFICANCE OF COLLECTIVE BAR GAINING
Collective bargaining enables management and workers to negotiate on the terms and conditions of 
employment for establishing amicable relationship and helps prevent industrial disputes, which are 
harmful for both the parties. The significance of collective bargaining may be understood from the 
observation of the Report of the Second National Commission on Labour (2002, p. 329) that “employ-
ment relations are best regulated, not by provisions of law, but on the basis of agreed procedures and 
systems that the managements and unions are able to arrive at, on the basis of what is commonly 
described as ‘collective bargaining’ or negotiations.” In fact, researches have indicated that countries 
where collective bargaining is highly prevalent tend to have lesser inequality in wages and lesser 
problems of unemployment. Such countries have fewer instances of strikes, which are shorter in com-
parison with countries that make lesser use of collective bargaining (ILO, n.d.). Republic of Korea 
was able to successfully face the Asian financial crisis and South Africa 
made a peaceful transition from the phase of apartheid into post-apartheid 
era due to well-established collective bargaining (Aidt and Tzannatos, 
2002). Thus collective bargaining is important not only for workers and 
management, but also for a nation.
Wages in the organised sector in India are decided mostly by collective bargaining, and much 
depends on the bargaining strength of the management and trade unions. Unions symbolise workers’ 
right to organise. Collective bargaining is a technique through which unions put forth their demands 
collectively and make their collective voice heard when decisions affecting their work-life are made, 
and thus promote industrial democracy.
Significance of the process of collective bargaining has been succinctly portrayed by the 
Supreme Court in Ram Prasad Vishwakarma vs. Industrial Tribunal (1961 SCR (3) 196) as: “It is 
well known how before the days of collective bargaining labour was at a great disadvantage in ob-
taining reasonable terms for contracts of service from his employer. As trade unions developed in the 
country and collective bargaining became the rule the employers found it necessary and convenient to 
deal with the representatives of workmen, instead of individual workmen, not only for the making or 
modification of contracts but in the matter of taking disciplinary action against one or more workmen 
and as regards all other disputes.”
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/1616269/ accessed on 15/1/2014.)Spotlight

Collective Bargaining 5.5
We will now explain the significance of collective bargaining for employers, workers, industry and 
the nation as a whole.
For Employers
rA means to resolve issues peacefully :Collective bargaining helps to resolve issues existing 
between workers and employers peacefully. This saves time that can otherwise be used gainfully 
in the production process and eliminates a lot of hassles.
rA chance to understand workers’ perspective :Sitting with workers’ representatives across the 
table and having a dialogue with them provides the management with an opportunity to get an 
insight into workers’ perspectives and problems. This also minimises the pitfalls of a unilateral 
decision.
rBelief in participative management : In the process of collective bargaining workers participate 
in finding solutions to problems and disputes. The very fact that management is negotiating with 
workers proves the belief of management in participative management and respect for workers 
and their rights.
rA means to increase productivity :Conflict resolution through 
law courts results in long drawn battles in which a lot of time and 
money are expended. If an agreement could be reached through a 
bipartite meeting between workers and management, the resources 
saved as a result can be utilised for increasing productivity. In fact, 
measures for increasing productivity often form the terms of agree-
ment between workers and management. The type of bargaining in which the workers’ demands 
are agreed upon in return for increase in efficiency on their part is called productivity bargaining .
rA mechanism to improve public image :If an organisation is able to resolve its conflicts with 
workers through dialogue, it creates a positive public image for itself at national and interna-
tional levels.
For Workers
rA legitimate platform : Collective bargaining provides a platform to workers to present their 
demands and concerns in a legitimate manner to employers.
rEqual status :The process of collective bargaining offers an equal status for workers vis-à-vis 
their employers. It ensures that labour is not merely a tool in the hands of employers for increas-
ing production. Collective bargaining empowers workers to object to the conditions existing in 
the organisation and demand improvement through negotiations.
rExercising rights :Collective bargaining allows workers to exercise their rights to organise 
themselves, choose their representatives and demand their legitimate benefits and rights assured 
to them through various legislations.
rSolidarity among workers :Collective bargaining can be successful only if there is unity amongst 
workers. Thus it requires workers to act as a united body that can pressurise the employer to 
concede to their demands.
rImproved facilities :Employers want to increase their profits through cost cutting, which may 
even amount to reduction in facilities for workers or denial of new benefits for them. Workers 
can demand for improvement of working conditions and oppose cutting down of their existing 
benefits and facilities through the mechanism of collective bargaining.Spotlight

5.6 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
rStrengthening the position of trade unions as bargaining agents : In Tamilnad Electricity Work-
ers’ Federation vs. Madras State Electricity Board (AIR 1965 Mad 111) the Madras High Court 
had observed that the whole theory of organised labour and its statutory recognition in industrial 
legislation is based upon the unequal bargaining power that prevails between the employer and 
an individual (or disunited) workman. Collective bargaining is the foundation of the trade union 
movement, and it is in the interest of labour that statutory recognition has been accorded to trade 
unions and their capacity to represent workmen who are members of these unions.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/1190603 accessed on 16/1/2014).
Thus whenever union leaders represent workers and negotiate with employers for their demands 
to be met or concessions to be granted, it reaffirms the position of a union in its role as a protec-
tor of the interests of workmen and their legitimate representatives.
rImproved quality of work-life : Since the process of collective bargaining aims at bringing about 
equality, improving overall work conditions, increasing facilities and bringing democracy in work 
sphere, its ultimate outcome is enhancing quality of work-life of workers.
For Industry
rMeans to industrial peace :As mentioned earlier, the process of collective bargaining helps in 
promoting peace and harmony by acting as a tool to resolve conflicts at a basic level between 
workers and employers, without the intervention of any third party. Employers and representa-
tives of workers negotiate to resolve their differences together by sitting across the bargaining 
table, rather than by indulging in exercising undue pressure tactics like gherao , pelting, etc.
rFacilitation of modernisation and restructuring : Liberalisation of the Indian economy has 
resulted in changes in organisations in terms of technology, professionalisation of systems and 
processes and restructuring. Trade unions today are adopting new roles that include involvement 
in educating and training workers. Multi-employer bargaining may facilitate modernisation and 
restructuring (OECD, 1994). Occupational training for workers in a particular industry may be 
regulated by a bargaining process involving multiple employers at industry level. Such training 
may be funded by collective financing, as in countries like Australia (Mitchell and Scherer, 1993) 
and France (Goetschy and Rozenhlatt, 1992). 
rContinuous production and profits: Industrial unrest is detrimental to the growth of any industry. 
Strikes, lock-outs, gheraos,  etc. result in huge losses in production and ultimately affect profits. 
Such undesirable situations may be eliminated through peaceful negotiations.
For Nation
rIncrease of productivity :Collective bargaining helps in avoidance of instances of strikes and 
lock-outs and resultant work stoppages. It assists in improving relations between employers 
and workers and helps in maintaining industrial peace and harmony. These conditions help in 
improving productivity at national level.
rStrengthening of the economy: Successful collective bargaining results in increased production, 
enhanced employment, better work conditions, improved wages and growth in industries. All 
these contribute to strengthening the economy of a country. Thus constructive agreements result 
in fairer economic development (ILO, 2004).

Collective Bargaining 5.7
Exhibit 5.2 Collective Bargaining between 
General Motors Corporation and the United Auto Workers
A historic collective bargaining agreement took place between one of the world’s leading auto-
mobile manufacturers, General Motors Corporation (GMC), USA and the United Auto Workers 
(UAW) in late 2007. GMC was under huge pressure due to its declining market share with the 
entry of Japanese auto companies in USA. In addition to other financial issues, the company 
was facing under-funded pension liabilities and rising employee and retiree healthcare costs. A 
nation-wide strike involving 74,000 UAW employees was called over job security concerns and 
retiree healthcare costs. The work stoppage affected 82 domestic General Motors assembly plants 
for 2 full days. An agreement was reached on a 4-year contract, and workers returned to work 
the same day. The Union ratified the contract with 65 per cent approval. Under the new contract, 
the company was required to establish a new healthcare trust to pay for retiree healthcare that 
would be funded by General Motors and managed by UAW. Employees were required to make 
quarterly fund contributions. GMC also agreed to stop outsourcing of positions for the duration 
of the contract. The agreement was seen by the management to be innovative, as it would provide 
a basis for improved competitiveness.
(Adapted from:  Schildkraut, J. L. (2008). Profiles of Significant Collective Bargaining Disputes in 2007,

Bargaining in different sectors may take place at different levels. In no country does it take place only 
at one level. Depending upon the coverage of the terms of agreement and involvement of unit-level, 
enterprise-level, regional-level or national-level trade unions, collective bargaining may take place at 
unit/plant level, enterprise-level, industry or national level.
Unit/Plant-level Negotiations that take place at unit/plant-level result in decentralised agreements. 
Sometimes such negotiations take place with trade union federations at company-level, involving 
representatives of unions of different plants of an establishment. As we have mentioned earlier, the 
agreement between TISCO and Tata Workers’ Union in 1956 was the first unit-level agreement in India.

5.8 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Exhibit 5.3 Levels of Collective Bargaining in other Countries
Levels at which collective bargaining takes place may differ across countries. The existence 
of strong employers’ organisations and powerful trade unions in many industrialised nations, 
particularly in Europe, has resulted in many important negotiations and agreements being con-
cluded at the national or industry-level, and some at enterprise-level. Collective bargaining at 
enterprise-level has been more common in USA, barring certain sectors like coal, steel, trucking 
and construction. In Japan enterprise-level bargaining has been more common, while national-
level bargaining appears to be an exception. This trend is due to the structure of unions which 
are enterprise-based. In many Asian countries enterprise-level bargaining has been more common 
as compared to national and industry-level bargaining. This is because of relatively low rate of 
unionisation, which does not support national-level agreements, and due to this reason employ-
ers’ organisations in such countries rarely get involved in collective bargaining. In Japan such 
collective negotiations taking place at unit-level and other participative methods at shop-floor 
level (such as joint consultation), have resulted in increased productivity by considering specific 
conditions existing in an enterprise.
(Adapted from: Silva, S. (1996). Collective bargaining negotiations, International Labour Organisation, 
ACT/EMP Publishers, p. 3. Retrieved from www.ilo.org/public/english/dialogue/actemp/downloads/publi-
cations/srscbarg.pdf on 2/1/2014.)Industry-level Industry or sector-level negotiations cover various companies in an industry. 
There may be involvement of one or more employers’ organisations and trade union federations 
in such bargaining. Industry-level bargaining includes a range of bargaining patterns and results in 
standardisation of the terms of employment and working conditions in 1 industry or sector. Depending 
upon the issues covered, bargaining may take place at sub-regional, regional or sometimes even at 
national-level. An advantage associated with such multi-employer bargaining is that the collective 
agreements at industry-level tend to standardise wages and working conditions and hence produce 
a ‘latent cartelisation’ among employers as they eliminate wages from competition (OECD, 1994).
Cotton, jute, textiles and transport are some industr ies in India in which such agreements commonly 
take place. Though the oil sector was nationalised way back in the 1970s, industry-level bargaining 
does not take place in this sector . Even if collective bargaining occurs at plant or enterprise-level,
the oil coordination committees are able to achieve a great deal of standardisation in pay and service 
conditions (Government of India, 2002).
National-level National-level negotiations usually take place in the industries or sectors which 
are controlled by the Government. Collective negotiations at this level generally involve more than 
1 national-level trade union federations and employers’ organisations. Examples of sectors in the Indian 
economy where national-level bargaining is common are iron and steel, postal department, banks, 
ports and docks, etc. Most of the mining industries such as coal, iron ore, copper, bauxite and zinc, 
the oil sector and the cement industry have evolved a system of national-level negotiations and 
settlements (Government of India, 2002).
Economy-level bargaining is an extension of national-level bargain-
ing. “Economy-wide bargaining may be a bipartite or tripartite form 
of negotiation or “concertation” between union confederations, central 
employer associations and government agencies” that provides a basis for Spotlight

In India there has been a trend towards decentralisation of collective bargaining in the key sectors,

PR OCESS OF COLLECTIVE BAR GAINING
The actual process of bargaining involves 3 steps: pre-bargaining preparations by management and 
unions, bargaining and contract administration. These steps have been described in this section.
I. Pre-bargaining Preparations by Management and Unions
Both management and unions have to make in-depth preparation for the actual negotiations. Let us 
elaborate on the preparation of each.
Preparations by management After a charter of demands has been presented to the 
management by workers, the former must begin the following preparations:
(i) The management must make a careful study of the charter and decide the objectives for collective 
bargaining and the gains expected from this process. The objectives may be to enhance produc-
tivity, to increase production level, to improve relations with workers, to gauge workers’ attitude 
towards management actions, and so on.
(ii) A team for negotiation comprising members with expertise in different areas must be finalised. It 
may include people like the human resource manager, an expert in industrial relations and labour 
legislations, a financial expert, production in-charge and others as necessary. The team leader 
must be given the authority to take decisions during the negotiation meeting within given limits, 
so that decisions may be taken instantly rather than waiting for approval from higher authorities, 
thus delaying the process.
(iii) Management must also try to identify if there is any ‘hidden agenda’ of workers that they may 
bring up at the negotiation table. This can be done by collecting information related to absentee-
ism, grievance issues, suggestions, turnover and disciplinary actions from different departments 
of the organisation. Other than this, management must collect figures on production, sales, loss 
by wastage, costs incurred, relevant expenditures, company performance in past years, etc. Hard 
facts in support of arguments are important in convincing the other party. For example, if sales 
are going down and workers are demanding increase in wages and salary, record of declining 
sales may help in convincing workers to review their demand.
(iv) Management must gather data on practices prevalent in industry on the issues present in the 
charter of demand and other factors that may impact the bargaining process. For example, if it is 
a demand related to increasing facilities for worker welfare, management must find out the facili-
ties provided by other organisations in the same industry. Proper ‘homework’ by management is 
essential for putting forth its arguments emphatically.
(v) Since it is a bargaining process whereby both the parties are expected to ‘give up’ something to 
‘take’ something, management must also try to gauge the extent to which workers are willing to 
accommodate and ‘give up’ on each of the demands. Though considered to be ‘not very ethical’, 
many companies resort to cooptation to get the inside story of the other party. Cooptation refers 
to the situation when management tries to influence one or more of the union member(s) by 
IR&LL_Ch_05.indd   9 1/1/2008   4:48:52 AM

5.10 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
offering them promotion or other benefits, in exchange for information about union strategies or 
for influencing workers, so as to get advantage during the negotiation process.
Preparations by workers Just like management, workers and their trade unions also need to 
make elaborate and in-depth preparations for their success in collective bargaining. Union leadership 
plays an important role in this process. While preparing the charter of 
demands, trade union leaders must ensure that it includes the interests 
of all categories of workers, including women workers, skilled workers, 
unskilled workers, etc. A term called intra-organisational bargaining  is 
used for a situation when there is a need for bargaining within a worker 
body due to differences between various worker-groups (or even within 
the existing groups in management).
The demands must be related to real issues, rather than those ‘created’ by union leaders in order 
to simply prove that they are the ‘real’ leaders of workers. If this is not ensured, a trade union cannot 
be considered a true representative of workers.
While preparing the charter of their demands, unions must carefully make an in-depth study of 
the practices existing in the industry. They must collect information from internal as well as external 
sources in order to justify their demands and pressurise the management for accepting such demands. 
Workers and their unions must also try to find out the level to which the management would be ready 
to bend and make concessions.
II. Bargaining
When management analyses union demands, these could come out to be of 3 types: those that can be 
accepted unconditionally, those that can be partly accepted, and those that must be rejected. For de-
mands that can be accepted unconditionally, the outcomes would be positive, while rest of the situations 
need to be handled deftly by management representatives at the bargaining table. Management may 
accept some demands partly and in return may put forth its demands on workers. Another possibility 
may be that it accepts some demands and buys time to consider others without direct refusal. Outright 
refusal may result in problems as workers may resort to pressure tactics like strike.
If negotiations are not successful, the next round of discussions would 
need to be planned. Deadlock must be avoided as it ultimately results in 
loss for both the parties.
Before we move on to the third and final step in the bargaining process, 
we will take a look at some of the processes related with collective bargaining.
Distributive bargaining Distributive bargaining involves bargaining over economic issues like 
wages, salaries and bonus. Here one party gains at the cost of the other party, so it results in a win-lose
situation and hence is a zero-sum game. Such a situation generates negative feelings in the losing side 
and may even breed mistrust and unhealthy labour-management relations. This type of bargaining is 
also known as conjunctive bargaining .
Integrative bargaining This type of bargaining involves a situation in which either both the parties 
have something to gain, or at least none of the parties loses anything. Thus it is a win-win  situation for 
both. For example, during economic slowdown management may demand increase in working hours 
in return for job security. This is the most ideal situation. This type of bargaining is sometimes known 
ascooperative  or interest-based bargaining .Spotlight
Intra-organisational bargaining 
is used to resolve conflicts 
between various groups  
within a worker body or within 
management.
Spotlight

sum game.

Collective Bargaining 5.11
Attitudinal structuring Attitudinal structuring means changing the attitudes and beliefs of 
workers and management regarding each other, so as to create an environment of mutual trust. This 
is required in the following situations:
rWhen it is a lose-lose situation, i.e., when none of the parties is ready to accommodate the 
interests of the other party. In such a situation, negotiations come to a dead end and resultantly 
both the sides have to lose.
rWhen there is a win-lose  situation that generates bitterness in the losing party.
Under both the situations the involved parties need to change their attitude in order to avoid gen-
eration of any hostility.
Good faith bargaining The principle of good faith bargaining is that both the parties meet each 
other with the intent to constructively communicate with each other over the issues of dispute and 
make honest attempts to arrive at a collective agreement. There is a readiness to make concessions, 
though it neither requires any party to shelve its own interests, nor does it compel any party to 
necessarily agree to a proposal, nor does it require any of the parties to make any undue concession. 
The principle of good faith is violated when:
rany of the sides indulges in surface bargaining , in which the meet-
ing is simply an eye-wash without any intention of reaching an 
agreement, or
rthe parties involved indulge in any unfair labour practice during 
negotiation and while administering the contract, or
rthe employer refuses to meet with union representatives, or
rthe employer refuses to provide any information to union, that can 
be used for holding discussions and negotiations.
III. Contract Administration
Once an agreement is signed between the trade union and management, the final phase in the process 
of collective bargaining is marked by contract administration. The parties must understand that they 
have come together to reach an agreement for improving the existing conditions. Thus, to achieve 
this objective they must administer the contract properly. The process of administering is included in 
the contract itself.
The management team and union representatives must make all the employees aware of the terms 
and conditions in the contract, so that everybody may understand what is expected of them. Collec-
tive bargaining agreements must contain formal procedures for resolving grievances that may arise 
over the interpretation and application of the terms of contract. Efforts must be made by workers and 
management to resolve these grievances at lower levels. Otherwise methods like conciliation, arbitra-
tion or ultimately adjudication may be resorted to. All these methods of settlement of disputes have 
been covered in Chapter 8.
PREREQUISITES OF SUCCESSFUL BAR GAINING
For collective bargaining to be successful, there are certain conditions that must exist to provide a strong 
base and to support the process. First, there must be support from the legal and political system of the 
country. Second, the attitude of the negotiating parties must be such that there is a willingness to reach 
an agreement and to accept and implement it. Also, for workers to get their demands accepted, their Spotlight
In good faith bargaining
employers and workers’  
representatives negotiate with 
each other with the honest intent 
to reach a mutually beneficial 
agreement.
