5.12 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
unions must be strong and powerful so as to exert pressure on the employer to listen to and accept 
their demands. These prerequisites for successful bargaining are reviewed as follows:
Legal and Political Framework
Workers must enjoy the right to organise and bargain. There must be a supportive legislation system 
to promote the use of bilateral negotiations as a means to resolve conflicts. The legal and political 
framework of the country must recognise the method of collective bargaining at par with other methods 
of settling disputes like conciliation, arbitration, etc. The Supreme Court of India has time and again 
encouraged the use of this process and has recognised the sanctity of bilateral agreements. 
Prakash (1991) has cited 2 examples in this context. In the case of State of Bihar vs. D.N. Ganguli 
(1959 SCR 1191), the Apex Court held that it would be wholly unreasonable for an Industrial Tribunal 
to which the matter may be referred for adjudication, to insist upon adjudication of a dispute on merits 
even after it has been informed that such dispute has been amicably settled between the parties. In 
such cases it should immediately make an award in terms of the settlement.
In the second case, namely that of Sirsilk Ltd. vs. Government of Andhra Pradesh (AIR 1964 SC 
160), though an award had already been sent for publication to the Government by the Industrial Tri-
bunal for its enforcement under the Act, the Court gave preference to a settlement arrived between the 
parties to the dispute. It was noted that there is no dispute left between the parties once they arrive at 
such a settlement, and therefore the Tribunal’s award itself should not be enforced by the Government 
by publishing it, as required under Section 17 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
The Trade Unions Act, 1926 provides workers the right to organise and form a union, though India 
has not yet ratified ILO Conventions No. 87 and No. 98. The former is regarding Freedom of Associa-
tion and Protection of the Right to Organise, and the latter is regarding Right to Organise and Collec-
tive Bargaining. Certain other measures like schemes for workers’ education, tripartite conferences, 
Code of Discipline, formation of joint management councils, works committees and shop councils, 
and the existence of grievances redressal machinery act as measures to promote collective bargaining. 
The Industrial Truce Resolution of 1962 has also influenced the growth of collective bargaining as 
it required management and workers to cooperate with each other in every possible way and resolve 
their disputes in a peaceful manner through mutual discussions, conciliation and voluntary arbitration 
(Singh and Bhatia, 2000).
Attitudinal Framework
Employers and trade union representatives must form a supportive attitude for negotiating with each 
other. Nature of the relationship between employer and workers affects the collective bargaining 
process. Management will indulge in bargaining at an equal level if it has respect for workers’ rights. 
Existence of mutual trust is thus an essential ingredient in the bargaining process. Style of manage-
ment is another factor affecting the willingness to use collective negotiations; negotiations have better 
chances to be successful if management believes in participative style. It is very essential that both the 
sides keep a flexible attitude and consider the concerns of the other side with an open mind. There is 
a need for proper coordination within and between different levels of employers’ organisations and 
union federations for successful implementation of agreements.
IR&LL_Ch_05.indd   12 1/1/2008   4:48:52 AM

Collective Bargaining 5.13
Existence of Strong Trade Unions
For collective bargaining to be successful there must be a strong trade union that can put up the de-
mands of workers emphatically and exert pressure on the employer to accept their demands. In fact, 
a strong union is a sine qua non  for collective bargaining.
HINDRANCES TO COLLECTIVE BAR GAINING
We have specified earlier that existence of a strong trade union is one of the prerequisites for successful 
collective bargaining. A proper legal framework is essential for the formation of strong unions and for 
their recognition. Pratap (2011) has observed that most of the famous workers’ struggles in 2009-2010 
were either on the issue of formation or of recognition of trade unions for collective bargaining. Workers 
of Hyundai Motors India Ltd. and MRF Tyres had struggled for recognition of their unions. Further, 
problems faced by trade unions directly affect their bargaining power. Such problems include falling 
union memberships, low finances, multiplicity, etc. Changing factors in the business environment due 
to economic liberalisation also have direct and indirect impact on trade unions. Let us quickly have a 
look at all such inhibitors to successful collective bargaining.
Multiplicity of Unions
The problem of multiplicity of unions weakens their bargaining power. There can be numerous small 
unions existing in an establishment, but none of them may actually be strong enough to pressurise 
the employer to accept workers’ demands. Moreover, multiplicity gives rise to rivalry between unions, 
which divides their power, and management stands at an advantage in such a situation. The already 
weak workers’ group loses its strength further. Multiplicity poses another challenge for collective bar-
gaining. Workmen in a unit or plant may be members of different unions. When a collective agreement 
is signed, it is assumed that all the interested parties are participating in it and that they have consent 
in the agreement. Every union, irrespective of whether or not it represents the majority, is supposed 
to be an interested party. Now, workmen may not choose to be the members of any union, and one or 
more unions may, for reasons of their own, may also not like to be a part of the settlement.
According to Section 2(p) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, settlement refers to a settlement 
arrived at in the course of conciliation proceeding that may be held by a conciliation officer or Board
of Conciliation under the Act. It also includes a written agreement between the employer and work-
men arrived at otherwise than in the course of conciliation proceeding where such agreement has been 
signed by the parties thereto in such manner as may be prescribed. A copy thereof must be sent to an 
officer authorised in this behalf by the appropriate Government and the conciliation officer. Section 
18(3) mentions that a settlement arrived at by agreement between the employer and workman otherwise 
than in the course of conciliation proceeding shall be binding on the parties to the agreement. Thus it 
may be implied that collective agreements are binding on all workmen, as conciliation officer’s pres-
ence is supposed to ensure that the agreement is bona fide .
The Amendment to the Trade Unions Act, 1926 in 2001, enforced with effect from 9th January 
2002 provides for reducing multiplicity of unions. It requires at least 10 per cent or 100 workmen, 
whichever is less, subject to a minimum of 7 workmen engaged or employed in an establishment, to 
be the members of a union before its registration.
IR&LL_Ch_05.indd   13 1/1/2008   4:48:52 AM

5.14 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Lack of Legislation on Recognition of Trade Unions 
The Trade Unions Act, 1926 provides only for the procedure for registration of unions. There are 
no provisions in either the Trade Unions Act, 1926 or the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 regarding 
recognition of trade unions as bargaining agents. Although the provision relating to recognition of 
trade unions was sought to be incorporated in the Act by introducing Chapter IIIA through the Trade 
Unions (Amendment) Act 1947, but it has not yet been put into operation. Only certain States like 
Maharashtra, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan have made provisions for recognition of unions 
in their laws. In the absence of any proper statute for recognition of a bargaining agent, employers 
may refuse to bargain with a particular trade union and select the one of its ‘choice’ for negotiations.
Unless the process of collective bargaining is given a strong support in the form of statutory provi-
sions, it will be difficult to popularise the use of this process in resolving disputes.
External Leadership
According to the Trade Unions Act, 1926 half of the total number of office bearers of any union can 
be outsiders. An outsider cannot understand the problem as a factory worker would, and so such a 
person may not be as effective while negotiating with employers. Even employers may not be very 
forthcoming in negotiating with a person who is hardly aware of the day-to-day happenings in the 
plant or workplace.
Most of the trade unions are affiliated to political parties and many a times leaders of these parties 
assume leadership positions in the unions. Employers may be averse to the idea of any person from a 
political party becoming a union leader as this would amount to political interference in the activities 
of the establishment. Thus involvement of outsiders may indirectly result in weakening of the roots 
of collective bargaining in industry.
Informalisation of Economy 
The process of globalisation and liberalisation has resulted in increased competition for business firms 
at domestic as well as international levels. Firms are finding the employment of casual labour or 
temporary workers more beneficial mainly for 2 reasons. First, it is difficult for these workers to form 
their registered unions. Second, most of the labour laws do not apply to casual labour, hence such 
workers fall outside the ambit of many statutory benefits that are required to be provided to permanent 
workers. The phenomenal increase in the number of casual labour has resulted in reduced membership 
of trade unions and has affected their strength.
Another issue that is worth mentioning here is that since workers in 
the unorganised (or informal) sector do not have a registered trade union, 
they cannot reap the benefits of collective bargaining. This is a grave 
situation, since majority of workers in India belong to the informal sec-
tor. The Report of the Second National Commission on Labour (2002, 
p. 602) notes that “collective bargaining has not been able to get any 
visible space in the unorganised sector…. this is a sector in which workers do not have protection or 
adequate bargaining power”. In the Third India-EU Seminar on Employment Relations and Resolution 
of Conflicts (2008), the key elements of an effective collective bargaining system for the informal 
sector have been identified, some of which are highlighted here:

RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE SECOND NATIONAL COMMISSION 
ON LABOUR
The Second National Commission on Labour (2002) has given certain recommendations on the issue 
of collective bargaining. Some of the important ones are mentioned here briefly.
rEvery worker must be ensured the right to organise and form trade unions and the right to col-
lective bargaining.
rTrade unions must be strengthened and collective bargaining must be encouraged in the country.
rA settlement entered into with a recognised negotiating agent must be binding on all workers. 
Provisions must be made in the law for determining negotiating agents, particularly on behalf 
of workers.
rIt is essential to recognise that collective bargaining or negotiations could be at different levels, 
namely at establishment-level, at corporate-level, at industry-level, at regional-level, at national-
level and so on.
rSince benefits of collective settlements are received by all workers in an establishment, whether 
or not they are members of any trade union, therefore it is desirable that a provision may be 
introduced in the law according to which, a worker who is not a member of any union will have 
to pay an amount equal to the subscription rate of the negotiating agent or the highest rate of 
subscription of a trade union not involved in the negotiation process.
rAn integrated labour judiciary system must be set up, with Labour Relations Commissions as a 
constituent body. These Commissions, amongst their other duties, should be responsible for the 
task of identifying collective bargaining or negotiating agents.
rWorkers’ education programmes must be so designed that they help workers understand their 
rights and their environment, so that their bargaining power may be improved.
rDemand for bonus in excess of prescribed annual bonus, either on the basis of profits earned 
in the accounting year or on the basis of production or productivity will be determined by col-
lective bargaining.
rCompetent bodies in the national system of labour administration should make their services 
available to employers’ and workers’ organisations, as may be appropriate under national laws or 
regulations or national practice, with a view to promoting the regulation of terms and conditions 
of employment by means of collective bargaining.
rThe vital role of trade unions in collective bargaining must be duly recognised in any institu-
tional arrangement.
rA comprehensive Industrial Relations Law is proposed, that will contain provisions for collec-
tive bargaining on issues relating to finances, wage structure, fringe and other benefits, bonus, 
housing, medical facilities, overall recruitment and personnel policies and norms and resolution 
of disputes pertaining to the areas of collective bargaining.

Contract administrationSummary
rThe term ‘collective bargaining’ was first used by the economic theorist Beatrice Webb in 1891 
in Britain. The process of collective bargaining strives at arriving at peaceful settlement of any 
dispute between labour and management.
rThe Trade Unions Act, 1926, the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and certain provisions of the 
Constitution of India give a boost to the process of collective bargaining in India.
rCollective bargaining is a voluntary and formal process of negotiation, and it also serves as 
a means of establishing industrial democracy. The process is important for management as it 
provides a means to resolve issues peacefully, a chance to understand workers’ perspective, to 
prove their belief in participative management, increase productivity and improve public image.
rCollective bargaining provides a legitimate platform to workers to present their demands to em-
ployers at an equal status and exercise their rights. It promotes solidarity amongst workers and 
renders them an opportunity to get improved facilities and better quality of work life. Moreover, 
it strengthens the position of trade unions as bargaining agents.
rThe actual process of bargaining involves 3 steps: pre-bargaining preparations by management 
and unions, bargaining and contract administration.
rBoth management and unions must carefully prepare their own demands and study the demand(s) 
of the other party through extensive research of practices existing in industry in order to decide 
their stance during negotiation.
rFrom the perspective of an employer, union demands can be of 3 types: those that can be accepted 
unconditionally, those that can be partly accepted and those that must be rejected.
rFor effective bargaining, attitudinal structuring may be required and bargaining must be done 
in good faith. Integrative bargaining results in a win-win  situation, while distributive bargaining 
results in a win-lose  situation.
rThe process of administering an agreement must be included in the contract itself. For proper 
contract administration the management team and trade union representatives must make aware 
all the employees about the terms and conditions in the contract, so that all may understand 
what is expected of them.
rPrerequisites for successful bargaining include existence of a supportive legal and political 
framework, supportive attitudinal framework of both employer and trade unions and existence 
of a strong trade union.
rDepending upon the coverage of the terms of agreement and involvement of unit-level, regional-
level or national-level trade unions, collective bargaining may take place at the enterprise, industry 
or national level. In India unit-level bargaining is the most common.
rFactors that pose as hindrance for success of collective bargaining include multiplicity of trade 
unions, lack of uniform legislation for recognition of unions, external leadership and increase 
in number of informal workers as compared to regular workers.

Collective Bargaining 5.19
C ASE
      TUDY
Labour Unrest at Manesar
Maruti Suzuki India Ltd. (MSIL), earlier known as Maruti Udyog Ltd. (MUL), came into existence in 
1981 as a public sector enterprise. It became a joint venture between MUL and Suzuki Motor Company, 
Japan in 1983. In 2002 the Government of India sold its share and the company was privatised, after 
which MUL changed its name to Maruti Suzuki India Ltd. The first plant was started in Gurgaon, 
Haryana in 1984 and the second was set up in Manesar in the year 2006. There were about 950 regular 
workers, 400 trainees, 700 contract workers and 400 apprentices at the Manesar plant. 
Poor working conditions and the structure of wage payment led the Manesar workers to demand 
a union with the name Maruti Suzuki Employees Union (MSEU) towards end-2010 or early-2011 
to negotiate with the management. MSEU had filed an application with the Labour Department of 
Haryana Government to get registered. The company wanted the workers to be part of the existing 
union, i.e., Maruti Udyog Kamgar Union (MUKU), supposedly formed by cooperation between la-
bour and management and active at the Gurgaon plant. When the company officials forced them to 
join MUKU, all the workers, including apprentices and contract workers (who were not members of 
either of the 2 unions), struck work by going for a sit-in strike on 4th June 2011. On 6th June 2011, 
the company dismissed 11 workers, including the 4 office bearers of the proposed union on grounds 
of indiscipline and striking work. The strike, supported by the All India Trade Union Congress, was 
joined by the workers of the neighbouring factories in sympathy. The strike ended after 13 days with 
joint negotiations. MSEU signed its first agreement with the management and the terminated work-
ers were reinstated. According to the agreement, both workers and management decided to cooperate 
with each other. 
After this strike the management changed the department of many workers; workers perceived 
this action as one of victimisation. Meanwhile, their application for a separate union registration was 
rejected by the Labour Commissioner. Through August 2011 workers adopted a go-slow policy. The 
impact was 50 per cent production cut in the plant. The management took a strict stance and on 29th
August 2011 the company locked the factory. Workers were denied entry into factory premises unless 
they signed a good conduct bond, to which they refused. The company terminated the services of 18 
trainees; 44 regular workers were either suspended or fired. During this period, the company hired 
contract workers, got its supervisors to work on the shop floor, allowed 170 workers who signed the 
bond to get in, and started production. 
Negotiations at this stage were made complex by the varied political influences on workers. Deep 
resentment amongst workers had set in and they favoured leaders with a more radical approach. An 
agreement was signed on 1st October 2011, under the terms of which, the workers agreed to sign the 
good conduct bond, and management committed not to work with malice against workers. But this 
agreement was allegedly breached by the management. As a part of the agreement, MSIL had agreed 
to take back all the workers. However the 44 regular workers who were dismissed earlier would 
now only be suspended and internal investigations would be conducted against them. Later the 
management refused to re-engage about 1,000 casual/contract workers who had also participated in 
the strike. When workers came back to work on 3rd October 2011, they demanded taking back of all 
contract workers and the 44 suspended workers.

5.20 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Another sit-in strike began on 7th October 2011 with the demand to reinstate the contract workers. 
Workers of 3 more Suzuki companies in the Gurgaon–Manesar belt joined the agitating workers in a

Manesar facility.

the violent incident at the Manesar plant was solely due to internal issues between the management

INTR ODUCTION
Any organisation aspiring to have a stable workforce needs to be aware of the actions it can take to 
deal with indiscipline of its employees, and equally, of the actions which employees can take to voice 
grievances they may have. Issues related to discipline and grievance redressal are time consuming and 
potentially costly and can damage employee relations and the image of the organisation as a good em-
ployer, if not handled properly. Nevertheless, many employers have to deal with these issues at some 
point of time or the other. The human resource approach tends towards a dislike of rules and procedures, 
in favour of a more individualised approach (Foot and Hook, 1999). However, organisations need to 
comply with legislations in managing their workforce, and hence discipline and grievance, though be-
ing individual issues in the area of industrial relations, must not be treated individually. This chapter 
deals with industrial discipline and grievance handling with the underlying philosophy that disciplin-
ary and grievance procedures promote good management practices and are invaluable tools to address 
performance issues in any organisation.
INDUSTRIAL DISCIPLINE
Employees are vital resource for any organisation and often a crucial differentiating factor from its 
competitors. Employees must not only work together as a team to achieve organisational success, but 
IR&LL_Ch_06.indd   1 1/23/2008   11:33:51 AM

6.2 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
also adhere to the rules and regulations of the organisation and conduct themselves in accordance with 
the standards of acceptable behaviour. Discipline refers to the process of systematically conducting of 
business by the organisational members who regulate their behaviour in accordance to the established 
rules and norms of the organisation.
No organisation can function properly and prosper without an effective disciplinary system; in fact, 
industrial discipline is essential for the smooth running of an organisation and also for the maintenance 
of industrial peace and harmony. Employee behaviour forms the basis of discipline in an organisation; 
discipline is a useful tool with the management for developing, improving and stabilising the behaviour 
of its workforce. Discipline with reference to employees implies complying with the predefined rules 
and regulations of the organisation, i.e., to conform to the code of conduct established by the organisa-
tion. Some commonly found disciplinary issues include absenteeism, tardiness, malingering, pilferage, 
damaging property, tampering with safety devices, misuse of equipment and other company resources, 
bribery, alcoholism, insubordination and negligence. Let us now understand the concept of discipline.
Concept and Meaning of Discipline
The term “discipline” can have various connotations. According to Calhoon (1963), discipline is the 
force that prompts individuals or groups to observe rules, regulations, standards and procedures deemed 
necessary for an organisation. Tead (1933) defines discipline as the orderly conduct of affairs by the 
members of an organisation who adhere to its necessary regulations because they desire to cooperate 
harmoniously in forwarding the end which the group has in view, and willingly recognise that to do this 
their wishes must be brought into a reasonable unison with the requirements 
of the group in action.
Summing up, discipline may be defined as an attitude which aims 
at inculcating restraint and orderly behaviour. In an organisational set- 
up, discipline connotes a state of order that must be adhered to by the 
members and a process of modulation of human behaviour for desired 
performance. It may also be looked upon as an employee’s self-control 
process, which prompts him/her to cooperate willingly with organisational rules and standards.
Nature of Discipline
Maintaining discipline at work ensures the successful attainment of 
organisational objectives. There are 2 broad aspects of discipline: positive 
discipline and negative discipline. Negative discipline  is somewhat traditional 
in approach, under which employees adhere to rules and regulations in fear 
of punishment. Such punitive action may be in form of penalties, fines, 
demotions or transfers. Thus fear of punishment dissuades employees from 
disregarding the norms and rules at work. Employees do not perceive organisational goals as their own 
goals and there is a lack of a feeling of oneness with the organisation.
Positive discipline , on the other hand, implies discipline without punitive actions. It involves cre-
ation of an atmosphere in the organisation whereby employees willingly conform to the established 
rules and regulations. A shift in approach from negative discipline, paving the way for the concept of 
positive discipline, can be attributed to changes at workplace like increase in the level of education 
and awareness of the working class and growth of trade unionism. The main aim of positive discipline 
is to inculcate self-discipline among employees, so that they adhere to the organisational rules and 
regulations not due to any fear of punishment but due to the inherent desire to ensure congruence Spotlight

modulation of human behaviour 
for desired performance.

Industrial Discipline and Grievance Handling 6.3
of individual objectives with group objectives and harmony in achieving organisational goals. Such 
discipline can be achieved through appropriate rewards and effective leadership.
Indiscipline
Employees may indulge in defiant behaviour when they violate organisational rules and norms, and such 
violation may prove to be detrimental to the functioning of the organisation. The term ‘indiscipline’ 
generally refers to such violation of or non-conformity to formal or informal rules and regulations 
in an organisation. Some of the causes for indiscipline are: unfair practices by management (like ir-
regularities in payment of wages, discrimination in wages, ineffective handling of grievances, etc.); 
policies and procedures of the organisation (like non-compliance with wage legislations and promo-
tional and transfer policies); absence of code of conduct; lack of effective leadership; communication 
barriers; and politicised trade unionism. Other reasons may include deliberate delay in disciplinary
proceedings, imposition of punitive measures like transfer to an inconvenient place at a short notice, 
aggressive attitude of trade unions, etc. Whatever be the cause(s), indis-
cipline brings with itself adverse effects on the morale of the workforce, 
thus affecting individual and organisational performance in a negative 
way. Hence organisations ensure preventive and curative measures on 
the earliest symptoms of indiscipline.
Misconduct
Before we move on to the ways of handling indiscipline, let us quickly touch upon a related concept, 
namely, misconduct. In a generic sense, misconduct refers to any unacceptable or improper behaviour 
by an individual. In an organisational context, misconduct is disobedience of some established and 
defined rules and breach of discipline on the part of an employee; it is violation of rules. Bhatia (2003) 
defines misconduct as a behaviour which is in breach of the accepted and expected norms of conduct; 
it presupposes wrongful intention and is not merely an error in judgment. 
Typical examples of misconduct by an employee would include habitual 
absenteeism and taking or giving bribes.
InShardaprasad Onkarprasad Tiwari vs. Divisional Superintendent, 
Central Railway Nagpur Division, Nagpur  and Satubhe K. Vaghele vs. 
Moosa Raza [(1969) 10 Guj LR 23], the High Court has noted the defi-
nition of misconduct in Stround’s Judicial Dictionary, as: “Misconduct 
means, misconduct arising from ill motive; acts of negligence, errors of 
judgment, or innocent mistake, do not constitute such misconduct.”
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/1454648 accessed on 25/12/2013.)
An act of misconduct by an employee is prejudicial to the interest of the employer and is likely to 
damage its reputation. What is notable here is that such acts can be performed even outside the prem-
ises of an establishment and beyond duty hours, subject to the provisions in the standing orders of the 
concerned establishment. The onus lies with the management to determine in its standing orders as to 
what all shall constitute acts of misconduct and to define the quantum of punishment for each of them.
It has been held in A. L. Kalara vs. The Project and Equipment Corporation of India Ltd.  (1984 
AIR 1361) that standing orders or rules require an employer to define with sufficient precision the 
terms of employment, particularly those pertaining to the definition of misconduct. Further, it would Spotlight

6.4 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Exhibit 6.1 Misconduct outside the Premises of an Establishment
In M/s Glaxo Laboratories Ltd. vs. Workmen (AIR 1984 SC 505) a worker had been chargesheeted 
for assaulting a coworker while the latter was coming to his office. The incident had occurred 
in a bus outside the premises of the establishment, but it had nexus to the disputes in the of-
fice. It had the effect of subversive of discipline and hence the management chargesheeted the 
worker for violating of a particular standing order which read as follows: “…assault or any act 
subversive of discipline….committed within the premises of the establishment”. The worker 
was ultimately dismissed from service, but the High Court ordered reinstatement on the ground 
that the act committed by him was not a misconduct because it was committed not within the 
premises of the establishment. The management thereafter filed a Special Leave Petition (SLP) 
in the Supreme Court.
The Supreme Court held that any act committed outside the premises of the establishment, even 
if it is subversive of discipline, does not amount to misconduct, unless it has been specifically 
incorporated as misconduct in the standing orders of the establishment. The Court disfavoured 
liberal interpretation of standing orders and held that wherever there are penal consequences, 
standing orders would be strictly construed.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/1513240/ accessed on 24/12/2013.)not be open to the employer to treat any act as misconduct, unless it was precisely so defined previ-
ously. No doubt, this is a salutary principle of law enunciated by the Supreme Court for guidance of 
all Courts and parties.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/1606318/ accessed on 25/12/2013.)
As per Schedule I of the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946, relating to Model
Standing Orders, the following acts and omissions on the part of workers shall be treated as misconduct:
(a) willful insubordination or disobedience, whether alone or in conjunction with others, to any law-
ful and reasonable order of a superior;
(b) theft, fraud or dishonesty in connection with the employers’ business or property;
(c) willful damage to or loss of employers’ goods or property;
(d) taking or giving bribes or any illegal gratification;
(e) habitual absence without leave or absence without leave for more than 10 days;
(f) habitual late attendance;
(g) habitual breach of any law applicable to the establishment;
(h) riotous or disorderly behaviour during working hours at the establishment or any act subversive 
of discipline;
(i) habitual negligence or neglect of work;
(j) frequent repetition of any act or omission for which a fine may be imposed to a maximum of 2 
per cent of the wages in a month;
(k) striking work or inciting others to strike work in contravention of the provisions of any law or rule 
having the force of law.
We would be talking more about the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 and its 
various provisions in Chapter 16.

Industrial Discipline and Grievance Handling 6.5
Handling Indiscipline
Discipline implies obedience, orderliness and maintenance of proper subordination on the part of 
employees. Employees who cannot be self-motivated to maintain such discipline may require some 
degree of extrinsic disciplinary action in the form of penalty or punishment. Stated in simple terms, 
employees who indulge in defiant behaviour are dealt with disciplinary proceedings, which refer to 
the steps taken by an employer to decide as to what and whether any penalty is warranted against an 
employee. Whenever an employee is sought to be awarded any penalty or dismissed, the employer, 
either himself or through a representative, holds disciplinary enquiry to 
ascertain as to whether the proposed penalty or dismissal is warranted. 
Article 311 of the Constitution of India puts limitation in the matter of 
award of major penalty or dismissal, by which no person who is a member 
of a civil service of the Union or on all-India service or a civil service 
of a State can be dismissed except after an enquiry that informs him of 
the charges against him and given a reasonable opportunity of being heard in respect of such charges. 
Therefore holding of disciplinary proceeding is a necessary pre-condition to impose any penalty.
In case of employees working in Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs), holding of disciplinary en-
quiry (also termed as departmental enquiry) is mentioned in the Conduct Discipline and Appeal (CDA) 
Rules and under the Certified Standing Orders. Even in case of employees of private sector establish-
ments, holding of departmental enquiry is laid down in the standing orders framed under the Industrial 
Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946. Such standing orders have the force of law and constitute 
statutory terms of employment in an establishment. In this connection let us touch upon the concept 
of vigilance here. The term “vigilance” means watchfulness and covers all kinds of deviations from 
standards of integrity as well as improper exercise of administrative discretion, nepotism, favouritism 
and conduct unbecoming of a public servant. Vigilance is an important tool with the management of 
any PSU to increase its productivity and profitability by plugging any seepage in its resources. It thus 
acts as a profit-generating centre for an enterprise.
Disciplinary actions, whether in PSUs or private sector, must conform to the following principles:
rPrinciple of natural justice: Natural justice in common sense means “that which is founded in 
equity, in honesty and right.” The main ingredients of natural justice are:
jNemo judex in causa sua : This means that no one should be made a judge in his own cause 
or the rule against bias.
jAudi alteram partem : This means “Hear the other side”. In other words, this pertains to the 
rule of fair hearing or the rule that no one should be condemned unheard.
The principle of natural justice is firmly grounded in Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution of 
India. Article 311 of the Constitution also follows this principle. The principle of natural justice 
must guide all enquiries and actions; this means that no person should be appointed to conduct 
an enquiry who himself is interested in the outcome, either as an aggrieved party or because 
he is hostile to the person proceeded against, or for any other reason. Overall, justice must not 
only be done, but should also seem to be done.
rPrinciple of impartiality or consistency : This principle implies that under identical situations 
where even the extenuating circumstances are alike, there should be no marked difference in the 
action taken.
rPrinciple of impersonality or consistency:  The disciplinary authority should not have a sense 
of elation or triumph or sadistic pleasure when a recalcitrant or delinquent employee is brought 
to book.Spotlight

proceeding is a necessary pre-
condition to impose any penalty.

6.6 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Steps in Disciplinary Procedure
The essential steps in a disciplinary procedure are as follows:
(i) Complaint and Preliminary Enquiry: The disciplinary procedure 
must be initiated by a complaint against indiscipline of the em-
ployee concerned (also regarded as the “charged officer” adverse to 
the interest of the company. Let us mention here that before starting 
the process of discipline it is essential to hold a preliminary enquiry 
to know if a prima facie  case of indiscipline and misconduct exists 
or not. Thus the preliminary enquiry report of the complaint must 
indicate ground(s) as to whether there is substance in the complaint, 
calling for disciplinary action. When an employee is alleged to have committed any of the of-
fences mentioned in the standing orders or service rules or under common law, the departmental 
manager must make a report, indicating action recommended. The management must thereafter 
depute a responsible officer of the company to enquire into the misconduct. On examining both 
sides of the case, the enquiry officer must ascertain if there is a prima facie  case for chargesheet, 
in which case, the accused must be chargesheeted. If the offence committed is only of minor 
magnitude, the employee may be excused or given warning orally or in writing.
(ii) Issue of Chargesheet: Once the prima facie  case of misconduct on the part of the concerned 
employee is established, the management should proceed to issue a chargesheet to him/her. A 
chargesheet can be issued by the Appointing Authority or authority higher than the Appointing 
Authority or Disciplinary Authority (DA) or by an authority senior in rank to the concerned 
employee, with the specific approval of the Appointing Authority or Disciplinary Authority. A 
chargesheet is merely a notice of the charge on the employee and provides the employee with 
an opportunity to explain his/her conduct; therefore chargesheet is generally known as a ‘show 
cause notice’. It needs to be drafted in a plain and simple language which can be understandable 
easily by the employee; charges also need to be specific, with a separate charge for each allega-
tion and without any vagueness.
(iii) Consideration of Explanation: In the next stage, on receipt of the written statement of defence 
of the charged officer against the chargesheet served, the explanation furnished should be 
considered by the Disciplinary Authority as to whether the reply of the charged employee is 
satisfactory or not. In case the reply is found to be satisfactory, there is no need to proceed with the 
disciplinary case and the chargesheet can be withdrawn on the basis of facts showing innocence 
of the employee. On the contrary, if the DA is not satisfied with the employee’s explanation, it 
can proceed with disciplinary enquiry. As another consequence, if the charged officer admits 
the charge, the employer can warn him/her or award punishment without further enquiry.
(iv) Suspension Pending Enquiry: In case the charge against the 
delinquent employee is grave and of serious nature, a suspension
order may be served on the employee along with the chargesheet. 
As per the provisions of the Industrial Employment (Standing 
Orders) Act, 1946, the suspended employee must to be paid a 
subsistence allowance equal to one-half of wages for the first 90 
days of suspension and three-fourths of wages for the remaining 
period of suspension if the delay in the completion of disciplinary proceedings is not due to 
the employee’s conduct. It must be noted here that what is grave as a charge would be the sole 
discretion of the management, and must be decided in accordance with the Code of Discipline.Spotlight
The preliminary enquiry report 
of a complaint must indicate 
ground(s) as to whether there 
is substance in the complaint, 
calling for disciplinary action.

IR&LL_Ch_06.indd   6 1/23/2008   11:33:51 AM

Industrial Discipline and Grievance Handling 6.7
(v) Holding of Enquiry: The Appointing Authority or an authority not subordinate to the charged 
officer and delegated with the powers as the Disciplinary Authority can appoint the Inquiring
Authority (IA) and Presenting Officer (PO) and a notice to this effect should be given to the 
concerned employee. The Inquiring Authority must preferably be of a rank higher than that of the 
charged employee or at least of equal rank. It should be of good knowledge and ability to assess 
the evidence to marshal the enquiry proceedings with due regards to the principle of natural 
justice. A copy of the chargesheet along with copy of article of charge, imputation of charge, list 
of documents and a list of witnesses must be given to the IA. The Presenting Officer must present 
the case before the IA through oral and documentary evidences. Further, the charged officer must 
be given sufficient notice to represent his/her case and make submission in own defence. Fair 
opportunity should be given to the employee to cross-examine the witnesses.
(vi) Order of Punishment: The Standing Orders or service rules of the organisation must provide 
that any employee who is adjudged to be guilty of misconduct is liable to be dismissed without 
notice, or discharged, or suspended from work with loss of pay for a specified period, or fined or 
warned, depending on the seriousness of the offence. Before making a final order in the case, the 
DA shall forward a copy of the IA’s report to the charged officer, to enable the latter to make a 
representation against the report, if he/she so desires. On receipt of the representation, if any, the 
DA shall record its findings against each article of charge as to whether in his opinion the charge 
stands proved or not. In case the Disciplinary Authority does not agree with findings of the IA on 
any article of charge, it shall also record the reasons for it while recording findings. The DA may 
remit the enquiry report to the IA in case a clear finding is not possible or there is any defect in 
the report of the IA against any article of charge. The DA, having regard to the aforesaid, shall 
record reasons that in its opinion which penalty(s) commensurate to the article of charge proved 
against the employee, would meet the ends of justice and accordingly issue the penalty order in a 
speaking manner. While deciding the nature of disciplinary action, the charged employee’s previ-
ous records, precedents, effects of the action on other employees, etc. have to be considered.
(vii) Appeal: Appeal may be preferred by the officer against the penalty awarded on him/her in case 
the punishment is not convincing and acceptable to him/her to the Labour Court or Industrial 
Tribunal. The criteria that a Labour Court or Industrial Tribunal would seek to establish when a 
case is being adjudicated by it is whether a proper domestic enquiry had been conducted or not, 
whether the principle of natural justice was observed or not, whether the enquiry proceedings 
were unbiased or not, and whether the affected party was heard in good faith or not.
   Remedies lie in the appropriate court of law for the charged employee if he/she is aggrieved 
with the decision of the Appellate Authority and when he/she has exhausted all the channels of 
appeal in his/her disciplinary case.
It has been held in Adinath s/o Narayanrao Jadhav vs. Chief General Manager (WP 2511.95.J. 
dated 14/1/2012) that in the case of departmental inquiries it is a settled law that even if one of the 
acts of misconduct is established and is of serious nature, courts cannot interfere in the quantum of 
punishment.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/192670095/ accessed on 25/12/2013.)

6.8 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Exhibit 6.2 Acceptance of Resignation Prior to Disciplinary Proceedings
A preliminary enquiry was being conducted against an employee working in a government 
company for some misconduct, who, on coming to know of the same submitted resignation en-
closing a draft of an amount equivalent to 3 months’ pay. The rules of the organisation provide 
its management a right not to accept resignation if any disciplinary proceedings are commenced 
against an employee. There is a further rule that any employee should give 3 months’ notice or 
3 months’ pay in lieu of such notice, if he submits resignation. After receiving the resignation let-
ter, the personnel department submitted this matter to the vigilance department, which advised the 
former not to accept the resignation, but to suspend him immediately in view of the investigation 
being conducted by the vigilance department on the complaints received against the employee. 
The personnel department accordingly suspended him and subsequently a chargesheet was issued 
to the delinquent employee.
The employee challenged the commencement of disciplinary proceedings. The High Court 
dismissed his writ petition, subsequent to which, he filed an SLP in the Supreme Court. The 
contention of the employee is that he had resigned from his job by paying an amount equivalent 
to 3 months’ pay in accordance to the rules. By that time no disciplinary proceedings were pend-
ing against him. The management cannot hence refuse the acceptance of resignation; therefore 
the actual acceptance is a mere formality. The management contended that as the employer is a 
government company and the vigilance department is expected to follow the Central Vigilance 
Manual, which directs non-acceptance of resignation if any case was being investigated by the 
vigilance department. It was also contended that the Government of India has issued executive 
instructions to follow the said manual and the management is bound by such executive instruc-
tions, even though these do not form a part of the rules framed by the company. The Supreme 
Court held that when once an employee submits his resignation by paying 3 months’ pay, there 
cannot be any departmental proceedings, even if the employee submitted resignation knowing 
fully well that showcause notice was being issued.
(Adapted from: V . P . Gindroniva vs. State of Madhya Pradesh (AIR 1970 SC 1494) www.indiankanoon.
org/doc/108995/ accessed on 23/12/2013.)
Forms of Punishment
In establishments covered by the Industrial Employment (Standing 
Orders) Act, 1946 the model standing orders or certified standing 
orders may specify the various forms of punishment for different acts 
of misconduct. As is obvious, misconduct of lesser gravity would fetch 
lesser form of punishment. Let us specify here that standing orders limit 
the management in awarding punishment from only those specified in the 
standing orders. Let us talk about the alternate forms of punishment here.
rWarning: Warning may be oral or written. An oral warning is a verbal interaction between the 
delinquent employee and his/her supervisor, wherein they discuss the problem behaviour and 
the expectations on the part of the management to change such defiant behaviour. Such a warn-
ing is issued as an informal reprimand; it may not have serious implications. When in writing, 
a warning forms a part of an employee’s service record and is reflective of the conduct and Spotlight

efficiency of the employee during his/her tenure with the organisation. Hence a written warning 
is more official and may even summarise the previous oral attempts, if any. It can be referred 
to by the management in case of a promotion due for the employee concerned. A warning, as 
is suggestive of the term, serves to be a reminder to an employee to be vigilant in future. A 
written warning can also be used in awarding severe punishment in future in case of habitual 
repetition of the same offence.
rPenalties: On the basis of the conclusions arrived at in the disciplinary proceedings, if any or all 
of the charges leveled against the charged officer are proved, then the management may impose 
appropriate penalty on him/her as per rules. The penalty levied should normally be imposed for 
good and sufficient reasons, commensurate with the gravity of the misconduct of the employee 
concerned. Management has the sole discretion to decide the appropriate penalty for a particular 
misconduct, subject to the obvious qualification that the penalty should not be unduly excessive. 
Minor penalties may include censure; withholding of promotion; withholding of increments of 
pay with or without cumulative effect; and recovery from pay or such other amount as may be 
due to him, of the whole or part of any pecuniary loss, caused to the company by negligence 
or breach of orders. Reduction to a lower grade or post or to a lower stage in a time scale and 
dismissal from service are examples of major penalties.
Exhibit 6.3 Quantum of Punishment
A police constable was chargesheeted on the ground of using abusive language against his superior 
officer. The disciplinary authority (DA) appointed an enquiry officer, who eventually submitted 
a “not guilty” report. DA disagreed with the same and issued a notice to the chargesheeted em-
ployee, stating such disagreement. No reasons thereof were given. Ultimately the said employee 
was dismissed from service. The High Court did not interfere, and the employee filed an SLP in 
the Supreme Court, contending that if DA disagrees with the “not guilty” report, it should give 
reasons thereof; opportunity should be given to represent against the tentative reasons. He further 
contended that the punishment was excessive.
The Supreme Court held that the disciplinary authority was required to give tentative reasons 
for the said disagreement. Also that no straight formula could be evolved in adjudging whether 
abusive language in the given circumstances would warrant dismissal from service. The Supreme 
Court finally set the dismissal order aside, but suggested reduction of 2 increments.
(Adapted from: Ram Kishan vs. Union of India and Others (1996 AIR 255) www.indiankanoon.org/
doc/1307831/ accessed on 23/12/2013.)
rSuspension: Suspension from duty means keeping an employee away from workplace temporarily 
for reasons of discipline, though it does not mean removal from service. The suspended employee 
shall not enter the work premises during the period of suspension without the permission of 
the Disciplinary Authority or any other competent authority; he/she shall not leave the station 
without the written permission of the competent authority. Such an employee is not granted any 
leave during the period of suspension. However, an employee suspended pending enquiry shall 
be paid subsistence allowance admissible to him/her, as per provisions of the Industrial Employ-
ment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946, already referred to in an earlier section.

6.10 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Suspension of an employee from duty often arises under the following situations:
jSuspension Pending Domestic Enquiry: We have already explained this under steps in 
disciplinary proceedings. Such suspension is till investigations are pending, though at this 
stage it cannot be called a punishment. Under normal circumstances the order of suspen-
sion is issued along with chargesheet, but if it is not possible, the charge-sheet must follow 
within 7 days of issue of suspension order. The Disciplinary Authority also has the right to 
keep a charged employee under suspension if he/she is accused in a court of law for any 
criminal offence, until the disposal of the trial.
jPunitive Suspension: The Disciplinary Authority may decide to punish a charged officer 
by way of suspension for the acts of misconduct committed by him/her after the conclusion 
of domestic enquiry. In case of punitive suspension, the suspended employee is prohibited 
from performing duties and wages of such employee are withheld for the period of suspen-
sion, since it is a punishment imposed on him/her.
rDismissal and Discharge: Both the terms ‘discharge’ and ‘dismissal’ refer to termination of 
service of an employee and are used only when other measures have failed to change unaccept-
able behaviour. The literal meaning of the term dismissal is ‘to let go’ or ‘to relieve from duty’; 
it is a punishment for some misconduct, though discharge is not always a punishment. Agarwal 
(1978) defines discharge to be termination of service by giving 
agreed notice or payment and acceptance of money in lieu of such 
notice. Removal from service in the form of discharge does not 
disqualify an employee from re-employment in the organisation, 
whereas dismissal from service does disqualify him/her from such 
re-employment. In fact, the stigma that is attached to the expression ‘dismissal’ may make it 
practically impossible for the person concerned to obtain another employment, unlike the case 
of discharge. Thus dismissal is considered to be the severest of all the penalties. Removal or 
dismissal is due to gross misconduct on the part of an employee. In case of dismissal, the em-
ployer can withhold the contribution of the employee to provident fund, bonus and gratuity 
payable and other dues, in order to make good of the loss caused to the organisation by his/her 
misconduct. In other words, a dismissed employee loses all termination benefits. Discharge 
simplicitor  refers to termination of services of an employee for loss of confidence and trust. 
Since it is a termination, it does not carry any st igma of misconduct, but chances of victimisation 
of the employee cannot totally be eliminated here.
As Chhabra and Suri (2007) have pointed out, disciplinary proceedings are essential to dis-
miss an employee, though the employer may or may not do so for discharging an employee. An 
employee can be discharged by giving a reasonable notice, as provided in the standing orders 
or contract of service, without being served with a charge sheet, receiving explanation thereof 
and holding an enquiry, as is usually done for dismissing an employee. No order of removal or 
dismissal from service shall be made by an authority lower than the appointing authority of the 
employee concerned, notwithstanding the fact that such appointing authority might have subse-
quently delegated the power of appointment of employees of the category or rank to which the 
employee belongs to such lower authority.

through tripartite consultation. Applicable to both public and private sector enterprises, the Code of 
Discipline is a set of self-imposed and mutually agreed upon voluntary principles of discipline and 
relations between the management and workers in the industry. It is a code of conduct both for work-
ers and management, and it provides for the voluntary and mutual settlement of disputes through 
mutual negotiation, voluntary arbitration and conciliation without the 
interference of an outside agency. While it dissuades both parties from 
unilateral action, the Code induces them to make the best use of the 
existing machinery for the settlement of disputes. Thus the Code of Dis-
cipline compels both the parties in dispute not to indulge in any strike or 
lock-out without exploring the avenues for the voluntary and mutual 
settlement of any possible misunderstanding or dispute. In this manner, 
it lays emphasis on an atmosphere of mutual regard and respect, in order 
to maintain harmonious relations and promote industrial peace.
The basic objectives of the Code of Discipline are to:
remphasise upon the employers and employees to recognise each other’s rights and obligations;
rpromote constructive criticism between the parties concerned at all levels;
rmaintain discipline in the industry;
ravoid work stoppages and litigation;
reliminate all forms of coercion, intimidation and violence in industrial relations;
rfacilitate the free growth of trade unions; and
rsecure settlement of disputes and grievances by mutual negotiation, conciliation and voluntary 
arbitration
To maintain discipline in industry there has to be a just recognition by employers and workers of the 
rights and responsibilities of either party, as defined by the laws and agreements (inducting bipartite 
and tripartite agreements arrived at all levels from time to time) and a proper and willing discharge 
by either party of its obligations consequent on such recognition. Towards this end, management and 
unions agree on not indulging into various actions, summarised as follows (Dhingra and Verma, 1995):
Management and Union(s) Agree that
rno unilateral action should be taken in connection with any industrial matter and such matter 
should be settled at appropriate level;
rthe existing machinery for settlement of disputes should be utilised with the utmost 
efficiency;

GRIEVANCE HANDLING
Employees have their own sets of aspirations and expectations from their employers. Whenever there 
is any incongruence between such expectations and what an employee actually gets from the organisa-
tion, he/she experiences a feeling of dissatisfaction or discontentment. A grievance is formed due to 
difference between employees’ expectations and management policies or practices. Grievance is not a 
rare feeling when it comes to someone’s job. Perhaps it is inherent in human nature to be dissatisfied 
about something or the other. The most commonly found reason of grievance is pay; if it is not pay 
structure, then some other aspect of work, say work environment, relation with superior or peer group, 
etc., with which an employee may have dissatisfaction and hence have grievance.
In the area of employment relations, employee dissatisfaction is commonly divided into 2 broad 
categories: organised  and unorganised dissatisfaction (Green, 1987; Rose, 2004). Organised dissatis-
faction leads to collective form of conflicts like strikes, go-slows and work-to-rule as attempts made 
by workers to change whatever condition is deemed to be unsatisfactory (Salamon, 2000; Rose, 2004). 
On the other hand, unorganised form of conflicts refers to individual-based forms of behaviour which 
are less-strategically oriented to the achievement of change (Mills, 1994; Fossum, 2000; Rose 2004). 
IR&LL_Ch_06.indd   12 1/23/2008   11:33:52 AM

Industrial Discipline and Grievance Handling 6.13
Definition of Grievance
The International Labour Organisation (ILO) defines grievance in an exhaustive way to include any 
complaint either by a worker, or a group of workers, or a trade union, or by an employer, or a group 
of employers, or an employer’s organisation, regarding some specific aspect of the employment rela-
tionship, or in case of workers, regarding employment conditions, or employer’s policy and practices. 
Britton (1982) proposes that a grievance is any dispute that arises between an employer and em-
ployee, which relates to the implied or explicit terms of an employment agreement. The First Na-
tional Commission on Labour (1969) in India has visualised grievances as being those “arising out of 
complaints affecting one or more individual workers in respect of their 
conditions of work and not disputes over matters of general applicability 
to all” (Paragraph 24.23). D’Cruz (1999) defines grievance as a matter 
raised by an employee to express dissatisfaction with management be-
haviour, and as an attempt to bring out changes. Grievance is any dis-
satisfaction regarding work and workplace filed by employee formally to 
his immediate supervisor (Rose, 2004). On the other hand, Michael Jucius 
defines grievance as any discontent or dissatisfaction, whether expressed 
or not, whether valid or not, and arising out of anything connected with 
the company that an employee thinks, believes, or even feels as unfair, 
unjust, or inequitable. What is noteworthy is that, according to Jucius, 
grievance may or may not be expressed, though Rose (2004) proposes that grievance is a written al-
legation.
Fairness at work is one of the pivotal aims of employment relations. Fairness, however, is a relative 
term, and is expected by every employee from his/her employer. When an employee feels something 
is unfair in the organisation, he/she is said to have a grievance. Whatever be the cause of such griev-
ance, it is surprising that any such feeling of dissatisfaction or grievance may be real or imaginary. 
In fact, it may so happen that an employee may not be able to ascertain on his/her own as to what 
is/are the reason(s) behind such dissatisfaction. And this may be due to 
ignorance, lack of knowledge of duties and rights, or even mental blocks. 
Thus grievance may be any real or imaginary feeling of injustice that an 
employee may perceive concerning his/her employment relations. This 
may become a tricky situation for any organisation, as it may not always 
be feasible for the management to understand the real reason behind dissatisfaction and grievance.
A grievance may take various forms; it may be overtly expressed, verbally or in writing, or it 
may be covert or kept within. The latter may have serious implications in itself because unexpressed 
grievance may result in frustration and detachment, ultimately affecting employee performance. In 
such cases the onus is on the management to perceive that employees have some grievance, and then 
ascertain the reason(s) behind such grievance. Mere discontent or dissatisfaction is not grievance; it 
may initially find expression in the form of a complaint. But if such a complaint remains unattended 
by the management, an employee would eventually feel a lack of justice or fairness on the part of 
management. This would increase his/her dissatisfaction, and eventually such dissatisfaction would 
assume the status of a grievance. According to Ratnam (2006), a complaint becomes a grievance under 
the following 3 conditions:
(i) When an employee feels that some injustice has been done to him/her.
(ii) When the complaint is formally expressed, either in verbal or written form.
(iii) When it is related to the policies, procedures and practices of the organisation.Spotlight
Grievance may be overtly 
expressed, verbally or in writing, 
or may be kept within.Spotlight

6.14 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
There are several ways in which employees may express their dissatisfaction; such expressions 
may even go to the extent of aggression and hostility. Other manifestations may include absenteeism, 
indiscipline, etc. If there is a manifestation of dissatisfaction, then it would be relatively easier for the 
management to address such issues; the situation may become difficult if the management is not able 
to perceive the real reason behind grievance. Why is it important for management to identify the fac-
tors that fuel employee grievance? Any unheard grievance would lead to symptoms like absenteeism, 
low morale and less enthusiasm towards work, and all of these would lead to serious problems like 
low productivity and poor work quality. As such it becomes imperative on the part of management 
to identify such symptoms and take corrective actions, such that whatever behaviour is manifested is 
not repeated again. Perhaps, the adage “a stitch in time saves nine” says it all: if the management is 
able to identify the symptoms and ameliorate any grievance at individual-level, this would prevent the 
issue getting extended any further and affecting a larger group of workers.
Nature and Causes of Grievance
A grievance may be expressed by a single worker, or by several workers, or even by a union of 
workers, if the subject matter of grievance is of such nature that it may affect several workers of the 
organisation, in which case it no longer remains restricted to a grievance .Ratnam (2006) proposes 
that when individual grievances are not redressed and other workers are also affected by the same 
situation, then it becomes a collective grievance, which normally comes under the purview of collec-
tive bargaining. As laid down in the Model Grievance Procedure by the First National Commission 
on Labour, “complaints affecting one or more individual workers in respect of their wage payments, 
overtime, leave, transfer, promotion, seniority, work assignment, and discharge would constitute griev-
ance where points of dispute are of general applicability or of considerable magnitude, they will fall 
outside the scope of this procedure”.
Although their nature is found to vary across organisations, in general grievances fall under the 
following categories in most Indian organisations (Ratnam, 2006): promotions (matters related to su-
persession, promotion, seniority and fixation of pay); compensation (issues on increments, payment 
and recovery of dues); amenities (like inequitable distribution, entitlement and medical benefits); ser-
vice matters (like transfers, continuity of service and superannuation); disciplinary action (including 
punishment, fines and victimisation); nature of job (like allocation of job); condition of work (like 
safety and hazards); and leave.
Handling of Grievances
By now it must be clear that any grievance in an organisation, whether explicitly expressed or not, 
must be addressed by the management with immediate effect. In fact, management is required to take 
appropriate steps to eliminate the cause(s) of such grievance, so as to ensure employees are committed 
to their work and to the organisation. Now there is a difference between 
how small and large organisations deal with issues of dissatisfaction lead-
ing to grievance. In small organisations handling of grievances is often 
devoid of any formal mechanism. In such an informal system grievance 
may be dealt with by the intervention of managers, who discuss such 
issues with their subordinates and sort these problems out. Large organisa-
tions, on the contrary, have a formal mechanism for grievance redressal. 
Grievances may be handled by a single official or may even include an 
entire department that would deal exclusively with employee grievances. A Spotlight
A formal grievance handling 
system provides an avenue 
to employees to vent their 
grievances; it assigns certain 
individuals to hear and refer or 
resolve employee grievances, 
usually at fixed times.

Industrial Discipline and Grievance Handling 6.15
formal system provides an avenue to employees to vent their grievances; it assigns certain individuals 
to hear and refer or resolve employee grievances, usually at fixed times. Such a procedure indirectly 
helps to improve relations between the parties to the collective agreement (Thomson, 1974), renders 
justice (Balfour, 1984) and improves perceptions of fairness and equity (Lewin and Peterson, 1988). 
The grievance procedure also serves as the mechanism by which management and union representa-
tives can ‘bargain’ over the applicability of the terms in question (Thomson and Murray, 1976; Lewin, 
1983). Both union officials and managers invest their time and energy in grievance procedures to ensure 
that employees’ complaints are dealt with in an effective manner (Bemmels and Lau, 2001). Such 
a formal system tends to be procedural and ritualised. In fact, employees may become disillusioned 
with the effectiveness of the mechanism if the system takes long time to find a workable solution to 
the grievance expressed. We would be talking more about a formal system of grievance handling in 
a subsequent section.
According to the First National Commission on Labour (1969), a grievance procedure should be 
simple and have the provision for at least 1 appeal. The Commission recommends a formal grievance 
procedure to be introduced in units employing 100 or more workers. Paragraphs 24.29 and 24.30 of the 
recommendations suggest that a grievance procedure should normally provide 3 steps: submission of a 
grievance by the aggrieved worker to the immediate superior, appeal to the departmental head/manager, 
and appeal to a bipartite grievance committee representing the management and the recognised union. 
In rare cases where unanimity eludes the committee in the third step, the matter may be referred to 
an arbitrator. The Commission prescribes 3 conditions necessary for any formal or informal system 
of grievance handling, namely: satisfaction of the individual worker, reasonable exercise of authority 
by the manager and participation by unions (Paragraph 24.29).
Discovering Grievances
Understanding grievances is always a difficult task for managers when there is no explicit manifesta-
tion. Managers need to be sensitive in understanding what may be bothering employees. In the absence 
of a formal mechanism, a useful source of information on grievances and the causes therein would 
be the grapevine. In fact, in organisations in which there is no formal grievance handling mechanism, 
employees may approach the trade union for removal of their grievances. As such, union may be an-
other source of information on issues of grievance. Let us focus on some of the most common ways 
of discovering grievances.
rDirect Observation:  In this method a manager generally observes any change in the behaviour 
of subordinates affecting their performance. Examples of changes in behaviour may include 
absenteeism, indiscipline, lack of enthusiasm at work, etc. Needless to say, this method would 
necessitate a manager to be sensitive to the difficulties subordinates may face at work and em-
pathise with them. A manager must also be efficient enough to observe changes in behaviours 
and other traits that may actually hint at a hidden issue of dissatisfaction.
rGripe Box:  The gripe box serves as an innovative way to discover 
grievances; it is a facility to employees to file complaints about 
anything that is causing dissatisfaction, maintaining their anonym-
ity. These boxes are kept at prominent locations in the organisation 
or factory premises for the convenience of employees to express 
their feelings or opinion about any aspect of the organisation. In 
many organisations employees are apprehensive of expressing their 
grievances in fear of facing the wrath of the management. Under such circumstances the gripe Spotlight
The gripe box is a facility to 
employees to file complaints 
about anything that is causing 
dissatisfaction, maintaining their 
anonymity.

6.16 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
box method is particularly useful, as it encourages an employee to provide information without 
the fear of being reprimanded or victimised.
rOpen Door Policy:  In this technique employees are encouraged to enter a manager’s chamber 
and express their grievance. This is a democratic way of securing information about grievances 
at work.
rExit Interview:  When an employee leaves an organisation for greener pastures, it often intrigues 
the management as to what instigated the employee to leave the present job. An exit interview 
is a useful source of information on such reasons. These interviews are nothing but interactions 
between the departing employee and management. The outcome of such interviews can provide 
valuable insights into what are the problem areas which compel an employee to leave, and in 
what all areas the organisation needs improvement. Exit interviews can thus go a very long way 
in improving work conditions if the management addresses the problem areas, thereby ensuring 
employee retention.
rOpinion Surveys:  Management can also conduct surveys at intervals to gauge the areas in which 
employees may be having grievances. This can be a proactive method to take corrective actions 
before dissatisfaction takes the shape of grievance.
Exhibit 6.4 ILO Standards on Grievance Handling
Recommendation No. 130 (1967) on the Examination of Grievances deals with a special category 
of labour disputes: grievances of one or several workers against specific aspects of their employ-
ment conditions or labour relations. The grounds for a grievance may be any measure or situation 
that concerns employer-worker relationship or that is likely to affect the conditions of employment 
of one or more workers in the enterprise, if the situation appears to be contrary to the provisions 
of collective agreement, individual employment contract, national laws or other rules. In case 
grievance procedures are established through collective agreements, the parties involved should 
be encouraged to promote the settlement of grievances using those procedures, abstaining from 
any action which would impede the effective functioning of such procedures.
Recommendation No. 130 explicitly calls for workers’ organisations and workers’ representa-
tives to be associated on an equal basis with employers and their organisations in the establish-
ment and implementation of grievance procedures. The Recommendation also highlights the 
various elements that form the basis of grievance procedure in any enterprise. An attempt should 
be made initially to settle the grievance directly between the workers or group of workers and 
the immediate supervisor. In the event of failure to settle the grievance at the initial level, the 
worker should have the right to have the case considered at a higher level, depending on the 
nature of the grievance as well as structure of the enterprise. Grievance procedures should be so 
formulated and applied that there is a possibility for settlement of dispute at every level. They 
should also be expeditious and simple. Workers concerned in any grievance should have the right 
to take part directly in the grievance procedure. During the procedure, workers may be assisted or 
represented by a trade union representative or any other person of his/her choice, in conformity 
with national law and practice.

Industrial Discipline and Grievance Handling 6.17
rGrievance Procedure:  A formal and systematic grievance procedure is perhaps the best way 
to understand what all aspects of the organisation are causing dissatisfaction to employees. It 
gives employees an avenue to vent their grievances. Presence of a robust grievance mechanism 
instills confidence in employees about their grievances being heard and corrective actions to be 
taken. In absence of such a procedure, employees may not be able to express their grievances, 
and this may eventually lead to union intervention, which may disrupt the harmony between 
employer and employees.
It may be noted here that there is no perfect method among those specified above. An 
organisation may actually use more than one of these ways to discover causes of grievances among 
employees.
Legal Framework of Grievance Handling in India
If we look back in time at the historical evolution of grievance handling in Indian organisations, we 
would find the first official reference to grievance in legislation given in the Model Standing Orders 
of the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946. As per Clause 29 of the First Schedule of 
the Act, all complaints arising out of employment, including those related to unfair treatment or wrong-
ful exaction on the part of an employer or his agent, shall be submitted to the manager or any other 
person specified in this behalf, with the right to appeal to the employer. Standing orders regulate the 
conditions of employment, discharge, grievances, misconduct, disciplinary actions, etc. of workmen, 
and faulty or inadequate application and administration of the standing orders by an employer may 
lead to grievances and misconduct, which may have adverse effect on industrial relations.
Section 49 of the Factories Act, 1948 provides for the appointment of such number of welfare 
officers as may be prescribed by State Governments in every factory employing 500 or more 
workers. One of the duties of such welfare officers is to bring to the notice of the factory management 
the grievances of workers, individuals as well as collective, with a view to securing their expeditious 
redressal and to act as a liaison officer between the management and workers. The Industrial Disputes 
Act, 1947 has included Section 9C in Chapter IIB, that prescribes setting up of a Grievance Settlement 
Authority for the settlement of industrial disputes connected with an individual workman employed in 
every industrial establishment in which 50 or more workmen are employed or have been employed on 
any day in the preceding 12 months. The Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Bill, 2010 passed by the 
Rajya Sabha on 3rd August 2010 seeks to establish 1 or more Grievance Redressal Committee within 
an industrial establishment having with 20 or more workmen, with 1 stage 
appeal at the head of the establishment for resolution of disputes arising 
out of individual grievances. With this amendment, a workman will get 
one more alternative grievance redressal mechanism for the resolution of 
his/her disputes within the organisation itself, with minimum necessity 
for adjudication. Setting up of a Grievance Redressal Committee would 
in no way affect the right of a workman to raise a dispute on the same 
issue under the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
Model Grievance Procedure
The 15th Session of the Indian Labour Conference held in 1957 had emphasised on the need for an 
established grievance procedure for the country as a whol e, that would be acceptable to unions as well 
as to management. In response to this, the Model Grievance Procedure was drawn up in the 16th
Session of the Indian Labour Conference in 1958 in pursuance of the Code of Discipline. We have Spotlight
