6.18 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
already explained the Code of Discipline under industrial discipline in this chapter. The procedure 
drawn up has successive time-bound steps with access to the next stage if satisfaction is not obtained 
in the previous stage. Let us describe the Model Grievance Procedure here in detail.
The process of grievance redressal, as per the “Model”, starts with a grievant worker who can 
make a verbal complaint to the supervisor or any other manager designated for the purpose. The 
supervisor must give a reply to the grievant within 48 hours of lodging of the grievance. If the reply 
or solution offered is satisfactory, the process of redressal ends there. However, if the employee is 
not satisfied, he/she can move the grievance to the departmental head or any other designated officer 
within 72 hours (or 3 days) after the receipt of the reply. If the employee is satisfied, the matter would 
end there; otherwise the grievance is referred again within 72 hours to the Grievance Committee, 
which must be a joint committee of at least 2 or 3 workers and 2 or 3 managers. The Committee 
would get a time limit of 7 days to consider the matter and suggest a suitable solution. If the decision 
given is unanimous, then it has to be implemented with immediate effect. If the grievant continues 
to remain dissatisfied, he/she can proceed further within another 72 hours to appeal to the Chief 
Executive of the enterprise or the head of the establishment, who gets 3 days to consider the problem. 
If the suggestion given by such authority satisfies the employee concerned, the problem is solved. If 
not, the grievant has 3 options: he/she may file a revision petition to the 
management for a complete review of the entire matter, or proceed for 
conciliation by moving the government labour procedure for redressal, 
or ask for voluntary arbitration. Whichever of these options is chosen by 
the grievant marks the final step in the process, since it is not possible to 
carry the redressal any further. Figure 6.1 gives a succinct explanation 
of the entire process.

Industrial Discipline and Grievance Handling 6.19
Recommendations of the Second National Commission on Labour
The Second National Commission on Labour (2002) recognises right to redressal of grievance as 
among those rights that are inalienable and hence must accrue to every worker under any system of 
labour laws and labour policy. Every establishment to which the general law of employment relations 
applies, i.e., those with 20 or more workers, shall establish a Grievance Redressal Committee consist-
ing of equal number of representatives of workers and employers. Such committee shall not be larger 
than 10 members or smaller than 2 members, depending on the employment size of the establishment, 
as may be prescribed. 1 member of the committee may be designated as the Chairman and another as 
the Vice Chairman. A system may be established to ensure that 1 of them is from the management, 
and the other from among employees’ representatives. The Grievance Redressal Committee shall be 
the body to which all grievances of a worker in respect of his employment, including his non-employ-
ment, will be referred for decision within a given time frame. Where the worker is not satisfied with 
the decision of the committee, he shall be free to seek arbitration of the dispute by an arbitrator, to be 
selected from a panel of arbitrators to be maintained in the manner prescribed, or seek adjudication 
of the dispute by the Labour Court. The decision of the Labour Court or the arbitrator shall be final.
As regards resolution of disputes between employers and workers, the Commission has recom-
mended that all matters pertaining to individual workers, be it termination of employment or transfer 
or any other mater, be determined by recourse to the Grievance Redressal Committee, conciliation 
and arbitration or adjudication by the Labour Court. These disputes need not be elevated to the rank 
of ‘industrial disputes’ which would then take the form of collective 
disputes. Individual disputes may be taken up by the affected workers 
themselves or by any registered trade union of which the worker is a 
member, provided the union has at least 10 per cent membership amongst 
the workers in that establishment, by referring the dispute to the Griev-
ance Redressal Committee for a decision. Where the Committee is not 
able to settle the dispute within 30 days, or if no such committee is in 
existence, the dispute may be referred for arbitration to a mutually agreed 
Arbitrator or Conciliation Officer or to a Lok Adalat or Labour Court in 
the prescribed manner.
Summary
rIndustrial discipline is essential for the smooth running of an organisation and also for the 
maintenance of industrial peace and harmony.
rDiscipline on account of employees implies complying with the predefined rules and regula-
tions of the organisation, i.e., to conform to the code of conduct established by the organisation. 
Maintaining discipline at work ensures the successful attainment of organisational objectives.
rThere are 2 broad aspects of discipline: positive discipline and negative discipline. Negative 
discipline is traditional in approach, under which employees adhere to rules and regulations in 
fear of punishment. Positive discipline implies discipline without punitive action.
rIn organisational context misconduct is disobedience of some established and defined rules and 
breach of discipline on the part of an employee. Disciplinary actions against misconduct must 
conform to principle of natural justice, principle of impartiality or consistency, and principle of 
impersonality or consistency.Spotlight

C ASE
      TUDY
Taking Bribe at Workplace
The appellant is aggrieved against the order of the learned Single Judge dated 21st April 2008, passed 
in WP(S) No. 5477 of 2007, whereby the appellant’s writ petition challenging the award dated 5th June 
2007 passed by the Labour Court, Jamshedpur has been dismissed.
The facts reveal that the petitioner in this case was caught red-handed on 24th January 1995 taking 
bribe of `150 when he was on duty in shift ‘E’. The Labour Court, after considering the evidence 
of the parties, held that the petitioner was in fact caught red-handed taking bribe and the amount of 
`150 was also recovered immediately thereafter. The punishment inflicted upon the workman was 
upheld by the award. The learned Single Judge also, after considering the facts of the case, dismissed 
the writ petition.
The counsel for the appellant submitted that the appellant was assigned the duty of receiving goods 
only and therefore there was no occasion and there could not have been any reason for taking as 
well as giving bribe in the present case. It was also submitted that another person was earlier caught 
red-handed taking bribe, but he had been reinstated in service. The counsel for the appellant further 
submitted that there is no sufficient evidence on record on the basis of which it can be inferred that 
money was taken as bribe in view of the defence of the appellant taken in the departmental proceeding 
and before the Labour Court. The defence of the appellant was that at about 11.00 am on 24th January 
1995, the concerned supplier came to the workman and asked for an amount of `150 to attend some 
urgent work. The said person normally and in past also had taken some money from the appellant. In 
the instant case, the supplier returned the said money of `150. The workman also admitted that at that 
time he was surrounded by other workmen and other persons of the respondent company and `150
was recovered from him. According to the counsel for the appellant, so far as demanding and taking 
of bribe is concerned, there is no evidence in view of the stand taken by the appellant.
It will be relevant to mention here that the writ petition was admitted on 2 counts. Firstly, whether 
the order of termination can sustain in law on the ground of non-examination of the person from whom 
the appellant is alleged to have received the illegal gratification. Secondly, whether the punishment 
was proportionate to the guilt, as the allegation is of taking bribe of `150 only.
The counsel for the respondent had submitted that the person from whom the amount was taken 
was examined in departmental proceedings and therefore the first ground does not survive. It was also 
IR&LL_Ch_06.indd   22 1/23/2008   11:33:52 AM

Industrial Discipline and Grievance Handling 6.23
submitted that the defence taken by the appellant also is unbelievable due to the fact that the appel-
lant himself had lodged complaint against the person from whom, as he was saying, was receiving 
the money back.
It is undisputed that on 24th January 1995, while on duty, the appellant had taken `150 from a 
person and admittedly, that person was a supplier of goods to the company. If the Labour Court, after 
appreciation of the evidence, has rejected the defence stand of the appellant that it was a case of return 
of money by the supplier to the appellant, then it is a pure question of fact.

bribe is grave enough to be awarded a punishment of dismissal?
3. Do you think that the petitioner ought to be discharged or dismissed?

Industrial Conflict and Disputes
Desired Knowledge Competencies
cTo comprehend the concepts of industrial conflict and dispute.
cTo discuss the various views of conflicts and the underlying reasons of industrial disputes.
cTo outline the typology of strikes and the concepts of lock-out, bandhs  and gheraos .
cTo develop an understanding of the trend of industrial disputes in India.
INTR ODUCTION
The entire gamut of industrial relations revolves around a cycle of expectations and aspirations, which 
depends on cooperation and teamwork. This cycle often creates a series of conflicting situations due 
to the divergent interests of employers and employees. When any such conflict is allowed to exist for 
long, it has negative implications for an organisation. Under the unitary approach to industrial rela-
tions, workplace conflict is seen as a temporary aberration resulting from poor management, and is 
considered not only as unnecessary, but also as destructive. The pluralistic approach however views 
conflicts between the management and workers as inevitable and, in fact, conducive for growth. The 
Marxist approach considers conflicts to be the outcome of the capitalist society.
Industrial dispute, on the other hand, refers to any disagreement between workers and employers on 
a wide range of issues like wages, working conditions and other employment matters. Disputes may 
also arise due to disagreement between rival unions regarding issues like jurisdiction, or even between 
employers and employers. Conflict and dispute are intertwined in industrial relations. In this chapter 
we would discuss both these concepts within the ambit of labour legislations in India.
INDUSTRIAL CONFLICT
Referred to as a “dramatic expression of the relationship between capital and labour (Korpi and Shalev, 
1979, p. 164), conflict is inherent in the interests of capital and labour as parties to the employment 
relationship. There are different views on what conflict is all about. Coser (1967, p. 8) has defined 
IR&LL_Ch_07.indd   1 1/1/2008   4:49:17 AM

7.2 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
conflict as “A struggle over values and claims to scarce status, power and resources, in which the 
aims of the opponent are to neutralize, injure or eliminate the rivals”. Willmot and Hocker (2001, p. 
41) look at conflict as “an expressed struggle”. It is apparent that the phenomenon of conflict in both 
these definitions has negative and destructive hues. On the contrary, Deutsch (1973) and Rahim (1983) 
consider conflict as “confronting interests” or “incompatible activities” existing between the parties 
involved in social situations. Thomas (1992, p. 265) considers conflict as “the process which begins 
when one party perceives that another has frustrated, or is about to frustrate, some concern of his”. 
This definition is broad enough to include a wide variety of conflict phenomena.
When people work together, conflict becomes an integral and in fact a normal part of doing business. 
Organisational conflict refers to an interactive process manifested in incompatibility, disagreement or 
dissonance within or between social entities (i.e., individual, group, organisation, etc.) (Rahim, 2002). 
It includes interpersonal, inter-group and inter-organisational conflicts. Numerous factors may be 
responsible for conflicts at workplace. In fact, there can be more than one reason that may come into 
play to give rise to a single instance of conflict. Hence it is not always easy to ascertain or single out 
the particular cause(s) involved. What may be more intriguing is that the apparent reason(s) behind any 
unrest may conceal the deep-seated and more fundamental causes. Nevertheless, the factors responsible 
for organisational conflicts can be clubbed under the following heads:
rIndustry-related factors:  These factors include industry-related policies or practices pertaining 
to employment, wage, hours of work, terms and conditions of employment, rights and obliga-
tions of employers and workers, etc.
rOrganisation-related factors:  Such factors may include wages 
(e.g., wage structure; deductions from wages; incentives; allow-
ances); work-related issues (e.g., authoritarian administration; 
methods of job evaluation; physical working conditions; usage 
of technology and machinery; plant layout); terms of employ-
ment (e.g., hours of work; shift working; promotion; leave rules; 
layoff; retrenchment; dismissal; job security); union issues (e.g., 
recognition of union; membership of union; subjects of collective 
bargaining); unfair practices (e.g., non-implementation of labour 
laws and regulations; ambiguity in standing orders; violation of 
collective agreements), etc.
rIndividual-related factors:  These factors are related to the personality and behaviour of an 
individual worker, like habits; behavioural maladjustments; lack of scope for self-expression 
and participation, etc.
rGovernment-related factors:  These include changes in economic policies and regulations; 
improper implementation of labour legislations; changes in administrative machinery, etc.
rMiscellaneous factors:  Other factors that may be instrumental in industrial conflicts are the 
growing intervention of political parties in union activities; unstable political situation; inter-
union rivalry; clashes within union; change in ownership of establishment, etc.
However, this list is not exhaustive. With increase in complexities of jobs, emergence of new 
industries and growing awareness level of workers, the goals, expectations and aspirations of both 
workers and employers are expanding their domains. Such new expectations and aspirations would 
invoke new kinds of clashes between the two groups and the causes of conflicts would continue to 
increase in number and complexities.Spotlight

Industrial Conflict and Disputes 7.3
All the reasons behind organisational conflicts can be summed up in accordance to the perspective of 
Rahim (2002), who proposes that organisational conflicts are likely to happen when the parties involved:
rare required to engage in an activity that is incongruent with their needs or interests.
rhold behavioural preferences that are incompatible with the implementation of each other’s 
preferences.
rwant some mutually desirable resource that is short in supply.
rpossess attitudes, values, skills and goals that are appropriate for directing their behaviour but 
contradict the attitudes, values, skills and goals held by others within an organisation.
rhave contradictory preferences regarding their joint actions.
Views on Conflict
Traditional View The traditional view, dated in the 1930s and 1940s, 
was primarily based on attitudes that prevailed about group behaviour. It 
had a negative, rigid and formalistic approach to conflict. Conflict was 
considered dysfunctional and had to be avoided at all costs by role players 
(Slabbert, 2004), primarily because of the adverse effects it could have 
on organisational productivity. The classical writers believed that conflict is indicative of malfunctioning 
within the organisation and that it represents management’s failure to bind the workers and organisation 
together in a cohesive unit. Conflict was denounced because conflicting groups would not cooperate 
in getting tasks completed. Managers would also have to devote extra efforts and time in resolving 
conflicts. All of these would lead to losses in productivity and hence the traditional view recommended 
suppression of conflicts.
Modern View The modern approach to conflict originated in the discourses of the human relations 
theorists, who proposed that conflict is a natural phenomenon that is inevitable and should be managed 
as such (Reynecke, 1997). Conflict is natural and inevitable because organisations are composed of 
individuals with different and divergent values, goals and perceptions. Faulty policies and structure of 
the organisation leading to blockage in communication also contribute to conflicts at work. Because of 
its inevitability in any organisational set up, conflict must be resolved amicably to achieve good human 
relations. Overall, the human relations school perceived conflict as harmful and advised resolution of 
conflicts in the interest of the organisation and its members.
The modern view proposes that conflict is not only a positive force in 
a group, but is also necessary for a group to perform effectively. Conflict 
should be measured in terms of functionality, i.e., whether it is func-
tional or dysfunctional. A functional conflict encourages the group to 
work for the attainment of its goals, improves its performance and con-
tributes to personal growth of the members and to overall organisational growth. A dysfunctional
conflict is destructive in nature as it hinders group or individual performance. Thus it is inappropriate 
to say that conflict is all good or bad. In fact, the modern approach encourages conflict on the ground 
that a minimum level of conflict is necessary to keep the organisational members alert and creative. 
It provides stability to a group and helps in the identification of power centers in and between groups 
(Chhabra and Suri, 2007). Conflict is also viewed to be integral to the 
process of change; a harmonious group that exhibits cooperation is prone 
to become static and non-responsive to change and innovation. The onus 
would lie on the group leader to allow any conflict to happen in order to 
make the group members innovative and imaginative. Further, conflicts 
must be kept under control to avoid their dysfunctional consequences.Spotlight

7.4 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
INDUSTRIAL DISPUTES
An industrial dispute may be defined as a disagreement or difference of 
opinion between management and workers over issues like pay, work-
ing conditions and other terms of employment. However, it would be 
wrong to suppose that industrial disputes are limited to employees and 
employers. Disputes also include any disagreement between worker and 
worker and between employer and employer. All these aspects are neatly 
summarised in the definition of industrial disputes as per Section 2(k) of 
the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 as “any dispute or difference between 
employers and employers, or between employers and workmen, or be-
tween workmen and workmen which is connected with the employment 
or non-employment or the terms of employment or with the conditions of 
labour, of any person.” We would be talking about the Act and its various 
provisions in detail in Chapter 15.
Disagreement or difference fuelling an industrial dispute could be on 
any matter concerning workers, either individually or collectively, connected with employment, like 
inequitable wage structure, or non-employment, or with the conditions of labour, like poor working 
conditions. When an industrial dispute occurs, both the parties try to pressurise each other and often 
adopt coercive methods to have their demands fulfilled. Management may resort to lock-outs, while 
workers may call on strikes, picketing or gheraos . Whatever be the method adopted, disputes lead to 
negative repercussions. Such implications of industrial disputes have been explained in a subsequent 
section. Let us first understand the differences between seemingly similar terms, namely conflict and 
dispute, and individual dispute and industrial dispute.
Difference between Conflict and Dispute
Is there any difference between conflict and dispute? Many a times these 
two terms have been found to be used interchangeably. Conflict is consid-
ered to be an unavoidable fact of organisational life; it is somewhat gen-
eral as a concept. However, when conflict acquires concrete and specific 
manifestations, it becomes an industrial dispute, i.e., industrial conflict is 
general, whereas industrial dispute is specific. More specifically, the term ‘industrial dispute’ is used in 
the literature including government publications to denote work-stoppage as well as those differences 
between labour and management that are settled through the industrial relations machinery (Chhabra 
and Suri, 2007). Be it dispute or conflict, either must be resolved for harmonious labour-management 
relations. When workers and their unions take an issue of conflict to the management for the purpose 
of negotiation, such a conflict becomes a matter of industrial dispute.
Difference between Individual Dispute and Industrial Dispute
There is a large divergence of opinions as to whether a dispute between an individual worker and 
employer (i.e., an individual dispute) can be considered as an industrial dispute under Section 2(k) of 
the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Let us analyse some relevant judgments to clarify the difference.
It would be worthwhile to note the provisions of Section 2A, added as per an amendment in the 
Industrial Dispute Act, 1947 in the year 1965. According to this section, where any employer discharges, 
dismisses, retrenches or otherwise terminates the services of an individual workman, any dispute or Spotlight

Industrial Conflict and Disputes 7.5
difference between that workman and his employer connected with, or arising out of, such discharge, 
dismissal, retrenchment or termination shall be deemed to be an industrial dispute, notwithstanding 
that no other workman or any union of workmen is a party to the dispute.
InThe Newspapers Ltd vs. The State Industrial Tribunal, U.P . [(1957) SCR 754] the Court held 
that any dispute between an employer and a single workman does not fall within the definition of 
“industrial dispute” under the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Though the applicability of the said 
Act to an individual dispute, as opposed to a dispute involving a group of workmen, is excluded and 
if workmen as a body or a considerable section of them make a common cause with the individual 
workman, then such a dispute would be an industrial dispute.
The Court has held in D. N. Banerji vs. P . R. Mukherjee and Others [(1953) SCR 302] that the 
words “industrial dispute” seemingly imply that the dispute must be such as would affect large groups 
of workmen and employers on issues such as wages, bonuses, allowances, pensions, provident fund, 
number of working hours per week, holidays and so on. Even with reference to a business, we would 
hardly opine that there is an industrial dispute where an employee is dismissed by his employer and 
the dismissal is questioned as wrongful. But at the same time, having regard to the modern conditions 
of society where capital and labour have organised themselves into groups for the purpose of fighting 
their disputes and settling such disputes on the philosophy that in union is strength, and with collective 
bargaining becoming a powerful tool in the hands of unions, a single employee’s case might develop 
into an industrial dispute when it is taken up by the trade union of which he is a member and there 
is a concerted demand by the employees for redress. Such an issue may not be limited to a single 
establishment or a factory, but may cover the industry as a whole in a case where the grievance, if 
any, passes from the domain of an individual complaint into a general complaint on behalf of all the 
workers in the industry. In such widespread extension of labour unrest even an industrial dispute in 
a particular business becomes a large scale industrial dispute, which the Government cannot afford 
to ignore as a minor trouble to be settled between the particular employer and workman concerned. 
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/162306/ accessed on 15/2/2014.)
MANIFESTATION OF CONFLICT
Workers resort to various methods like strikes, go-slow and work-to-rule 
as a manifestation of their discontentment and conflict with the employer, 
while lock-out is the weapon in the hands of the employer to manifest 
an industrial dispute. Let us elaborate on each of these weapons now.
Strike
A strike is a powerful weapon in the hands of workers and their trade unions to get their demands 
accepted. A strike generally involves quitting of work by a group of workers for the purpose of pres-
surising their management. Section 2(q) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 defines a strike as “a 
cessation of work by a body of persons employed in any industry acting in combination or a concerted 
refusal, or a refusal under a common understanding, of any number of persons who are or have been 
so employed to continue to work or to accept employment”.
We have already referred to strikes under the method of direct action adopted by unions in Chapter 
3. Let us talk about the types of strikes here.Reflection

7.6 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Types of Strikes
There can be several bases of classifying strikes. Let us explain types of strikes in terms of such bases.
I. On the Basis of Consent of Union
(a)Authorised strikes:  Strikes which are called with the consent of the union are authorised strikes.
(b)Unauthorised strikes:  An unauthorised strike, popularly known as a 
lightning strike or a “wildcat strike” is one which is called without 
prior consent of the union concerned and without giving proper no-
tice to the employer. Hence a wildcat strike is an unofficial strike. 
Such a strike is normally the outcome of an emotional upsurge due to provocative circumstances 
between employer and workers. Many authors are of the opinion that such strikes occur in viola-
tion of the no-strike pledge in collective bargaining agreements. The characteristic feature of this 
type of withdrawal of labour, as Srivastava (1990) points out, is that workmen suddenly withdraw 
their labour and bargain afterwards. The union concerned is under obligation to use its best ef-
forts to end a wildcat strike.
   Such strikes are prohibited in public utility services under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 
and in all industrial establishments in public utility services in Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, 
Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat, where notice of strike is required to be given. We shall be deliber-
ating about regulation of strikes and notice of strike in Chapter 15. Further, the standing orders 
of an industrial establishment generally require notice of strike. Since no notice is required in 
industrial establishments other than public utility concerns, a question therefore arises whether a 
wildcat strike would be misconduct or unjustified in such establishments; this is a subject-matter 
of judicial controversy (Srivastava, 1990).Spotlight
A wildcat strike is an unofficial 
strike.
Exhibit 7.1 Wildcat Strike at Maruti Suzuki
A wildcat strike had exploded on 4th June 2011 and continued till 17th June 2011 at the Manesar 
plant of Maruti Suzuki, with around 2,000 workers demanding the recognition of a new union, 
namely, Maruti Suzuki Employees Union (MSEU), formed by those working at the Manesar 
plant, and for improving working conditions and wages of the workers.
Without previous notice to strike, the workers brought production to a complete halt. They 
spent almost two weeks in the factory. The strike delayed the production of 13,200 cars and the 
company was hit in a phase of full production capacity. Damages caused were worth 100 mil-
lion Euros to the company. The workers continued with the strike, even though it was officially 
declared illegal on 10th June and police were stationed within the factory.
The outcome was however a defeat for the majority of the workers, with their most important 
goal, i.e., improvement in wages not being attained. Instead, the agreement with the manage-
ment contained a penalty wage cut of two days per strike day. The agreement also included 
re-employment of the eleven union members who had been fired during the protests, though 
subject to investigation.

II. On the Basis of Tactics Used to Halt Work
(a)Ordinary strike: This type of strike is characterised by employees quitting their workplace during 
prescribed working hours; the striking workers also prevent others from coming to work. Rallies, 
picketing and demonstrations are also made by the workers to draw the attention of the manage-
ment to their grievances and demands.
(b)Slow-down strike:  In this type of strike, the striking workers remain on their jobs. They do not 
stop work as such, but restrict the volume of output produced in an organised manner. If we go by 
the definition of strike as provided by the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, in slow-down there is no 
“cessation of work” or “refusal to continue to work” or “refusal to accept employment”. Never-
theless the economic implications of slow-down are very serious as adoption of such techniques 
raises the costs of production. These strikes are resented by employers on grounds of immorality.
Exhibit 7.2 Slow-down at IISCO, Burnpur
The workers of Indian Iron and Steel Co. (IISCO) Ltd. had started a slow-down on 19th January 
1953 at the Burnpur unit without any declared reason or demand from the management. The com-
pany had no knowledge of the intrigues and the animosities which had engendered the trouble until 
10th February 1953. It was also unable to recognise the Action Committee which was set up as a 
representative body, as the Committee was not constituted by any lawful election and especially 
as it had been actively engaging in subversive activities, including the slow-down of production.
On account of the continued illegal stoppage of work, ‘slow down’ tactics and strikes indulged 
in by the workmen despite the advice of their union, IISCO issued a notice dated 23rd August 
1953 that in consequence of the illegal strike the management had no option other than declaring 
a lock-out of the entire works except the special shifts with effect from 24th August 1953.
(Adapted from: Labour Trouble at Burnpur, The Economic Weekly, 15th August, 1953. Retrieved 
from www.epw.in/system/files/pdf/1953.../labour_trouble_at_burnpur.pdfý, www.indiankanoon.org/
doc/1919374/ on 28/2/2014.)
   Let us throw light on “go-slow” here as a variant of slow-down, in which workers deliberately 
slow-down the pace of production by pretending to be engaged in the factory. As Mamoria et al. 
(2008, p. 231) point out, “The go-slow is a technical word which is used to describe the tactics 
of workers when they intentionally reduce the speed of work to adopt dilatory tactics to reduce 
production or efficiency while pretending to be engaged in the factory.” There is no “cessation 
of work” or “refusal to continue to work” or “refusal to accept employment” in such type of 
strikes as well. Workers adopt the practice of “go-slow” to circumvent the statutory restrictions 
on strike; however, when they are disciplined for misconduct, these workers assert that the prac-
tice amounts to strike (Srivastava, 1990).
   In M/s Bharat Sugar Mills Ltd vs. Shri Jai Singh and Others , the Supreme Court had observed 
that: “Go slow which a picturesque description of deliberate delaying of production by workmen 
pretending to be engaged in the factory is one of the most pernicious practices that discontented 
or disgruntled workmen sometime resort to. It would not be far wrong to call this dishonest. 
For, while thus delaying production and thereby reducing the output the workmen claim to have 
remained employed and thus to be entitled to full wages.” Besides, go-slow is likely to be much 
more harmful than total cessation of work by strike. This is because while during a strike much 
IR&LL_Ch_07.indd   7 1/1/2008   4:49:17 AM

7.8 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
of the machinery can be fully turned off; however during go-slow the machinery is kept going on 
at a reduced speed, which is often extremely damaging to machinery parts.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/774563/ accessed on 28/2/2014.)
(c)Quickie:  In a quickie workers remain at their work stations, but halt their work for a brief while, 
say a few minutes to a few hours (Sinha, Sinha and Shekhar, 2006). The implications of such 
work-stoppage, even though for a few minutes, can be very serious, especially in assembly-line 
production.
(d)Sit-down strike:  In a sit-down strike a group of workers keeps control over the production facili-
ties; these workers stop production and refuse access to the owners or to any one else desiring to 
work. Thus workers do not absent themselves from their place of work when they are on strike, 
though they do not work. It is a strike in the traditional sense, to which is added the element of 
trespass by strikers upon the property of the employer. A sit-down strike is also known as a ‘pen
down’ or ‘tool down’ strike.
   Another variant of a sit-down strike is a “sit-in” strike. In this 
type of strike an organised group of protesting workers sits and 
occupies an area where it is not wanted and refuses to move out 
until its demands are met. In The Punjab National Bank Ltd. vs. its 
Workmen (1960 SCR (1) 806) the employees of the appellant Bank 
had commenced a pen-down strike followed by a general strike, 
pending arbitration of an industrial dispute between them. In con-
sidering whether this pen-down strike is actually a strike within the 
scope of Section 2(q) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 or not, the Court held that on a plain 
and grammatical construction of the definition of a strike it would be difficult to exclude a strike 
where workmen enter the premises of their employment and refuse to take their tools in hand and 
start their usual work. Refusal under common understanding to continue to work is undoubtedly 
a strike and if in pursuance of such common understanding the employees had entered the prem-
ises of the Bank and refused to take their pens in their hands that would surely be a strike under 
Section 2(q). The main grievance of the Bank is that these employees not only sat in their places 
and refused to work, but they would also not vacate their seats when asked to do so by their supe-
rior officers. Such conduct may introduce an element of insubordination. The Court was finally 
of the opinion that the pen-down strike in which the employees had participated cannot be said to 
be outside Section 2(q) of the Act.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/1395554/ accessed on 26/2/2014.)
   Let us sort out the difference between quickie and sit-downs. The basic distinction between 
these two variants of strikes is the duration involved. Obviously a quickie is for shorter duration 
than a sit-down. The similarity between the two is in the stoppage of work.
(e)Stay-in strike:  A stay-in strike is one in which the striking workers report to their duties, but 
refuse to work and they do not leave the plant premises. The owner of the plant (or factory) is de-
prived of the use of the plant and the machinery and further operations are at a halt. Besides, the 
owner has to incur additional expenditure on the safety and security 
of the plant and machinery when the striking workers remain inside 
the factory or establishment.
(f)Work-to-rule strike: Work-to-rule is a kind of concerted activity in 
which employees remain on job, but perform their work literally in 
accordance with the rules prescribed for the purpose. These work-Spotlight

   As Srivastava (1990) observes, usually under work-to-rule, rules

shelter of complying with rules the very purpose of these rules, 
namely, harmonious working for maximizing production, is frustrated. As such, workers literally

rule”. Work-to-rule is generally employed as an alternative to a traditional strike, particularly in 
situations when the latter cannot be called. It amounts to bringing about a lot of pressure on the 
management by the employees.
Exhibit 7.3 Work-to-rule at Neyveli Lignite Corporation
The employees of Neyveli Lignite Corporation (NLC) gave up their 13-days-old strike and re-
turned to work soon after the Tamil Nadu Government clinched the deal with the Securities and 
Exchange Board of India to buy 5 per cent NLC shares at `500 crore. However, in response to 
this deal, the employees have decided to adhere to the work-to-rule procedures. The rules stipulate 
eight-hour shift for employees, with rightful breaks in between for refreshment. Prior to the strike 
the employees and workers never went by the clock but would always put in extra work of about 
two to two-and-half hours daily beyond their shift obligations. The foremen, numbering about 
2,000, used to work extra hours to facilitate smooth change over from one shift to the other as it 
would normally take some time before the fresh batch of employees would replace the previous 
batch by a practice that is termed as “man-to-man relieving”.
According to S. Rajavanniyan, General Secretary of the Labour Progressive Front (Neyveli 
Unit), the proposed action of the employees should not be construed as either a threat to the man-
agement or an anti-management move. He specified that “Taking time-off is indeed the legal right 
of the employees which they will duly exercise hereafter.” The employees and the workforce in 
the mines and thermal power stations would unfailingly take the tea/tiffin break in such manner 
that during such intervals the officials could not take over, as the entire functionality would be 
with the employees. Rajavanniyan reiterated the point that “it would not be a vengeful act but a 
rightful act on the part of the employees as provided under the law.” 
(Adapted from: Strike given up, but NLC staff to go by work-to-rule, Neyveli, 17th July, 2013, Retrieved

(g)Sick-in strike: The sick-in (also known as sick-out) is an interesting variant of a strike; instead 
of calling a conventional strike, a majority or all the workers call in sick simultaneously. The 
employer cannot initiate any action against such workers because these workers do not break any 
rules; they just avail of their sick leave that they are entitled to, on the same day. Sick-in is thus 
a good way to strike without striking; it provides a signal to the employer of the repercussions if 
the workers really went on strike.

strike”, and “tool-down strike” are often used as synonymous to each other.Spotlight

7.10 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
III. On the Basis of Miscellaneous Purposes
(a)Sympathetic strike:  As the name itself suggests, a sympathetic strike is borne out of sympathy; 
the striking workers do not have any grievance against their employer. However they join the 
other group of workers, whether the latter are on strike or not, to express their solidarity and com-
monness to the cause of these workers.
Exhibit 7.4 Expressing Solidarity to the Maruti Cause
The strike by workers of Maruti Suzuki at its Manesar factory was under threat to spread to other 
auto and component makers in the Manesar-Gurgaon belt, which makes about half of all the cars 
and bikes in the country. The demand placed by Maruti workers for an independent workers’ 
union had struck a sympathetic chord among workers in neighbouring units including Hero Honda, 
Honda Motorcycle and Scooter India (HMSI), Rico Auto, Omaxe Auto and Lumax Industries. 
Unions of these companies are now threatening to strike work against their respective companies.
The secretary of HMSI Employees’ Union said that “We have decided to call a one day strike 
to protest against the indecisive Maruti management. We will give them some time before taking 
a final call on the issue.” The president of Rico Auto’s workers’ union at the Daruhera plant near 
Manesar said that “If Maruti Suzuki fails to act on workers’ demands, we will resort to a strike 
at our plants in coming days.” The president of Employees’ Union at Hero Honda’s Daruhera 
plant said that “We will extend all support to Maruti employees and may go on strike to express 
our solidarity. If required, we will come to a common location and protest for joint demands.”
(Adapted from: www.libcom.org/news/india-wildcat-strike-maruti-suzuki-continues-may-spread-09062011 
accessed on 28/2/2014.)
(b)Hunger strike: Hunger strike features fasting by some or all the striking workers for a limited 
period. However, the ulterior motive of workers involved in the strike is to exert moral pressure 
on the management for acceptance of their demands and to attract the attention of the public. 
Srivastava (1990) holds the view that the usage of hunger strike as a weapon is complicated 
because, like the term ‘strike’, it is used to describe all protest fasts, 
whether or not the particular protest activity is in furtherance of 
an industrial dispute. Typical examples are of students on hunger 
strike to press their demands against educational authorities, politi-
cal leaders on hunger strike to compel the government to redress 
their grievances, and sections of the community on hunger strike in 
support of their stand against various authorities or bodies.
(c)Jurisdictional strike:  Typically American in concept, jurisdictional strike is an outcome of a dis-
pute between the members of different unions over work assignments or disagreement between 
two or more unions as to which of them should have the exclusive right to bargain collectively 
with the employer. Needless to mention, such strikes can occur only in such establishments that 
have multiple trade unions which are rivals.
(d)Economic strike:  As is evident from the name itself, this type of strike is initiated to enforce the 
economic demands of workers, such as wages, bonus and various types of allowances.
(e)Token strike:  A token strike is generally of a very short duration intended to convey the strength 
of feeling of workers on a disputed issue. It serves more as a kind of signal for the real threat Spotlight
Workers on hunger strike intend 
to exert moral pressure on the 
management for acceptance of 
their demands and to attract the 
attention of the public.
IR&LL_Ch_07.indd   10 1/1/2008   4:49:18 AM

Industrial Conflict and Disputes 7.11
of a strike ahead in case the demands of the workers are unheeded by the employer. The motive 
behind such a strike is moral persuasion.
(f)Political strike:  Political strikes are called with the objective of challenging the government or 
influencing its policy decisions in favour of the working class. Such strikes are not the outcome 
of any industrial dispute.
(g)General strike:  General strikes are wide-spread in terms of coverage and scope, with participa-
tion of members of all or most of the unions in a region or an industry. These strikes are usually 
directed to create political pressure on the government, and in this sense general strikes are simi-
lar to political strikes.
(h)Picketing and Boycott: Picketing is an action taken by union members to prevent employees from 
attending work after a strike has been called. It is accompanied by patrolling of striking workers 
in front of the premises of the employer and displaying banners and placards to show their protest 
verbally. Picketing is a tool in the hands of workers to generate public awareness of their dispute 
with their employer. Peaceful picketing is not illegal; however adoption of coercive methods and 
persuasion by threat or violence may fail to restrict picketing within peaceful limits.
   Boycott refers to the rejection by workers of specific products or services provided by the 
employer. As per Mamoria et al. (2008), a boycott is an appeal for voluntary withdrawal of 
cooperation, and so it is persuasive in nature, but negative in approach; however, picketing 
is positive in approach as it involves adopting necessary and adequate measures to prevent 
cooperation by others in the normal functioning of a business.
(i)Gherao:  The term gherao  literally means encirclement. In Jay Engineering Works Ltd. and Oth-
ers vs. State of West Bengal and Others (AIR 1968 Cal 407), the Court has defined gherao  as a 
physical blockade of a target, either by encirclement or forcible occupation. It has described two 
kinds of gherao . The ordinary kind is encirclement and blockade of an industrial establishment, 
where the person gheraoed  is generally in managerial or supervisory position present at the prem-
ises. Blockade can also be outside the premises on a public thoroughfare; the persons blockading 
may trespass into the land belonging to an industrial establishment. The second kind of gherao
is encirclement in depth, i.e., forcible possession of the industrial establishment and ouster of the 
real owner and the managerial and other staff. A gherao  can last for several hours or even days, 
and the staff are prevented from going out pending fulfillment of the demands of workers.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/140181/ accessed on 28/2/2014.)Exhibit 7.5 Hunger Strike: Saty agraha
InPipraich Sugar Mills Ltd vs. Pipraich Sugar Mills Mazdoor Union [(1956-57) X FJR 4113 
LAT]  certain workmen who held key posts in the factory went on hunger strike on a holiday at the 
residence of the Managing Director of the factory and continued to do so on other working days. 
The Labour Appellate Tribunal observed that the mere fact that the hunger strike was staged on 
a holiday does not reduce the essential characteristics of a strike from this hunger ‘ satyagraha ’.
This is because the intention of the strikers was to continue the strike till their demands were met 
or till they died of starvation. It was not claimed on behalf of the satyagrahi  workers that they 
did present themselves for their duty on 2nd April 1953. So it must be held that the ‘ satyagraha ’ 
was continued on 2nd April 1953 and amounted to ‘strike’.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/1252531/ accessed on 26/2/2014.)

7.12 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
   According to the First National Commission on Labour (1969), 
gheraos  strike at the very root of trade unionism apart from their 
adverse effects on industry and the economy of the country. The 
Commission hence deprecated resort to gheraos  which invariably 
tend to inflict physical duress on the person(s) affected and not only 
endanger industrial harmony but also create problems of law and order. If such means are to be 
adopted by workers for realisation of their claims, trade unions may come into disrepute; it is 
hence the duty of all union leaders to condemn this form of labour protest as harmful to the in-
terests of the working class itself. As per the Commission, gheraos  cannot be treated as a form of 
industrial protest since they involve physical coercion rather than economic pressure, thus affect-
ing national interest in the long run. The incidence of gherao  was initiated amidst violent trade 
unionism in West Bengal, followed by Kerala, though it is not much in practice nowadays.
   Blockade under gherao  is occasionally supplemented by assault, criminal trespass, mischief 
to person and property, unlawful assembly and various other criminal offences. Many a times 
the offences reported are cruel and inhuman, e.g., confinement in a small space without lights or 
fans and for long periods without food or communication with the outside world. The persons 
confined are beaten, humiliated by abuse and not allowed even to answer calls of nature and 
subjected to various other forms of torture. In short the officials “ gheraoed ” are completely at the 
mercy of the besiegers. The Court has held that workers have no right to resort to coercive meth-
ods like wrongful restraint, wrongful confinement and criminal trespass, which are all cognizable 
offences as per the Indian Penal Code. Often such strikes are referred to as “secondary action’. 
The legality of such strikes is found to vary across countries.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/140181/ accessed on 28/2/2014.)
(j)Secondary strike: Secondary strikes are those in which pressure is not applied against the primary 
employer, but against some third person who has good trade relations with the employer and thus 
the latter incurs losses.
(k)Bandh:  The literal meaning of the term bandh  is “closed”, implying that everything is to be 
closed during a bandh .
   In Communist Party of India (M) vs. Bharat Kumar and Others  [(1998)1 SCC 201] the Kerala 
High Court has laid down that: “… which the organiser of a bandh, call for a bandh, they clearly 
express their intention that they expect all activities to come to a standstill on the day of the 
bandh.” A call for a bandh  is different from that for a general strike or a hartal . The Court further 
held that: “The intention of the callers of the bandh  is to ensure that no activity either public or 
private if carried on that date… It is no doubt true that while calling for a bandh  it is not also an-
nounced that any citizen not participating in the bandh  will be physically prevented or attacked.” 
However experience has shown that when any attempt is made to move out, such a person has 
been threatened with harmful consequences.
   In Railway Board, New Delhi vs. Niranjan Singh (AIR 1969 SC 966), the Supreme Court 
has observed that: “The fact that the citizens of this country have freedom of speech, freedom 
to assemble peaceably and freedom to form associations or unions does not mean that they can 
exercise those freedoms in whatever place they please. The exercise of those freedoms will come 
to an end as soon as the right of someone else to hold his property intervenes. Such limitation 
is inherent in the exercise of those rights.” Keeping this verdict in perspective and if the call for 
bandh  and holding of it entails restriction on the fundamental freedoms of the citizen, the court, 
inRama Prasad Sarkar vs. The State of West Bengal (WP 23617 (W) of 2013), has held that no 
political party has the right to call for bandh  on the plea that it is part of its fundamental right of Spotlight

of a target, either by encirclement 
or forcible occupation.

ing for a general strike or hartal  that is not accompanied by express or implied threat of violence 
to enforce it. It is not possible to accept that the calling of a bandh  is the only measure to demon-
strate the protest of a political party to a given decision or in a given situation.

Lock-out
The use of the term “lock-out” to describe the instruments of economic 
coercion in the hands of employers dates back to 1860s; as a practice 
lock-out is younger than its counterparts in the hands of workers, i.e., 
strike, by about a hundred years (Srivastava, 1990). Formerly lock-out 
as an instrument of coercion was resorted to by an employer or group of 
employers to ban union membership; later lock-out was declared generally 
by a body of employers against a strike at a particular establishment by 
closing all factories until strikers would return to work. Section 2(l) of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 defines lock-out as “the temporary closing 
of a place of employment or the suspension of work, or the refusal by 
an employer to continue to employ any number of persons employed by him”. As mentioned earlier 
in the chapter, lock-out is a weapon in the hands of the employer to coerce labour to come down in 
their demands, thus restraining their militant spirit.
InPresidency Jute Mills Co. Ltd. vs. Presidency Jute Mills Co. Employees’ Union [(1952) LAT 
62] the Court has held that the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 treats strikes and lock-outs on the same 
basis as counterparts of each other. If we look at these instruments of industrial disputes, we can find 
plentitude of negative impacts of each. It is just that in lock-out it is the employer who first draws 
the sword. Neither a strike, nor a lock-out would severe the relation of employer and workers. The 
Supreme Court describes a lock-out as the antithesis of strike.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/301159 accessed on 25/2/2014.)
We shall be discussing the other aspects of lock-out, including notice of lock-out by an employer on 
any public utility service and illegality of a lock-out in the chapter on Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
ANAL YSIS OF TRENDS IN CONFLICT IN INDIAN INDUSTR Y
The Industrial Relations machineries at both Centre and State levels under the aegis of the Ministry 
of Labour & Employment strive on a continuous basis towards maintenance of harmonious indus-
trial relations in the country. The Departments of Labour in the States and Union Territories and 
Regional Labour Commissioners (Central) are responsible for collecting basic information in respect 
of work-stoppages from the affected primary units in the State and Central Spheres respectively, 
whenever such occurrence of a work-stoppage becomes known either directly or from supplementary 
sources like police records. Such information is furnished in standard format to the Labour Bureau, 
Ministry of Labour & Employment, on or before the 25th of each succeeding month. The statistics 
on industrial disputes brought out by the Labour Bureau include information in respect of those 
temporary work-stoppages only which include strikes, lock-outs and gheraos  followed by lock-
outs, and involving 10 or more workers, whether directly and/or indirectly. Work-stoppages which 
involve less than 10 workers are not included in such records. Similarly, political strikes, sympa-Spotlight

Industrial Conflict and Disputes 7.15
EFFECTS OF INDUSTRIAL DISPUTES
Whatever by the type adopted, strikes have far-reaching impacts on not only the employers, but also 
the striking workers themselves, the consumers of the products of the affected industry, the suppliers to 
the establishment(s) and the economy as a whole. Though a lock-out is in the hands of the employer, 
but otherwise its consequences are similar. Let us enumerate the effects of industrial disputes as a 
whole in this section.
Effects on Workers
The most immediate impact of industrial disputes on the workers is through their wages. The question 
that would come in sequence is that whether striking workers should be entitled to wages from their 
employer or not. The Supreme Court has held in Syndicate Bank and Another vs. K. Umesh Nayak 
(AIR 1995 SC 319) that the right of workmen to receive strike wages is when the strike is not only 
legal, but is also justified. What needs to be understood here is that every strike is not illegal, and that 
workers enjoy the right to resort to strike in order to express their grievances or demands. The Court 
has opined in All India Central Government Health Scheme Employees’ Association (Delhi Branch) vs. 
Union of India and Others (WP(C) No. 5471 of 2008) that if the strike is illegal, there is no question 
of payment of any wages. Even if a strike is legal, but unjustified, there have been instances in which 
courts have refused wages for the period of such illegal strike. It hence follows as a corollary that where 
the strike is illegal or unjustified, the concerned workmen would not be 
entitled to strike wages. In addition, as held in Crompton Greaves Ltd. vs. 
Workmen (AIR 1978 SC 1489), whenever workers would resort to the use 
of coercion, violence or acts of sabotage during the strike period, they 
would render themselves disentitled to claim wages for the strike period.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/1650811/ accessed on 28/2/2014.)
The entire discussion hence boils down to the simple fact that workers would normally not earn 
wages for the period for which the dispute would continue, and this loss of earnings exerts tremendous 
pressure on their own selves and their dependents. With an already low level of earning, workers would 
seldom have any savings to fall back on. They may even get into debt traps to sustain their livelihood. 
Workers also suffer from physical injuries in case there are incidents of violence during the industrial 
dispute. Facing the wrath of the employer in the form of victimisation is another risk that workers may 
be exposed to. There have been instances when union leaders who are actively involved in protests 
and strikes have been suspended on various charges (Das and Gupta, 2013).
Such losses can of course be made good of if the dispute ends at a favourable note for the agitating 
workers. They can get rid of their hardships following increase in wages and other allowances, subject 
to the demands put forth by the workers and their fulfillment by the management.
Effects on Employers
The very first impact of an industrial dispute on the employer is stoppage of work, which, in turn, 
affects production adversely. As per the provisional figures obtained by the Labour Bureau ( Source: 
Indian Labour Journal, Vol. 5 No. 9, September 2013, p. 898) , there were 276 instances of industrial 
disputes (strikes and lock-outs taken together) during 2012 in both State and Central spheres. Work-
stoppages as a consequence involved 1,225,042 workers with a time-loss of 3.39 million man-days. 
Though large in themselves, these figures are still redeeming, as against 389 disputes involving 734,723 Spotlight
When the strike is illegal or 
unjustified, the concerned 
workmen would not be entitled 
to strike wages.

workers with a time-loss of 14.33 million man-days during 2011 ( provisional ). In 2012 the public 
sector had accounted for 1.71 million man-days or 50.43 per cent of the total time-loss. Among the 
States, Tamil Nadu alone was responsible for a time loss of 0.82 million man-days (i.e., 24.25 per 
cent), followed by Haryana, West Bengal, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka with 0.38, 0.37, 
0.33, 0.28 and 0.26 million man-days respectively of the total time loss. Amongst the various industry 
divisions, ‘manufacturing’ had registered a time-loss of 1.55 million man-days (i.e., 45.65 per cent of 
the total time-loss). 
As a simple rule of economics, the average cost of production goes on increasing during any industrial 
dispute leading to work-stoppage due to fixed expenses that continue to be incurred though the variable 
costs (e.g., wages and cost of raw materials) are nil during the stoppage. It also results in a fall in sales, 
leading to a fall in profits. Stoppage of production not only reduces the profit-making capacity of the 
employer, but also affects delivery commitments. Idle machinery may get dysfunctional during the 
phase of work stoppage. The employer may also have to incur additional expenses on the safety and 
security of the factory premises during the period of unrest. Losses may be incurred due to destruction 
of property and physical intimidation if the dispute takes a violent turn. Economic costs of a dispute 
are escalated in case the dispute ends with a decision favouring the economic demands of the workers.
Apart from the immediate economic effects, industrial disputes may have non-economic implica-
tions like loss of goodwill of the employer and bitter labour relations. Psychological distress out of 
the dispute can also have a bearing on the employer’s peace of mind. Incidences of disputes may mar 
the image of the establishment as a good employer to prospective job applicants.
The employer can resort to various methods in order to make good of the economic loss as a re-
sult of a dispute. The unsold stock of goods in the inventory can be sold during the dispute to meet 
prior business commitments. The employer can speed up production with additional facilities and 
overtime. Following the principles of economics, whereby excess demand for a commodity fetches a 
higher price, the commodity produced by the employer can be sold at a higher price once the dispute 
is resolved. In case the employer has multiple plants, production facilities can be shifted to the other 
plant(s) which are out of the ambit of the dispute. The employer can simply conduct a cost-benefit 
analysis in such a case. As Sinha, Sinha and Shekhar (2006) point out, if the employer ascertains 
that the costs of agreeing to the terms of the agitated union are less than the anticipated costs of the 
dispute, the employer would avert the strike or alternately face the strike. However, the analysis may 
come out to be incorrect and the dispute may turn to be in favour of the workers, thus imposing ad-
ditional expenses on the employer. 
Effects on Other Stakeholders and Economy
The effects of industrial disputes are not restricted only to the two parties involved in such dispute, 
i.e., workers and employers; disputes have their impact on others as well, like the consumers of the 
commodity, suppliers to the establishment which is facing the dispute, and the economy as a whole. 
The direct effects of a strike on the affected firm may be only one component of the total impact 
resulting from the action; the existence of indirect or “spillover” effects can have important implica-
tions for the economic performance of competing firms as well (McDonald and Bloch, 1999). Cus-
tomers of the affected commodity also face inconveniences due to limited supply of the commodity 
in the market. The more essential the commodity the greater would be the inconvenience. Strikes and 
lock-outs in public utility services create greater inconvenience to the public at large. As long as the 
dispute continues and production is halted, the business of the suppliers to the affected firm would 
also suffer. Prolonged industrial disputes also lead to wastage of national resources and thus have an 
adverse effect on national productivity and national income. Overall there is an air of negativity and 
bitterness in the industrial relations of the country.

Industrial Conflict and Disputes 7.17
Exhibit 7.6 Nationwide Bank Strike: Crippling Trade and Industry
Public sector bank employees had embarked on a two days’ countrywide strike on August 22 and 
23 2012, in opposition to the proposed reforms in the Banking Regulation Act, that would ease 
mergers and allow more private capital, including foreign investment in the banking sector. The 
strike was called by all major unions, including the All India Bank Employees’ Association and 
the All India Bank Officers’ Association under the banner of the United Forum of Bank Unions 
(UFBU). Traders and industrialists raised their protests against the strike that was scheduled on 
a Wednesday and Thursday, Monday already being a gazetted holiday.
The UFBU declared the strike to be successful on the very first day, with all public and private 
sector banks and even rural banks closing their shutters in opposition of the reforms. Though 
ATMs remained operational, they were apprehended to run out of cash by the end of the second 
day of the strike.
(Adapted from: Banks down shutters, trade and industry suffer, The Telegraph, Ranchi, 23/8/2012.)
Summing up the discussion we may say that the issue of industrial peace has assumed vital impor-
tance to the Government. The effects of industrial disputes are a reminder that unless there is a proper 
equilibrium between the capabilities and demands of the employers and the legitimate expectations of 
the working class, not only these two parties to dispute but also the industry, the general public and 
the economy as a whole would have to bear all the consequences.
Summary
rConflict is inherent in the interests of capital and labour as parties to the employment relation-
ship. Industrial dispute refers to any disagreement between workers and employers on issues 
like wages, working conditions and other employment matters, between rival unions, or even 
between employers and employers.
rFactors behind organisational conflicts can be clubbed as: industry-related factors, organisation-
related factors, individual-related factors, government-related factors, and miscellaneous factors. 
rThe traditional view on conflict has a negative, rigid and formalistic approach to conflict and as 
per the modern view, conflict is considered to be an unavoidable fact of organisational life and 
should be measured in terms of functionality.
rConflict is somewhat general as a concept; when conflict acquires concrete and specific mani-
festations, it becomes an industrial dispute.
rWorkers resort to various methods like strikes, gherao,  go-slow and work-to-rule as a manifesta-
tion of their discontentment and conflict with the employer. A strike is a powerful weapon in the 
hands of workers to get their demands accepted by the management. Strikes can be classified 
on the basis of consent of union, techniques adopted, generic purpose, etc.
rA lock-out is the weapon in the hands of the employer to manifest an industrial dispute. It is the 
employer who initiates a lock-out. Neither strike nor lock-out can severe the employer-employee 
relation in an organisation.
rWhatever is the form of manifestation of disputes, both strikes and lock-outs have far-reaching 
impacts not only on the workers but also on the employers, the consumers of the products of the 
affected industry, the suppliers to the establishment(s), and the economy as a whole.

rUnless there is a proper equilibrium between the capabilities and demands of the employers 
and the legitimate expectations of the working class, not only these two parties to dispute but 
also the industry, the general public and the economy as a whole would have to bear all the 
resultant adversities.

Objective Type Questions
I. State True or False
(i)General strikes are similar to political strikes.
(ii)The traditional view of conflicts is proposed by human relations theorists.
(iii) Workers involved in a legal strike can get strike wage even if the strike is unjustified.
(iv) Terms of employment can be categorised as an individual-related reason of conflicts.
(v)A quickie is for shorter duration than a sit-down.
Answers:  (i) True, (ii) False, (iii) False, (iv) False, (v) True

(i)Work-stoppages which involve less than ____ workers are not included in records compiled by 
the Labour Bureau.
(ii)A ______ is persuasive in nature, but negative in approach.
(iii) Encirclement in ____ involves forcible possession of the industrial establishment and ouster of 
the real owner.
(iv) Modern view proposes conflicts to be measured in terms of ____.
(v)In ___ strikes no pressure is applied against the primary employer.

      TUDY
Air India: Grounded by Strikes
The national carrier of India, Air India (AI) is reeling under one problem or the other. Steeped in losses 
and thriving on taxpayers’ heard-earned money, AI pilots struck work yet again on 7th May 2012, over 
demands for better career progression. The airlines management took a tough stand by sacking 101 
pilots, including 10 office bearers of the Indian Pilots’ Guild (IPG), the 450-member association of 
erstwhile AI pilots which was also derecognised. This marked the sixth strike in the company since 
2009 and the fourth by its pilots in less than a year. The IPG reacted with the allegation that the man-
agement had created a ‘hostile environment’ by sacking the striking pilots and also derecognizing the 
Guild. The management took a hard stand with the opinion that the pilots have been in complete dis-
obedience of the court’s orders for the last two months and they need to call off the strike first before 
talking to the management regarding their demands. The 58 days’ protracted strike by Air India pilots 
was finally called off in early July 2012 after the Delhi High Court asked them to join duty within 48 
hours and advised the airline management to sympathetically consider their grievances, including the 
aspect of reinstatement of those pilots whose services were terminated as a consequence of their strike.
Last May when pilots had struck work by calling in sick, the national carrier had lost around `200
crores. The airline management had initially given pilots time till 6.00 pm to return to work; it even-
tually decided to act sooner and sent a team of doctors to check on the claims of the ‘sick’ pilots. It 
soon became apparent that no one needed a medical report on the pilots to know that ‘sick leave’ was 
just an excuse to be on strike. With around 300 pilots having reported sick, the Government reacted 
by sacking 10 of the striking pilots. It also derecognised the IPG, and sealed its offices. It was decided 
not to talk to the sacked pilots. On 9th May the Delhi High Court declared the strike illegal. The initial 
repercussions of the pilots calling in sick affected three international flights; however the airline was 
reported to have managed the situation by operating all the international flights in the afternoon of the 
particular day the pilots had reported sick. Flights on long-haul routes are operated by the agitating 
pilots who were demanding first class travel in routes that cost the airline the heaviest.
Pilots of AI, the highest paid employees of the organisation, are reportedly the biggest trouble-
mongers for the management. An AI captain earns somewhere around `6-12 lakhs a month. Pilots 
get to stay in five-star hotels on outstation duty and spend up to 3 nights for every flight they operate. 
Travel allowances of pilots are provided by the company.
The national carrier is plagued by several problems including poor management, excess manpower, 
apathetic attitude of its employees, few routes to fly, governmental red-tapism and bureaucracy, and last, 
but not the least, the ‘infamous’ and ill-conceived merger of AI and Indian Airlines. The Government 
is perturbed by the inconvenience faced by the passengers. The latest strike leading to cancellation of 
AI Express flights has jeopardised the career of several hundred poor workers migrating to the Gulf 
IR&LL_Ch_07.indd   20 1/1/2008   4:49:18 AM

Industrial Conflict and Disputes 7.21
for job opportunities. The agitation of the pilots has affected operations of seven prime international 
destinations in North America and Europe. It has led to a daily loss to the tune of `10-15 crores in 
addition to the existing operating losses of `21 crores. Overall the AI has incurred a record loss of 
`7,853 crores in 2011-2012. Its outstanding loans and dues amount to more than `70,000 crores, with 
no option left with the Government than clearing a `30,000 crores helpline from taxpayers’ money in 
order to keep the airline alive.

Settlement of Industrial Disputes
Desired Knowledge Competencies
cTo discuss various ways of settlement of industrial disputes.
cTo describe different statutory and non-statutory measures of dispute settlement.
cTo develop an understanding of the processes involved in conciliation machinery, reference of 
disputes to adjudication machinery, etc.
INTR ODUCTION
We have already discussed industrial disputes, the underlying causes of disputes and their all-pervasive 
impact on workers, employers, consumers, suppliers and the economy in Chapter 7. A dispute is not 
an end in itself; every conflict or dispute must be followed by its settlement, leading to cooperation, 
thus completing a full cycle. The effects of industrial disputes necessitate striking a proper balance 
between the capabilities and demands of employers on the one hand and the legitimate expectations 
of workers on the other, to ensure cordial industrial relations and lasting industrial peace. Settlement 
of disputes thus assumes paramount importance in the domain of industrial relations. Both employers 
and workers should strive to settle any discontentment or rift in their mutual relation with the help of 
the preventive machinery. Whenever the preventive machinery fails, the dispute settlement machinery 
should be brought into operation by the government to settle disputes. Overall, such machinery should 
be fair and independent for the peaceful settlement of industrial disputes to ensure the establishment and 
maintenance of good industrial relations. In this chapter we would elaborate on prevention and settle-
ment of disputes and the machinery involved therein, within the realm of labour legislations in India.
PREVENTION AND SETTLEMENT OF DISPUTES
The simplest way to settle any dispute between an employer and workers is by mutual discussions; 
this process is termed as “bargaining”. If such a bargaining process faces obstacles then the parties 
involved may ask for the intervention of a third party; the settlement process in such a case is known 
as bargaining with conciliation. However, it is not necessary that the dispute gets settled at this stage. 
IR&LL_Ch_08.indd   1 1/9/2008   11:48:13 AM

8.2 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
In case it is continued, the parties would have two possible options. They may either resort to coer-
cive methods to arrive at a settlement, or may refer the dispute to a third party for a process known 
as ‘arbitration’. We have exhaustively covered strikes and lock-outs as coercive methods of settling 
industrial disputes in Chapter 7. The focus of this chapter is on the ways to prevent and settle disputes 
beyond such coercive methods.
There are several perspectives of looking at prevention and settlement of industrial disputes. We 
have mentioned about preventive and settlement machineries in the previous section. Understanding 
the implications of industrial disputes and to protect the interests of the working class, the management 
of industrial establishments and the society, the Government has designed certain mechanisms (statu-
tory and non-statutory) to prevent the occurrence of disputes and ensure their settlement. The statu-
tory machinery comprises the following: Works Committee, conciliation, Court of Inquiry at the 
central and State-levels, and adjudication authorities consisting of Labour 
Courts, Industrial Tribunals and National Tribunals. With the sharp growth 
in the number of laws and litigations, the legal system is under great 
pressure. In order to reduce this already heavy pressure on courts efforts 
need to be made to resolve disputes by resorting to Alternative Dispute 
Resolution (ADR) methods, before they reach the court (Medha, n.d.). Spotlight

Arbitration, conciliation and mediation are the most popular tools of Alternative Dispute Resolution. 
However, the ADR is considered to be in an experimental phase in India. Hence is the necessity of 
non-statutory measures for the prevention of industrial disputes internally. These measures consist of: 
Workers’ Participation in Management (WPM), collective bargaining, grievance procedure, tripartite 
bodies, Code of Discipline and Standing Orders. Tripartite bodies include the Indian Labour Confer-
ence (ILC) and Standing Labour Committee (SLC) operating at national-level; Wage Boards and In-
dustrial Committees functioning at industry-level; and State Labour Advisory Boards at State-level. 
We can also develop an insight into dispute settlement from the point of view of the stages involved 
in the process of settlement, i.e., settlement with State-intervention and without State-intervention. 
We have explored this perspective in a subsequent section. Figure 8.1 depicts the various statutory 
and non-statutory measures of settling industrial disputes, to be explained in the very next section.
I. Statutory Measures of Settlement of Industrial Disputes (or Settlement 
Machinery)
Various statutory measures to settle industrial disputes given in the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 
have been explained here. The sections mentioned at appropriate places imply those given in the Act.
(i) Works Committee [Section 3] A Works Committee is bipartite in composition. The 
Statement of Objects and Reasons appended with the Industrial Disputes Bill, 1946 refers to Works 
Committee as an institution for the prevention and settlement of industrial disputes. The duties of such 
committees were specified to include removal of causes of friction between the employer and workmen 
in the day-to-day working of an establishment and to promote measures for securing amity and good 
relations between them. It was also mentioned in the Statement that industrial peace will be the most 
enduring where it is founded on voluntary settlement, and that Works Committees would render recourse 
to the remaining machinery provided for in the Bill for the settlement of disputes as infrequent.
Section 3 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 mandates any industrial 
establishment employing 100 or more workmen to constitute a Works 
Committee consisting of representatives of employers and workmen 
engaged in the establishment. Further, the number of representatives of 
workmen in the Committee shall not be less than the number of repre-
sentatives of the employer. The workers’ representatives shall be chosen 
in the prescribed manner from among the workmen engaged in the es-
tablishment and in consultation with their trade union, if any. It shall be 
the duty of the Works Committee to promote measures for securing and preserving amity and good 
relations between the employer and workmen and, to that end, to comment upon matters of their 
common interest or concern and endeavour to compose any material difference of opinion in respect 
of such matters. These bipartite committees are empowered to settle differences between workers and 
their employers and thus they act as a safety valve in settling disputes. We shall be talking briefly 
about bipartite committees in the section on dispute settlement with the intervention of the State. Both 
Central and State Governments have framed relevant rules under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 
concerning the size of Works Committee, selection of representatives of workers, terms of office, etc.
However, let us specify here that we have included Works Committees under statutory measures of 
dispute settlement, as the establishment of such committees is a legal binding on organisations. At the 
same time, Works Committees are also considered as an integral component of Workers’ Participation 
in Management. Hence we have mentioned these committees under non-statutory measures of dispute 
settlement as well.Spotlight
