8.4 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
(ii) Conciliation The dictionary meaning of the term ‘conciliation’ 
is “bringing of opposing parties or individuals into harmony”. As one of 
the most important methods of dispute settlement, conciliation refers to 
the process of reconciling the views of parties to a dispute and bringing 
them to an agreement. The first step in conciliation is the selection of a 
qualified conciliator, who is a neutral third party. In the next step, a 
decision is taken as to who will attend the conciliation and the cost to be 
incurred in the process. The parties are thereafter encouraged to explain 
their case and share their feelings. The process involves discussions among the parties in the presence 
of the conciliator, with the objective of exploring equitable resolutions, thus paving the way for a 
mutually acceptable settlement. The role of the conciliator is to simply listen to the parties and identify 
the issues without being judgmental. Thus the conciliator does not decide anything on behalf of either 
of the parties, but essentially provides a supportive role in finding a viable solution. The conciliator 
facilitates negotiations between the disputing parties and helps them in understanding both their conflicts 
and interests. A brainstorming session follows and possible solutions are explored. At the final stage 
when the parties reach a consensus, a written agreement is drawn up. The process of conciliation is 
not binding on the parties till they sign this agreement, which has the effect of an arbitration award.
Conciliation Machinery The conciliation machinery, as provided 
under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, is analysed here briefly. Section 
4 provides for the appointment of Conciliation Officers, to whom the 
industrial disputes shall be referred for conciliation. As per provisions of 
Section 11, a Conciliation Officer enjoys the powers of a Civil Court; he examines all facts relevant 
to the disputed matter and then gives his judgment. He is charged with the duty of holding conciliatory 
proceedings for the purpose of bringing about a fair and amicable settlement of any industrial dispute 
without delay, as given in Section 12. On the failure to arrive at a settlement, the Conciliation Officer 
shall send a full report to the appropriate Government.
The Act also empowers the Government to appoint a Board of Con-
ciliation for promoting the settlement of disputes [Section 5(1)] where 
the Conciliation Officer fails to do so within 14 days. The Board of 
Conciliation is a tripartite ad hoc body consisting of a Chairman and 
two to four other members. The mode and procedure of the functioning 
of the Board are similar to those of the Conciliation Officer. As per Sec-
tion 10(3), where the dispute is referred to the Board, the appropriate Government may prohibit the 
continuance of any strike or lock-out in connection with such dispute which may be in existence on 
the date of reference.
Section 13 of the Act provides that when a dispute has been referred to the Board of Conciliation, 
the Board may take suitable steps to induce the parties to come to a fair and amicable settlement. If 
a settlement is arrived at, the Board is required to send a report and a memorandum of the settlement 
signed by the parties to the appropriate Government. If no such settlement is arrived at, the Board is 
required to send a full report to the appropriate Government, along with its recommendations for the 
determination of the dispute. It is required to submit its report within two months of the date of the 
reference of the dispute, or within a shorter period, as determined by the appropriate Government.
Section 19 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 lays that settlement comes into operation on the 
date agreed upon by the parties to the dispute and in case no date is agreed upon, the date on which 
the memorandum of settlement is signed by the parties to the dispute. A settlement is binding for such Spotlight

10 during the pendency of conciliation proceedings.
(iii) Court of Inquiry [Section 6] In case the conciliation proceedings fail to settle an industrial 
dispute, a Court of Inquiry is appointed by the appropriate Government, as provided in Section 6 of 
the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
According to Section 6(2), a Court of Inquiry may consist of one or more independent persons as 
the appropriate Government may appoint; where it consists of two or more members, one of them 
shall be appointed as the Chairman. Sub-section 3 empowers the Court having the prescribed quorum 
to act even if the Chairman or a member is absent; however, the Court shall not act if the services of 
the Chairman have ceased to be available and till a new Chairman has been appointed. Section 11(5) 
empowers a Court of Inquiry, if it so thinks fit, to appoint one or more persons having special knowl-
edge of the matter under consideration as assessor(s) to advise it in the proceeding before it. Under 
Section 14 the Court shall inquire into the matters referred to it and report thereon to the appropriate 
Government within six months from the date of commencement of inquiry.
(iv) Adjudication The ultimate legal remedy for the settlement of 
an unresolved dispute is marked with the reference of such a dispute 
to adjudication by the appropriate Government. Adjudication may be 
described as the process which involves intervention by a third party 
appointed by the appropriate Government, with or without the consent 
of the parties to the dispute, for the purpose of settling such a dispute. 
If both parties to the dispute agree to refer the dispute for adjudication 
at their own accord, then such reference of dispute to adjudication is 
considered voluntary; however it is compulsory when reference is made 
to adjudication without the consent of either or both the parties.
Adjudication Machinery The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 empowers the appropriate 
Government to provide a three-tier adjudication machinery with the following constituents: Labour 
Courts, Industrial Tribunals and National Tribunals. Let us talk about each of these constituent members 
of the machinery in details now.Spotlight

8.6 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
(a) Labour Courts Labour Courts as a component of the adjudication machinery apart from 
Industrial Tribunals came into existence under the Industrial Disputes (Amendment and Miscellaneous 
Provisions) Act, 1956, by which the original Section 7 was substituted by a new one. The present 
Section 7 empowers the appropriate Government to constitute one or more Labour Courts for the 
adjudication of industrial disputes relating to any of the following matters (as enlisted in the Second
Schedule of the Act) and for performing such other function as may be assigned to them under the Act: 
1. The propriety or legality of an order passed by an employer under standing orders;
2. The application and interpretation of standing orders;
3. Discharge or dismissal of workmen including re-instatement of, or grant of relief to, workmen 
wrongfully dismissed;
4. Withdrawal of any customary concession or privilege;
5. Illegality or otherwise of a strike or lock-out; and
6. All matters other than those specified in the Third Schedule.
According to Section 7(2), a Labour Court shall consist of only one person who shall be appointed 
by the appropriate Government. Sub-section 3 of Section 7 provides that no person shall be appointed 
as the presiding officer of a Labour Court, unless:
1. he is, or has been, a judge of a High Court; or 
2. he has, for a period not less than three years, been a District Judge or an Additional District 
Judge; or
3. he has held any judicial office in India for not less than seven years; or 
4. he has been the presiding officer of a Labour Court constituted under any Provincial Act for not 
less than five years.
As the Court mentions in Ramkrishan Ramnath Bidi Factory vs. Labour Court, Nagpur [(1963)
ILLJ 417 Bom], the Labour Court is essentially an authority for the avowed purpose of adjudication 
of industrial disputes, and would be governed by all the principles of industrial adjudication. (Adapted
from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/751360/ accessed on 2/1/2014.)
We shall be reviewing the powers and duties of Labour Court in Chapter 15, under the Industrial 
Disputes Act, 1947.
(b) Industrial Tribunals Industrial Tribunals were created for the first time by the Industrial 
Disputes Act, 1947. Section 7A of the Act empowers the appropriate Government to constitute one 
or more Industrial Tribunals for the adjudication of industrial disputes relating to any matter, whether 
specified in the Second Schedule or the Third Schedule and for performing such other functions as 
may be assigned to them under the Act. Similar to a Labour Court, a Tribunal shall consist of only 
one person to be appointed by the appropriate Gover nment. Further, a person shall not be qualified for 
appointment as the presiding officer of a Tribunal unless he is, or has been, a Judge of a High Court, 
or he has, for a period of not less than three years, been a District Judge or an Additional District 
Judge. It is provided by Section 7A(4) that the appropriate Government may appoint two persons as 
assessors to advise the Tribunal in the proceedings before it.
InThe Bharat Bank Ltd., Delhi vs. The Employees of the Bharat Bank Ltd., Delhi and the Bharat 
Bank Employees’ Union Delhi (AIR 1950 SC 188), the Supreme Court had considered the question as 
to whether an Industrial Tribunal constituted under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 was a Court for 
the purpose of Article 136 of the Constitution. It was held that though the Tribunal has all the trap-
pings of a Court, but its award was not appealable to the Apex Court. (Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.
org/doc/653417/ accessed on 3/1/2014.)
IR&LL_Ch_08.indd   6 1/9/2008   11:48:14 AM

Settlement of Industrial Disputes 8.7
The Industrial Tribunal is a judicial body that is responsible for the ad-
judication of industrial disputes relating to any matter whether specified in 
the Second Schedule or the Third Schedule of the Industrial Disputes Act, 
1947. Matters related to the Second Schedule have already been covered 
under Labour Courts. Those related to the Third Schedule are as follows:
1. Wages, including the period and mode of payment;
2. Compensatory and other allowances;
3. Hours of work and rest intervals;
4. Leave with wages and holidays;
5. Bonus, profit sharing, provident fund and gratuity;
6. Shift working otherwise than in accordance with standing orders;
7. Classification by grades;
8. Rules of discipline;
9. Rationalisation;
10. Retrenchment of workmen and closure of establishment; and
11. Any other matter that may be prescribed.
Industrial Tribunals, as given in Section 11, shall have the same powers vested in a Civil Court 
when trying a suit, in matters like: enforcing the attendance of any person and examining him on oath; 
compelling the production of documents and material objects; issuing commissions for the examina-
tion of witnesses, etc. A Tribunal shall hold its proceedings expeditiously and shall submit its award 
to the appropriate Government within the specified period (Section 15).
(c) National Tribunals As per Section 7B of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the Central Govern-
ment may constitute one or more National Tribunals for the adjudication of industrial disputes which 
involve questions of national importance or are of such a nature that industrial establishments situated 
in more than one State are likely to be interested in, or are affected by them. In other words, these 
tribunals are meant for those disputes which, as is suggestive of the name, involve issues of national 
importance or issues which are likely to affect the industrial establishments of more than one State. It 
is thus evident that the span of jurisdiction of National Tribunals is wider than those of the other two 
components of the adjudication machinery discussed earlier.
Sub-section 2 of Section 7B provides that a National Tribunal shall 
consist of only one person to be appointed by the Central Government; 
sub-section 3 lays that a person shall not be qualified for appointment 
as the presiding officer of a National Tribunal unless he is, or has been, 
a Judge of a High Court. Similar to Industrial Tribunals, the Central 
Government may, if it so thinks fit, appoint two persons as assessors to 
advise the National Tribunal in the proceeding before it. According to the 
provisions of Section 7C, presiding officers of National Tribunals should 
be independent persons, below the age of 65 years. We shall be taking 
into account the powers and duties of National Tribunals in Chapter 15.
It may be noted here that the procedures and powers of different authorities laid down under 
Section 11 of the Act are equally applicable in the case of Conciliation Officers, Board of Conciliation, 
Court of Inquiry, Labour Court and Tribunals.Spotlight

8.8 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Exhibit 8.1 Central Government Industrial Tribunal-cum-Labour Courts
The Central Government Industrial Tribunal-cum-Labour Courts (CGIT-cum-LCs) are set up 
as per the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 for adjudication of industrial disputes 
arising in the Central Sphere. The objective of setting up CGIT-cum-LCs is maintaining peace 
and harmony in the industrial sector. Due to increasing awareness about their rights and about 
labour laws among the workers, there is a gradual increase in the number of cases being filed 
under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 before these courts. Restructuring of workforce with the 
application of latest technology in the industries has also resulted in retrenchment, declaration 
of surplus, etc., which has further led to an increase in workers’ grievances. The CGIT-cum-LCs 
aim at quick and timely disposal of industrial disputes through adjudication, such that industrial 
growth does not suffer on account of any widespread industrial unrest.
There are 22 CGIT-cum-LCs set up in various States, out of which 10 are under Non-Plan 
and 12 under Plan Scheme. The CGIT-cum-LC No.1, Mumbai and CGIT-cum-LC, Kolkata also 
function as National Tribunals. These courts are headed by presiding officers who are selected 
from amongst serving or retired High Court Judges or District or (serving or retired) Additional 
District Judges.
(Adapted from: www.labour.gov.in/content/division/central-govt-industrial-tribunal.php accessed on 
2/1/2014.)
Reference of Disputes to the Adjudication Machinery [Section 10] Now that we have 
explained the three-tier structure of the adjudication machinery, let us quickly describe the process 
of reference of disputes to the adjudication machinery. The appropriate Government may refer an 
unresolved dispute to a Labour Court or Industrial Tribunal or National Tribunal for adjudication. We 
have already specified that any matter which is important for the industry as a whole and is listed in 
the Second or Third Schedule may be referred for adjudication to a Labour Court or Industrial Tribunal. 
However, as per Section 10(1)(d), where a dispute is pertaining to a matter specified in the Third 
Schedule, and is not likely to affect more than one hundred workmen, the appropriate Government may 
refer it to a Labour Court. In case a dispute involves any question of national importance or is of such 
nature that industrial establishments situated in more than one State are likely to be interested in or be 
affected by the dispute, then as per Section 10(1A), the Central Government may refer such dispute or 
any relevant matter that is related to the dispute to the National Tribunal. Further, sub-section (2) of
this section provides that where the parties to an industrial dispute apply in the prescribed manner, 
whether jointly or separately, for a reference of the dispute to a Board, Labour Court, Tribunal or 
National Tribunal, the appropriate Government, if satisfied that the persons applying represent the 
majority of each party, shall make the reference accordingly.
II. Non-Statutory Measures of Settlement of Disputes (or Preventive Machinery)
(i) Workers’ Participation in Management Workers’ Participation in Management is a 
mechanism by which the workers of an establishment are allowed to participate actively in the decision-
making process of the establishment and to have a say in its management. Hailed as a powerful 
behavioural tool, WPM promotes a sense of belongingness in workers and checks any kind of 
IR&LL_Ch_08.indd   8 1/9/2008   11:48:14 AM

Settlement of Industrial Disputes 8.9
exploitation of workers by the owners or top management. Workers involve themselves in the 
management of an organisation by way of information sharing, joint consultation and suggestion 
schemes. Thus WPM is essentially democracy at work, and is instrumental in reducing industrial unrest 
and in ensuring higher productivity, increased commitment and overall increased growth of the economy.
The various forms of WPM prevalent in India are: Works Committee, 
Joint Management Council, Shop Council, Joint Council andUnit Coun-
cil. Works Committees are intended to promote measures for securing 
and preserving cordial relations between employer and workmen and 
to opine on matters of common interest or concern. These committees 
comprise equal number of representatives of employers and employees in 
the industry concerned. Joint Management Councils  are established in any 
establishment employing 500 or more workers and have equal representation of workers and manage-
ment. These councils are charged with the general duty of promoting and assisting in the management 
of the undertaking in a more efficient, orderly and economical manner, ensuring amiable relations 
between the employer and workers and building understanding and trust between them. These councils 
were established for the first time in 1950; further, since 1975 the two-tier participation called Shop
Councils  at shop-level and Joint Councils  were introduced. Shop Councils  have been incorporated 
in big industrial establishments employing more than 500 workers, with each council having equal 
representation of workers and management. The functions of these councils are to achieve increased 
production, productivity and overall efficiency of the shop or department, eliminate wastage, utilise 
capacity and manpower of the establishment to the optimum level, and to support the management in 
achieving the monthly or yearly production targets. Joint Councils  are prescribed for every industrial 
unit employing 500 or more workers. These councils are responsible for the settlement of matters un-
resolved by Unit Councils . Each organisation shall decide on the number of councils to be set up for 
the services it has, in consultation with the recognised union(s). A Unit Council  is required to be set 
up in each unit of an organisation or service employing 100 or more persons. Such a council would 
have equal number of representatives of workers and management as its members. The number of Unit 
Councils  and the departments to be attached to each council of the establishment is to be decided by 
the employer in consultation with the recognised union(s). The decisions of Unit Councils  are to be 
taken on the basis of consensus and not by a process of voting.
For detailed explanation of Workers’ Participation in Management and its various aspects, refer to 
Chapter 11.
(ii) Collective Bargaining Collective bargaining is the term used 
to describe a situation in which “the essential conditions of employment 
are determined by a bargaining process undertaken by representatives 
of a group of workers on the one hand and of one or more employers 
on the other” (Yoder, 1959). It includes negotiation, administration and 
enforcement of written contracts between workers and their employers and the process of resolving 
labour-management conflicts.
We have explained collective bargaining and its various facets in Chapter 5.
(iii) Grievance Procedure The First National Commission on Labour (1969) in India visualised 
grievances as being those “arising out of complaints affecting one or more individual workers in 
respect of their conditions of work and not disputes over matters of general applicability to all”. 
An organisation establishes a grievance procedure to give avenue to an employee to file his/her 
dissatisfaction (Mante-Meija and Enid, 1991). The Model Grievance Procedure was drawn up in the Spotlight

Successful handling of grievances helps an organisation to contain mat-

(iv) Tripartite Bodies The term “tripartite” refers to representatives of three bodies. Industrial 
peace being an area of concern, the Government of India, after Independence, had laid stress on the 
need for consultation between the representatives of labour, management and the Government in 
tripartite and bipartite forums. With its tripartite structure, the International Labour Organisation (ILO) 
has been a proponent of strong tripartite cooperation, in which the “social partners” play an important 
role in shaping government policy on a wide range of issues (Trebilcock, n.d.). In response to the 
constant pressure of the ILO to implement tripartite structures in the area of industrial relations, the 
Government of India constituted various tripartite bodies like the Indian Labour Conference, the 
Standing Labour Committee and Industrial Committees to deliberate on various issues relating to 
labour and management that would have formidable impact on the country’s labour policies and 
legislations. Tripartism and its evolution in India have been covered extensively in Chapter 10.
The principal aim of the tripartite consultative machinery is “to bring 
the parties together for mutual settlement of differences in a spirit of 
cooperation and goodwill” (Chhabra and Suri, 2007, p. 178). The tripar-
tite Indian Labour Conference and its tripartite Standing Labour Com-
mittee are the premier policy advisory bodies in the field of industrial 
relations at the national-level, constituted to suggest ways to prevent 
industrial disputes. The Government had adopted the annual tripartite 
conference, initially known as the Tripartite National Labour Conference, 
held for the first time in the year 1942, on the model of the Interna-
tional Labour Conference. It was subsequently renamed as Indian Labour 
Conference since 1944. The underlying philosophy was to attain active 
and willing cooperation of capital and labour post-World War II through State-consultation with these 
two partners of industrial production during such annual conferences. As an apex national-level tri-
partite body, the ILC is the testing ground of tripartite consultations. The primary functions of the ILC 
are: to promote consistency in labour legislations; to streamline the procedure for settlement of indus-
trial disputes; and to discuss matters of national importance between employers and workers. The ILC 
advises the Government on any matter referred to it for advice, considering suggestions made by the 
States and representatives of the organisations of workers and employers (Chhabra and Suri, 2007).

In the 1950s and 1960s the Government had constituted various Wage

8.12 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
The concept of Industrial Committees as tripartite bodies with equal representation from employers 
and workers sides had emerged in the Indian Labour Conference of 1944. The very first Industrial 
Committee was formed in the year 1948 in the plantation industry, which is considered to be one of 
the industries having the highest labour absorption in the country. This was followed by other indus-
tries like coal mining, jute, minerals other than coal, leather, cotton textiles, etc. The basic objective 
behind setting up of these committees was to deal with problems specific to the industries in which 
they were set up.
State Labour Advisory Boards, as is indicated by the name itself, are tripartite bodies set up in 
nearly all States, with equal representation of workers and employers to advise the State Governments 
on all matters pertaining to labour. A typical example is the State Level Child Labour Advisory Board 
established in various States to look into issues related to child labour. 
(v) Code of Discipline The Code of Discipline is a set of self-imposed and mutually agreed 
upon voluntary principles of discipline and cordial relations between management and workers of both 
public and private sector enterprises. In the 15thIndian Labour Conference held in July 1957, certain 
general principles to be followed by both labour and management for their mutual interest as also for 
the common interest of the society and the nation were laid down through tripartite consultation. The 
Code of Discipline was finally approved by the 16th Indian Labour Conference held in the next year. 
It is a code of conduct both for workers and management, and it provides for the voluntary and mutual

(vi) Standing Orders The Standing Orders of any establishment 
regulate the conditions of employment of a worker from the stage of 
his entry to the establishment to that of exit from the establishment. 
The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 was passed 
so that employers of industrial establishments define with sufficient 
precision the conditions of employment under them and to also make the said conditions known to 
workmen employed in such establishments. Standing Orders define the conditions of employment in 
an organisation and matters related to discharge, misconduct, etc. and act as a code of conduct for 
workers during their tenure with their employer. Thus Standing Orders form a regulatory pattern for 
industrial relations.
STAGES IN THE SETTLEMENT OF INDUSTRIAL DISPUTES
As mentioned earlier, we can also view the process of settlement of disputes in terms of the stages 
involved in lines with Sinha, Sinha and Shekhar (2006). For this purpose, we may split the process 
into two parts: settlement with State-intervention and without State-intervention. However, most of 
the stages as per this classification have previously been reviewed under statutory and non-statutory 
measures of settling disputes. Settlement without State-intervention includes collective bargaining and 
voluntary arbitration. Settlement with State-intervention includes: compulsory setting up of bipartite 
committees; compulsory collective bargaining; initiation of compulsory investigation; compulsory 
conciliation and mediation; and compulsory arbitration and adjudication. This section features expla-
nation of all these measures.
I. Settlement without State Intervention
(i) Collective Bargaining We have already touched upon collective bargaining as a non-statutory 
measure in a previous section.
(ii) V oluntary Arbitration Let us first understand the concept of arbitration here. Generally 
speaking, arbitration refers to the process by which the parties to any dispute submit their differences 
to the judgment of an impartial person (or group) appointed by mutual 
consent or by any statutory provision. An arbitration system authorises 
a third party to decide how a dispute should be resolved (Padhi, 2012). 
Arbitration process may be either binding or non-binding. Binding 
arbitration produces a third party decision that the parties to the dispute 
must follow, even though they may disagree with the decision. Non-
binding arbitration, on the other hand, produces a third party decision 
that the parties concerned may not accept.Spotlight

8.14 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Arbitration finds application in the settlement of conflicts since quite a 
long time in India. Mahatma Gandhi had propagated the practice of vol-
untary arbitration in the textile industry in Ahmedabad. In fact, the Textile 
Labour Association Ahmedabad provides for voluntary arbitration. In 1957 
provisions for voluntary arbitration were inserted in Section 10A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Arbitration was incorporated in the Code 
of Discipline in 1958. In the Indian Labour Conference in 1962 it was decided that arbitration would 
be preferred after conciliation method fails, except in cases where the employer prefers adjudication.
In voluntary arbitration the parties willingly and by mutual consent refer their dispute to a third 
party, known as the arbitrator, under such circumstances in which both parties disagree on their own 
argument and they feel that any bargaining process is ineffectual and coercive methods would not 
yield positive outcomes. An arbitrator may be a single person or a panel. As per Section 10A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, there must be an arbitration agreement signed by the parties thereto. 
Employers and workmen who are not parties to the arbitration agreement but are concerned in the 
dispute, shall be given an opportunity of presenting their case before the arbitrator(s). The arbitrator(s) 
shall investigate the dispute and submit to the appropriate Government the arbitration award signed by 
the arbitrator(s). However, the award given by the third party is not binding on the parties to dispute, 
whereby the significance of voluntary arbitration is diluted. Nevertheless, it is usually a less expensive 
and speedier method of settling a dispute than resolving it in court.
The First National Commission on Labour (1969) had foreseen that with the growth of collective 
bargaining and the general acceptance of recognition of representative unions and the improved at-
titude of management, there would be wider acceptance of voluntary arbitration. It had even advised 
employers to encourage voluntary arbitration and wean away reluctant employers from recourse to 
third party intervention.
II. Settlement with State Intervention
Role of State Before we get into the details of the process of 
settlement of industrial disputes, let us understand the role of State in 
dispute settlement. Industrial peace being a serious issue, the Government 
makes continuous efforts to ensure peaceful and harmonious industrial 
relations. The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 is reflective of this very 
concern of the State. In Narendra Kumar Sen vs. All India Industrial Disputes (Labour Appellate) 
Tribunal [(1953) 55 Bom. LR 125], the Court has observed that the Act was passed with the following 
objectives: to bring about industrial peace in the country; to avoid conflicts between employers and 
labour; to prevent strikes and lock-outs; and to ensure that production does not suffer by reason of 
constant and continuous labour troubles.
Industrial relations are not restricted to the concern of labour and management alone; the State is 
an equally important stakeholder. Justification of the need for intervention of the State in industrial 
disputes is guided by the question as to whether the dispute is of such magnitude as to disturb industrial 
peace and hamper production. Thus the concern of the State in matters relating to labour, especially 
settlement of industrial disputes, is a product of its obligations to protect the interests of working class, 
while at the same time boosting the manufacturers, thus fostering economic growth.

353], the Court is of the opinion that if the Government considers that the workmen have no such Reflection

The following are the ways in which State intervention is possible in settlement of industrial disputes:
(i) Compulsory setting up of bipartite committees
(ii) Compulsory collective bargaining
(iii) Initiation of compulsory investigation
(iv) Provision for conciliation and mediation
(v) Compulsory arbitration and adjudication
Let us describe each of these measures now.
(i) Compulsory Setting up of Bipartite Committees As is evident from the name itself, a bi-
partite committee is made up of two parties: representatives of workers and their employer at the 
plant-level or at industry-level. The bipartite machinery to settle industrial disputes in India was es-
tablished as early as in 1920; a few joint committees were set up by the Government of India in 
Indian Railways and Government Printing Presses. TISCO in Jamshedpur was the pioneer in private 
sector to set up joint committees. Chapter 10 provides a comprehensive coverage of bipartism in 
Indian context.
(ii) Compulsory Collective Bargaining To refuse to bargain collec-
tively in good faith by a recognised trade union and an employer has been 
included in the list of unfair labour practices in the Fifth Schedule of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Collective bargaining has been explained 
earlier in this chapter. However, in certain cases, the State may intervene 
and mandate workers and employers to enter into a formal collective 
bargaining process through their representatives; the underlying objective is to ensure that the parties 
settle their disputes through mutual discussions and negotiations before they resort to coercive methods.Spotlight

8.16 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
(iii) Initiation of Compulsory Investigation Court of Inquiry is a statutory machinery responsible 
for investigation into matters of industrial dispute. We have detailed about Courts of Inquiry, their 
structure and functioning under statutory measures of dispute settlement.
(iv) Provision for Conciliation and Mediation ‘Conciliation’ and 
‘mediation’ are two terms that are often used interchangeably. ILO 
(1983) has defined conciliation as “the practice by which the services 
of a neutral third party are used in a dispute as a means of helping the 
disputing parties to reduce the extent of their differences and to arrive 
at an amicable settlement or agreed solution. It is a process of orderly 
or rational discussion under the guidance of the conciliator.” Brown and Marriott (2011) view media-
tion as a facilitative process in which the disputing parties engage the assistance of an impartial third 
party, the mediator, who helps them to try to arrive at an agreed resolution of their dispute. According 
to these authors, the mediator has no authority to make any decisions that are binding on them, but 
uses certain procedures, techniques and skills to help them to negotiate an agreed resolution of their 
dispute without adjudication. The authority of the mediator vests on the approval of the parties that 
he should facilitate their negotiations.
The Parliament of India has made a clear distinction between conciliation and mediation by way 
of two distinct statutes. Section 30(1) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 permits the arbitral 
tribunal to “use mediation, conciliation or other procedures” for the purpose of reaching settlement; 
this makes it evident that the two terms are used with different connotations. As per the various provi-
sions in the Act, the ‘conciliator’, apart from assisting the parties to reach a settlement, is also permit-
ted to make “proposals for a settlement” and “formulate the terms of a possible settlement” or “refor-
mulate the terms” (Rao, n.d.). The Civil Procedure Code (Amendment) Act, 1999 also speaks of 
‘conciliation’ and ‘mediation’ as different concepts. Several authors opine that the role of the ‘con-
ciliator’ in India is pro-active and interventionist, while the role of the ‘mediator’ is restricted to that 
of a ‘facilitator’. Nevertheless, both these terms refer to some kind of third-party intervention in vol-
untary settlement of disputes.
(v) Compulsory Arbitration and Adjudication We have talked about 
voluntary arbitration under settlement of disputes without intervention 
of State, whereby the parties willingly and by mutual consent refer their 
dispute to a third party, known as the arbitrator. Compulsory arbitration, 
on the other hand, is a non-binding, adversarial process in which parties to 
the dispute have to accept the arbitration without any willingness on their 
part. In case one of the parties feels aggrieved by any act of the other, it may apply to the appropriate 
Government to refer the dispute to adjudication machinery. The State may decide to adopt compul-
sory arbitration to resolve a dispute under circumstances in which it thinks that industrial production 
should not be compromised due to work-stoppage as a consequence of a strike or lock-out. Thus, 
under compulsory arbitration, the parties are forced to arbitration by the State when they fail to arrive 
at a settlement by a voluntary method. In this process one or more arbitrators hear the arguments of 
the parties to the dispute and issue a non-binding judgment on the merits after an expedited hearing. 
Compulsory arbitration leaves no scope for strikes and lock-outs; it takes away a party’s right to have 
any dispute with the other party.Spotlight

RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE SECOND NATIONAL COMMISSION
ON LABOUR
Following are the recommendations of the Second National Commission on Labour (2002) on matters 
pertaining to settlement of industrial disputes:
rIt is necessary to provide a minimum level of protection to managerial and other employer 
against unfair dismissals or removals through adjudication by Labour Court or Labour Relations 
Commission or arbitration.
rPresently Central legislations relating to labour relations are the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, 
the Trade Unions Act, 1926 and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946. In addi-
tion, there is the Sales Promotion Employees Act, 1976 and some other Acts for particular trades 
or employments, besides State-level enactments. The Commission recommends that provisions 
of all these laws may be judicially constituted into a single law called the Labour Management 
Relations or the Law on Labour Management Relations. 
rIn case of socially essential services like water supply, medical service, sanitation, electricity and 
transport, when a dispute is not settled through mutual negotiations, there may be a strike ballot. 
If the ballot shows that 51 per cent of workers are in favour of a strike, it should be taken that 
a strike has taken place, and the dispute must forthwith be referred to compulsory arbitration.
rA system of Labour Courts, Lok Adalats and Labour Relations Commissions has been envisaged 
as the integrated adjudicatory system in labour matters.
rLabour Courts and Industrial Tribunals should be merged, and this system will deal not only with 
matters arising out of employment relations but also trade disputes in matters such as wages, 
social security, safety and health, welfare and working conditions and so on.
rIndustrial disputes that are not settled in conciliation should go for either voluntary arbitration 
or by arbitrators maintained by the Labour Relations Commission or adjudication. In the case 
of essential services the dispute should go for compulsory arbitration; in other cases, it should 
go for adjudication. Arbitrators should be chosen from eminent persons in industry, conciliators, 
trade unionists and labour judiciary.
rLabour Courts must be given powers to issue decrees or initiate contempt proceedings for non-
implementation or non-compliance of awards.
rA Central Labour Relations Commission (LRC) should be set up for establishments in Central-
Sphere, and a State Labour Relations Commission should be set up for those in the State-Sphere. 
Above both the Central and State Labour Relations Commissions, there will be the National 
Labour Relations Commission to hear appeals against the decisions of the two other Commis-
sions. The National LRC, Central LRC and the State LRCs will be autonomous and independent. 
rTo make conciliation effective, it is necessary to improve the status, competence and calibre of 
conciliation officers through proper recruitment, training and placement. A Labour and Judicial 
Service can be formed.
rV oluntary resolution of disputes should be encouraged over legalistic approach of settlement of 
disputes through adjudication. Labour administration should encourage better human resource 
management practices.
rThere should be a legislative framework for voluntary dispute settlement. A basic prerequisite 
is to place a system of recognition of negotiating agency on the statute. The responsibility of 
conducting verification of trade union membership for recognition of trade unions should be 
vested in the Central and State LRCs.

8.18 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
rThe Works Committee required to be constituted under Section 3 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 
should be substituted by an Industrial Relations Committee to promote in-house dispute settlement.
rThe Indian Labour Conference should be an effective forum for review, consultation and formu-
lation or evolution of perspective and policies; it has to be as representative as possible. Some 
means must be found to include representatives from the unorganised sector and from central 
organisations that are not affiliated to central trade union federations.
rIn lines with the proposals in the Draft Indian Labour Code for the strengthening of the Indian 
Labour Conference, the ILC can be used as a sounding board for proposals of legislations. Sug-
gested functions of the ILC would include: review of labour situation; consideration of Conven-
tions and Recommendations of the ILO for adoption; sounding board for legislative proposals, etc.
rThe ILC should set up Tripartite Standing Committees to consider and review problems, legisla-
tions and implementation into main areas. 
rLabour disputes between a foreign invested enterprise and its employees may be settled through 
consultations between the concerned parties, failing which, the parties may apply to the labour 
dispute mediation committee of the enterprise. Further, if mediation fails, the parties may apply 
to the labour dispute arbitration committee. Either party that is not satisfied with the adjudica-
tion of arbitration may bring the case to the people’s court of the district or country where the 
enterprise is located within 15 days upon the reception of the adjudication.
Summary
rSettlement of disputes is of paramount importance in the domain of industrial relations. Both 
employers and workers should strive to settle any discontentment or rift in their mutual relation 
with the help of the preventive machinery, failing which the Government should intervene with 
the dispute settlement machinery.
rThere are several perspectives of looking at prevention and settlement of industrial disputes: 
statutory and non-statutory measures of settlement; preventive and settlement machinery; and 
settlement with or without State intervention.
rThe statutory machinery comprises the following: Works Committee, Conciliation, Court of 
Inquiry at the central and State levels, and adjudication authorities consisting of Labour Courts, 
Industrial Tribunals and National Tribunals. 
rThe non-statutory machinery is used for the prevention of industrial disputes, and consists of: 
workers’ participation in management, collective bargaining, grievance procedure, tripartite bod-
ies, Code of Discipline and Standing Orders. 
rTripartite bodies include the Indian Labour Conference and Standing Labour Committee operat-
ing at national-level; Wage Boards and Industrial Committees functioning at industry-level; and 
State Labour Advisory Boards at State-level. 
rThe process of settlement of disputes can be split into two parts: settlement with State-intervention 
and without State-intervention. Settlement without State-intervention includes collective bargain-
ing and voluntary arbitration. 
rSettlement with State-intervention includes: compulsory setting up of bipartite committees; com-
pulsory collective bargaining; initiation of compulsory investigation; provision for conciliation 
and mediation; and compulsory arbitration and adjudication.
rRecommendations of the Second National Commission on Labour (2002) include: amalgamation 
of all Central legislations related to labour relations into a single law; establishment of legislative 
framework for voluntary settlement of disputes, etc.

      TUDY
Settlement of Industrial Disputes: the Situation in West Bengal
West Bengal has been one of the five States in India which have accounted for over 50 per cent of 
the total Indian workforce in the industrial and service sectors in 2006. The major industries in the 
State are leather, tea, jute, engineering and paper. There is substantial public sector presence in West 
Bengal and in more recent years an emerging joint sector as well.
IR&LL_Ch_08.indd   20 1/9/2008   11:48:15 AM

Settlement of Industrial Disputes 8.21
Significantly, there is no law on collective bargaining or on union recognition at the all-India level 
and different States have framed their own laws. But enforcement is not easy, since employers are 
not homogeneous. The State Government also does not have a large enough body of inspectors to 
enforce legislative provisions. In the organised sector trade unions apply pressure on management to 
enforce legislative provisions. Bargaining takes place at various levels, that too only once in 3 to 4 
years, although there is no national-level agreement on any issue. Since there is a significant number of 
industry-wide agreements in the State, there have to be mechanisms at the plant or establishment level 
through which industrial relations problems can be tackled. Wages, major allowances and productivity 
levels are determined at the industry-level, but smaller agreements on detailed issues may be signed 
from time to time at the plant-level. There would not be contradictions between these agreements, 
because the issues dealt with would be different. This is clearly demonstrated in the case of jute and 
steel industries. The industry-level agreement in the jute industry includes vague clauses on productivity 
and mentions merely that cooperation is required from unions. The company-level or unit-level agree-
ments, on the other hand, have ample details on specific outputs, machines, operations and processes.
Wages are fixed in different ways in the organised and unorganised sectors. For the organised sec-
tor there are two methods. If we include all units registered under the Factories, Mines or Plantations 
Acts, then the organised sector is large. But in reality large establishments in the organised sector are 
those which implement the major legal requirements for employment and labour and employ 100 or 
more workers. Those employing below this number can be clubbed as smaller units in the organised 
sector but have characteristics very similar to that of the unorganised sector. The method of collec-
tive bargaining is used to fix wages in large-sized organisations and a mixture of unilateral (by the 
employer), collective negotiations and statutory methods is used for the smaller units, depending on 
the size of the workforce and the degree of unionisation. 
Joint labour management bodies at the enterprise-level are as follows:
Works Committees:  A Works Committee is a statutory body for all manufacturing units employing 
100 or more workers with worker representatives elected on the basis of departmental constituencies 
and not nominated by unions. The main industries where this body still exists are jute and engineer-
ing, that too without holding regular elections. Very few other industries even constitute such bodies. 
In others, they may have existed at one time, but have fallen into disuse. Up to December 2006, the 
West Bengal Government had ordered 1,005 establishments to constitute Works Committees through 
elections; only 119 units were compliant. Even though this is a tool of industrial relations, there ap-
pears little urgency in this matter.
Industrial Relations Committees:  These committees are formed voluntarily by enterprises, especially 
in large central public sector undertakings, to resolve day-to-day problems at the local level. They 
are not required by any statute and have been set up by management of various enterprises with trade 
union concurrence.
Joint decision-making bodies:  These bodies exist in those enterprises, again mainly the public sector 
steel plants, where participative management has been formally introduced. This is also not required 
by any statute and can be looked upon as a strategy in industrial relations.
The total number of disputes raised in West Bengal for conciliation fell steadily from 3,103 in 1994 
to 2,053 in 2002, and 1,852 in 2003. Lock-outs have however increased. Statistical data also indicate 
that even the percentage of disputes disposed off by the Labour Directorate is declining from a sub-
stantial 45 to 50 per cent between 1994 and 2001, to just 37 to 38 per cent in the post-2002 period. 
This declining tread does not mean that relations between management and unions have become very 
harmonious; instead it implies that both parties have perceived that it is better to resolve disputes 
IR&LL_Ch_08.indd   21 1/9/2008   11:48:15 AM

8.22 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
amicably and jointly, so that employees do not lose wages and employers production. Such a trend 
of industrial disputes could also indicate reduced dependence on the State labour machinery. Unions 
too are in no position to agitate for workers’ benefits since workers themselves prefer to get smaller 
benefits rather than face industrial closure. This has happened in the case of some strikes, for example 
in the jute industry, where workers have pressurised unions to call off strikes after a very short period.
The State Government refers to all government intervention in dispute settlement as tripartism. 
Industry-wide settlements in jute, tea and engineering are all tripartite. The main tripartite body op-
erating in West Bengal is the State Labour Advisory Board which discusses issues that have defied 
solution in other forums and suggests possible methods for solution.
(Adapted from Sen, R. (2009). The Evolution of Industrial Relations in West Bengal, ILO Subregional Office 
for South Asia, New Delhi. Retrieved from www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/@asia/@ro-bangkok/@sronew_

Labour Welfare
Desired Knowledge Competencies
cTo describe the concept of labour welfare and trace its evolution in India.
cTo discuss the theories of labour welfare.
cTo outline the types of labour welfare measures.
cTo explain the concept of workers’ education and training.
INTR ODUCTION
Labour welfare is an important aspect of industrial relations. Welfare activities in an industry encompass 
not only workers, but their families also, as well-being of a worker cannot be seen in isolation (Report 
of the Committee on Labour Welfare, 1969). The Royal Commission on Labour (1931) was of the 
view that, “the term welfare as applied to industrial workers is one which must be necessarily elastic, 
bearing a somewhat different interpretation in one country from another, according to the different 
social customs, the degree of industrialisation and the educational development of workers”(cited in 
Sharma, 2004, p. 298). Labour welfare is a broad term encompassing various benefits, amenities and 
facilities provided by employers to workers and their families, over and above wages/salaries. It helps 
in improving safety, general well-being and efficiency of workers.
The concept of labour welfare finds its origin in the Directive Principles of State Policy enshrined 
in the Constitution of India. Article 38 directs the State to secure a social order for the promotion of 
the welfare of people. Article 41 requires that within the limits of its economic capacity and develop-
ment, the State shall make effective provisions for securing the right to work, to education, and to 
public assistance in case of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement, and in other cases of 
undeserved want. Article 42 mandates that the State should make provision for securing just and 
humane conditions of work and for maternity relief. According to Article 43, the State shall endeavour 
to secure, by suitable legislation or economic organisation or in any other way, to all workers, agri-
cultural, industrial or otherwise, work, a living wage, conditions of work ensuring a decent standard 
of life and full enjoyment of leisure and social and cultural opportunities. According to Article 47, the 
IR&LL_Ch_09.indd   1 1/1/2008   4:49:50 AM

9.2 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
State should regard the raising of the level of nutrition and the standard of living of its people, and 
improvement of public health, as among its primary duties.
Labour welfare refers to “Such facilities and amenities as adequate 
canteens, rest and recreation facilities, sanitary and medical facilities, 
arrangements for travel to and from and for accommodation of workers 
employed at a distance from their homes, and such other services, ame-
nities and facilities including social security measures as contribute to 
conditions under which workers are employed” (Report of the Committee 
on Labour Welfare, 1969, p. 24). We may thus define labour welfare as the 
whole range of benefits, amenities and facilities, including social security, 
provided by employers to workers besides their wages/salaries, that helps 
in maintaining and improving their health, safety and quality of life.
EVOLUTION OF THE CONCEPT OF LABOUR WELFARE
The concept of labour welfare, as we understand today, has developed over a period of time. The 
evolution of labour welfare in India may be broadly divided into 3 phases. This section provides a 
depiction of all these phases.
Phase I: 1850-1900
This was the phase when industrialisation was growing and labour was exploited by employers for 
increased profits by way of long working hours, poor working conditions, no job security and low 
wages. Some enactments were passed by the government during this phase, with the objective of im-
proving the working and living conditions of workers. Though these had limited scope, but a beginning 
was nevertheless made. The Apprentices Act, 1850 aimed at helping poor children to learn trades and 
crafts; the Fatal Accidents Act, 1853 had the provision for giving compensation to families of workers 
who lost their lives; and the Merchant Shipping Act, 1859 had provisions for the health of seamen. 
Enactment of the Indian Factories Act, 1881 was a significant step towards labour welfare, though it 
was limited in scope and was applicable only to factories employing not less than 100 persons.
Phase II: 1900-1947
During this phase the efforts of expanding the scope of labour welfare gained some momentum. The 
Indian Factories Act passed in 1911 had a wider scope in terms of applicability, working hours for 
children and provisions for health and safety. The discontentment caused among workers due to con-
ditions arising out of World War I (1914-1918), the Russian Revolution 
of 1917, and setting up of the International Labour Organisation (ILO) 
in 1919 gave impetus to welfare activities taken up by employers and the 
State. The Government of India passed the Indian Factories (Amendment) 
Act, 1922 with wider applicability; the amended Act contained provisions 
for limiting the working hours for both men and women, and other wel-
fare provisions for women and children. The Workmen’s (now Employees’) Compensation Act, 1923 
introduced provisions for compensation in case of injury at work, resulting in disablement or death. 
The Royal Commission on Labour (1931) had a considerable influence on welfare activities in the Spotlight

country. With its recommendations, the Factories Act, 1934 came into force; this Act reduced the 
working hours for children and women and provided for crèches at workplace. It also recommended 
health insurance and maternity benefits. The Indian Dock Labourers Act was passed in 1934, provid-
ing for safety at working places on shore and of any regular approaches over a dock, wharf, quay or 
similar premises. The Labour Investigation Committee (also known as the Rege Committee) was ap-
pointed by the government in 1944 to investigate into labour welfare measures. In its report submitted 
in 1946, the Committee recommended extension of the scope of labour welfare to include measures 
like education, healthcare, relief in case of old age and death, etc.
After World War II, many welfare measures were introduced in enterprises. In 1942, welfare of-
ficers were appointed in the Labour Department by the government. Welfare activities were initiated 
for mica and coal mine workers and their families (Sharma, 1998) and a welfare fund was created for 
coal mine workers in 1944.
Exhibit 9.1 Earl y Initiatives in Labour Welfare in India
Tata Steel was the first to establish labour welfare practices in India, even before these were made 
statutory laws across the world. Tata Steel, even in its nascent years, brought in social scientists 
like Sidney and Beatrice Webb to work on welfare schemes. In fact, some of the initiatives in-
troduced by the company were not only the first of their kind in India, but also in many Western 
countries at that time. Apart from building housing blocks for its employees, and offering civic 
amenities and infrastructure, the company introduced 8-hour working days as early as 1912; 
free medical aid was started in 1915; initiatives like leave with pay, Workers’ Provident Fund 
Scheme and Workmen’s Accident Compensation Scheme were introduced in 1920; maternity 
benefits were offered as early as in 1928. Profit sharing bonus was granted for the first time in 
the country by the company in 1934, and a scheme of retiring gratuity was introduced for the 
Tata employees in 1937.
(Adapted from: Chattopadhyay, S.S. (2008, Jun. 21-Jul. 04). Steel with soft core, Frontline, 
25(13). Retrieved from www.frontline.in/static/html/fl2513/stories/20080704251310600.htm on 
17/4/2014.)
Phase III: 1947 Onwards
After India attained Independence, industrialisation begun and employment level started increasing. 
The Government was concerned for improving the condition of workers. Many welfare legislations 
were enacted towards this end, including the Factories Act, 1948, the Plantations Labour Act, 1951,
the Mines Act, 1952, the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970, etc. Labour Welfare 
Funds were created for workers under legislations like the Coal Mines Labour Welfare Fund Act, 
1947, the Iron Ore Mines Labour Welfare Cess Act, 1961 and the Beedi  Workers Welfare Fund Act, 
1976. Welfare provisions for workers in almost every industry were made in industry-specific legisla-
tions like the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, the Motor Transport Workers Act, 1961 and the Beedi
and Cigar Workers (Conditions of Employment) Act, 1966, etc. In addition to these legislations, many 
other welfare and social security legislations were enacted by the Central Government and various 
State Governments.

9.4 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
OBJECTIVES OF LABOUR WELFARE
Labour welfare activities are a reflection of the nature of industrial rela-
tions of a nation. The main objective of such activities is to improve the 
condition of workers, and thereby enhance productivity of an enterprise. 
Other objectives are to improve employee morale and preserve efficiency 
level of workers by providing a richer quality of life and improved stan-
dard of living to workers and their families. Welfare activities directly or 
indirectly aim at reducing absenteeism and labour turnover in industries. Welfare measures contribute 
to the maintenance of industrial peace (Mamoria and Mamoria, 1980) and enhance the image of an 
employer (Thomas, 1990); this induces many employers to embark on labour welfare activities.
There may be three approaches that underlie the welfare activities taken up by employers. These 
are discussed as follows:
rHumanitarian approach:  This may viewed as a sense of social responsibility of employers 
towards workers and concern for providing such amenities as would help workers live a life 
with frugal level of comfort.
rUtilitarian approach:  Under utilitarian approach expenditure on welfare amenities are seen as 
investment that would preserve employee efficiency for the benefit of an organisation.
rPaternalistic approach:  The paternalistic approach propagates an employer as the guardian of 
workers, who undertakes welfare activities due to a sense of responsibility towards them and 
to protect them.
THEORIES OF LABOUR WELFARE
Several theories have been proposed to explain how and why labour welfare measures are undertaken. 
Some of the important theories are briefed here.
rPolice Theory:  This theory assumes that owners and managers of industrial undertakings have 
a lot of wealth and power, which they use for their own benefits. They overlook and neglect 
the welfare of workers, and even exploit workers for their own advantage. The State must enact 
legislations that would coerce employers to provide for workers’ welfare in the form of minimum 
wages, healthcare, good working conditions, etc. The basis for taking up welfare activities is 
fear and compliance.
rPhilanthropic Theory:  Humanitarian by approach, this theory is based on the assumption that 
welfare measures are undertaken with the objective of providing benefits to workers for improv-
ing their condition. Many philanthropists believed that investment in labour welfare will be 
ultimately beneficial for industry.
rPaternalistic or Trusteeship Theory:  This theory is paternalistic in 
approach and proposes that the owner of an industrial undertaking 
is the guardian or ‘father’ of all the workers. The employer owns 
the property and profits which he uses for the benefit of workers 
and the society as a whole. Due to lack of awareness, workers know 
little about their rights. Though not bound, the employer must take 
care of the interests of workers. Mahatma Gandhi strongly believed 
in the trusteeship theory.
rPlacating Theory:  The placating theory believes that as workers are becoming more aware of 
their rights, they are adopting a militant attitude to pressurise employers for higher wages and Spotlight
Labour welfare activities may 
be guided by humanitarian, 
utilitarian or paternalistic 
approach.

assumes that welfare measures 
are undertaken with the objective 
of providing benefits to workers 
for improving their condition.

Labour Welfare 9.5
improved working conditions. Given such situations, undertaking welfare measures can appease 
workers and peaceful industrial relations can be attained.
rPublic Relations Theory:  This theory proposes that welfare activities of an industrial undertak-
ing not only help in improving relations between workers and employer, but also in enhancing 
public relations. When labour welfare measures of an undertaking are publicised, they create 
goodwill in the society. Sales and profits of such an establishment may go up. Thus it gives 
two-way benefits to employers: increased profits and better industrial relations. This theory may 
be said to be based on the utilitarian approach.
rFunctional Theory:  Utilitarian by approach, this theory rests on the assumption that welfare 
measures help to preserve the efficiency and productivity of workers. Also known as the effi-
ciency theory, the functional theory propagates the essentiality of collaboration between union 
and management with the common objective of increasing production, as such a collaboration 
would benefit employers in getting higher profits and workers in earning higher wages.
rReligious Theory:  This theory is based on the belief that doing good deeds is an investment. 
In this context, investing in labour welfare is a good deed that would reap fruits in future. Pain 
and problems are a result of sins done in the past. Providing benefits to workers in the form of 
canteens, health benefits, crèches, etc. can also help in atonement of sins.
TYPES OF LABOUR WELFARE
Welfare amenities provided to workers may be of several types, namely, voluntary, statutory and mu-
tual. Certain facilities are taken up voluntarily by employers for the benefit of workers because of the 
feeling of humanitarianism, irrespective of statutory requirements. There are other facilities that are 
to be provided by employers because of statutory requirements. Some welfare measures are mutual 
in nature, in which both workers and employers contribute.
Statutory measures may be of two types (Sills, 1968):
rMeasures which have to be provided irrespective of the size of the organisation or the number 
of people employed therein. These include washing, storing and drying of clothes, first-aid, 
drinking water, and latrines and urinals.
rMeasures which are to be provided subject to employment of speci-
fied number of people, such as canteens, rest shelters, crèches and 
ambulance rooms.
Statutory measures may also be categorised as: welfare legislations  that 
provide for general well-being and some degree of comfort, and social
security legislations  that are protective in nature.
Depending upon whether welfare amenities are provided within the premises of an establishment 
or outside, welfare measures may be of two types: intra-mural  and extra-mural . Intra-mural facilities 
are those that are provided by the employer to the workers within the premises of an establishment, 
e.g., drinking water, canteen, rest room, crèche, etc. Extra-mural facilities are provided outside the 
premises of an establishment, e.g., housing, transport, etc.
Statutory Welfare Measures
The Government of India has laid down various labour enactments from time to time, many of which 
contain provisions for worker welfare. These measures have to be taken up by an employer as a legal 
obligation and any negligence in implementing these provisions results in penalty. Some of the important Spotlight
Intra-mural facilities are

facilities are provided outside

Exhibit 9.2 Recommendation Concerning Welfare Facilities for Workers
The R102-Welfare Facilities Recommendation, 1956 (No. 102) adopted on 26th June 1956 by 
the General Conference of ILO, convened at Geneva by the Governing Body of the International 
Labour Office is as following:
Whereas it is desirable to define certain principles and establish certain standards concerning 
the following welfare facilities for workers:
(a) feeding facilities in or near the undertaking (canteen, buffet and trolley, mess room and other 
suitable rooms, mobile canteens, other facilities, use of facilities);
(b) rest facilities in or near the undertaking and recreation facilities excluding holiday facilities; 
(c) transportation facilities to and from work where ordinary public transport is inadequate or 
impracticable.
The Conference also recommended that the provisions should be applied as fully and as rapidly 
as national conditions allow, by voluntary, governmental, or other appropriate action, and that 
each Member should report to the International Labour Office as requested by the Governing 
Body concerning the measures taken to give effect thereto.

The Factories Act, 1948
This is a legislation dedicated to labour welfare and it contains extensive provisions for workers’ health, 
safety and welfare. Chapter 14 discusses all such provisions in detail. Annexure I gives the number of 
canteens, shelters, rest rooms and welfare officers (which are statutory requirements under the Act) 
in factories in the year 2010.
The Mines Act, 1952
The issue of health and safety of mine workers is governed by the Mines Rules, 1955 (hereinafter 
referred to as ‘Rules’), created under the jurisdiction of the Mines Act, 1952. Under the Act and the 
Rules, an employer has to provide the following facilities for the health and welfare of mine workers: 
adequate and suitable shelters for taking food and rest at every mine where 50 or more persons are 
employed (Section 62 of the Rules); canteens in mines employing 250 or more workers (Section 64 of 
the Rules); appointment of a welfare officer in mines employing 500 or more workers and where the 
number of workers in a mine exceeds 2,500, such welfare officer to be assisted by a suitably qualified 
additional welfare officer for every additional 2,000 persons or part thereof employed (Section 72 of 
IR&LL_Ch_09.indd   6 1/1/2008   4:49:50 AM

the Rules); sufficient supply of cool and wholesome drinking water (Section 19 of the Act); sufficient 
number of latrines and urinals separately for males and females in every mine (Section 20 of the Act); 
and maintenance of first-aid boxes or cupboards in every mine and first-aid rooms in mines employing 
more than 150 workers (Section 21 of the Act).
The Plantations Labour Act, 1951
The welfare measures that are to be provided to plantation workers by employers are: clean and whole-
some drinking water (Section 8); separate latrines and urinals for male and female workers (Section 
9); medical facilities for workers as prescribed by the State Government (Section 10); one or more 
canteens in every plantation ordinarily employing 150 workers (Section 11); crèches in plantations 
employing 50 or more women workers (Section 12); recreational facilities for workers and their chil-
dren (Section 13); educational facilities for children of workers employed in any plantation between 
the age of 6 and 12 exceeding 25 in number (Section 14); housing facilities for every worker and his/
her family residing in the plantation (Section 15); workers to be provided with prescribed number and 
type of umbrellas, blankets, raincoats or other like amenities for protection from rain or cold (Section 
17); and appointment of a welfare officer in plantations employing 300 or more workers (Section 18).
The Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970
A contractor is liable to provide the following amenities to contract labour: canteen, wherein con-
tract labour numbering 100 or more is ordinarily employed (Section 16); rest room wherein contract 
labour is required to halt at night in connection with the working of the establishment (Section 17); 
arrangements for sufficient supply of wholesome drinking water, latrines and urinals, washing facilities 
(Section 18); and first-aid facilities (Section 19). In case of failure on the part of the contractor to 
provide these facilities, the principal employer is liable to provide the same.
The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958
Welfare provisions in the Act include: supply of sufficient provisions and drinking water of good 
quality (Section 168); maintenance of proper weights and measures on board (Section 171); supply 
of beddings, towels, medicines, medical stores, and provision of surgical and medical advice (Section 
172); crew accommodation (Section 175); appointment of Seamen’s Welfare Officer at such ports in 
or outside India as the Government may consider necessary (Section 13); setting up of an advisory 
board to be called the National Welfare Board for Seafarers for advising the Central Government 
on the measures to be taken for promoting the welfare of seamen (whether ashore or on board ship) 
generally, and in particular the establishment of hostels or boarding and lodging houses for seamen, 
the establishment of clubs, canteens, libraries and other like amenities for the benefit of seamen, the 
establishment of hospitals or the provision of medical treatment and of educational and other facilities 
for seamen (Section 218).
SOCIAL SECURITY
The concept of social security is based on the principles of human dignity and social justice (ILO, 
1969). According to ILO (2005, p. XXI), “Social security is the protection that a society provides 
to individuals and households to ensure access to health care and to guarantee income security, par-
ticularly in cases of old age, unemployment, sickness, invalidity, work injury, maternity or loss of a 
IR&LL_Ch_09.indd   7 1/1/2008   4:49:50 AM

9.8 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
breadwinner.” Thus we may define social security as assurance provided 
by the State against various types of adverse situations to which individu-
als may be exposed in events like old age, sickness, financial distress, 
disablement, unemployment, maternity or death. Social security may be 
of two types: social insurance and social assistance. A social assistance 
scheme provides financial benefits to persons of small earnings as a right, 
which can sufficiently fulfill the minimum standard of need; its source 
of finance is taxation. ILO defines a social insurance scheme as one that 
provides benefit for persons of small earnings granted as a legal right in amounts which is the com-
bined contributory effort of the insured person, the employer and the State (as cited in Mishra, 1999, 
p. 10). Social security measures are significant for a nation to achieve the goal of a welfare state and 
to maintain the efficiency of workers. ILO has been instrumental in setting standards of social security. 
The Social Security (Minimum Standards) Convention adopted in 1952 embodies universally accepted 
basic principles and common standards of social security.
Some of the important social security legislations in India are the Employees’ Compensation Act, 
1923, the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, the Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948, the Employees’ 
Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952, the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 and the 
Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972. These Acts have been covered as separate chapters in this book.
Social Security for Unorganised Workers
As discussed in Chapter 2, the majority of the workforce in India consists 
of workers in the unorganised sector. They are involved in activities like 
agriculture, construction, mining, manufacturing and services. On account 
of lack of organisation and unionisation due to low literacy and awareness 
levels, these workers do not get adequate social security and welfare.
Many of the unorganised workers, particularly agricultural labour, work under highly insecure condi-
tions. There are no social security measures for these workers for maintaining basic living standards and 
risk coverage, especially in crisis situations such as unemployment, sickness or disablement. Neither 
there is any law to ensure suitable and safe working conditions. Even the working hours are not fixed 
and wages are governed by local factors. The situation is the same in the case of migrant labour and 
forced labour. The only exceptions are the Governments of Gujarat, Kerala, Karnataka and Madhya 
Pradesh, which have insurance schemes for the landless agricultural labour.
The unorganised sector does not get much benefit out of the existing framework of labour laws. 
However, the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 stands out as a legislation that is widely applicable to un-
organised workers, including agricultural labour. The Act empowers both Central and State Govern-
ments to fix or revise the minimum rates of wages in respect of scheduled employments under their 
respective jurisdiction. The basic objective of minimum wage fixation is to improve the standard of 
living of these workers. We have talked about the Act exhaustively in Chapter 18. 
Some welfare schemes are being implemented by the Central Government for specific occupational 
groups of the unorganised sector, such as beedi  workers, non-coal mine workers, cine workers, hand-
loom weavers, fishermen, etc. Certain initiatives of the Government like the National Rural Employment 
Guarantee Act, 2005, the National Rural Health Mission and the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyaan  address the 
problems of employment, health and education, respectively. Some of the State Governments and non-
governmental organisations have also been implementing welfare programmes for certain categories 
of unorganised workers. Despite various efforts, there is still a wide gap in coverage of such workers 
under social security measures.Reflection

Labour Welfare 9.9
WELFARE FUNDS
Labour welfare funds have been set up by the Government to provide welfare and social security to 
workers in certain industries. There are 5 welfare funds governed by different legislations, which are 
administered by the Ministry of Labour & Employment; their corresponding legislations are: 
rThe Mica Mines Labour Welfare Fund Act, 1946
rThe Limestone and Dolomite Mines Labour Welfare Fund Act, 1972
rThe Iron Ore, Manganese Ore and Chrome Ore Mines Labour Welfare Fund Act, 1976
rTheBeedi  Workers Welfare Cess Act, 1976
rThe Cine Workers’ Welfare Fund Act, 1981
The purpose of these welfare funds is to provide housing, medical care 
(prevention of diseases), transportation, water supply, educational and rec-
reational facilities, social insurance and security to workers employed in 
non-coal mines and beedi  industry and to cine workers. For building and 
construction workers, the welfare boards and welfare funds are required 
to be set up by the concerned State Governments.
Welfare funds fall broadly in two groups: tax (cess)-based and contributory. The Central Govern-
ment funds are tax-based, while welfare boards for mine workers, beedi  and cigar workers, etc. are 
financed by the cess levied on these commodities. Under the Beedi  Workers Welfare Cess Act, 1976, 
a fixed cess is levied per thousand beedis  manufactured. Similarly there is a cess for building and 
construction workers. Cess is levied on the mica mines and under other welfare laws on mine products 
on the basis of quantum of production. Under the Cine Workers Welfare Cess Act, 1981, cess is levied 
on the basis of production of films and not on the basis of collection.
Among the different States, Kerala has set up more than 20 welfare funds for workers in the un-
organised sector, including toddy workers, agricultural workers, handloom workers, auto-rickshaw 
workers, cashew workers, construction workers, motor transport workers, some artisans and others. 
These funds provide a wide range of benefits including old age benefit, medical care, education, as-
sistance for marriage, housing, etc. to the beneficiaries. The funds set up by the Kerala Government 
are mostly contributory, and hence are similar to social insurance. The schemes are administered by 
autonomous boards and are financed by contributions from employers, workers and others. In Maha-
rashtra, the Mathadi Boards exist for various groups of headload workers. The Tamil Nadu Welfare 
Fund established under the State law for manual workers has established labour welfare centres that 
provide childcare facilities and tailoring classes for the wives and wards of workers.
LABOUR WELFARE PRACTICES IN INDIA
Labour welfare in India is carried out by the efforts of Government, employers, trade unions and vol-
untary organisations. We have already mentioned the legislations enacted and enforced by the Central 
Government that have provisions for labour welfare earlier in this chapter. These apart, there are labour 
laws enacted and enforced by various State Governments, which apply to respective States. A typical 
example is of the Shops and Establishments Act, enacted by every State to regulate conditions of work 
and provide for statutory obligations of employers and rights of employees in the unorganised sector 
and other employments in their jurisdiction. The Government may introduce new welfare provisions 
or amend the existing ones while implementing the recommendations made by bodies like National 
Commission on Labour and Pay Commission. Child Care Leave for employees of Central Government Spotlight
