was introduced as a result of recommendations of the Sixth Central Pay Commission, with effect from 
1st September 2008. Women employees having minor children may be granted Child Care Leave by 
a competent authority for a maximum period of 2 years (i.e., 730 days) during their entire service for 
taking care of up to 2 children, less than 18 years of age, whether for rearing or taking care or any 
other needs like examination, sickness, etc. During the period of such leave, women employees shall 
be paid leave salary equal to pay drawn immediately before proceeding for leave. It may be availed 
of in more than 1 spell. Child Care Leave shall not be debited against leave account; such leave may 
also be allowed in the third year as leave not due (without production of medical certificate).
Employers, depending upon their capacity, make different welfare facilities available to workers. 
Large establishments provide facilities even beyond the level required by laws, while small ones may 
just provide statutory benefits. Non-statutory or voluntary benefits provided by employers to workers 
include loans for purposes like house building; recreational facilities; education of children; purchas-
ing of personal vehicle; conveyance; leave travel concession; fair price shops; and many other such 
facilities. 
Amongst voluntary organisations, there are some social organisations 
like the Bombay Social Service League, the Seva Sadan Society, the 
Maternity and Infant Welfare Association and the Young Men’s Christian 
Association, that undertake voluntary welfare activities like night schools, 
promotion of public health, organising recreational activities and lectures, 
etc. (Agalgatti, 2008).
Though trade unions have limited financial resources, they are actively undertaking labour welfare 
activities within their means. A notable example is of the Textile Labour Association Ahmedabad, 
which provides maternity care, education and development of children, workers’ education and train-
ing programmes, medical and healthcare, recreation, etc. The Rashtriya Mill Mazdoor Sangh, Mumbai 
provides similar amenities to workers and their families. The Mazdoor Sabha, Kanpur, the Railwaymen’s 
Union and Indian Federation of Labour in Uttar Pradesh are some other trade unions that are engaged 
in labour welfare by providing facilities like legal defence and running of cooperative societies. The 
Steel Employees’ Welfare Association at Bhilai provides social security to workers of the Bhilai Steel 
Plant in the form of financial assistance to the families of deceased member-workers and assistance 
to member-workers for medical care, retirement, etc. (Agalgatti, 2008). Trade unions at the Unchahar 
plant of National Thermal Power Corporation were found to have a fair involvement in labour welfare 
activities (Ghosh, Nandan and Gupta, 2009).
WORKERS’ EDUCATION AND TRAINING
Education is important for workers as it helps them improve their under-
standing in a holistic manner regarding their status problems and rights 
and responsibilities in various roles as workers, as union members, as 
consumers and as citizens (Peterson, 1952). The Indian workforce is char-
acterised by low level of education. The Government of India had realised 
the need for educating workers to ensure large scale industrialisation in the 
country after Independence, and towards this end, it initiated the Workers’ 
Education Scheme in 1958. This scheme was administered by the Central 
Board of Workers’ Education (CBWE), which is an autonomous body under the Ministry of Labour 
& Employment, registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860. The CBWE gets grants-in-aid 
from the Ministry of Labour & Employment to operate its activities.Spotlight

IR&LL_Ch_09.indd   10 1/1/2008   4:49:50 AM

Labour Welfare 9.11
The objective of the Workers’ Education Scheme is to create a well-aware and disciplined workforce 
in the organised, unorganised and rural sectors ( www.labour.nic.in ). The First National Commission 
on Labour (1969) had observed that the beneficiaries of the Workers’ Education Scheme were found 
to show more interest in union activities than others who did not receive education under the Scheme 
(National Commission on Labour Recommendations, n.d.). Educated workers were also found to have 
high interest in participation in management activities (Sethi, 1973, as cited in Sen, 2012). The Indian 
Institute of Workers’ Education (IIWE) was established by the CBWE in March 1970 at Mumbai 
as the apex training institute. To achieve its objectives, various training programmes are conducted 
by the CBWE for the workers of formal and informal sectors at national, regional and unit levels 
through a network of 50 regional and 9 sub-regional Directorates spread in various parts of the country 
(www.cbwe.gov.in ).
Under the Constitution of India, vocational training is a concurrent subject. The term ‘vocational 
training’ refers to lower level education and training for the population of skilled or semi-skilled work-
ers in various trades; however, it does not enhance their level with respect to general education (Goel, 
n.d.). The national vocational training system provides training for development of skills. The Central 
Government is responsible for developing policies and training schemes at the national level, setting of 
training standards, procedures, certification, etc. The National Council for V ocational Training (NCVT), 
a tripartite body under the Ministry of Labour & Employment, supervises training activities. It has 
representation from employers, workers and Central/State Governments. State Councils for V ocational 
Training are constituted at State-level monitoring training programmes by the respective State Govern-
ments. Training is provided through Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs), run by State Governments, 
and through various industrial establishments that provide apprentice training.
The main vocational training schemes consist of Craftsmen Training Scheme, Apprenticeship Train-
ing Scheme, Training of Skilled Workers and Supervisors, Training of Craft Instructors, Training of 
Women, Staff Training and Research, Development of Instructional Materials and Hi-Tech Training 
Scheme. Since women constitute a significant part of the workforce, women’s vocational training has 
also been given special attention. The Directorate General of Employment and Training has launched 
the Women’s V ocational Training Programme in 1977. 
Some of the challenges faced by the Government in training workers include uneven distribution of 
ITIs in different parts of the country; small coverage of persons including both school pass-outs and 
drop-outs, trade obsolescence, lack of training infrastructure and inadequate number of experienced 
staff (Chandra, 2004). In view of the tremendous growth of the service sector in India, skills need be 
imparted to workers by introducing appropriate training schemes for enhancing their employability 
in this sector.

Labour research is an activity aimed at collecting, analysing and dissemi-
nating knowledge about various dimensions of labour by using scientific 
methods. Globalisation, changing work technology, information technol-
ogy, socio-economic factors, etc. are affecting the nature of workforce 
and adding new dimensions to it. This calls for labour research.
Nanda (2011) has classified labour research into three categories: basic
(concerned with theoretical and conceptual studies related to labour eco-
nomics), applied  (the objective of which is to give such findings as can Spotlight

The Government of India relies on scientifically conducted researches in formulating its policies 
(Ministry of Labour & Employment, 2011). The main purposes of most of the labour research under-
taken by the Government are: to identify measures to solve problems, to assist in devising policies, and 
to comprehend and understand the depth of the socio-economic conditions of workers for comparison 
at national and international levels. Research on labour-related issues is conducted by several bodies 
in the country. The Ministry of Labour & Employment has a separate research division. The National
Labour Institute also conducts labour research. This apart, State Governments have their research 
studies. The Second National Commission on Labour (2002) has expressed the need for coordination 
between all these bodies to enhance the effectiveness of labour research.
LABOUR STATISTICS
Labour statistics provide an insight into the socio-economic development of a country; such statistics 
are necessary for planning developmental activities and improving the industrial relations scenario 
of a nation.
The Report of the Second National Commission on Labour (2002) lists the following government 
agencies engaged in collection, compilation and dissemination of labour statistics in the country:
rMinistry of Labour & Employment and its affiliates Directorate 
General of Factory Advice Service and Labour Institutes, 
Employees’ State Insurance Corporation and Employees’ Provident 
Fund Organisation).
rOther agencies (Office of the Registrar General of India, National
Sample Survey Office, Planning Commission and State Govern-
ments).
Of these, the Labour Bureau is the main agency engaged in collecting statistics on different aspects 
of labour since its inception in 1946. It also conducts labour research by way of studies and surveys 
covering the unorganised sector, SC/ST labour in urban areas, women workers and contract labour; oc-
cupational wage surveys in the organised sector; family budget enquiries; rural labour enquiry; Annual 
Survey of Industries; and the Digest of Indian Labour Research. The Labour Bureau is also responsible 
for the collation, collection and publication of statistics and related information on wages, earnings, 
productivity, absenteeism, labour turnover, industrial relations, working and living conditions, evaluation 
of working of various labour enactments, etc. Since the informal sector employs a major proportion 
of the workforce in many countries (including India), a resolution concerning statistics of employ-
ment in the informal sector was adopted by the 15th International Conference of Labour Statisticians 
in 1993. The Resolution requires that countries in which the informal sector has a significant role in 
the national economy should develop a comprehensive system for collecting statistics on employment 
in this sector, so as to create a statistical database for various uses. This system should contribute in 
the improvement of labour statistics, macroeconomic analyses, planning, policy formulation for the 
informal sector in specific and economy in general, and in integration of the informal sector with the 
development process. Such a system would also help in developing assistance programmes for work-
ers in this sector. The Resolution emphasises the need for monitoring of such data every year and an 
in-depth examination every 5 years.Spotlight

Labour Welfare 9.13
EMPLOYMENT SECURITY AND MANAGEMENT OF REDUNDANCIES
Employment security implies that a worker enjoys permanent employment without any fear of losing 
job. The policy of economic liberalisation in India had resulted in intense competition and to meet 
this challenge organisations adopted several strategies, including technological upgradation and re-
structuring, which often gives rise to redundancy. The Oxford Dictionary defines redundancy as ‘the 
state of being no longer in employment because there is no more work available’ ( www.oxforddiction-
aries.com ). Budget constraints and/or change in work technology may be the major drivers of redun-
dancy.
An employer may terminate a worker’s employment for reason of 
redundancy in accordance with the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, which 
refers to such termination as ‘retrenchment’. Section 2(oo) of the Act 
defines retrenchment as the termination of workmen’s services by the 
employer for any reason other than termination by way of disciplinary 
action; retirement (whether voluntary or superannuation); non-renewal 
of the term of contract; and continued ill-health. The prime reasons for 
retrenchment have been found to be financial stringency, shortage of raw 
material, shortage of power and lack of demand for the product (Ministry 
of Labour & Employment, 2013).
It may be noted that employers are prohibited from terminating the employment of a female em-
ployee at any time during maternity leave or pregnancy, where the employee would have otherwise 
been entitled to maternity benefit or medical bonus under the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961.Spotlight

The ILO Convention No. 160 and Recommendation No. 170 concerning Labour Statistics ad-
opted in 1985 contain the general provisions regarding collection, compiling and publication of 
basic labour statistics. Such statistics should include the following subjects:
(a) Economically active population, employment, where relevant unemployment, and where 
possible visible under-employment;
(b) Structure and distribution of the economically active population, for detailed analysis and to 
serve as benchmark data; 
(c) Average earnings and hours of work (hours actually worked or hours paid for) and, where 
appropriate, time rates of wages and normal hours of work; 
(d) Wage structure and distribution; 
(e) Labour cost; 
(f) Consumer price indices; 
(g) Household expenditure or, where appropriate, family expenditure and, where possible, 
household income or, where appropriate, family income; 
(h) Occupational injuries and, as far as possible, occupational diseases; and 
(i) Industrial disputes.

9.14 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Employees may also be separated from work by way of lay-off or closure. Lay-offs, retrenchment 
and closure are three separate concepts and reflect increasing degrees of severity (Debroy, 2012). 
Section 2(kkk) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 defines lay-off as the failure, refusal or inability 
of an employer on account of shortage of coal, power, or raw materials, or accumulation of stock, 
breakdown of machinery, natural calamity, or for any other connected reason, to give employment to 
a workman whose name is borne on the muster rolls of his industrial establishment and who has not 
been retrenched. Closure is defined in Section 2(ff) of the Act as the permanent closing down of a 
place of employment or a part thereof, and is taken as one which may have occurred due to industrial 
disputes or also because of reasons other than industrial disputes, such as financial stringency, shortage 
of power or raw material or coal, inter or intra union rivalries, accumulation of stock, lack of demand, 
breakdown of machinery, indiscipline, violence, etc.
In general, there has been a decrease in the number of units retrenching workers and the number 
of workers affected thereby (Table 9.1). In the year 2010, there were 13 cases of retrenchment in the 
Central and State spheres, in which 559 workers were affected. This reflects a decrease of 55.17 per 
cent in respect of retrenchments, as well as 79.24 per cent in respect of the number of workers re-
trenched over the previous year. Similarly, during the year 2010, 23 cases of lay-off, showing a decline 
of 53.06 per cent from the previous year, were reported, which affected 1,494 workers and resulted 
in a time-loss of 1,46,978 man-days. During this period, number of workers laid-off and man-days 
lost had also decreased by 89.64 per cent and 47.69 per cent respectively as compared to the previ-
ous year (Ministry of Labour & Employment, 2013). During 2010, 42 industrial units were closed, 
thus affecting 2,401 workers, as compared to 68 units closed in 2009, affecting 3,571 workers. This 
decrease in the number of units and persons affected may be taken as an indication towards increas-
ing informalisation of labour, as employing informal workers saves an employer from the burden of 
paying compensation for retrenchment or lay-off.

Labour Welfare 9.15
Managing Redundancy
rNeed Assessment:  An employer must ensure that there is a genuine need for redundancy. For 
this, a works committee may be consulted on issues related to retrenchment. However, the 
employer has no obligation to follow any such recommendation.
rEmployee Entitlements:  An employer is required to provide 1 month’s notice to any retrenched 
workman indicating the reasons for retrenchment. The State-specific Shops and Establishments 
Act specifies notice requirements for all non-workmen employees. Most States usually require 
employers to provide at least one month’s notice or the period specified in the employment 
contract. Employers are required to pay retrenchment compensation equivalent to 15 days’ 
average pay for every year of continuous service to all workmen who are made redundant. For 
non-workmen, the amount payable is specified in the contract of employment or the relevant 
Shops and Establishments Act. Gratuity is also payable under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 
to all employees (whether “workmen” or not) with more than 5 years of continuous service.
RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE SECOND NATIONAL COMMISSION 
ON LABOUR
The Second National Commission on Labour (2002) has given several recommendations for labour 
welfare and social security, some of which are mentioned in this section.
rThe need for crèches not to depend on the number of women workers or the number of children 
(up to 6 years of age). Every establishment employing 20 or more workers must run a crèche 
properly manned and equipped either singly or in association with other employers and/or local

treatment and other rights of for home-workers, including right to organise, occupational safety 
and health, remuneration, social security, etc. would offer substantial safeguards to millions of 
workers.
rSimplification of judicial procedures related to statutory provisions that would enable unorganised 
workers to obtain legal redress.
rIntroduction of a system of registration for domestic workers; these workers should be entitled 
to benefits of all the schemes that the Commission has recommended for self-employed workers.
rTransformation of welfare funds into instruments of social security by way of: expanding their 
coverage; broadening the range of benefits; modifying the financial arrangements for providing 
benefits and decentralising the administration of the funds; and setting up of a Central Fund from 
which welfare and social security measures for women workers should be financed.
rEstablishing a separate wing for unorganised workers in Labour Departments, with adequate 
number of women employees.
rFormulation of an umbrella-legislation for workers in the unorganised sector that should be 
capable of being implemented and monitored easily.
rConversion of the Employees’ Compensation Act, 1923 from an employers’ liability scheme 
to a social insurance scheme. Its coverage should be progressively extended to cover more

Summary
rLabour welfare may be viewed as the whole range of benefits, amenities and facilities including 
social security provided by employers to workers. Such benefits are provided besides wages/
salaries of workers and help in maintaining and improving their health, safety and quality of life.
rThe concept of labour welfare finds its origin from Articles 28, 41, 42, 43 and 47 of the Direc-
tive Principles of State Policy.
rLabour welfare activities may be guided by humanitarian, utilitarian or paternalistic approach.
rVarious theories explaining the reasons for existence of labour welfare are: police theory, pater-
nalistic theory, religious theory, philanthropic theory, placating theory, public relations theory 
and functional theory.
rWelfare measures may be categorised as statutory, voluntary and mutual, or as intra-mural and 
extra-mural; provisions in enactments constitute the statutory measures.
rSocial security is an assurance provided by the State against various types of adverse situations 
to which individuals may be exposed in events like old age, sickness, financial distress, disable-
ment, unemployment, maternity or death. Social security may be of two types: social insurance 
and social assistance.
rUnorganised sector workers in India do not enjoy any social security by way of labour enact-
ments, with the exception of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948.

rBesides employers, trade unions and certain voluntary organisations are also involved to some 
extent in labour welfare in India. 
rThe scheme for workers’ education initiated in 1958 is administered by the Central Board of 
Workers’ Education (CBWE); the national vocational training system provides training for 
developing skills.
rThe Labour Bureau is the main agency in India engaged in collecting statistics on different 
aspects of labour.
rLabour welfare funds have been set up by the Government to provide welfare and social security 
to workers in certain industries; 5 legislations govern such welfare funds.
rRedundancy of workforce may arise due to cost constraints and change in technology. An em-

C ASE
      TUDY
Protection of the Rights of Jethwai’s Mine Workers
The State of Rajasthan has numerous kinds of metallic and non-metallic minerals. The workforce 
employed in the State’s mining industry is second only to agriculture. The workers in mining predomi-
nantly constitute  adivasis  (tribals) and dalits  (low castes). These seasonal mine workers engage in hard 
labour for 12 to 13 hours a day. They work in hazardous conditions, with temperature as high as 50°C
in summers and freezing cold in winters. They are prone to a number of occupational diseases and 
physical injuries due to the poor safety conditions; the mines lack basic facilities and do not provide 
even statutory benefits to the workers. The employers, i.e., the mine owners, are least concerned about 
the plight of the workers, as their main motive is earning profit.
There is a blatant violation of laws and safety measures in most of the mining activities of the State. 
For example, certain mining companies operate on illegal or expired leases; they practice improper 
dumping of mine debris; and pay less than the minimum wage to mine workers. Mine owners try to 
increase profitability by paying miners less for long hours of work and frequently fail to pay cess or 
royalties. Small huts are provided to miners as shelters that can barely accommodate them or protect 
them from weather. It appears to be a tough task for the State Mining Department to control the 
situation probably due to lack of political will and the actual resources to fully monitor and control 
the operations of thousands of leases spread across Rajasthan. This neglect has further aggravated 
the already oppressive working conditions of a large number of people. Majority of mine workers 
are males. Women are engaged mainly in activities like clearing debris and pebbles from the mines. 
They are usually paid far less than male workers. Contravening all the norms of the Child Labour 
IR&LL_Ch_09.indd   19 1/1/2008   4:49:51 AM

9.20 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
(Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986, children are engaged in work under hazardous conditions and 
are exploited in every manner.
Jethwai, a small village in the Jaisalmer district of  western Rajasthan, is predominantly a Bhil tribal 
village. Apart from Bhils, there are many migrant workers from the neighbouring districts of Jodhpur, 
Barmer and Ajmer. A large majority of Jethwai’s population is engaged in one sort of mining-related 
activity or the other. Migrant population is preferred by mine owners as they are often more compliant, 
and rarely complain about unfair treatment or violation of their rights as they fear losing job. Since 
they are worried about earning their living, such migrant workers agree to work for much lower wages 
and rarely participate in village-based activities.
In general the mining industry only reserves some 4 to 5 per cent of total production costs for labour. 
The mine owners pay wages in two different ways: daily-wages and piece-rate wages. Although the 
mine operators guarantee wages to their workers at the end of every month, usually such wages are not 
paid regularly, and workers may have to wait for several months to get their wages. To support their 
families and in circumstances like marriages, illness or funerals, these mine workers have to borrow 
large amounts of money from mine owners. Unable to pay off the loan, they very often are pushed 
into debt bondage, when they are forced to work off their debts. They are given lower wages on this 
account. This situation arises as these workers do not have any other source of financial support. If 
they change jobs they are required to repay the whole debt or, often, the new employer repays the 
debt and the loan is transferred. 
Safety conditions in the minefields are far from satisfactory. Accidents frequently take place in 
mines due to the primitive manual tools like heavy hammers, chisels, etc. used by the workers. Fre-
quent accidents result in high rate of injuries and number of deaths every year. Even in this situation 
the mine workers have no assistance and are forced to borrow from mine owners, and thus falling 
into debt trap. Family members of deceased workers get very little compensation, largely being left 
to fend for themselves.
Disillusioned with the Government’s apathy and the attitude of mine owners, a group of environ-
mentalists, lawyers and activists came together to form the Mine Labour Protection Campaign (MLPC) 
in 1994 with the objective of improving the lives and working conditions of Rajasthan’s mine work-
ers. The MLPC began its work with the determination to protect the rights of mine workers, promote 
environmental justice, provide adequate healthcare, ensure occupational safety and guarantee fair 
wages. After remaining dormant for some time, the Campaign became active again in 1999 with the 
formation of a series of mine workers’ unions in Rajasthan. In 2001, the Stone Mineworkers’ Union 
(Pathar Khan Mazdoor Union) was formed with a total of 95 members. It had the objective to protect 
the miners’ rights and ensure them safe working conditions. The union worked to ensure that mine 
workers received payments on time, and were provided with safe working conditions, adequate hous-
ing, regular employment, and a legally binding assurance for full compensation in the case of fatal 
and non-fatal accidents. 
The Mine Labour Protection Campaign encouraged Jethwai’s mine workers to take ownership of 
mining resources by forming a cooperative. This was seen as an effort to give mine workers a sense 
of dignity and a stake in their own land. Their cooperative, the Pathar Khan Shramik Theka Sahkari 
Samiti Ltd. (PKSTSSL) was formed in 2002. It aimed to help the mine workers take up mining leases, 
and is one of India’s first mining co-operatives for the indigenous people. The PKSTSSL engages in 
profit-earning activities from mining activities. One of the basic principles of the cooperative is that 
any profit earned must be distributed equally among all the cooperative members. The wages of work-
ers have increased significantly as compared to that paid by private mine owners. The cooperative has 
been earning considerable profits ever since successful acquiring of leases to extract minerals, though 
IR&LL_Ch_09.indd   20 1/1/2008   4:49:51 AM

Labour Welfare 9.21
private mine owners create problems for them. The PKSTSSL educates workers on their legal rights 
related to fair wages, working hours and other benefits. Mine workers of cooperative-owned mines 
have facilities like clean drinking water and proper shelter rooms. 
Inspired by this cooperative, the women of the village have formed their own Self Help Group 
(SHG) that helps its members in developing skills for making products like candles, detergents, etc., 
and then selling them through SHG shops, thus becoming independent and supporting their households.

INTR ODUCTION
Harmonious relations between workers and employers and lasting industrial peace are the desired goals 
in all industrialised economies. However, the responsibility of ensuring such harmony is not restricted 
to employers and workers and their trade unions. The State, as the third stakeholder in industrial re-
lations, takes steps through appropriate legislations and other machinery to ensure industrial peace. 
The role of State in settlement of industrial disputes in India has been broadly covered in Chapter 8. 
However, settlement of disputes is actually a fraction of the overall role the State plays in shaping the 
industrial relations framework, which we shall be elaborating in this chapter. The concept of tripartism 
involving three parties (i.e., trade unions of workers, employer and the government) as a participative 
mechanism for settlement industrial disputes has also been discussed in Indian context.
Wages paid to labour are a source of their livelihood and a cost to the employer at the same time. 
This chapter presents the different theories of wages and elaborates on Wage Boards, their evolution in 
India and their functions. The Planning Commission was set up by a resolution of the Government of 
India in March, 1950. It was charged with the responsibilities of assessing 
all resources of the country, augmenting deficient resources, formulating 
plans for the most effective and balanced utilisation of resources and 
determining priorities (www.planningcommission.nic.in) . The Five Year 
Plans, formulated, executed and monitored by the Planning Commission, Spotlight

10.2 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
form an integral component of the planning process in India. Issues pertaining to employment and 
employability considered critical for a labour-abundant country like India, and labour policy (including 
industrial relations, employment, wages, welfare, working conditions and productivity) have always 
occupied pivotal position in the Five Year Plans. Initiating with the First Five Year Plan (1951-1956), 
the Planning Commission has travelled a long way, with the on-going Twelfth Five Year Plan (2012-
2017). We have captured various policies and recommendations related to labour across all the twelve 
Five Year Plans in this chapter. Separate sections have been devoted to deliberations on labour law 
reforms, and provisions and measures meant for women workers and child labour.
R OLE OF STATE IN INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS
The State is an endogenous player of the industrial relations system (Aoki et al., 1997 as cited by 
Jeong. 2010) of any nation. The existence of State is projected in the one of the most widely ac-
cepted approaches to the analysis of industrial relations proposed by Dunlop (1958). Yesufu (1985) 
describes State intervention as entailing all actions, whether direct or indirect, by which a government 
promotes, sustains or participates to influence or determine the conditions of employment and the 
relations between those directly involved in the employment contract (i.e., employers or managers on 
one hand, and employees or trade unions on the other).
Four distinct roles of the State that affect industrial relations are 
identified by Jeong (2010) as: a third party regulator of labour relations; 
a regulator of markets; an establisher of the welfare system; and its own 
employer and policymaker. Ratnam (2006) observes that the role ascribed 
to the State in industrial relations depends on the ideological, political 
and socio-economic bent of the State, and that it varies depending on the 
level of development or industrialisation and the level of interactions.
According to Silva (n.d.), following are the commonly found means 
of State intervention:
rStatute law  represents the most direct means of State intervention and is one of the specific means 
used by the State to condition industrial relations outcomes. Statutory regulation of minimum 
terms and conditions such as minimum wages, working conditions, safety and health, social 
security and protection are integrated with the terms and conditions in contracts of employment, 
which employers must conform to.
rThe system of labour courts, tribunals or arbitration  is a more indirect method through which 
the State influences industrial relations.
rAdministrative role  is another method of State intervention, e.g., as conciliator or mediator.
Ratnam (2006) suggests the following as the major means of State intervention in industrial rela-
tions: policy framework in the sphere of labour and labour management relations; legislation (includ-
ing both hard laws and soft laws); and institution (classified as facilitative, executive, and judicial). 
Otobo (2000) has noted five areas that are the most frequently subjected to State regulations, namely: 
employment and manpower development; wages and salaries; union government and administration; 
collective bargaining; and industrial conflict.
In Indian context, the First National Commission on Labour (1969 p. 307) has observed that “The 
concern of the State in labour matters emanates as much from its obligations to safeguard the interests 
of workers and employers as to ensure to the community the availability of their joint product/service 
at a reasonable price. The extent of its involvement in the process is determined by the level of social Reflection

TRIPAR TITE MODEL OF INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS
Concept of Tripartism
As the term suggests, tripartism involves three parties that participate in 
settlement of matters of industrial dispute. The three participants are the 
trade unions of workers, employer and the government, with the pivotal 
role played by the government. Tripartism promotes the idea of partner-
ship between labour and management and rests on the following principles 
(www.indialabourarchives.org ):
rManagement and workers should share a relation of partnership and synergy.
rThe community as a whole must be responsible for protecting the interests of workers, so that 
they enjoy their due share in the fruits of development of the nation.
Tripartism operates at industry and national levels. As a mechanism it plays a vital role in settle-
ment of disputes especially when bipartism does not help in reaching a consensus. Meetings of the 
participants are conducted to review all aspects of a dispute, advise each other and try reaching a 
consensus by peaceful means.
Evolution of Tripartite Bodies in India
The need for consultation on labour matters in lines with the International Labour Organisation (ILO) 
was recommended by the Royal Commission on Labour in India (also known as the Whitley Com-
mission) in 1931. The Commission envisaged a statutory organisation that should be large enough to 
ensure adequate representation of the divergent interests of the parties involved; however, such an 
organisation was also projected as not to be too large to stifle individual contributions by the members 
to the discussion. The Commission had recommended that the representative of employers, workers 
and government should meet regularly. Further, worker members should be elected by their registered 
trade unions and employers’ representatives should be elected by their associations. However, the then 
British government did not immediately accept these recommendations. The Government of India Act, 
1935, which was an important milestone in itself, placed the subject of labour in the Concurrent List. 
The Centre and the Provinces having concurrent jurisdiction with respect to matters in the Concurrent 
List were thus empowered to enact their own legislation with respect to labour among other matters. 
It was in the wake of such events that the need for tripartite consultation was perceived by both em-
ployers and workers’ representatives. During the Second World War separate consultations with the 
representatives of labour and employers were held successively in 1941 and 1942 by the Government. 
The experience of these consultations highlighted the necessity of holding joint meetings of the rep-
resentatives of these three entities on a common platform. The objective of such meetings was seen 
to be the resolution of disputes and clearing of differences between workers and employers by means 
of constructive discussions and mutual understanding.
In the year 1942, India set up two tripartite bodies on the model of 
the International Labour Conference, the Tripartite National Labour Con-
ference, which was eventually named as the Indian Labour Conference 
(ILC) and the Standing Labour Advisory Committee, re-named later as Spotlight

consensus.

10.4 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
the Standing Labour Committee (SLC). After Independence, the Government of India put emphasis 
on the need for consultation between the representatives of labour, management and the government 
in tripartite and bipartite forums. India ratified the Tripartite Consultation (International Labour Stan-
dards) Convention, 1976 (No. 144) concerning tripartite consultations to promote the implementation 
of International Labour Standards in 1978, the same year it was adopted by the ILO. At present there 
are 44 national-level tripartite committees in the country.
Tripartite Bodies in India
TheIndian Labour Conference  and the Standing Labour Committee  are 
two important national-level tripartite bodies that play a significant role 
in shaping the industrial relations framework of the country. The objec-
tives set before these two tripartite bodies at the time of their inception 
in 1942 were:
(i) promotion of uniformity in labour legislation;
(ii) laying down of a procedure for the settlement of industrial disputes; 
and
(iii) discussion on all matters of all-India importance between employers and employees. (Report of 
the First National Commission on Labour, p. 311)
The ILC was instituted to advise the Government on matters brought to its notice by the Govern-
ment itself. The First National Commission on Labour (1969) had noted that earlier the SLC used to 
deliberate on its own or over such matters that were sent to it by the ILC and the latter would make 
the final recommendations. However, eventually both the ILC and the SLC have become deliberative 
bodies, ILC being more representative. Both these tripartite bodies consist of representatives of the 
Central Government, Governments of States and Union Territories and representatives of Employers 
and workers’ organisations nominated by the Central Government in consultation with all-India or-
ganisations of workers and employers. The meetings of the ILC are held annually, whereas the SLC 
meets as and when necessary.
The decision to constitute Industrial Tripartite Committees  or Indus-
trial Committees  with equal representation from employers and workers 
sides was mainly the outcome of tripartite deliberations at the ILC in 
1944. The functions of these committees are to study and debate on 
problems related to labour and specific to an industry, with a view to 
ensure better understanding between labour and management, and to advise the Government in solving 
problems related to such industry. Industrial Committees are found in industries like plantation, coal 
mining, jute, minerals other than coal, leather, cotton textiles, etc.
Wage Boards  were constituted by the Government at the industry-level in the 1950s and 1960s to 
solve the problems related to wage fixation. These boards have representatives of workers, employers 
and independent members who participate and finalise the recommendations. We shall be explaining 
the functions, composition and other aspects of Wage Boards in a subsequent section.
State Labour Advisory Boards  are tripartite advisory bodies set up in nearly all States to provide a 
forum of the representatives of the Government, employers and employees for discussing problems in 
order to maintain and promote harmonious industrial relations and to increase production.Reflection

LABOUR AND FIVE YEAR PLANS
This section presents the thrust areas and various policies and recommendations related to labour 
from the First Five Year Plan (1951-1956) to the on-going Twelfth Five Year Plan (2012-2017) (www.
planningcommission.nic.in) .
First Five Y ear Plan (1951-1956)
In the context of labour, the primary objective of the First Five Year Plan was to increase employment 
opportunities and to raise the standard of living of the masses. Towards this end, primary attention was 
given to the rural sector of the Indian economy on account of the magnitude and seriousness of the 
problem in the sector. Measures were directed towards ensuring a better distribution of the educated 
labour force among different occupations, thus diverting workers from ‘crowded’ occupations to those 
where there is a shortage.
The First Five Year Plan emphasised the need for overall industrial peace in industry and the ultimate 
oneness of interest; it propagated the virtue of harmonious relations between capital and labour. The 
Plan encouraged mutual settlements, collective bargaining and voluntary arbitration. It was observed 
that it is incumbent on the State to arm itself with legal powers to refer disputes for settlement by 
arbitration or adjudication, on failure of efforts to reach an agreement by other means. The Plan con-
centrated on five aspects of labour policy: industrial relations, wages, working conditions, employment 
& training and productivity.
Second Five Y ear Plan (1956-1961)
Driven by the objective of developing a socialist pattern of the society, the Second Five Year Plan was 
framed with suitable alterations in the existing labour policy. The underlying principle of the Plan was 
that a socialist society is built up not solely on monetary incentives, but also on the ideas of service to 
society and the willingness on the part of the latter to recognise such service. Therefore the creation 
of industrial democracy was considered a pre-requisite for the establishment of a socialist society.
Provision was made for the certification of employers’ associations as representatives of industry 
in an area. Any agreement entered into by such associations would then be binding on all members as 
well as on non-members of the associations. The Plan emphasised the need for industrial discipline. 
The necessity of a suitable framework for labour legislations and enforcement machinery was consid-
ered in the Second Five Year Plan for ensuring industrial peace. For this, the importance of preventive 
measures, including the last stage of mutual negotiations, namely conciliation, for achieving industrial Reflection
State Labour Advisory Boards 
have equal representation of 
workers and employers.
IR&LL_Ch_10.indd   5 1/1/2008   4:50:03 AM

10.6 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
peace was stressed upon. Emphasis was also placed on facilitating the stages of mutual negotiations 
and voluntary arbitration.
The Plan recommended appointment of a wage commission and an authority like a tripartite wage 
board, consisting of equal representatives of employers and workers, to be instituted for individual 
industries in different areas. The Employees’ Provident Fund (EPF) Scheme, which was instituted 
on a statutory basis during the First Five Year Plan, was extended in the Second Plan phase to cover 
industries and commercial establishments having 10,000 or more workers in the country as a whole. 
The main development programmes proposed under the Plan were: expansion of training of craftsmen 
and instructors, the Employment Service Organization and the Central Labour Institute; financing of 
housing schemes; and setting up of a Film Unit.
Third Five Y ear Plan (1961-1966)
The development of industrial relations in the Third Five Year Plan was 
contingent on the foundations created by the working of the Code of 
Discipline. Full awareness of the obligations under the Code to all the 
constituents of the central organisations of employers and workers was 
emphasised in the Plan.
The Third Plan stressed on increasing the application of the principle 
of voluntary arbitration for resolving differences between workers and employers. It spelt out the need 
to strengthen workers’ participation in management through Works Committees and Joint Management 
Councils. A large scale expansion of the Workers’ Education Scheme was also visualised for the period 
of the Third Plan. Apart from minimum wage, the Plan suggested to fix fair wages for different classes 
of workers. An urgent consideration was given to the conversion of the various Provident Fund schemes 
into a statutory scheme for old age, invalidity and survivorship pension-cum-gratuity. Emphasis was 
given on the problem of safety at workplace. The Plan proposed to set up a Standing Advisory Com-
mittee to promote measures for bringing down the incidence of accidents in factories and a National 
Mine Safety Council for safety education and propaganda in the mining industry.
Fourth Five Y ear Plan (1969-1974)
The Fourth Five Year Plan did not have any fresh direction or any shift in the Government’s indus-
trial relations policy; it further extended the training and employment schemes implemented in the 
previous Plan. The activities of the Employees’ State Insurance (ESI) Corporation were proposed to 
be expanded. Greater emphasis was placed on promoting safety practices and on the development of 
indigenous mine safety equipment. Stress was laid on strengthening labour administration for better 
enforcement of labour laws. The Fourth Plan recommended that studies should be undertaken to get 
estimates on unemployment and information on different segments of the labour force. It laid consid-
erable emphasis on labour-intensive schemes such as roads, minor irrigation, soil conservation, rural 
electrification, village and small scale industries, housing and urban development.
Fifth Five Y ear Plan (1974-1979)
The Fifth Five Year Plan laid emphasis on generation of employment, labour welfare and greater mobil-
ity of labour especially from labour surplus to labour starved areas. The Plan stressed on strengthening 
industrial relations and conciliation machinery, better enforcement of labour legislations, research in 
labour and labour statistics, and undertaking studies in the field of wages and productivity.Reflection

Sixth Five Y ear Plan (1980-1985)
One of the principal objectives of the Sixth Five Year Plan was the progressive reduction of unemploy-
ment in the country. Labour force estimates were obtained through surveys by the National Sample 
Survey Office (NSSO) on the basis of usual status participation rates. Special attention was paid to 
women and educated manpower both for the purpose of analysis of the existing employment market 
and for the formulation of suitable policies for these categories.
Seventh Five Y ear Plan (1985-1990)
The emphasis of the Seventh Plan was on employment and manpower policy. Technological upgrada-
tion, modernisation and scientific advances in production process in organised industry, agriculture and 
small industry were envisaged as the essence of growth of productivity. The Plan also ensured suitable 
arrangements and adjustment policies in terms of education, training, retraining and re-orientation of 
workers to avoid dislocation effects and to ensure smoothening of the process of technology adoption.
Eighth Five Y ear Plan (1992-1997)
The Eighth Plan aimed mainly at reducing unemployment. The Plan echoed concerns of the earlier 
Plan with particular reference to workers’ participation in management, skill, training, productivity, 
equitable wage policy and the informal sector. It also expressed concerns about rationalisation of the 
regulatory framework with a view to provide reasonable flexibility for workforce adjustment for ef-
fecting upgradation of technology and improvement in efficiency.
Ninth Five Y ear Plan (1997-2002)
The Ninth Five Year Plan attempted to create conditions for improvement in labour productivity in 
general and for provision of social security. It aimed at reducing the number of laws which determine 
the relations between workers and employers so that a much smaller number of laws can reach out 
to the entire workforce.
Attempts at providing social security were targeted specifically at the poor through special em-
ployment generation programmes and provision of free or heavily subsidised basic needs like health, 
nutrition, housing and education. Efforts were made to extend the coverage of the National Social 
Assistance Programme to the casual and self-employed workers in the informal sector both in rural 
and urban areas with the objective to cover the economically active population outside the organised 
sector. The Ninth Plan directed efforts to modify the existing National Child Labour Project (NCLP) 
by establishing special schools to provide non-formal education, vocational training, supplementary 
nutrition, stipend, healthcare, etc. to children withdrawn from employment.
Tenth Five Y ear Plan (2002-2007)
Unemployment was a major concern in the Tenth Plan; hence provision 
of gainful employment opportunities was a thrust area. During the Plan 
period efforts were made to ensure universal access at least to primary 
health care facility and to promote vocational training as a measure to 
generate employment opportunities.
The Tenth Plan envisaged reorganisation and strengthening of the Labour Department. It also un-
dertook affirmative measures to eradicate child labour by way of the Child Rehabilitation Scheme that Spotlight
Provision of gainful employment 
opportunities was a thrust area of 
the Tenth Plan.

Eleventh Five Y ear Plan (2007-2012)
The employment strategy for the Eleventh Plan was to ensure rapid growth of employment while 
ensuring an improvement in the quality of employment, especially in the unorganised sector. The 
aim was to achieve substantial increase in the share of regular employment, with a reduction in that 
of casual employment. Employment of women was encouraged in this Plan period. The Eleventh 
Plan highlighted the significance of programmes for skill development to aid the desired growth in 
employment. Services like Information Technology (IT) enabled services, telecom and tourism were 
identified to have prospects for high growth in output and for creation of new employment opportuni-
ties. Need for ensuring a under provision of social security and welfare of unorganised workers was 
also perceived in the Plan period.
Twelfth Five Y ear Plan (2012-2017)
The focus of the Twelfth Five Year Plan is to improve the outreach of skill development, both quan-
titatively and qualitatively; to bridge the spatial, sectoral regional and gender divides; and to have an 
institutional mechanism focused solely on skill development. The Plan has stressed on provision for 
necessary support mechanisms to enable the financial requirements/skill loans for poor students (i.e., 
the Credit Guarantee Fund). As regards issues of employment, the Plan has suggested an outcome-based 
approach to ensure that employability created is manifested in immediate, measurable and tangible 
employment or self-employment of trainees.
The Twelfth Five Year Plan has recommended activating the State Skill Missions and making 
them nodal points for receiving most of the skill-related funding from Centre. Greater interaction is 
encouraged among industry academia and skill providers to narrow the demand-supply gap of skilled 
manpower. The intervention of IT is clearly evident from the following thrust areas of the Twelfth 
Five Year Plan: development of Information and Communication Technology (ICT)-based real time 
labour market information system; development of an online national register of skilled persons; all 
employment exchanges to come online and act as pro-active counseling and placement centres; and 
setting up of a National Skill Registry having the facility to link various databases across Ministries 
and States. Other focus areas of the Plan include: focus on training of trainers; promotion of Public 
Private Partnership; and development of a model on the informal sector that reaches out to people.
LABOUR POLICY AND LABOUR LAW REFORMS
Labour policy in India is mainly based on labour laws. The dignity of 
human labour and the need for protecting and safeguarding the interest of 
labour has been enshrined in various articles of the Constitution of India. 
As we have mentioned earlier, labour is a subject in the Concurrent List 
in the Constitution, which empowers both the Central and State Governments to enact legislations. 
As a result, a large number of labour legislations have been enacted at Central and State levels that 
cater to different aspects of labour, including employment, occupational health and safety, fixing of 
minimum wages, payment of wages, compensation against injury at work leading to disablement or 
death, bonded labour, various categories of labour (namely, contract labour, women labour, child la-
bour, migrant labour, etc.), settlement and adjudication of industrial disputes, social security (including 
provident fund, gratuity, bonus, etc.), industry-specific categories of workmen (like mines, plantations, Spotlight
Currently there are 45 labour 
legislations in India.
IR&LL_Ch_10.indd   8 1/1/2008   4:50:03 AM

Wages, Government Policies on Labour and Five Y ear Plans 10.9
beedi,  and cigar, etc.). India has 45 labour legislations as on date, including the latest Sexual Harass-
ment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013. A complete list of 
all these laws has been provided in the appendix of the chapter. Apart from these laws, both Central 
and State Governments have formulated Rules to facilitate implementation of these laws. We have 
mentioned some of these Rules in relevant parts of this chapter. The Planning Commission observes 
that laws need to be reviewed from time to time, especially in a dynamic context, and hence stresses 
on the review or updating of labour laws on a continuous basis in order to bring them in tune with the 
emerging needs of the economy, including attaining higher levels of productivity and competitiveness, 
increasing employment opportunities and attracting more investment for growth.
It is obvious from this deliberation that the entire gamut of labour legislations, both at Central 
and State levels, the Rules appended with many of these laws, the enormous number of sections and 
clauses within each Act and their implementation invite an element of complexity in the industrial 
relations framework.
Flexibility in labour laws is an important matter to ensure all pervasive structural reforms. Further, 
the growing dynamism in the Indian labour market has also brought with itself notable instances of 
labour disputes in big industrial houses like Maruti Suzuki and Honda Motorcycle. In the face of such 
circumstances, more flexibility in labour laws has been widely perceived as an urgent need.
Datta and Sil (2007) observe that the main accusation against the labour laws in India, especially 
by employers, is that they are excessively pro-worker in the organised sector; this has led to serious 
rigidities with adverse consequences in terms of performance of this sector and the operation of the 
labour market. Thus growth of output in the organised sector is not leading to a proportionate growth 
in employment, which is compelling employers to resort to more capital intensive production pro-
cesses. This brings us to an interesting dichotomy: labour laws that are meant to protect the jobs of 
the workers are themselves impeding the scope for creation of more job opportunities in future.
The Planning Commission and different committees have been recom-
mending reform of labour laws by highlighting the need for flexibility in 
the existing laws that would give impetus to the industry to compete in 
international markets. Let us now understand the perspective of employers 
and workers on this issue. Employers view flexibility as a pre-requisite for 
promoting economic growth and generating jobs, whereas trade unionists 
consider this as a strategy of employers for profit maximisation and reduc-
tion in the bargaining power of unions, without commensurate employment opportunities (Datta and 
Sil, 2007). Unless we have labour reforms, as Debroy (2001) portrays, India’s comparative advantage 
of enormous labour abundance will not be adequately utilised because of the high wage lands created 
by the labour legislation in the organised sector.

Updating labour laws is a continuous process and changes are implemented in these laws from time 
to time by the Government to bring the various provisions in tandem with the emerging needs of the 
economy. The Working Group on Labour Laws and Other Regulations for the Twelfth Five Year Plan 
(2012-017) set up by the Planning Commission has given recommendations on amending certain 
legislations, some of which have been discussed in this section. ( www.planningcommission.nic.in)

10.10 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
rThe Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 is proposed to be amended to ensure 
that in case contract labour performs the same or similar kind of work as those directly appointed 
by the principal employer, such a worker shall be entitled to the same wage rates, holidays, hours 
of work and social security provisions. Further, whenever a contract worker is engaged through 
a contractor, the contract agreement between the principal employer and the contractor must 
clearly indicate the wages and contribution towards social security schemes and other benefits 
to be paid by the contractor to the contract labour concerned.
rThe Factories Act, 1948 must be amended to introduce new terms like ‘hazardous substance’, 
‘disability’, etc.; to redefine certain other terms; and to add new provisions on health, safety, 
hazardous process, welfare, working hours for adults, employment of young persons, annual 
leave with wages; and penalties & procedures, including provision of flexibility in the matter 
of employment of women during night in factories.
rThe Employees’ Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 may be amended to 
bring down the threshold limit of workers from the existing ‘20 and above’ to ‘10 and above’ 
as regards coverage of establishments.
RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE WORKING GR OUP
On the basis of views of various stakeholders (i.e., employers, workers and State Governments) the 
Working Group has given broad recommendations on labour legislations, some of which have been 
mentioned under specific heads in this section.
I. Consolidation, Simplification and Rationalisation of Labour Laws
The Working Group has agreed with the suggestion of the Second National Commission on Labour 
(2002) and National Commission for Enterprises in the Unorganised Sector (NCEUS) (2007) that 
labour laws should be consolidated in the following cognate groups to reduce their multiplicity that 
would ensure better enforcement and more effective compliance:
rLaws Governing Industrial Relations: The Working Group has recommended consolidation of 
the laws pertaining to industrial relations (i.e., the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, The Industrial 
Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 and the Trade Unions Act, 1926) into one law, i.e., 
the Industrial Relations Act.
rLaws Governing Wages: The legislations governing wages (i.e., the Equal Remuneration Act, 
1976, the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 and the Payment of 
Wages Act, 1936) may be consolidated into one Act, named the Payment of Wages Act.
rLaws Governing Social Security: There are more than one definition of a single concept 
available across legislations. The Working Group has hence recommended that the definitions 
of establishments, eligibility criteria, etc. in the various social security legislations (i.e., the 
Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948, the EPF and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 and the 
Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972) may be harmonised for purposes of consolidation.
rLaws Governing Working Conditions and Welfare: The Working Group has recommended 
clubbing of the Acts on working conditions and labour welfare (i.e., the Factories Act, 1948, 
the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961, the Workmen’s (now Employees’) Compensation Act, 1923, 
the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 and the Inter-State Migrant Workmen 
(Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) (RECS) Act, 1979).
rWelfare Cess Laws: The Working Group opines that all Cess Acts and Welfare Fund Acts may 
be clubbed into one Act.
IR&LL_Ch_10.indd   10 1/1/2008   4:50:03 AM

Wages, Government Policies on Labour and Five Y ear Plans 10.11
II. Common Definitions
At present different terminologies and definitions used in various labour laws lead to confusion and 
complications in the effective compliance and enforcement of these laws. One of the pre-requisites 
for codification or consolidation of labour laws is thus to have common definitions.
III. Protecting Interest of Workers in the Unorganised Sector
The Working Group has recommended provisions of minimum living wage, improved regulatory 
activities, basic social security and labour welfare schemes, and improved health and safety facilities 
to workers in the unorganised sector.
IV . Amendments in Certain Acts
Certain Acts like the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 
1970 and the Factories Act, 1948 have far reaching impact on the living standards of workers and 
have certain proposed amendments at various stages of consultation. Such considerations have been 
recommended to be put on fast track during the Twelfth Five Year Plan.
V . Enhancing Eligibility Criteria and Indexing of Benefits
The eligibility criteria in terms of wage ceiling in Acts like the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, the ESI 
Act, 1948, the EPF and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 and the Employees’ Compensation Act, 
1923, etc. should be reviewed at a given periodicity, say 3 to 5 years, considering the erosion in the 
wage ceiling limits through amending the rules rather than the Acts.
VI. Improving Enforcement of Labour Laws
The Working Group has suggested a complete review of the strength of the enforcement machinery 
of labour legislations; creation of an All India Service for labour administration; induction of greater 
professionalism, etc. Holding Lok Adalats  has also been encouraged to enable faster disposal of cases. 
A database should be built on all aspects relating to industrial relations and the officers of the Labour 
Departments should have access to such database through computer connectivity. In addition to codi-
fication and simplification of labour laws, the Working Group also suggested for creating an online 
‘single window system’ for making compliance simple and user friendly and for bringing transparency.
VII. Easing Compliance Burden of Labour Laws
For minor offences for which punishment by way of fine is provided, a senior officer of the Labour 
Department should be empowered to adjudicate these cases. This would reduce the time taken in 
disposing complaints and also lessen the burden on courts. The Working Group has recommended 
identification of the reasons for non-implementation of certain Acts.

Employment
rSection 27 of the Factories Act, 1948 prohibits employment of women in any part of a factory 
for pressing cotton in which a cotton-opener is at work.
rSection 46(1)(a) of the Mines Act, 1952 prohibits employment of women in any part of a mine 
which is below ground.
Remuneration
rArticle 39 of the Constitution of India envisages that the State shall direct its policy, among 
other things, towards securing equal pay for equal work for both men and women. The Equal
Remuneration Act, 1976 gives effect to this constitutional provision. It provides for the payment 
of equal remuneration to men and women workers and for the prevention of discrimination on 
the ground of sex against women in the matter of employment and for matters connected there-
with or incidental thereto.
rA Central Advisory Committee has been set up at the Centre under the Equal Remuneration Act, 
1976 to advise the Government on providing increasing employment opportunities for women 
and generally reviewing the steps taken for effective implementation of the Act.
Health and Safety Measures
Sections 22(2) and 34(2) of the Factories Act, 1948 provide for health and safety of women workers. 
These sections have been dealt with in details in Chapter 14.
Prohibition of Night Work
Section 66(1)(b) of the Factories Act, 1948, Section 25 of the Beedi and Cigar Workers (Conditions 
of Employment) Act, 1966 and Section 46(1)(b) of the Mines Act, 1952 stipulate working hours for 
women between 6 AM and 7 PM.
Provisions for Separate Latrines and Urinals
Provisions for separate latrines and urinals for female workers exist in: Section 19 of the Factories 
Act, 1948; Section 20 of the Mines Act, 1952; Section 9(1) of the Plantations Labour Act, 1951; Rule 
51 of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970; and Rule 42(1) of the Inter-State 
Migrant Workmen (RECS) Central Rules, 1980.
Provisions for Separate Washing Facilities
Provisions for separate washing facilities for female workers are given in: Section 42(1)(b) of the 
Factories Act, 1948; sub-section (1) of Rule 57 of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) 
Act, 1970; and Rule 43(1) of the Inter-State Migrant Workmen (RECS) Act, 1979.

Provisions for Crèches
Provision for crèches exists under the following legislations:
rSection 48(1) of the Factories Act, 1948 mandates every factory employing more than 30 women 
workers to provide and maintain suitable room(s) for the use of children under the age of 6 years 
of such women. As per sub-section (2) of the Section, these rooms must have adequate accom-
modation, adequate lighting and ventilation and maintained in a clean and sanitary condition, 
under the charge of women trained in the care of children and infants.
rAs per Section 12(1) of the Plantations Labour Act, 1951, in every plantation wherein 50 or 
more women workers (including those employed by any contractor) are employed, or where the 
number of children of women workers (including women workers employed by any contractor) 
is 20 or more, there shall be provided and maintained by the employer suitable rooms for the 
use of children of such women workers.
rSection 14(1) of the Beedi and Cigar Workers (Conditions of Employment) Act, 1966 mandates 
the provision and maintenance of suitable room(s) for the use of children under the age of 6 
years of female employees in industrial premises where more than 50 female employees are 
ordinarily employed. 
rSection 35(1) of the Building and Other Construction Workers (RECS) Act, 1996 provides for 
suitable room(s) for the use of children under the age of 6 years of female building workers in 
every place wherein more than 50 such female workers are ordinarily employed. 
rAs per Rule 44(1) of the Inter-State Migrant Workmen (RECS) Act, 1979, in every establish-
ment where 20 or more workmen are ordinarily employed as migrant workmen and in which 
their employment is likely to continue for 3 months or more, the contractor shall provide and 
maintain two rooms of reasonable dimensions for the use of the children of these workers under 
the age of 6 years.

rThe Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 regulates the employment of women in certain establishments 
for periods specified before and after childbirth and provides maternity benefit and certain other

rThe Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of

Exhibit 9.2 Sexual Harassment of Women Workers: The Legal Perspective
In its landmark judgment in Vishakha and Others vs. State of Rajasthan and Others (AIR 1997 
SC 3011) the Supreme Court of India has categorically held that any incident of sexual harass-
ment results in violation of fundamental rights of gender equality and the right to life and liberty. 
Thus any such incident is a clear violation of the rights guaranteed under Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(g) 
and 21 of the Constitution of India, which are enforceable under Article 32 of the Constitution. 
The Apex Court has further observed that sexual harassment includes such unwelcome sexually 
determined behaviour as physical contacts and advances, sexually coloured remarks, showing 
pornography and sexual demands, whether by words or actions. Such conduct can be humiliat-
ing and may constitute a health and safety problem. Equality in employment can be seriously 
impaired when women are subjected to gender-specific violence such as sexual harassment at 
workplace, and safeguards against sexual harassment are implicit therein.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/635207/ accessed on 6/6/2014.)Sexual Harassment of Women Workers

POLICIES AND PR OVISIONS FOR CHILD LABOUR
The affirmative attitude of the State towards prevention of child labour is evident from various Articles 
in the Constitution of India. Article 21A, under the title Right to Education, says that the State shall 
provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of 6 to 14 years in such manner as 
the State may determine by law. Article 24 prohibits employment of children below the age of 14 years 
in any factory or mine or in any other hazardous occupation. Article 39(e) states that the health and 
strength of workers, men and women, and the tender age of children are not abused and that citizens 
are not forced by economic necessity to enter avocations unsuited to their age or strength.
State intervention in various dimensions to eradicate employment of children has resulted in in-
stances of child labour witnessing record decline in the last few decades, both in terms of magnitude 
and workforce participation rate. Table 9.1 presents the details of inspections carried out, prosecutions 
launched and convictions made under the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 between 
2007 and 2012 on the basis of data received from various States.

On the basis of data generated by the National Sample Survey Office (2009-2010), working children 
in India are estimated at 49.84 lakhs. Further, as per the Report of the Working Group on Employment, 
Planning and Policy for the Twelfth Five Year Plan, the percentage of child labour has been found to 
have declined steadily from 6.2 per cent in 1993-1994 to 3.3 per cent by 2004-2005 to 2.4 per cent

Global Report on Child Labour published by ILO in 2006 revealed that the activity rate of children in

the activity rate of children  is 5 per cent as per 2001 Census (Ministry of Labour & Employment, 
2012-2013, p. 91) . However, child labour still exists in different industries and the Government has 
to play a proactive role in the eradication of this menace.

10.16 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
The National Policy on Child Labour, declared in August, 1987, 
contains a three-pronged action plan for tackling the problem of child 
labour. As a part of the legislative action plan , the Government of India 
has enacted the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 to 
prohibit the engagement of children below the age of 14 years in 18 oc-
cupations and 65 processes and to regulate the conditions of work of children in certain other employ-
ments. The onus of enforcement of the various provisions of the Act lies with the State Governments, 
as provided in Section 2 of the Act. The Government monitors the enforcement of the legislation from 
time to time. Special drives on enforcement and awareness generation are also launched regularly.
Rescue and repatriation is another crucial component of the legislative policy. During inspections 
and raids conducted under the Act, child labour is identified and rescued; rehabilitative measures are 
set forth thereafter by way of repatriation in case of migrant child labour; and bridge education is 
provided with the ultimate objective of mainstreaming such children into the formal system of educa-
tion. The Government also provides pre-vocational training to the rescued children.
As a part of the convergence action plan , a Core Group on convergence of various welfare schemes 
and general development programmes of the Government for benefiting children has been constituted 
under the aegis of the Ministry of Labour & Employment. The primary aim of the Core Group is 
to ensure that the families of child labour are given priority for their upliftment. The Government is 
aware of the fact that poverty and illiteracy are the root cause of child labour; hence it is necessary that 
educational rehabilitation of children is supplemented with economic rehabilitation of their families, 
so that they are not compelled by economic circumstances to send their children to work.
Under project-based action plans , the National Policy on Child Labour also envisages launching of 
projects for the welfare of working children in areas of high concentration of child labour. With regard 
to educational rehabilitation, the Government has implemented the National Child Labour Project 
(NCLP) Scheme in 1988. The Scheme seeks to adopt a sequential approach towards rehabilitation of 
children working in hazardous occupations and processes in the first instance. A survey of child labour 
engaged in such occupations is conducted, following which, children are to be withdrawn and then put 
into special schools, to be eventually mainstreamed into formal schooling system. Project Societies 
at the district level are fully funded for opening of such special schools or Rehabilitation Centres. As 
per figures revealed by the Ministry of Labour & Employment, presently about 7,311 special schools 
are in operation, with enrolment of 3.2 lakh children. About 8.95 lakh children have already been 
mainstreamed into the formal system since inception of the NCLP.
Exhibit 9.3 Eradicating Child Labour through Convergence of Schemes
The Ministry of Labour & Employment is taking various proactive measures by converging 
schemes of different Ministries. Some of such schemes are highlighted here.
The Ministry of Women and Child Development is working in supplementing the efforts of 
this Ministry in providing food and shelter to the children withdrawn from work through their 
schemes of shelter homes, etc. The Ministry of Human Resource Development (MHRD) is work-

Wages, Government Policies on Labour and Five Y ear Plans 10.17
WAGES
The term ‘wage’ refers to a payment made under contract by an employer to a worker in lieu of the 
services rendered by the latter. The most commonly accepted unit to measure such service is time. 
Wages may thus be paid on basis of hours, days, month or even year.
Over time thoughts on wages have developed from mere subsistence theory  and standard of living 
theory  to broader aspects of human resource management, and wages and salary are now clubbed 
as compensation (Geetika, Ghosh and Choudhury, 2011). Let us quickly touch upon the concepts of 
money wage and real wage here, before we move on to the theories of 
wages. Money wage  is evaluated with reference to the money that is paid, 
instead of the equivalent purchasing power; it is also known as nominal 
wage. However, money wage may not depict what a worker really earns; 
it is real wage that determines the standard of living of a worker. Real
wage  is income of a worker after taking into consideration the effects of 
inflation on his/her purchasing power.
THEORIES OF WAGES
Subsistence Theory
Proposed by David Ricardo, the subsistence theory states that the price of labour depends on the sub-
sistence of labour. Wages tend to settle at a level that is just sufficient to maintain the bare minimum 
subsistence level of a worker and his/her dependents. Such price, according to Ricardo, is equal to the 
amount of commodities necessary for the existence of a worker and his/her family. If wages rise above 
the subsistence level, workers are encouraged to marry and have large families, which would eventually 
add to the labour force, bringing wages down to the subsistence level. If however wages fall below this 
level, marriages and births are discouraged and impoverishment would increase death rate. This would 
again lower labour supply, until wages rise to the subsistence level.
The subsistence theory is completely outdated and has no practical application, especially in de-
veloped countries. It also ignores the importance of demand for labour and the role of trade unions 
in determining wages.Spotlight
