10.18 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Wages Fund Theory
According to the Wages Fund Theory proposed by J. S. Mill, wages depend upon two quantities, 
namely, the fixed wage fund (or circulating capital) set aside for the purchase of labour and the num-
ber of workers seeking employment. Since the wage fund is fixed, only a reduction in the number 
of workers could raise wages. There is another dimension to the fixed wage fund: if trade unions of 
workers succeeded in raising wages in one trade that could only be possible at the expense of another. 
Therefore unions cannot raise wages for the labour class as a whole.
This theory has been widely criticised on several grounds, the strongest 
of them being that wages are not necessarily paid out of circulating capital 
alone. The Wages Fund Theory is applicable at best in an under-developed 
country that has capital deficiency, and stands rejected now.
Purchasing Power Parity Theory
The classical economists, most notably Pigou, had argued that a cut in wages during unemployment 
and depression in the economy would help in restoring full employment. This viewpoint was criticised 
by Keynes, who propounded a new theory applicable to the economy as a whole and not particularly 
wages. Keynes considered determination of wage rate from a macro viewpoint, as an income for the 
wage earners. If the wage rate is high, workers would have more purchasing power, which, in turn, 
would increase the aggregate demand for goods and the level of output. Conversely, if the wage rate 
is low, purchasing power of labour would be less, which would lower the aggregate demand. Low 
aggregate demand would have an adverse impact on the level of employment and output. Therefore 
a cut in the wage rate instead of removing unemployment and depression would further accentuate 
the problem.
Residual Claimant Theory
The Residual Claimant Theory has been proposed by Walker, according to whom, wages are the residue 
after the other factors of production have been paid. In other words, after rent, interest and profit have 
been paid, the remainder of the total output would go to workers as wages. Several authors consider this 
theory to be optimistic, as it suggests the possibility of increase in wages through increased efficiency 
of workers, whereas the Subsistence Theory and Wages Fund Theory were pessimistic in approach. 
However this theory has been rejected by economists on several grounds.
Marginal Productivity Theory
One of the most prominent of neoclassical theories of wages, the marginal productivity theory, is as-
sociated initially with John Bates Clark and was developed later by Marshall, Jevons and Walras. It is 
basically a theory of distribution, and can be applied to any factor of production, although it has been 
most prominently used for determination of wages.
The marginal productivity theory rests on the assumptions of a per-
fectly competitive market and profit maximisation motive of employers. 
It postulates that demand for labour is determined by the value of output 
of an additional worker. The marginal product of labour is the amount by 
which the output would be increased if a unit of labour was increased, 
with the quantities of other factors of production remaining constant. Spotlight
The wage fund (or circulating 
capital) is fixed.

IR&LL_Ch_10.indd   18 1/1/2008   4:50:04 AM

Wages, Government Policies on Labour and Five Y ear Plans 10.19
Since the employer works for profit, therefore he would like to pay as low as possible, and definitely 
not more than the marginal productivity of the factor (here labour). Due to perfect competition, no 
factor input would be willing to accept a return lower than its marginal productivity. Thus in an open 
market marginal productivity determines the equilibrium factor price (here wage).
The marginal productivity theory invites criticism on account of the assumption of perfect competi-
tion. Further, labour is assumed to be perfectly mobile, which does not hold in the real world. Because 
of such reasons this theory becomes just a theoretical explanation of wage determination, whereas in real 
life wages are determined by other considerations like efficiency of labour, bargaining and negotiation.
Bargaining Theory of Wages
Proposed by John Davidson, this theory of wage determination is based on negotiations between em-
ployers and unions, with the assumption that the two parties, labour and employer, have conflicting 
objectives. Each wants the maximum share of the firm’s profits and is aware of the costs of a strike 
and the risks of participating in one.
Efficiency Wage Theory/Hypothesis
The term ‘efficiency-wages’ was coined by the noted economist, Alfred Marshall. The efficiency 
wage hypothesis is a complete digression from the marginal productivity theory explained earlier. It 
postulates that in certain situations employers may find it more beneficial to pay wages to their work-
ers higher than their marginal revenue product. The underlying idea is that the value of a worker may 
depend on how much he/she is paid, because richer workers are more productive or better motivated 
to avoid unemployment. This theory is more modern and practical in approach as it takes a holistic 
view of wages.
Demand and Supply Theory
According to this theory, wages are determined by the interaction of 
demand and supply, just like any commodity. Demand for labour partly 
reflects productivity of labour and partly the market value of the prod-
uct at different levels of production. Factors that determine the demand 
for labour include derived demand, elasticity of demand for labour and 
technical progress. Supply of labour, on the other hand, depends on the 
number of workers and the number of hours per day they are prepared to work. It is governed by the 
prevailing wage rate in the market and preference of labour for leisure. Workers earn to meet their 
needs, which may include basic necessities of food, clothing and shelter, education and health and 
entertainment of self and dependents.
Due to the trade-off between hours of work and hours of leisure, the supply curve of labour is not 
normally upward sloping, but is backward bending beyond a particular wage.

Evolution of Wage Boards in India
Tracing the evolution of Wage Boards in India we can see that as early 
as 1931 the Whitley Commission on Labour had recommended the set-
ting up of a Wage Board for the determination of wages in lines with 
concern of the ILO to evolve an international instrument for minimum 
wage fixation. Subsequently the First Five Year Plan also drew a scheme 
for permanent wage boards to be set up in each State with a tripartite composition and dealt with at 
the level of the Central Government. This was envisaged in the Second Plan as well. Finally the Wage 
Board system was introduced in March, 1957; the very first of its kind was set up for the cotton textile 
industry in the name of Central Wage Board. This was followed by establishment of such boards in 
other industries like sugar, cement, and jute. Though Wage Boards were initially meant to deal with 
the problems which arise in wage fixation, eventually it was felt that wage fixation can be left to the 
concerned industry without State intervention. As on date, wages are decided by Wage Boards for 
journalists and non-journalists newspaper and news-agency employees. Since 1955, the Government 
has constituted six wage boards for these employees, presented in Table 9.2.

Constitution of Wage Board
A Wage Board is tripartite by structure, consisting of a chairperson, an equal number of representatives 
of employers and employees (two members each) and two other independent members (an economist 
and a consumers’ representative) nominated to the Board. The Chairman is appointed by the appropri-Spotlight
The first Wage Board in India 
was set up for the cotton textile 
industry in 1957.
IR&LL_Ch_10.indd   20 1/1/2008   4:50:04 AM

Wages, Government Policies on Labour and Five Y ear Plans 10.21
ate Government in consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned or the Supreme 
Court of India. Any person who is or has been eligible to be appointed as a Judge of a High Court 
shall be qualified for appointment as the Chairman. Usually a Member of Parliament is nominated to 
represent consumers. The appropriate Government appoints workers’ and employers’ representatives 
on the recommendations of the most representative workers’ and employers’ organisations respectively 
in the sector concerned.
Functions of Wage Board
A Wage Board adjudicates industrial disputes referred to it with the assistance of independent mem-
bers. As per the First National Commission on Labour (1969), a Wage Board serves as an effective 
machinery for determination of wages, and for this purpose it attempts to fix wages within the broad 
framework of the Government’s economic and social policy. It is required to work out a wage struc-
ture based on the principles of fair wages formulated by the Committee on Fair Wages. In addition to 
the considerations relating to fair wages, a Wage Board must take into account the following aspects:
(i) the needs of the industry in a developing economy,
(ii) the system of payment by results,
(iii) the special characteristics of the industry in various regions and areas, 
(iv) the categories of workers to be covered (this may be according to the definition in the Industrial 
Disputes Act, 1947), and
(v) the working hours in the industry.
Besides, a Board may be assigned additional tasks like working out the principles that should govern 
payment of bonus and framing of gratuity schemes to workers in the concerned industry.
Exhibit 9.4 R ole of Wage Boards
InSindhudurg District Central Cooperative Bank Ltd., Kudal vs. Sindhu Sahakari Bank Karam-
chari Sanstha ((1997) IILLJ 1217 Bom) the Court has observed that Wage Board is a platform 
where the conflicting and contradictory views of employers and workmen are sought to be har-
monized within the narrowest possible limit in the presence of the Chairman, with an impartial 
attitude to reach harmonious decisions. The very object of constituting a tripartite Wage Board 
can bring to bear on the discussions and examinations of the questions by persons having a close 
and intimate knowledge of the working of the industries. The presence of such persons in the 
Board leads to competent handling of industrial disputes. Thus the Board ensures more acceptable 
decisions. The decisions of the Board are also based on the spirit of compromise.
It has been pointed out that from the time these Boards have been incepted, the efforts of the 
Chairman and members have gone a long way in maintaining harmonious industrial relations in 
the undertakings appearing before them. Such decisions, when taken unanimously, are naturally 
and legally free from appeal to the higher Courts. In this spirit, they have greater value in terms 
of collective bargaining and industrial peace than decisions imposed on the parties by a single 
statutory authority like the Industrial Court. The scheme of Wage Boards thus introduces a dual 
adjudication process, which is a unique feature of this tripartite machinery: one is to plead their 
case and the other is to decide their case.

10.22 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Evaluation of Wage Boards
The Committee on the functioning of the system of Wage Boards set up by the First National 
Commission on Labour (1969) had identified major problems from which Wage Boards suffer, some 
of which are discussed here:
rA section of employers’ organisations opposed this single machinery for wage fixation in all 
types of industrial undertakings and preferred collective bargaining or adjudication for wage 
determination. The composition and functioning of the Boards was also criticised.
rWage Boards take an unduly long time. Their working can be improved only if procedural 
delays are removed.
rMajority of the recommendations of these boards are not unanimous; such recommendations 
should be implemented only if they are unanimous.
rWorkers’ organisations were generally dissatisfied about the manner of working of the Boards on 
grounds of time taken, ad hoc increase in emoluments, that too on the lower side recommended 
by these boards, the non-statutory nature of recommendations and adjudication in the event of 
non-implementation.
The Committee made some important recommendations, including selection of the Chairman of a 
Wage Board by common consent of the organisations of workers and employers in the industry con-
cerned; functioning of the Boards essentially as a machinery for collective bargaining; assistance by 
technical assessors and experts; setting up of a Central Wage Board in the Union Ministry of Labour 
on a permanent basis to serve all Wage Boards through the supply of statistical and other material and 
lending of necessary staff, etc. (Report of the First Commission on Labour, 1969).
The importance of non-statutory Wage Boards has declined over time since recommendations made 
by these boards are not enforceable under the law. Simultaneously trade unions have grown in strength 
and are themselves able to negotiate their wages with the management. No non-statutory Wage Board 
has been set up after 1966, with the exception of the sugar industry, in which the last such Board was 
constituted in 1985 (www.labour.nic.in) . Nevertheless, Wage Boards have succeeded in promoting 
industry-wise negotiations and have thus ensured industrial peace.
RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE SECOND NATIONAL COMMISSION 
ON LABOUR
The Second National Commission on Labour (2002) has made certain significant recommendations in 
the areas of labour legislations, women and child labour and wages. We have included some of these 
recommendations in this section.
Labour Laws
rThe organised sector should be defined as consisting of establishments which have a minimum 
employment limit. Whatever be such limit, certain provisions like maternity benefit, child care, 
employees’ compensation, medical benefits and other elements of social security and safety 
must be applicable to all workers, irrespective of the employment size of that establishment or 
the nature of its activity.

rThe Government may lay down a list of highly paid jobs like airline pilots who are presently 
deemed as workmen category as being outside the purview of the laws relating to workmen and 
included in the proposed law for the protection of non-workmen.
rThe existing set of labour laws should be broadly grouped into four or five groups of laws per-
taining to industrial relations, wages, social security, safety and welfare and working conditions.
rCoverage as well as definition of the term ‘worker’ should be the same in all groups of laws, 
subject to the stipulation that social security benefits must be available to all employees includ-
ing administrative, managerial, supervisory and others excluded from the category of workmen 
and others not treated as workmen or excluded from the category of workmen. The Commission 
preferred the gender-neutral expression ‘worker’ instead of the currently used word ‘workman’ 
that we find in the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and some other Acts.
rTo rationalise and simplify the existing labour laws it was proposed that persons engaged in 
domestic service are better covered under the proposed umbrella legislation, particularly in regard 
to wages, hours of work, working conditions, safety and social security.
Women Workers
rThe laws and systems of social security should prevent and eliminate discriminatory attitudes 
and practices towards women workers. All recommendations for policies meant for this segment 
of the workforce must be combined with an enhancement of their own strength, i.e., women’s 
empowerment.
rA separate wing should be set up in the Labour Departments for unorganised workers with 
adequate number of women employees.
rA Central Fund must be set up from which welfare and social security measures for women 
workers should be financed. A Welfare Fund should be set up with employers’ contribution in 
the form of a cess with provisions for maternity leave for women agricultural labour.
rThe existing provisions for maternity benefit in the organised sector should be extended to be 
applicable to all women workers. There is a need for separate legislation for providing maternity 
benefits to women in the unorganised sector. Its implementation is possible through Welfare Funds 
or area-based schemes. A statutory scheme for the implementation of maternity entitlements 
should cover all women under income criteria. The scheme should provide financial support 
for childbirth, childcare and breast-feeding in the first few months of the child’s life. Funds to 
support such a scheme should be raised from a basket of sources.
rBoth underground work in mines and work between certain hours for women workers must be 
prohibited. There need not be any restriction on night work for women if their number in any 
shift in an establishment is not less than five and if the management is able to provide satisfac-
tory arrangements for their transport, safety and rest after or before shift hours.
rLabour legislation should include provisions for crèches where there are 20 or more workers, 
irrespective of the gender of the worker.
Child Labour
rPublic action is recommended to be mobilised along all fronts to change the attitude towards child 
labour and to build public pressure against hiring children. The entire strategy would have to be 
based on promoting the norm that no child should work and that all children should be in schools.

Summary
rThe State is an endogenous player of the industrial relations system of any nation. Tripartism 
involves three parties (i.e., trade unions of workers, employer and government) that participate 
in settlement of matters of industrial dispute. In India the main tripartite bodies are: ILC, SLC, 
Industrial Committees, Wage Boards and State Labour Advisory Boards. 
rThe Planning Commission and different committees have been recommending reform of labour 
laws in India by highlighting the need for flexibility that would give impetus to the industry to 
compete in international markets.
rThe main recommendations regarding amendment of labour laws are: consolidation, simplification 
and rationalisation, common definitions in laws, provisions of minimum living wage, improved 
regulatory activities, basic social security and labour welfare schemes, and improved health and 
safety facilities to unorganised workers.
rAmendment is recommended in certain key acts like the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, the Contract 
Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 and the Factories Act, 1948. 
rGovernment has been playing a crucial role in protecting the class of women workers through 
policy measures and legislations. Some important provisions for safeguarding the interests of work-
ing women available in various legislations are in the categories of prohibition of employment, 
provision for equal remuneration, health and safety measures, prohibition of night work, provi-
sions for conservancy, separate washing facilities, crèches and maternity benefit. Other important 
provisions are related with training and education and sexual harassment of women workers.
rThe National Policy on Child Labour contains a three-pronged action plan for tackling the prob-
lem of child labour: legislative action plan, convergence action plan, and project-based action plan.
rAs a part of the legislative action plan, the Government has enacted the Child Labour (Prohibition 
and Regulation) Act, 1986 to prohibit the engagement of children below the age of 14 years in 
18 occupations and 65 processes and to regulate the conditions of work of children in certain 
other employments.
rThe term ‘wage’ refers to a payment made under contract by an employer to a worker in lieu of the 
services rendered by the latter. Wages may be paid on basis of hours, days, months or even year.
rVarious wage theories are subsistence theory, wages fund theory, purchasing power parity theory, 
residual claimant theory, marginal productivity theory, bargaining theory, efficiency wage theory/ 
hypothesis and demand and supply theory.

C ASE
      TUDY
Child Labour in India: Justice Denied
Children are not any commodity; they are precious and one of the most important assets for any nation. 
The welfare and development of any community is largely contingent on the health and well-being 
of its children. However, it is a matter of disgrace that millions of children today are forced to work 
in various economic activities in return of very nominal wages. As domestic help they have to clean 
clothes and floors, cook food and take care of children in the house. Children also work as bonded 
labour out of perceived obligations to landlords or money lenders, to whom they are mortgaged for 
small loans taken for purposes like treatment of sickness and social ceremonies. Thus the provision 
of child labour becomes a part of a family rent or debt settlement.
Practically there in no industry in which children do not work. More specifically, as many as 90 per 
cent of children in the carpet industry in Mirzapur in the State of Uttar Pradesh have been bonded, i.e., 
sold into virtual slavery. They also have to work in exploitative and hazardous conditions. According 
to an estimate, approximately 50,000 children ranging from 3.6 to 15 years of age work in the match 
and fireworks industries in and around Sivakasi in the State of Tamil Nadu, perhaps the most publicised 
center of child labour in India. As many as 150 to 200 children are loaded in buses and vans which 
start off from 3 to 5 in the morning from neighbouring villages within a radius of about 20 miles, to 
get to the factories at 6 AM or 7 AM. These children return home between 6 and 9 in the evening. They 
work for about 12 hours daily in dark sheds, handling dangerous and toxic chemicals, but effectively 
are away from home for 15 hours. Three quarters of these child workers are girls. Each village in the 
neighbourhood of Sivakasi has an agent who enrolls the children and ensures that they are awake when 
the transport arrives. These agents receive a monthly salary of `150. They may give an advance of up 
to`200 per child labour enrolled to the parents; the advance is then deducted from the child’s salary. 
In the glass industry of Firozabad in Uttar Pradesh almost 25 per cent of the total workers are not 
even of 15 years of age. They have to undertake almost all the processes involved in bangle making, 
including carrying molten glass from the furnace to adult workers and back to the furnace, in which 
temperature approaches 700 degree Centigrade. Children who are often hired along with their parents 
for construction work also have to engage in hard physical labour while digging earth, carrying head 
loads of mud and mortar, breaking stones and soldering heavy iron rods.
The ILO has also pointed in its studies that millions of children work under exploitative conditions. 
They are beaten up, treated cruelly, and provided little food and insufficient rest. No medical treatment 
is made available to these children by their employers. Some child workers have even been found to 
go to the extent of consuming liquor, opium, ganja  and charas . Such a disturbed and undisciplined 
childhood makes criminals out of innocent children. They are denied education and their development 
is retarded, as they work long hours in the fields, glass factories, carpet weaving industry and in homes.
The causes behind this problem are many. Undoubtedly the existence of child labour in India, in 
most of the cases, is the gift of poverty; but there are certain other causative dimensions. The social 
structure is also one of reasons; child labour is mostly from the scheduled castes, scheduled tribes 
and other backward classes and religious minorities. Policy makers argue that the State ought not to 
intervene in the issue of child labour, since poor parents depend upon the income of their children, 
and hence it is a matter of social justice that the children of the poor are allowed to work.

Workers’ Participation in Management
Desired Knowledge Competencies
cTo comprehend the concept of workers’ participation in management and its levels.
cTo understand the objectives and need for workers’ participation in management.
cTo outline the forms of workers’ participation in management.
cTo develop an insight into workers’ participation in India.
INTR ODUCTION
There has been an increasing concern in industrial establishments for involving workers in organisational 
matters, particularly in those aspects that have an impact upon them. Workers’ participation generally 
encompasses different forms of workers’ involvement in decision-making pertaining to various activi-
ties of an organisation. It may be understood as an advanced form of cooperation between labour and 
management. Participation may also exist at higher levels, i.e., industry or sector-level and even at 
national-level through tripartite bodies. The idea of workers’ participation 
had originated in Europe (Ozaki and Trebilcock, 2011). A beginning in 
this direction was made when the concept of ‘industrial democracy’ was 
proposed by Sydney Webb and Beatrice Webb. Cole (1917) believed 
that political democracy could be achieved by extending democracy to 
industry. It is important to understand that ‘industrial democracy’ and ‘workers’ participation’ are two 
distinct terms. The difference between the two has been clarified in a succinct way by Rasmussen 
(2009, p. 494), according to whom, participation, “whether it involves having a say in decisions or 
sharing in financial benefits, does not necessarily give employees (individually or collectively) any 
control over those decisions …Although participating employees have potential influence within an 
organisation, management is free to ignore their views and opinions if it so chooses. Underlying the 
idea of industrial democracy, in contrast, is the possibility of employee control of various aspects of 
the enterprise’s operations.” 
Simultaneously, an interesting relationship is observed between workers’ participation in manage-
ment (WPM) and industrial democracy. WPM is a means for establishing industrial democracy, and 
the belief of management in industrial democracy may actually act as a precursor for bringing about Spotlight
The concept of industrial 
democracy was given by Sydney 
and Beatrice Webb.
IR&LL_Ch_11.indd   1 1/1/2008   4:50:15 AM

11.2 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
workers’ participation in management. If an employer wants workers’ involvement and commitment, 
specific mechanisms, structures and institutions would be required through which they can participate 
and function in a democratic set up (Pateman, 1970; Rhodes and Steers, 1981). The nature of par-
ticipation may differ across enterprises in terms of power given to workers, as it may range from just 
being consultative to co-determination of certain matters together with the management. Whatever the 
mode may be, it allows employees to control their work and working conditions to a certain extent 
(Strauss, 1998).
Thus, we may define workers’ participation in management as the shar-
ing of decision-making power by workers through their representatives 
in the entire range of activities of an organisation, by direct or indirect 
involvement. Participation usually takes place through joint committees 
of workers and management. Workers’ participation may be known by 
different names in different countries, for example in Germany it is termed 
as co-determination, while in Yugoslavia it is known as self-management.
In India, the beginning of joint committees of workers and employers be-
gun in 1920, when the Government of India constituted joint committees 
in railways and Government printing presses. A similar joint committee was formed in the Tata Iron 
and Steel Works, Jamshedpur. A joint committee was also constituted in the Carnatik Mill in Madras 
(now Chennai) in 1922 (Ministry of Labour & Employment, 2002).
The Government of India considers workers’ participation as an important means to achieve social 
justice and economic prosperity. The Industrial Policy Resolution adopted by the Government in 1956 
declared that in a socialist democracy, labour is a partner in the common task of development, and 
should be asked to participate in it with enthusiasm (Ministry of Labour & Employment, 2002, p. 1282). 
OBJECTIVES AND NEED OF WORKERS’ PAR TICIPATION IN 
MANAGEMENT
The objectives of workers’ participation in management may differ from one country to another, 
depending upon the socio-economic context. In India, soon after Independence, the Government had 
initiated various schemes for workers’ participation as a necessary ingredient for the growth of in-
dustrialisation and to create a socialist society through this process. In Germany one of the objectives 
of ‘co-determination’ was prevention of exploitation of workers by management (Virmani, 1978). In 
Japan the objective of ‘joint consultation’ is to share information between workers and management on 
various issues ranging from management to working conditions in the organisation (Shimada, 1994).
In general, some of the general objectives of workers’ participation in management are:
rSharing of power:  Power in industrial establishments has, as a practice, remained in the hands 
of management. Participation is actually a distribution of social power in industry so that it tends 
to be shared among all those who are engaged at work, rather than getting concentrated in the 
hands of a few (Mamoria, Mamoria and Gankar, 2008). Including workers in decision-making 
gives them the opportunity to share power with management.
rStimulate cooperation:  Through the process of WPM both management and workers come 
together with the objective of identifying problems of the organisation and cooperate with each 
other in finding solutions to these problems.
rIncrease labour-management communication:  Regular meetings between labour and manage-
ment help in maintaining interaction between them. It creates a system of communication and 
consultation by formal and informal means, by which workers are kept informed about the affairs Spotlight

of decision-making power

organisation, by direct or indirect 
involvement.

Workers’ Participation in Management 11.3
of the organisation. It provides a forum through which they express their opinion and contribute 
to management decisions (Eaton, 1995).
rEmpowerment of employees:  The process of WPM facilitates employee empowerment by giv-
ing them a voice in matters that affect them.
rPromotion of industrial peace:  Association of management and workers ensures better under-
standing between them. It changes the feelings and attitude of workers such that suspicion gives 
way to mutual trust and a stable relationship, a sense of belongingness and participation are built 
up, that would result in industrial peace (Davis, 1997).
The Second Five Year Plan (1956-1961) had emphasised the importance of association of manage-
ment with labour. Such association helps in increasing productivity for the general benefit of employees, 
enterprise and community. It gives employees clarity in understanding their role in the working of the 
industry and the process of production. Association satisfies the urge of workers for self-expression, 
as also observed by French (1987), thus leading to industrial harmony, 
better relations and increased cooperation. Studies have shown that par-
ticipation in management increases job satisfaction and decreases work 
apathy (e.g., Saini, 1983 and De, 1984 as cited in Gani, 1991, p. 48); 
such participation also reduces industrial conflicts (Thakur and Sethi, 
1972 and Chaudhari, 1981, as cited in Gani, 1991, p. 48).
Shimada (1994) considers WPM important as it fulfills the following needs:
rProductivity and quality improvement:  The purpose of workers’ participation in management 
is to increase their involvement in the production process, generate a sense of belongingness and 
help in improvement of quality. This improves their efficiency and strengthens their abilities, 
which results in productivity increase.
rLabour adjustments:  Changing business conditions require modifications in work structure and 
work schedules, and introduction of new technology. Work adjustments may require transfer of 
workers to new jobs in the same or to a different plant and sometimes even their retrenchment 
and lay-off. Such readjustment plans are discussed in joint consultations in Japan before they 
are actually implemented. Thus workers are informed a priori  about the situation, though the 
issues may be negotiated later through collective bargaining.
rAdaptation to economic changes:  Participation and communication with workers at various 
levels aid organisations in moderating the effects of economic shocks and help both management 
and workers in better adjustments. With cooperation of workers, organisations have been found 
to be able to adjust wages and working hours more flexibly, thereby leading to more stability. 
Participation also gives a sense of employment security to workers.

rFinancial participation:  Such participation takes place through profit-sharing or stock owner-

Sen (2012) classifies the methods of participation adopted by various enterprises into the following 
three types:
rSuperficial participation:  Such participation comprises information-sharing and suggestion

rIntermediate participation:  Intermediate participation involves collective bargaining in both 
traditional and non-traditional areas and consultation on restricted issues.
rReal participation:  Such participation covers consultation on unrestricted issues and co-deter-

every aspect of running of an enterprise, and hence may be equated to democracy. Bhattacharya 
(1986, p. 173) defines “industrial democracy as the exclusive control of productive organisa-
tions by their total workforce on the basis of equality of vote.” This means that workers do not 
merely have a superficial participation. They participate with the management at an equal level 
in deciding issues on the governance of core issues of the enterprise.
Monappa (1995) has identified four types of participation: consultative, associative, administrative 
and decisive. Other ways of distinguishing WPM may be on the basis of its advisory and mandatory 
nature, and as a voluntary or statutory measure.
Forms of Workers’ Participation in Management
There are various forms of workers’ participation, like information-sharing, consultation, association, 
joint decision-making and implementation (Klein, 1987). Some forms give employees influence (by 
way of giving a say), while others provide them power (by way of potential control) (Rasmussen, 
2009). These forms are used in different types of WPM. The types of workers’ participation deliber-
ated about in this section may involve the following forms:
rWorks Committee:  The concept of Works Committee has already been introduced as a dispute 
settlement measure in Chapter 8. The term ‘works committee’ describes arrangements for the 
representation of workers, usually at the plant or unit-level, although they may exist at higher 
levels (company, group of companies, industry, nations or group of nations). Extensive use of 
such committees, also known as works councils, workers’ committees and cooperation commit-
tees, is well established in a number of European countries such as Belgium, Denmark, France, 
Germany and the Netherlands.
rCollective Bargaining:  In collective bargaining workers’ represen-
tatives negotiate with the representatives of management on issues 
like wages, working conditions and other labour-related issues 
through exchange of dialogue. It involves active participation of 
workers. Collective bargaining results in collective agreements, 
which lay down certain rules and conditions of service in an es-
tablishment. Such agreements are normally binding on the parties. 
Theoretically speaking, collective bargaining is based on the principle of equality of power, but 
in actual practice, each party tries to overpower the other and get the maximum advantage for 
itself by using means like threats, strikes, lock-outs and other direct actions, if necessary. Thus 
collective bargaining represents the confrontational aspect of labour-management relations, Spotlight

rSuggestion Schemes:  Many organisations have implemented suggestion schemes as a form of 
WPM, in which workers are encouraged to give their suggestions on various issues and problems 
related to production and administration. Accepted suggestions may even be rewarded. Here 
workers have no power and employers are under no pressure to accept the suggestions.
rQuality Circle:  Quality Circles (QCs) are small groups of six to twelve volunteers from the 
same work area, who meet regularly to identify, analyse and solve quality and performance-
related problems in their area of responsibility (Munchus, 1983). QCs may be viewed as a 
participative management technique that had originated in Japan. They are based on the prin-
ciples of voluntary participation and collaborative decision-making (Gray, 1993).
Successful implementation of a QC programme requires that 
workers must have interest in the programme; they must believe that 
their support and participation would benefit themselves as well as 
the organisation; participants in a QC must be well-trained in human 
and technical skills (Wood, Hull and Azumi, 1983). 
QCs have been criticised as a limited form of empowerment as 
employees can take decisions only in specific areas, due to which 
they cannot enjoy the real power (Turban, 1985; Gray, 1993; Tang 
and Butler, 1997; Abo-Alhol, Ismail, Sapuan and Hamdan, 2006).Spotlight

Maruti Suzuki India Ltd., India’s largest car manufacturer, has implemented the Suggestion Scheme 
for its employees, which has benefited the company in various ways. This scheme rewards employ-
ees for their suggestions and was adopted from the parent company Suzuki Motor Corporation.
The Suggestion Scheme, which is based on a Japanese practice of engaging employees, has 
seen participation of employees across levels, plants, facilities and business functions, in improv-
ing work practices within the company. The number of suggestions has been increasing steadily 
over the years and so has been the saving resulting therefrom. In the year 2011-12, over 320,000 
suggestions were offered by the employees, which lead to cost savings of over `294.2 crore. 
Savings of `354 crore were registered during the financial year 2012-13, with over 3.96 lakh 
suggestions from the employees received during this period.
Most suggestions relate to improving quality and reducing costs, ways to speed up opera-
tions, improving efficiencies and streamlining supplies. Some of them have even helped improve 
efficiencies of the robots that are used on the shop floor. The Scheme has also been beneficial 
in improving ergonomics in the shop floor and in reducing fatigue of the workers, along with 
various other benefits. The company has been making innovations in the Suggestion Scheme. An 
online version, Sujhav Sangrehika , has also been made available to employees; it gives real time 
updates on an employee’s suggestions.

rStock Ownership:  Many employers and governments have been known to propose workers’

LEVELS OF WORKERS’ PAR TICIPATION IN MANAGEMENT
Worker involvement in labour-related affairs may take place at different levels, namely, at the level 
of enterprise or industry or region or nation or even at international level. This section gives a brief 
overview of such levels of participation.
rUnit or Enterprise-level:  Workers’ participation in decisions through modes like collective 
bargaining and works committees takes place at unit or enterprise-level.
rIndustry-level:  Workers discuss and decide upon issues related to the entire industry through 
their representatives in industrial committees, wage boards, etc.
rRegional-level:  Workers’ participation may occur at the regional-level through bodies like State 
Labour Advisory Boards.
rNational-level:  At the national-level there is a tripartite labour machinery, which comprises 
representatives of employers, employees and government. Various problems of industrial rela-
tions and policy-related issues are analysed and decided at this level.
rInternational-level:  Workers are represented at international-level in conferences, seminars and 
in bodies like ILO.
We have talked about all these measures in detail in Chapter 8.
WORKERS’ PAR TICIPATION IN MANAGEMENT IN INDIA
The need for some form of worker involvement in the management of an enterprise was felt in the 
mid-1950s and 1960s in India, well after Independence. This was realised more by the Government 
than by employers to ensure rapid industrialisation. However, there was no urge as such among unions 
for greater involvement in the management of industrial enterprises. It was observed by Punekar (1957) 
that workers’ participation in those times would take the form of joint committees for such functions 
as safety measures, social and cultural activities, production and productivity, personnel counseling, 
control of working conditions, auditing, profit sharing, recruitment and dismissal and overall man-
agement of an enterprise. Since then several forms of participation have emerged, some of which are 
elaborated here.
Shop Councils and Joint Councils
In 1975 a scheme of shop councils and joint councils was formulated by the Government. This was 
applicable to all enterprises in manufacturing and mining employing 500 or more people in the public, 
private and cooperative sectors, irrespective of whether joint consultative machineries had been set up 
and were functioning in such enterprises.
In the same year, in accordance with this scheme, during the Emergency period in the country the 
Constitution was amended and Article 43A was introduced, that formed part of the Directive Principles 
of State Policy. The purpose of this amendment was to increase productivity, promote industrial peace, 
IR&LL_Ch_11.indd   6 1/1/2008   4:50:15 AM

Workers’ Participation in Management 11.7
and inculcate a sense of involvement among the workers. It directed the State to take suitable measures 
to ensure participation of workers in the management of industrial establishments.
Shop Council The two-tier scheme of 1975 provided for the appointment of shop councils in each 
department or shop of an enterprise. The employer was expected to set up a shop council in consultation 
with the recognised union or other registered unions of workers, depending upon the local conditions.
Each council consists of an equal number of representatives of em-
ployers and workers. The employer determines the number of members 
in each council in consultation with union. Employers’ representatives 
are nominated by the management from among the persons employed in 
the unit concerned, while all representatives of workers are required to 
be from amongst those engaged in the shop or department concerned. 
The manner of representation was not specified in the two-tier scheme.
Each shop council is supposed to function for 2 years and meet at least once a month. The chairman 
of the council is nominated by the management and the vice-chairman by the workers. Decision-making 
is by consensus and decisions have to be implemented within a month.
The functions of shop councils are to assist the management in achieving production targets, improv-
ing production, productivity and efficiency, eliminating wastage and utilising capacity and manpower 
to the optimum level. They should specifically identify areas of low productivity, study absenteeism 
and recommend measures for their improvement. The councils should also concern themselves with 
safety, working conditions, discipline and two-way communication.
Joint Council The Scheme of 1975 envisaged that there should be one joint council for a single 
plant, its constitution being similar to that of shop councils. The chief executive of the unit would be 
the chairman; the vice-chairman was to be nominated by the worker members of the council. The joint 
council was required to meet at least once in 3 months. Any one of the council members could be the 
secretary of the council.
The functions of joint councils were to discuss production and produc-
tivity, achieve efficiency, eliminate wastage, arrest absenteeism, ensure 
safety measures, etc.; the physical conditions of working and welfare mea-
sures are the other areas of their concern. These councils were expected 
to ensure a two-way flow of communication between the management 
and workers. They must also give suggestions for improving the skills 
of workers and for providing adequate facilities for training.
In 1977 the Government of India introduced another scheme for participation; this scheme was 
meant for commercial and service organisations having large scale public dealings, such as hospitals 
and post and telegraph, which employ 100 or more workmen. Under this scheme, unit councils and 
joint councils were to be set up. The functions of unit and joint councils under this scheme were almost 
similar to those laid down under the 1975 scheme, with the exception that emphasis was also laid in 
the new scheme on discipline, elimination of pilferage and all forms of corruption.
Since the scheme was flexible in nature, various forms of workers’ participation had emerged 
with respect to levels of participation, size of councils, duration of schemes, frequency of meeting 
and mode of selection of representatives. This probably explains the initial increase in the number of 
enterprises controlled by the Central Government, which had adopted this scheme. By 1977-78, 545 
Central Government undertakings, 167 State Government undertakings, 1,132 private enterprises and 
99 cooperative sector units had introduced this scheme (Gupta, 1979). However there was a sharp 
decline in the number of units or enterprises having shop and joint councils after 1979.Spotlight

11.8 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Both the schemes (1975 and 1977) generated a lot of confusion and controversy due to various 
reasons including lack of criteria for determining representation, exclusion of grievance redressal, re-
strictions imposed on consideration of work-related issues, inadequate sharing of information, lack of a 
supportive and participative culture and indifference of management. Improper handling of schemes by 
union leaders also contributed to the ineffective functioning of many forums and their eventual decline. 
Works Committees
Section 3(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 provides for the setting up of a Works Committee 
consisting of representatives of management and employees in every industrial establishment employ-
ing 100 or more workmen. The objective of the committee, according to sub-section 2 of Section 3, is 
“to promote measures for securing and preserving amity and good relations between the employer and 
workmen and to that end, to comment upon matters of their common interest or concern and endeavour 
to compose any material difference of opinion in respect of such matters”.
The Act provides that the total number of representatives in the Works 
Committee, including those of the employer, should not exceed 20, and 
that the number of representatives of workers should not be less than 
that of the employer. The workers’ representatives are to be chosen from 
among the workmen engaged in the establishment, in consultation with 
their registered trade union, if any.
The main duties of Works Committee are: to promote measures for 
securing and preserving harmonious industrial relations;  discuss matters of common interest or concern; 
and endeavour to compose any material difference of opinion between the employer and workmen in 
respect of such matters.
The 17th Session of the Indian Labour Conference held in 1959 reviewed the functions of Works 
Committees and approved a list of functions which could be assigned to such committees. Accord-
ingly Works Committees were allotted discussions on lighting, ventilation, temperature, sanitation, 
drinking water, canteens, dining and rest rooms, medical and health services, safe working conditions, 
administration of welfare funds, educational and recreational activities and encouragement of thrift 
and savings among workers.
According to the statistics presented in the Report of the First National Commission on Labour 
(1969), the number of Works Committees set up in 1951 was 1,142, which rose to 2,574 in 1959-60, 
when 4,730 committees were required to be set up. Further there were 3,133 committees in 1965-66, 
as against 5,091 committees that were required to be set up.
Joint Management Council
Soon after the adoption of the Industrial Policy Resolution by the Gov-
ernment in 1956, which exhorted public sector enterprises to set an 
example in workers’ participation, a tripartite committee was set up. It 
visited UK, Sweden, France, Belgium, West Germany and Yugoslavia, 
and recommended the setting up of Joint Management Councils (JMCs) 
in all undertakings. The scheme was to be voluntary and consultative in 
nature. These councils were to deal with all matters except those falling within the area of collective 
bargaining, such as wages, bonus, hours of work, etc.Spotlight

Workers’ Participation in Management 11.9
The objectives of JMCs are to identify measures to build up trust and understanding and hence 
promote cordial relations between management and labour; increase productivity; secure effective 
welfare and other facilities; and train workers in understanding and sharing responsibilities. JMCs 
generally function as a consultative body.
A JMC has equal representation from workers and management. The size of the Council should 
be restricted to 12 persons, the majority of workers’ representatives ideally with workers themselves. 
Outside members, if inducted by the local trade unions, should not exceed 25 per cent of the workers’ 
representatives.
Following are the criteria to be followed in selecting undertakings in which JMCs should be es-
tablished:
rThe undertaking should have well-established and strong trade unions.
rThere should be willingness among employers and workers or their unions for establishing JMCs.
rThe size of the undertaking in terms of employment should be at least of 500 workers.
rThe employer, if in the private sector, should be a member of one of the leading employers’ 
organisations and the trade union should be affiliated to one of the central federations.
The scheme prescribed that JMCs are entitled to be consulted on certain specified matters that 
included administration of standing orders and their amendments as and when needed, retrenchment, 
rationalisation, closure and reduction in or cessation of operations. In some matters the management 
is expected to share information with the Council, like the general economic situation of the concern, 
the state of the market, production and sales programmes, methods of manufacture and work, annual 
balance sheet and profit and loss statements, as well as long-term plans 
for expansion. In other matters, administrative responsibilities have to 
be given to JMCs, like welfare and safety measures, vocational training 
and apprenticeship schemes, suggestion schemes, schedules for working 
hours, breaks and holidays, etc.
It was initially decided that JMCs would be set up in 50 selected enterprises, to be gradually ex-
panded to others, using the experience of the first 50. But ultimately the total number never exceeded 
140, and even that gradually decreased (Sen, 2010). The main problem was management’s reluctance 
to share decision-making with workers, which lay at the root of the failure of JMCs and the schemes 
that followed (Sheth, 1972). 
A tripartite seminar in 1958 had emphasised a basic requirement for establishing JMCs. “The 
Seminar was convinced that Joint Councils will thrive only in an atmosphere of mutual confidence 
and goodwill. It took note of the gradual improvement in the attitude of employers and trade unions 
towards each other and felt that there was a need for continuous educative work both on the side of 
labour and management” (Ministry of Labour & Employment, 1969, p. 344).
The First National Commission on Labour, which reviewed the working of JMCs, observed that 
there was not much support for these councils. The Commission held the view that “when the system 
of recognition of Trade Unions becomes an accepted practice both management and unions would 
themselves gravitate towards greater cooperation and set up JMCs” (Ministry of Labour & Employ-
ment, 1969, p. 345).Spotlight

11.10 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Worker Director
Another means of workers’ participation in management is having a representative of workers, regarded 
as Worker Directors, in the Board of Directors of an enterprise. Involvement of workers at such a high 
level gives them equality with the management. They directly participate in making of a policy and 
monitoring its implementation at organisational level. Worker Directors thus act as lining pin between 
workers and top management. They look into issues put up at board level with workers’ perspective, and 
at the same time, communicate management’s perspective to the workers.
The Nationalised Banks (Management and Miscellaneous) Scheme, 
1970, initiated by the Government in 1970, provided for the appointment 
of a Worker Director and a Director representing the officers’ cadre on 
the Board of each nationalised bank. The Worker Director was to be a 
nominee of the recognised union.
For introducing Worker Directors in banks statutory amendments 
were made in 1973 in the State Bank of India Act, 1959 and the Bank-
ing Regulation Act, 1969, that provided for the appointment of one Worker (non-executive) Director 
and one Non-Worker (officer/executive) Director in each bank. Implementation of the scheme was 
delayed both by managements of various banks and unions. Unions protested against Officer Direc-
tors, contending that officers were in any case represented. The performance of Worker Directors was 
also a concern, as they rarely spoke in the board meetings. Workers felt their number was too small 
to make an impact, and in many cases the Worker Directors felt intimidated by the presence of many 
Non-Worker Directors, who all came from social and educational strata superior to that of workers Spotlight

Tata Iron and Steel Company at Jamshedpur set up a three-tier machinery in 1956 after an agree-
ment reached with the recognised unions. The components of the machinery were:
rJoint Consultative Council of Management  is the highest level, which comprises 10 rep-
resentatives of management and an equal number of workers. It meets once in every 3 
months, and its main function is to advise management on issues pertaining to production, 
welfare, financial matters, etc.
rJoint Works Council  has 12 members each from workers and management. It meets once 
every month and its functions include studying production problems, monitoring functioning 
of other committees, etc. It also coordinates the activities of the Departmental Councils.
rJoint Departmental Council  exists at the lowest level and operates at the level of every 
department or a combination of two or more departments. It has representation from both 
management and workers. Size of the council may vary between 4 to 10 members. It 
meets once in 15 days. Suggestions received from employees are analysed in a meeting 
for further action.
Apart from these councils, there are various other forums like the General Safety Committee, 
the Safety Appliances Committee, the Suggestion Box Committee and the Canteen Management 
Committee.

Workers’ Participation in Management 11.11
(Ghosh and Gupta, 1992). At that time most of the recognised unions in Public Sector Undertakings 
(PSUs) controlled by the Centre were affiliated to Indian National Trade Union Congress (INTUC). 
Hence it became easy to nominate the national INTUC president or the general secretary on most

Joint Consultative Machinery
The Joint Consultative Machinery (JCM) was set up in 1966 by the Government on the basis of the 
recommendations of the Second Pay Commission constituted in 1959; the prime motive was to facili-
tate communication and cooperation between the Government and its employees. The Commission 
defined the objectives of the machinery as “promoting harmonious relations and securing the greatest 
measure of cooperation between the government in its capacity as employer and the general body of 
its employees in matters of common concern and with the object further of increasing the efficiency 
of public service” (Ministry of Labour & Employment, 2002, p. 1284).
The scheme of Joint Consultative Machinery, established mainly on 
the model of the Whitley Councils in the UK, provides a platform for 
constructive dialogues between representatives of workers and manage-
ment for peaceful resolution of all disputes in organisations where the 
Government is the employer. The objective of the scheme was to promote 
harmonious relations and ensure cooperation in matters of common 
concern, which would further increase the efficiency of the public ser-
vice and welfare of employees. The scheme is non-statutory and mutually agreed upon between the 
management and employees.
The JCMs have three-tier structure, e.g., office-level, department-level and national-level councils. 
Meetings of JCM must be held at least once in 4 months. There is a provision for compulsory arbi-
tration on certain matters such as pay and allowances, hours of work and leaves, in case there is a 
disagreement at the national-level JCM.
Another scheme was notified in December 1983 for Central PSUs excluding those which are run 
by Government Departments because they already had an existing stricture of JCMs. The functions 
of such councils to be set up under this scheme included consultation on production facilities, storage 
facilities, material, economy, operational problems, wastage control, safety issues, quality improve-
ment, planning, implementation and fulfillment of monthly targets, development of new products, 
encouragement to and consideration of suggestions, work system, profit and loss statement, balance 
sheet, operational expenses, absenteeism, administration of social security schemes, workers’ training 
programmes, issues pertaining to women, and welfare issues like housing, medical benefits, transport 
facility, canteens, etc.
Besides the methods of participation covered in this section, many Indian companies have also 
adopted methods like quality circles and suggestion schemes for workers’ participation.
Challenges in Implementing Workers’ Participation in Management in India
The various schemes for workers’ participation in India have not been able to deliver the desired re-
sults, as they have faced a number of challenges. Bisht (1986) found several reasons for the failure of 
participative schemes, which include: non-commitment of the management to the schemes; alienation 
of workers arising from non-implementation of decisions; and a general apathy among workers.Spotlight

11.12 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
One central element of all such participative institutions is sharing of information (Bernstein, 1982; 
Cornforth, Alan, Jenny and Spear, 1988; Lawler III, 1989); management is often reluctant to share 
information or even responsibility with workers. Sethi (1973 cited in Sen, 2012, p. 11) observed that 
“managers ... do not think that participation will unleash the creative talents of their subordinates. On 
the contrary, they seem to have a rather low opinion about their subordinates’ ability to understand 
and participate in organisational decision-making.”
Often there are perceived differences in social status, education and awareness between manage-
ment and workers that create a barrier for bringing them at an equal level. This obstructs transparency 
and trust. Certain variables related to workers also affect their willingness to participate. Sethi (1973) 
found that interest to participate was the highest among educated workers. Bisht (1986) reported that 
workers in the age group of 30 to 40 years were the ones who are the most interested in participation. 
A regular communication flow between unions and management is an essential ingredient for the 
success of WPM. A mere scheme of participation without an accompanying system of regular com-
munication does not work. Moreover, participation of workers must not be just in occasional situa-
tions; it needs to be sustained as a regular practice. The concept of WPM can be successful only if 
management and workers adopt it in the spirit with which the measures thereof are formulated. There 
are certain pre-requisites for this participation to be successful; existence of a powerful trade union is 
the most important of them. Worker representatives must feel strong enough to put forth their points 
of view in front of the more powerful management. Employers must also support workers’ participa-
tion by considering them as equal partners in the working of organisations. If management wants a 
serious and meaningful contribution of workers in decision-making, it must educate them by sharing 
the complete and right information.
RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE SECOND NATIONAL COMMISSION 
ON LABOUR
The Second National Commission on Labour (2002) has given certain observations regarding WPM 
in India. We will highlight some of the important ones here.
rThough employers’ organisations in India have been against introducing schemes of WPM 
by law, such schemes as established by law have been successful in countries like Germany, 
Japan and many member nations of the European Union. A legal base should be provided for 
institutionalising WPM in India, particularly in the context of liberalisation and globalisation.
rThere is a need for mutual dialogues between workers and management for improving indus-
trial relations, worker welfare and efficiency of organisations in view of changing technology, 
organisation structures and global competition.
rIn many countries a well-structured system of WPM exists where frequent interactions give rise 
to clearer understanding of common interests. Modern means of communication have made it 
easier to procure and exchange information related to processes of organisations.
rChanging nature of work and technology require greater understanding of the need for voluntary 
and imaginative cooperation, which can come with awareness of the common objectives and 
the identity of interests.
rIn today’s scenario there is a need to have an appropriate system that can ensure contact, coopera-
tion and co-determination at as many levels as possible from the plant-level to the board-level.

Workers’ Participation in Management 11.13
Summary
rThe term ‘workers’ participation’ is generally used to encompass various forms of workers’ 
involvement in decision-making, usually at plant-level or corporate-level. Workers’ participa-
tion in management may be seen a means for establishing industrial democracy and a belief of 
management in industrial democracy.
rObjectives of WPM are sharing power, promoting cooperation, increasing communication 
between labour and management, ensuring employee empowerment and promoting industrial 
peace. Need for WPM arises as it helps to improve productivity and quality, to bring about labour 
adjustments and to support organisations in adapting with economic changes.
rForms of WPM may be classified as direct, indirect and financial participation. Other classifica-
tions may be superficial, intermediate and real participation; advisory and mandatory participa-
tion; and voluntary or statutory participation.
rVarious methods of workers’ participation include Works Committee, collective bargaining, 
suggestion schemes, quality circles and stock ownership.
rCollective bargaining is the process by which workers’ representatives negotiate with the rep-
resentatives of management through dialogue on issues like wages, work, working conditions 
and other labour-related issues.
rQuality Circle is a participative management technique in which small teams of 6 to 12 workers in 
an enterprise are voluntarily formed to identify and solve quality or performance-related problems.
rWorkers’ involvement in labour-related affairs may take place at different levels, namely, enter-
prise-level, industry-level, regional-level, national-level and international-level.
rIn 1975 a scheme of shop councils and joint councils was formulated by the Government. This 
was applicable to all enterprises in manufacturing and mining, employing 500 or more workers 
in the public, private and cooperative sectors.
rShop council exists at shop floor or department-level, consisting of an equal number of repre-
sentatives of employers and workers; joint council exists at plant-level, and is required to hold 
meetings at least once in a quarter.
rThe Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 provides for the setting up of a Works Committee consisting 
of representatives of management and employees in every undertaking employing 100 or more 
workmen to promote healthy relations between employers and workmen.
rRecommended by a tripartite committee of the Government, joint management councils could 
be set up in undertakings employing at least 500 workers. The objectives of JMCs are to pro-
mote cordial relations between management and labour and to build up trust and understanding 
between them.
rA Worker Director is the nominee of a recognised union who would represent workers at the 
Board of Directors of the organisation.
rThe Second Pay Commission had recommended the setting up of Joint Consultative Machinery 
to facilitate communication and cooperation between the Government and its employees. 
rThe challenges for success of WPM in India include reluctance of employers to share power 
and information, lack of interest among workers to participate, etc.

      TUDY
Workers’ Participation in Management in a Cooperative
New Central Jute Mills (NCJM), an undertaking of an employees’ cooperative credit society in West 
Bengal operating in the private sector. It has about 7,000 employees, out of which almost 60 per cent 
are migrants from rural areas of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh. Most of the employees have been living in 
the company premises for more than 10 years.
The cooperative was formed from the remnants of a deserted family-owned company. In April 1986, 
the former owners declared lock-out on the ground of ‘labour unrest’ that had lasted for about a year. 
The workers suffered a lot during this period. Socio-economic conditions were becoming poor as the 
main business of the locality, i.e., jute mills, was in poor condition. Following a discussion with the 
Managing Director (MD) of the company, the local government and local political leaders, a cooperative 
of the remaining employees, who were around 2,500, was formed primarily to save the workers’ jobs. 
Thus in April 1987 the employees took over and the company resumed its operations. Some employees 
who had left, came back. The cooperative got its legal existence in 1989. The management consulted 
the All Union Advisory Committee (AUAC) of trade union representatives before holding discussions 
with external agencies like financiers, governmental agencies, local government, etc. 
IR&LL_Ch_11.indd   16 1/1/2008   4:50:16 AM

Workers’ Participation in Management 11.17
Though the cooperative became a legal body, workers could not accept the new system, as they 
viewed it as a ‘game’ of union leaders and the management to take away their money. This doubt was 
deepened when some workers could not sell off their shares, as the shares were made non-transferable. 
Neither the management nor the union leaders clarified the doubts of workers regarding financial mat-
ters. Workers of the plant complained that union representatives were not concerned with the problem 
at shop floor level. The MD felt the need to involve workers in decision-making at the plant-level, 
which would also increase their interest in work. Thus a Plant Level Consultative Committee (PLCC) 
was constituted in 1989 with the objective to provide a platform for democratic decision-making, to 
share problems and remove misunderstandings with management, and to enhance interest of workers 
in their work.
Along with PLCC, there were four more modes of workers’ participation:
1.Joint memorandum of all unions meeting:  All union representatives and committee members 
used to have a joint meeting to deliberate on issues of common interest, usually through consen-
sus. The memorandum of the meeting was distributed to workers. 
2.Union group meeting:  This meeting between union leaders and union members was to make 
them aware of shop-level problems in the various sections.
3.Works Committee meeting:  This was intended for exploring problems primarily related to 
workers’ welfare and work conditions, which helped in creating awareness among the leaders 
regarding shop-floor conditions, so that they could be taken up with shop floor managers or su-
pervisors.
4.Gate meeting:  This meeting served as a platform for general information sharing and venting off 
grievances by workers.
These meetings served as information channels and helped in increasing workers’ involvement in 
their work. Disciplining process improved considerably after evolution of these meetings. A process 
for settling disciplinary issues was developed, that involved settling issues at the plant-level between 
management and workers, without the need to refer it to Labour Office.
But despite all efforts, discontent grew amongst workers as the cooperative was not able to provide 
full wages/salary on a regular basis. They noticed that union representatives were spending most of their 
time in attending these meetings and they hardly worked. In addition, these representatives were given 
some extra allowances, whereas workers were not even given full wages. Moreover, workers came to 
know of the plans of the management to increase production using contract labour. This generated a 
feeling of job insecurity amongst casual workers, and with the objective to protect their interests they 
formed their own union called Shramik Samiti . The Sharmik Samiti  accused both management and 
union leaders of not being concerned about welfare of workers, and demanded that members of the 
Samiti , who did not get jobs through the year, be given jobs rather than jobs going to outside workers. 
Many workers left their union and joined the Samiti . They also opposed union’s role in disciplining. 
From that time, issues discussed in PLCC also changed and ‘payment of wages’ became a frequent 
matter of discussion. Unions were also accused of biased attitude in nominating workers for PLCC, 
who knew nothing about the real problems of workers. Therefore unions were forced to nominate 
shop-floor workers. These workers often took up the issue of wages at the meetings, to which the 
Committee Chairman showed displeasure. This resulted in disturbances in meetings, which gradually 
increased. Demonstrations, etc. by workers gained intensity and disrupted normal working. Ultimately 
the Sharmik Samiti  was invited to attend the Board meeting. Gradually normalcy returned. There was a 
period of stability between 1991 and 1994. But outside, the entire jute industry was hit by labour unrest.
Committees like PLCC, Works Committee, etc. were all active. Financial issues were also taken 
up in PLCC meetings, though it was considered a higher-up matter by management. Discussions took 
IR&LL_Ch_11.indd   17 1/1/2008   4:50:16 AM

11.18 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
place on rationalisation of employment and consequent increase in workload. Some joint memoranda 
were signed and distributed to workers for their information and the workers were asked to clarify 
their doubts with their respective sectional union leaders.
Reduction in number of employees and increased workload was taken into account at the PLCC 
meeting. Union representatives explained the rationale for job reduction to the worker mass in gate 
meetings and in union group meetings. Workers opposed any change in workload, but due to pressure 
from the operating agency and urgency of the situation, the management went ahead. Unions tried to 
convince workers of the situation and finally workers accepted workload change. Many permanent 
workers even volunteered to be transferred to new jobs with additional responsibilities. Some came 
up with suggestions on sharing of new responsibilities.
This was followed by a period of turbulence during 1994-1996. The cooperative was not making 
the expected progress and financiers became reluctant in continuing their support. It became difficult 
to pay timely wages or any other financial support to workers. There was a general lack of trust and 
management refused to talk about issues of wages in PLCC. Differences emerged between workers 
on one side and union representatives and management on the other. Due to disruptions the frequency 
of holding PLCC meetings decreased and ultimately the cooperative had to be cancelled as became 
more of a platform for fighting than amicable discussions.

INTR ODUCTION
The beginning of the process of industrialisation in Europe had initiated the labour movement that 
gradually grew and spread to different countries, having varying degrees of impact. Labour and 
management are the two most important aspects of an industry. The nature of relationship between 
them depends upon the legal, political, economic, social and cultural contexts of a country, and hence 
industrial relations system is found to vary from one country to another.
In Asia most of the countries have been under foreign dominance in the past, and when they became 
independent, the governments’ approach towards economic development was the deciding factor in 
shaping the industrial relations systems in these countries. Governments commonly became the larg-
est employer and hence influenced labour-management relations. The political developments in each 
of these nations were also different. With democratisation in many East Asian countries such as Korea, 
Indonesia and the Philippines in the late 1980s and 1990s, development of independent trade union 
movements and collective bargaining has picked up (Yoon, 2009).
If we take a look at industrial relations system in the European Union 
(EU) at the Union level, it has specific features which relate to various 
economic, political and social developments in the EU. These features 
include the European social dialogue, the European Employment Strategy, 
the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, cross-border Spotlight

coordination of collective bargaining, macroeconomic dialogue and the European Works Councils 
(www.eurofound.europa.eu ).
Industrial relations systems and practices are shaped by three main actors: government, workers and 
their unions, and employers/employers’ organisations. In many Asian countries, for instance, govern-
ments have had a significant impact on industrial relations. On the contrary, in Continental Europe, 
workers’ unions in some countries (e.g., Germany and the Nordic countries) have been found to have 
a major influence on shaping industrial relations, while in USA it has been more employer-driven 
(De Silva, 1997).
The role and functions of trade unions also depend upon the country context. The extent to which 
trade unions take up the responsibility to promote the interests of their members and that of com-
munity, and the mode they adopt to pressurise employers depend not only on their strength, but also 
the socio-economic compulsions and industrial structure in the nation. Labour legislations existing in 
a country have an important role to play in this connection.
Various aspects of labour-management relations like labour welfare, workers’ participation in 
management (WPM), labour laws, etc. are markedly distinct across countries and these give a unique 
shape to the industrial relations in these countries. The affluence of a country will determine if labour 
welfare has to be imposed upon employers or if they willingly undertake such activities. In general, the 
amount of benefits provided to workers will be contingent on the economic condition of the country. 
Different modes of workers’ participation in management have been discussed in Chapter 11. The 
extent and nature of workers’ involvement in decision-making in industrial undertakings depend on 
government policies and nature of trade unions and hence vary from country to country.
The International Labour Organisation (ILO) plays an important role in shaping labour-management 
relations at the international level. Many of ILO’s Conventions and Recommendations have influenced 
labour legislations in member-countries. India is a founder-member of ILO and industrial relations in 
India, to a considerable extent, have been influenced by ILO. 
In this chapter we will discuss aspects of industrial relations in some select countries and the impact 
of ILO on Indian industrial relations. 
NEED FOR UNDERSTANDING INTERNATIONAL 
INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS
We have already mentioned that the industrial relations system in a country is influenced by the unique 
characteristics of its environmental factors. In light of this view, such a system which has been suc-
cessfully implemented in one country may or may not be successful in another one. Despite this fact, 
it is essential to be aware about practices in other nations. It is important to learn from successful 
models in other countries and identify the aspects that may be replicated in order to improve labour-
management relations in a country. Today in the era of globalisation, when business organisations are 
expanding across boundaries of their nations, they hire local people. In this context, understanding 
industrial relations scenario and practices in other countries would help in managing operations and 
workforce of the enterprise in these countries successfully.
Perhaps the best example of learning from the practices in other nations and implementing such 
learning in designing own industrial relations system in Indian context is when after Independence, 
the Government of India had formed a tripartite committee that visited UK, Sweden, France, Belgium, 
West Germany and Yugoslavia to learn the prevalent practices and on returning the committee made 
certain recommendations. It agreed upon the constitution, functions and administration of Joint Councils 
and also recommended the setting up of Joint Management Councils.
