Industrial Relations: International Perspective 12.3
INTERNATIONAL INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS SYSTEMS: A
COMPARATIVE FRAMEWORK
In this section we will study the industrial relations systems in other regions/countries including the 
European Union, the United States of America and several Asian countries with respect to characteristics 
like bipartism/tripartism, trade unionism, collective bargaining, workers’ participation in management 
and labour welfare.
Bipartism/Tripartism
Industrial relations system in a country in general may have a bipartite
or tripartite nature. In many of the Asian countries the State has adopted 
a paternalistic approach and considers itself as protector of workers and 
holds itself responsible for their welfare. This is because most of these 
countries are still developing economies and a practice of pluralism may 
not be very helpful in achieving economic development. In fact, indus-
trial relations in these countries have been shaped by the active role of 
the State in their industrial development. Their governments intervene directly or indirectly (through 
formal mechanisms and institutions like adjudication, labour tribunals, etc.) in labour issues. The main 
objectives are to protect the weak labour and to maintain harmony in industry.
In the EU we may analyse industrial relations at two levels: at EU level and at the level of member-
countries. At the EU level, there may take place a dialogue between European-level trade union fed-
erations and employers’ organisations in the form of discussions, consultation etc., that may be either 
bipartite (involving only unions and employers’ organisations), or tripartite (where there is intervention 
of the European Commission). Across EU member-countries, both bipartite and tripartite agreements 
take place. Tripartite agreements are common and may be practiced for deciding wage policy and 
similar issues in some countries like Ireland, Italy and Portugal, or aspects like employment and social 
security in countries like Portugal and Spain. Bipartite agreements between unions and employers at 
inter-sectoral level are commonly done for laying down guidelines for lower-level bargaining on pay 
and work conditions in Belgium, Finland and Greece. UK has a few such formal systems (Carley and 
SPIRE Associates, 2001).
In Japan tripartite discussions and consultations commonly take place at national-level. Issues like 
labour legislations or major labour policy changes are usually discussed in tripartite councils and 
consensus is arrived at before reaching a final decision. However changes initiated in 1995 in the 
process of revision of labour laws have diluted the powers of Rengo, a major trade union confederation 
(Nakamura, n.d.). We have talked about Rengo in further details in the very next sub-section on trade 
unions.
USA is characterised by the absence of bipartite or tripartite formal institutions or mechanisms for 
any dialogue at national-level. There is no representative employers’ organisation. The government 
may bring together trade unions and employers’/business organisations for consultation or discussion 
on specific issues through means like seminars and conferences. The Department of Labour may also 
consult trade unions and employers’/business organisations separately.

12.4 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
resort to strikes and other pressure tactics to get their demands accepted. Trade unions in general are 
concerned with a wide range of economic and social issues—from wages to workers’ rights.
An important feature of trade unionism in EU is a high degree of unity and coherence at continent 
level, but there is huge diversity and sometimes division at national-level. All the major trade union 
confederations in EU countries and outside EU are members of the European Trade Union Confed-
eration (ETUC). Certain European industry federations that group most of the major EU trade unions 
in their respective sectors, are also affiliated to the ETUC. A number of trade union organisations are 
also affiliated to the European Confederation of Independent Trade Unions. 
At country-level in EU the pattern of trade union organisation varies. For instance, in Austria and 
Germany there are a few industrial unions that comprise a single dominant confederation. There are 
a few other small workers’ organisations in Germany but none in Austria. In UK and Ireland, on the 
other hand, there is a single major national centre but the number of member unions is larger and 
these unions are industrial, general and occupational unions. In Belgium, France, Italy, Luxembourg, 
the Netherlands, Portugal and Spain there are multiple confederations that differ on their views related 
to various issues, mainly political and religious.
Exhibit 12.1 Models of Industrial Relations System in European Union
Following are the four main models of industrial relations systems that exist in European Union 
nations:
i. Nordic corporatism : The Nordic corporatism model features high levels of trade union 
membership, negotiations at industry-level (sectoral) and relatively centralised bargaining 
arrangements. Generally social groups are more integrated into the system and union den-
sity is high. Hence collective agreements apply to majority of workers, without the need for 
government intervention. This model is followed in Scandinavian countries like Denmark, 
Finland and Sweden.
ii. Social partnership : This model is based on existence of employers’ associations and trade 
union confederations as it depends on strong negotiating parties who can make agreements 
survive. The social partnership model exists in countries like Austria, Belgium, Germany, 
Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Slovenia.
iii. Liberal pluralism : Labour-management relations are largely based at company-level and 
can be confrontational (with the exception of Ireland’s social pacts). In general, there are 
fewer laws concerning the labour market, social security, etc. Union density rates tend to 
be lower and therefore collective bargaining coverage is restricted, as negotiations are not 
centralised and there is no legal means of extending company-level deals industry-wide. 
This model is followed in Ireland, UK, Cyprus and Malta.
iv.State-centred : Governments in this model exercise more control; unions and employers 
are also accommodated to a certain extent to avoid social confrontation. Union density is 
often lower in these countries, but collective bargaining coverage may be wider because of 
the potential for extension of agreements to non-unionised workplace both by law and via 
employers’ associations. It exists in France, Greece, Italy, Portugal and Spain.
(Adapted from: European Trade Union Confederation (2010). Trade unions and industrial relations in 
EU. Brussels. Retrieved from www.etuc.org/IMG/pdf/TURKISH_4.pdf  on 27/92014.)

Industrial Relations: International Perspective 12.5
The number of major confederations in these countries varies from 2 in Portugal and Spain to 5 in 
France, many of them being made up of several sectoral trade union federations. In Italy and France, 
there are other major trade unions besides these large confederations. In Nordic countries there are 
separate confederations for workers in different occupations, made up of industrial and occupational 
unions, whereas in Greece, separate confederations exist for public and private sectors, each made up 
of different types of unions.
The structure of trade unions in USA is almost similar to that in Ireland and UK. The apex body 
is the American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations (AFL-CIO), which is 
made up of a large number of industrial and occupational unions. There are a few other unions that 
are not affiliated with the AFL-CIO umbrella.
Asian countries have both similarities and differences in their trade union structure and function-
ing. China and Vietnam have a communist regime. In China workers are represented by the All China 
Federation of Trade Unions and in Vietnam by the Vietnam General Confederation of Labour, both 
being the official national centres of trade unions and affiliated with the ruling parties. At a lower 
level there are sectoral unions and regional unions. Regional unions are formed on the basis of ad-
ministrative hierarchy, at district, city and State levels, and are more important than sectoral unions. 
All these lower level unions work under the official national federation, while enterprise-level trade 
unions work under the management.
Japan and Korea have had strong enterprise-level unions. Japanese trade union organisations have a 
three-tier structure: enterprise-based unions, industrial federations and the national center at the top. In 
the past national trade union centres were divided but were later united in 1989 into a national centre 
called the Japanese Trade Union Confederation, or Rengo, which organises majority of the unionised 
workers. Various enterprise-level unions that are organised into sectoral unions are the members of 
Rengo and, in this respect, trade union structure in Japan resembles that in France. Rengo works with 
the national government and employers’ organisations on issues including labour standards, tax systems 
and social security, that cannot be dealt with at the industry or enterprise-level. Table 12.1 gives the 
basic trade union organisation in the EU, Japan and USA.

A common trend across the EU (at both European and national levels), Japan and USA has been 
towards consolidation and merger of trade union organisations; consequently the number of industry 
federations affiliated to ETUC (in EU) and to AFL-CIO (in USA) has declined. A similar trend is seen 
in union membership across the industrialised market economies in recent decades, which is largely 
due to a decline in employment in the traditionally high-unionisation manufacturing industry and 
the growth of lower-unionisation services sector, increasing levels of contract employment and even 
corporate restructuring. This decrease has been witnessed in countries like France, the Netherlands, 
UK, USA and Japan.

12.6 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Collective Bargaining
The collective bargaining process and levels therein may differ across countries depending on the 
extent of involvement of the State in industrial relations, the issues ‘open’ for negotiation and the 
strength of trade unions.
Enterprise-level bargaining is a common approach in East Asian countries. In Malaysia and 
Singapore the governments have adopted a policy of enterprise or ‘in house’ unionism for securing 
cooperation, though sectoral bargaining is also picking up gradually. Both these governments have 
imposed restrictions on collective bargaining as in both the countries certain issues like transfer, pro-
motion, retrenchment, lay-off, etc. are considered management prerogatives and collective agreements 
on these issues require certification by the Industrial Court, which can even refuse the certification if 
the provisions are harmful to the national interest. Government intervention is sanctioned in Korea, 
Japan, Thailand and the Philippines when industrial disputes pose a threat to the growth of the national 
economy. Due to legal restrictions on workers in most of the countries in East Asian region, collec-
tive bargaining in the public sector is not much developed. The fragmented nature of trade unions in 
countries like Cambodia, Indonesia and the Philippines weakens their strength and limits their power 
in collective bargaining. Even at the national-level, they have little impact in influencing the policies. 
In China, the process has developed in a real sense only after 2000.
The mechanism of coordination of collective bargaining at Union level in the EU has been devised 
to avoid downward pressure on wage costs. However, issues like pay and work conditions are not sub-
ject to collective bargaining at sectoral or inter-sectoral EU level. In many States centralised national 
bargaining has been replaced by more decentralised systems of bargaining, but there is still a role for 
national-level bargaining. The Member States have widely differing dominant systems of collective 
bargaining over pay and working conditions. It is at the company-level in Bulgaria, Czech Republic, UK 
and Poland; at industry-level in Austria, Germany and the Netherlands; at company and industry-level 
in Spain, Sweden, Norway, Italy and France; at national-level in Belgium, where it sets framework. 
Industry and national levels co-exist in countries like Norway and Slovenia and bargaining takes 
place at all the three levels in Finland (Coordination of Collective Bargaining, www.eurofound.europa.
eu). However, despite these differences and a widely-observed trend towards the decentralisation of 
bargaining, it can be said that most countries have relatively centralised systems. There are countries 
like UK and most of the countries of Central and Eastern Europe where industry-level bargaining has 
largely disappeared, particularly in the private sector, and company-level negotiations predominate 
(www.worker-participation.eu ).
Under the Federal National Labor Relations Act, 1935 (or Wagner Act), workers in USA have 
gained the right to bargain collectively over wages, hours of work and other terms and conditions with 
their employers. Historically collective bargaining in USA is rooted deeply in the values of industrial 
democracy (Summers, 1978). The predominant bargaining-level for pay and all other issues is the 
individual company. Inter-sectoral or sectoral bargaining is virtually unknown in USA (with some 
exceptions at industry-level). Many unions seek to conduct ‘pattern bargaining’, whereby an agree-
ment is arrived at in a particular company or companies and then extended to other firms in the sector.
The predominant bargaining level in Japan for pay and all other issues is the individual company; 
inter-sectoral or sectoral bargaining just like in USA is virtually non-existent. Enterprise-level bar-
gaining is characterised by almost complete autonomy of the employer and enterprise-based unions, 
with no external participation (Shirai, 1999 as cited in Oh, 2006, p.15). However, it may be noted 
that there is coordination from both trade union and employers’ sides during the annual spring-time 
negotiations or Shunto. The pattern followed in these negotiations is that major manufacturers in lead-

later by small enterprises.
Collective bargaining may be said to be much more centralised in EU than Japan and USA, though 
there is no uniformity between the members of EU (UK, for example, has a highly decentralised 
bargaining structure).
LABOUR WELFARE AND SOCIAL SECURITY
The Report of the First National Commission on Labour (1969) observed that there are several 
factors deciding the standards of welfare facilities in organisations located in different countries, viz., 
an understanding of human dignity; pressure from labour; level of industrial prosperity and support 
from public opinion. Many facilities that have to be enforced by law in developing countries may 
be a matter of daily life in developed countries and are provided by employers without waiting for a 
demand from workers. Thus welfare amenities provided to workers essentially depend on the level of 
economic development of a country.
The emphasis and scope of social security system also varies across countries, depending on gov-
ernment policies and the amount of benefits may be said to depend upon the economic status of the 
nation.
Social security schemes in Japan include the public pension system to provide income security for 
the elderly, survivors and persons with disability. Healthcare systems to protect public health include 
health insurance, public health and maternal and child health systems. There are provisions of care 
services and financial support for persons with disabilities, a system to protect workers through em-
ployment insurance, work-related accident insurance, etc. Universal health insurance was implemented 
in both South Korea and Taiwan during the 1990s. Both the countries provide pension benefits. In 
addition to the Basic Livelihood Allowance Programme, the Mother-Child Welfare Scheme and long-
term elderly care, South Korea provides unemployment insurance that also covers part-time workers, 
most of whom are women (Lee and Park, 2003; Tchoe, 2003).Exhibit 12.2 Spring Labour Offensive: 
A Centralised Collective Bargaining System in Japan
With the objective of overcoming the limitations of enterprise-based unions in Japan, the Spring
Labour Offensive (known as Shunto ) began in 1956 as an annual unified struggle by labour unions 
in all industries, in which they come up with the central demand of simultaneous wage increases. 
This system has had a significant impact in shaping the Japan’s economy and industrial rela-
tions system. However under a prolonged national depression since the 1990s the Spring Labour 
Offensive experienced significant changes over the last decades. Rengo changed its name from 
‘the Spring Labour Offensive’ to ‘The Spring Struggle for a Better Life’, indicating its changed 
objectives and character. Now its objectives also include comprehensive improvement of workers’ 
living standards. The Spring Labour Offensive has shown diversification of demands that include 
shorter working hours, lump sum payments, welfare benefits and change in management policies.
(Adapted from: Oh, H. (2006). Report on the Survey on Industrial Relations in East Asia: Collective 
Bargaining in Japan. ILO- Japan Multi-Lateral Project, 2006. Thailand: ILO. )

12.8 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
In the EU there are rules regarding social security at EU level, but 
these rules do not replace national systems with a single system. EU coun-
tries have their own social security legislations that decide their specific 
beneficiaries and benefits, though EU has framed certain common rules 
to protect social security rights of citizens when moving within Europe 
(EU 28 Member States, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland). 
Nevertheless, a lack of common norms has resulted in a large disparity in 
social protection between EU Member States (Dijkhof, 2011).
National insurance in UK accounts for over half of the expenditure on 
social security in the country (Spicker, n.d.). Social security benefits in 
UK include income support for people with low income, job seeker’s allowance, child benefit, housing 
benefit that supports in paying all or part of house rent, council tax benefit, disability living allowance, 
invalid care allowance, state pension etc. French social security benefits can be categorised into five 
branches: sickness, maternity, paternity and death; accidents-at-work and occupational-diseases; retire-
ment; family benefits; and unemployment benefits ( www.cleiss.fr ). The Belgian social security system 
is based on the payment of social contributions that finance the social security system. Employer and 
employee both contribute to the social security fund. Social security is provided in events of sickness, 
unemployment, incapacity for work through sickness or invalidity, accidents at work and industrial 
disease, family allowances and pensions. The self employed can also claim social security for which 
they pay a social contribution ( www.belgium.be ).
In USA there are two principal federal programmes offering support for the elderly: Old Age, 
Survivor’s and Disability Insurance (OASDI), commonly known as Social Security, and Medicare. 
Social Security provides retirement income to the elderly, while Medicare provides health insurance 
coverage for the aged and disabled and is funded partly by payroll taxes and premium payments by 
retirees, and rest by the federal government. In addition, the Supplemental Security Income (SSI) pro-
gramme serves as a safety net to ensure that the elderly and disabled have a minimum level of income 
if their pension benefits are very low or if they do not qualify for Social Security. These apart, USA 
has a wide second-tier of private pension plans and plans sponsored by employers (Velloso, 2006).
WORKERS’ PAR TICIPATION IN MANAGEMENT
The idea of workers’ participation had originated in Europe, though its 
systems and forms profoundly differ from one country to another. Chapter 
11 discusses various forms of WPM. If we look at the institutional set up 
of workers’ participation in various countries like Germany, Japan and 
many of the EU member nations, we can clearly deduce that they have 
been established by law. A number of developing countries have also adopted legislative initiatives 
with a view to having works councils or similar structures set up (e.g., Pakistan, Thailand and Zim-
babwe) as a means of promoting labour-management cooperation. Extensive use of works councils, 
sometimes called workers’ committees, cooperation committees, etc. is well established in several 
European countries such as Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany and the Netherlands.
Board representations are also a common form of workers’ representation in EU. The majority of 
EU Member States have provisions in their legislation for some kind of employee representation at 
board-level (Kluge and Stollt, 2007, as cited in Rehfeld et al., 2011, p. 14).Spotlight

Industrial Relations: International Perspective 12.9
Workers’ participation may have a direct form as in Japan and USA, or indirect form, prevalent in 
Germany and Australia. In Germany co-determination occurs at plant-level through workers’ councils. 
In many Japanese companies a consensus is sought at all levels before 
taking a decision. It is called ringi. Through this process employees put 
considerable influence in decision-making. Though it slows down the 
decision-making process, but it ultimately results in quick implementation 
of decisions. Workers’ participation in USA stands, in general, for nego-
tiation, administration and collective bargaining, and is based on free choice. Unlike in Germany 
(where the German Work Councils Act, first passed in 1952 and subsequently amended, provides a 
legal basis for representation), the law does not impose a system of representation by requiring the 
creation of works council, but protects employees in choosing whether or not to have a system of 
representation and in choosing a union that represents them (Summers, 1978). Reflection
Co-determination aims  
at preventing exploitation of 
workers by management.
Quality circles comprise a form of worker participation originated in Japan and adopted in many 
countries. They are generally expected to achieve two goals: enhancement of quality and productivity, 
and fostering of a sense of participation in decision-making among work-
ers, resulting in better industrial relations. Emphasis has been placed more 
on the former in Japan and on the latter in Europe and North America. 
Another difference is that while circle leaders are normally appointed by 
management in Japan, they are often elected in Germany.
INTERNATIONAL LABOUR OR GANISATION
The International Labour Organisation is a specialised agency of the United Nations Organisation 
(UNO) that aims at improving labour standards at global level. It has a tripartite structure having rep-
resentatives of governments, employers and workers, and provides a forum for discussion of labour 
issues and policies. Currently the ILO has 185 Member States.Reflection
Quality circles are based on 
the principles of voluntary 
participation.Exhibit 12.3 Works Council in Germany
The Works Council in Germany represents interests of employees within an establishment. Elected 
separately for manual and non-manual workers, it enjoys certain rights to information, consultation 
and co-determination. Co-determination covers participation in arrangements on health and safety 
at work, deciding ‘social plan’ in situations like plant closure, setting guidelines for staff selection 
and appraisal, in-service training, etc. In the areas of obligatory collective co-determination like 
accident prevention and health protection, works rules, working time, fixing of performance-related 
pay rates, and others, the employer cannot take action without the Works Council’s agreement. 
The Council can refer a matter to the establishment-level arbitration committee for enforcement. 
Works Council is empowered to conclude works agreements at the enterprise-level and can initi-
ate complaints where it believes the agreement is not being honoured.

12.10 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Origin
The ILO was created in 1919, as part of the Treaty of Versailles that 
brought an end to World War I. ILO’s main objectives are to establish 
social justice for maintaining peace and harmony in the world, and to 
promote human and labour rights. Its Preamble states that:
1. Whereas universal and lasting peace can be established only if it is 
based upon social justice;
2. And whereas conditions of labour exist involving such injustice hardship and privation to large 
numbers of people as to produce unrest so great that the peace and harmony of the world are 
imperiled; and an improvement of those conditions is urgently required;
3. Whereas also the failure of any nation to adopt humane conditions of labour is an obstacle in the 
way of other nations which desire to improve the conditions in their own countries.
In its 26th Session in 1944, the General Conference of ILO brought 
out the ‘Declaration of Philadelphia’, which was incorporated into ILO’s 
Constitution. It reaffirmed the principles of ILO, which are as following:
rlabour is not a commodity;
rfreedom of expression and of association are essential to sustained 
progress;
rpoverty anywhere constitutes a danger to prosperity everywhere;
rthe war against want requires to be carried on with unrelenting 
vigour within each nation, and by continuous and concerted international effort in which the 
representatives of workers and employers, enjoying equal status with those of governments, 
join with them in free discussion and democratic decision with a view to the promotion of the 
common welfare.
The Declaration set forth the ten objectives of ILO, which are:
rFull employment and the revising of standards of living.
rThe employment of workers in the occupation in which they can have the satisfaction of giving 
the fullest measure of their skill and make their contribution to the common well being.
rThe provision, as means to the attainment of this end, and under adequate guarantees for all 
concerned, of facilities for training and the transfer of labour, including migration for employ-
ment and settlement.
rPolicies in regard to wages and earning, hours and other conditions of work calculated to ensure 
a just share of the fruits of progress to all, and a minimum living wage to all employed and in 
need of protection.
rThe effective recognition of the right of collective bargaining, the cooperation of management 
and labour in the continuous improvement of productive efficiency and the collaboration of 
workers and employers in social and economic measures.
rThe extension of social security measures to provide a basic income to all in need of such pro-
tection and comprehensive medical care.
rAdequate protection for the life and health of workers in all occupations.
rProvision for child welfare and maternity protection.
rThe provision of adequate nutrition, housing and facilities for recreation and culture.
rThe assurance of equality of educational and vocational opportunity.Spotlight

Industrial Relations: International Perspective 12.11
Membership
The States that were the members of ILO on 1st November 1945, any original member of UNO and 
any State that attained membership of the United Nations by a decision of the General Assembly may 
become a member of the ILO. The concerned State must give its formal acceptance of the obligations 
of the Constitution to the Director-General of the International Labour 
Office, also referred to hereafter as ‘the Office’. The General Conference 
of the ILO may also admit a State as member by a vote of two-thirds of 
the delegates attending the session, including two-thirds of the Govern-
ment delegates present and voting.
The Constitution of ILO provides that any member of ILO may withdraw its membership after 
giving notice to the Director-General of the Office. Such notice shall take effect 2 years after the date 
of receipt, subject to the condition that the member has fulfilled all financial obligations arising out 
of its membership at that time.
Structure
ILO carries out its functions through three main bodies: the International Labour Conference, the 
Governing Body and the International Labour Office. 
The International Labour Conference The International Labour 
Conference is also called as the international parliament of labour. Its 
main function is to set labour standards and general policies of ILO. It 
provides a forum for discussion of social and labour-related issues. It also 
adopts the ILO’s budget and elects the Governing Body. The Conference 
meets once a year in Geneva and has been continuing to meet every year since its first session in 1919, 
except for the interruption due to World War II. The annual meeting is attended by the delegates of 
governments, workers and employers of ILO Member States. The delegation of each Member State 
consists of two government delegates, one employer delegate, a worker delegate and their respective 
advisers. Generally the government representatives are ministers and officials responsible for labour 
affairs, while the employer and worker delegates are nominated by the respective government in 
agreement with organisations of employers and workers important at national-level. Every delegate 
has equal rights and has one vote. 
The Governing Body The Governing Body is the executive body of 
the ILO. It meets thrice in a year. Its main functions are to: take decisions 
on ILO policy; decide agenda of the International Labour Conference; 
scrutinise the budget of the ILO for submission to the Conference; elect the Director-General of the 
Office; and look after the implementation of the Recommendations and Conventions of ILO.
The work of the Governing Body and that of the Office are aided by tripartite committees covering 
major industries. The Governing Body is also supported by committees of experts on such matters 
as vocational training, management development, occupational safety and health, industrial relations, 
workers’ education and special problems of women and young workers.
It has 56 titular members (28 governments, 14 employers, and 14 workers) and 66 deputy members 
(28 governments, 19 employers and 19 workers). Out of 28 titular government seats, 10 are perma-
nently held by States of chief industrial importance. Since 1922 India has been holding one of these 
10 seats. The other government members are elected by the Conference every 3 years. The employer 
and worker members are elected in their individual capacity.Reflection
India is a founder member of 
the ILO.

12.12 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Prior to the adoption of a Convention or Recommendation, the Governing Body ensures proper 
preparation on the subject and adequate consultation of the concerned members by means of a pre-
paratory conference or other means.
International Labour Office The International Labour Office is the Secretariat of the ILO. The 
Office has a Director-General, who is elected every 5 years by the Governing Body. The Director-
General is responsible for the efficient conduct of the Office and other duties as may be assigned. It 
is the centre of the activities of ILO. It has headquarters in Geneva and many field offices around the 
world. The Office has a research and documentation centre. Some of the important functions of the 
International Labour Office include the following:
(i) Collection and distribution of information on all matters related to labour conditions in the world, 
particularly those subjects which it proposes to bring before the Conference with the objective to 
conclude international Conventions and Recommendations.
(ii) Conduct of research on certain matters as may be ordered by the Conference or by the Governing 
Body.
(iii) As per the directions of the Governing Body the Office must:
(a)prepare the documents on the various items of the agenda for the meetings of the Conference;
(b) provide assistance to governments at their request in framing of laws and regulations on the 
basis of the decisions of the Conference, and in improvement of administrative practices and 
systems of inspection;
(c) carry out the duties regarding the effective observance of Conventions; 
(d) prepare and bring out publications on problems labour and employment of international 
interest.
In general, the Conference or the Governing Body may assign other powers and duties to the 
Office from time to time.
Conventions and Recommendations
ILO draws international labour standards that are legal instruments and 
set out basic principles and rights at work. These standards may either 
take the form of Conventions , which are legally binding international 
treaties that may be ratified by Member States, or Recommendations ,
which act as non-binding guidelines. In many cases, a Convention lays 
down the basic principles to be implemented by ratifying countries, while 
a related Recommendation supplements the Convention by providing 
more detailed guidelines on how it could be applied. Recommendations can also be autonomous, i.e., 
not linked to any Convention.
Conventions and Recommendations are drawn up by representatives of governments, employers 
and workers and are adopted at the International Labour Conference. Once a standard is adopted, 
Member States are required under the ILO Constitution to submit  them to their competent authority 
(normally the parliament) for consideration. In the case of conventions, 
this means consideration for ratification . If it is ratified, a Convention 
generally comes into force for that country a year after the date of rati-
fication. Ratifying countries have to apply the Convention in their laws 
and practice and must report on its application at regular intervals. If the 
countries violate the Convention they have ratified, there is a provision 
of moving representation and complaint against them. Spotlight

Industrial Relations: International Perspective 12.13
If a member has ratified any International Labour Convention and later withdraws from the mem-
bership of ILO, such withdrawal shall not affect the continued validity for the period provided for in 
the Convention of all obligations arising thereunder or relating thereto.
India and the International Labour Organisation
The ILO Recommendations and Conventions have provided useful guidelines and framework for the 
evolution of legislative and administrative measures for the protection and advancement of the interest 
of workers in India. India has so far ratified 43 Conventions of ILO, including the 4 core Conven-
tions (out of the total 8), which are Forced Labour Convention (No. 29), Abolition of Forced Labour 
Convention (No. 105), Equal Remuneration Convention (No. 100), Discrimination (Employment Oc-
cupation) Convention (No. 111). Annexure I presents the list of ILO Conventions ratified by India. 
Regarding the ratification of any Convention, India has adopted a policy that first the national laws 
and policy will be brought into conformity with the provisions of the Convention, which is done 
through an amendment. The entire process of ratification begins when the Director-General of Inter-
national Labour Office sends a certified copy of the Convention or Recommendation to the Central 
Government, which then circulates it to all the State Governments, concerned Ministries of the Gov-
ernment of India and the employers’ and workers’ organisations. These bodies give their observations 
and suggestions. The Central Government then prepares a statement on action proposal which is placed 
before the Parliament for discussion. Copies of the statements are thereafter forwarded to the ILO and 
to the State Governments, and employers’ and workers’ organisations.
Many provisions in various labour legislations in India have been 
incorporated as a result of ratification of ILO Conventions by the Gov-
ernment. Thus provisions regarding working hours and weekly rest were 
incorporated in protective legislations like the Factories Act, 1948, the 
Mines Act, 1952, the Plantations Labour Act, 1951 and the Beedi and 
Cigar Workers (Conditions of Employment) Act, 1966 as a result of 
ratification of Hours of Work (Industry) Convention, 1919 in 1921 and 
the Weekly Rest (Industry) Convention (No. 14), 1921 in 1923. Many 
Conventions and Recommendations related to health, safety and welfare have resulted in incorpora-
tion of provisions in the Factories Act, 1948 and other welfare Acts. Similarly, the Minimum Wage 
Fixing Machinery Convention (No. 26), 1928 and the Minimum Wage Fixing Machinery Convention 
(No 121), 1970 have influenced the Minimum Wages Act, 1948. Several Conventions on employment 
of children and young persons and that of women have been ratified by India, and appropriate provi-
sions have been included in relevant Acts.
Conventions and Recommendations of ILO on social security like Workmen’s Compensation 
(Occupational Diseases) (No. 18), 1925 and Equality of Treatment (Accident Compensation) (No. 19), 
1925 have been ratified by India and the provisions of these two conventions have been incorporated 
into the Workmen’s (now Employees’) Compensation Act, 1923 and the Employees’ State Insurance 
Act, 1948. Many provisions in the Employees’ Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 
and the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 are a result of other Conventions related to old age benefits 
like Old Age Insurance (Industry) Convention (No. 35). Conventions aimed at promoting and regulat-
ing harmonious industrial relations namely, Rural Workers Organization Convention (No. 141), 1975, 
Tripartite Consultation (International Labour Standards) Convention (No. 144) have also been ratified, 
with the former being included in the Trade Unions Act, 1926 and the latter in the Minimum Wages 
Act, 1948 and the Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948.Spotlight

12.14 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Even the Conventions not ratified and many Recommendations related to such Conventions have 
influenced labour legislations. For example, certain provisions of Employment Injury Benefits Con-
vention (No. 121), 1964 and Workmen’s Compensation (Occupational Diseases) Recommendation 
(No. 24), 1925 have been incorporated in the Employees’ Compensation Act, 1923. Thus the ILO 
Conventions and Recommendations play an important role in shaping Indian industrial relations by 
way of influencing labour legislations.
Summary
rLegal, political, economic, social and cultural factors have an impact on all the actors in industrial 
relations scenario, i.e., employers, workers and the government of a country. Hence industrial 
relation systems differ across countries.
rIt is important to learn from successful models in other countries in order to improve labour-
management relations in a country.
rThe governments in most Asian countries intervene directly or indirectly in labour issues. While 
USA is characterised by the absence of bipartite or tripartite formal institutions or mechanisms 
for any dialogue at national level, EU countries have both bipartite and tripartite systems.
rIn EU the pattern of trade unionism varies in different member countries, from a few industrial 
unions comprising a single dominant confederation in Austria and Germany to multiple confed-
erations in Belgium, France, Italy, etc.
rJapan and Korea have strong enterprise-level unions; USA has a strong confederation to which 
many of workers’ unions are affiliated.
rEnterprise-level collective bargaining is a common approach in East Asian countries; in many 
EU States centralised national bargaining has been replaced by more decentralised systems of 
bargaining, but there is still a role for the national-level bargaining. The predominant bargaining 
level for pay and all other issues in USA is that of the individual company.
rThe mechanism of coordination of collective bargaining at European level in EU has been devised 
to avoid downward pressure on wage costs.
rSocial security schemes in Japan include the public pension system to provide income security 
for the elderly, survivors and disabled persons.
rIn EU there are rules regarding social security at EU level, but these rules do not replace national 
systems with a single system. These countries have their own social security legislations.
rWorkers’ participation may have a direct form, as in Japan and USA or indirect form, as in 
Germany and Australia. In Germany co-determination occurs at plant level through workers’ 
councils.
rILO is a specialised agency of UNO that aims at improving labour standards at global level, hav-
ing a tripartite structure. It carries out its functions through three main bodies: the International 
Labour Conference, the Governing Body and the International Labour Office. 
rILO’s Recommendations and Conventions have had a strong impact on Indian labour legislations.

      TUDY
Challenges for Workers’ Participation in the United Kingdom
Trade unions are a strong force in the British public sector and key private sector companies, but with 
changing times, trade union membership is declining at workplaces and so unions have not remained 
as the only means for workers ‘voice’. Various alternative approaches have been evolved for this pur-
pose that include direct involvement and communication methods, employee engagement, consultative 
committees and non-union and hybrid forms of consultation. 
In the mid-twentieth century there existed big trade unions, with large membership base, that partici-
pated in collective bargaining and thus regulated work conditions and employment. Unions participate 
in decision-making through consultative committees or partnership agreements and recognised trade 
unions play a statutory role in finding solutions to issues related to collective redundancy and business 
transfers. Trade unions not only represent workers in collective bargaining but also give individual 
representation in grievance and disciplinary matters, and even in work organisation and training issues. 
Such a trend is declining now as the density of membership and the use of collective bargaining pro-
cess both have fallen in public and private sector companies in recent years. Though unions are still a 
strong force in British industrial relations and are functioning actively in the public sector and within 
many large companies in the private sector in key industries (like vehicle manufacturing, aerospace 
and banks), but due to various changes in internal and external environment of organisations they no 
longer remain the only ‘voice’ of workers, as about three quarters of the employed people are not 
union members and have no access to union representation at work. In a large part of private sector 
and small part of the public sector recognised unions do not even exist. There is a representation gap 
for a large number of employees and they have expressed doubts about union effectiveness in giving 
voice to workers. 
Significant changes in employment relations in the past two decades have given rise to new meth-
ods in UK by which employees receive regular information about their organisation and can have a 
voice. Besides formal meetings of employers and trade union representatives, direct communication 
and involvement have become common. Researches have shown that the more the voice workers have 
in organisations, the better it is for increasing productivity and decreasing absenteeism; and the voice 
systems that combine direct forms of involvement with indirect forms through representative bodies 
increase organisational commitment. 
Indirect methods like Consultative Committees especially in the private sector, whether non-union 
or combining union and non-union representatives in a ‘hybrid’ body are becoming common and are 
operating alongside direct methods of involvement. There has been a remarkable growth in the use of 
direct communication in the last 25 years, having face to face meeting with employees. The preference 
for direct methods has been found to be strong.
IR&LL_Ch_12.indd   17 1/1/2008   4:50:26 AM

12.18 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
A drawback of methods like Consultative Committees and joint negotiating committees is that that 
they are less frequent than the direct methods like team briefing sessions and workforce meetings. 
But direct methods too have limited scope in terms of time limitations, and for meaningful dialogue, 
which is important for real participation. 
The advent of social media may change the way employers communicate with staff and open up new 
opportunities for employees to link with each other. Social media can help employees gain a stronger 
collective voice as employees can respond rapidly to issues discussed in Consultative Committees.
Consultative Committees have a long, if not very distinguished, history in British employment rela-
tions. Such a committee must have representatives of employees, drawn from recognised trade unions 
or directly elected by employees, or both. Trade unions have not been very positive towards these 
committees and prefer collective bargaining as a participation process as they fear that Consultative 
Committees might be used as their substitutes.
Though employers favour various forms of employee involvement but their object to legal enforce-
ment of Consultative Committees especially where these appear to limit their prerogatives. In 2004, 
only around a quarter of workplaces with 200 or more employees did not have a Consultative Commit-
tee. It is interesting to note that two-thirds of these committees were non-union and only 11 per cent 
were organised exclusively by the recognised unions. Around 1 in 5 were ‘hybrids’, having a mixture 
of union and non-union representatives. The power of these committees depend upon the attitude of 
management towards them, that may be decided to discuss important organisational decisions with 
them or may simply take them as a means of communication with workers. Management is always 
the dominant partner in consultation since it is they who are setting the key parameters to the agenda. 
In 2008, the Information and Consultation of Employees Regulations came fully into force for under-
takings with 50 or more employees. The way the regulations are drawn up in UK gives considerable 
freedom to choose the form and frequency of consultation.
Regarding the non-union Consultative Committees, there is evidence that managers often discuss a 
wider range of issues with these committees and take their views seriously. It is important to recognise 
that non-union representatives, for the most part, have a more restricted role than their union counter-
parts since their only function is to attend Consultative Committees. Consultation is a very different 
process from collective bargaining as it does not rely on arriving at agreement since the purpose is 
to discuss management plans and allow employees to raise matters concern. Where unions engage 
in both collective bargaining and consultation, the processes are often complementary. The resultant 
pattern of relationship is usually referred to as a ‘partnership’. Scotland is an example where there is 
a country-wide ‘Labour-Management Partnership’ in the National Health Service. 
In several hybrid councils trade unions have maintained their collective bargaining role but took 
part with non-union representatives in the Consultative Committee. A drawback with the hybrid form 
is the role of non-union members. If management wants a serious consultation with workers it must 
have an authoritative body to talk with, the one that represents workers in real sense. A confidential 
issue can be discussed with a representative, not the delegate, whose authority and powers are limited. 
Collective consultation in union and non-union organisations has the capacity to provide a meaning-
ful forum where employees have access to senior managers and are able to express their opinion on 
major decisions which have implications for the workforce. The necessary requirements for active 
consultation to be developed include readiness and preparedness of management to share information 
on major changes in time with workers, and discussion of a wide range of issues. Employee representa-
tives need to be able to develop a collective voice, and consultation has to be supported by a culture 
of mutual cooperation and trust.

13
Industrial Health and Safety
Desired Knowledge Competencies
cTo discuss the concept of and need for industrial health and safety.
cTo identify the causes of accidents and ways to avoid them.
cTo develop an understanding of the statutory and non-statutory measures for maintaining workers’ 
health and safety. 
INTR ODUCTION
Ever since the Industrial Revolution begun and expanded in Europe and later to different parts of the 
globe, there have been concerns regarding occupational health and safety. With increasing industri-
alisation and advancements in technology, dangers of manual jobs have undoubtedly been reduced, 
but risks of new kinds have developed. As machines and processes are becoming technologically 
advanced, they are also becoming more complicated, inviting potential hazards to the health of work-
ers and safety at workplace. The new economic order has resulted in demands for higher productivity, 
leading to work stress, besides the pressure to deal with mechanisation. Health and safety are the 
responsibility of management as well as workers, and negligence on the part of either of the two may 
result in risk to human life.
Let us first understand the concept of industrial health and safety 
before we move on to the various related aspects at workplace. The term 
‘industrial health’ encompasses all the measures undertaken to promote 
physical well-being, maintain sanitation at workplace and prevent oc-
cupational diseases amongst workers. Industrial safety includes all the 
activities undertaken to generate awareness amongst workers and imple-
mentation of safety measures so as to prevent accidents in industry. It 
may be noted here that the term ‘occupational safety and health’ (OSH) 
has the same connotation as ‘industrial safety and health’. OSH has been defined by Alli (2008, p. 
vii) as “the science of anticipation, recognition, evaluation and control of hazards arising in or from 
the workplace that could impair the health and well-being of workers, taking into account the possible 
impact on the surrounding communities and the general environment”. In this chapter we shall use 
both the terms interchangeably.Spotlight

13.2 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
The Government of India recognises that health and safety of work-
ers has a positive impact on their productivity and on the economic and 
social development of the nation. The National Policy on Occupational 
Safety and Health is drawn out of various parts of the Constitution of 
India. For example, the Directive Principles of State Policy provide safe-
guards to workers; Article 24 prohibits employment of children below 
14 years for work in any factory or mine or in any other hazardous employment; Article 39 requires 
the State to direct its policy towards securing the health and strength of workers, men and women, 
and the tender age of children and that they are not abused at workplace; Article 42 directs the State 
to make provision for securing just and humane conditions of work and for maternity relief. Thus the 
Constitution assures occupational health and safety to all workers, irrespective of their age, gender or 
sector of employment. On the basis of these Directive Principles and various international instruments,
the Government is committed to regulate all economic activities for the management of safety and 
health risks at workplace, and to provide measures to ensure healthy and safe working conditions for 
every working person in the nation.
NEED FOR INDUSTRIAL HEALTH AND SAFETY
Maintaining healthy and safe work conditions is a need for every organisation, small or big. A neg-
ligent attitude towards these aspects may result in various types of problems for organisations and 
workers. According to the Health and Safety Authority (HSA), Ireland, accidents and ill-health can 
result in losses to an organisation in terms of money, time, skill and public image, besides the hassle 
of being involved in legal proceedings ( www.hsa.ie ). We will throw light on these issues here in turn.
rFinancial loss : Whatever may be the nature of accident or ill-health resulting out of work, an 
organisation has to bear heavy cost for it. There could be a loss of physical assets like machine 
and material, besides harm to workers. Moreover, a large amount of compensation is required 
to be paid to the victims in compliance with legal enactments. Besides these direct costs, there 
may be indirect costs arising out of accidents. There is loss of productivity; manpower lost is 
required to be replaced through fresh recruitment and these workers must be trained before they 
start working on machines or equipment. Such recruitment and training process would again 
have cost implications.
rTime loss : When an accident takes place, work may be stalled for some period. Time and efforts 
are also required for fulfilling formalities laid down in the Employees’ Compensation Act, 1923 
(discussed in Chapter 26). A typical example is of notice as per Section 10(1) of the Act, by 
which no claim for compensation shall be entertained by a Commissioner unless notice of the 
accident has been given in prescribed manner as soon as practicable after the accident and unless 
the claim is preferred before him within 2 years of the occurrence of the accident. Production 
may get behind schedule as a result of such activities. 
rSkill loss : Employee skill is an asset for any company and is, in fact, a differentiating factor with 
other companies in the same industry. Little negligence on the part of management or workers may 
result in accidents or ill-health, causing partial or permanent disablement in workers, and in many 
cases, even death. Thus an organisation loses its human asset and skills due to these conditions.
rHassles of legal proceedings: Involvement in legal proceedings may consume a lot of time, 
energy and resources for an organisation. For example, in the case of Union Carbide disaster 
in Bhopal, it took 26 years for the verdict of the Supreme Court of India to see the light of the 
day (Business Standard, 2011).Spotlight

ACCIDENTS
Let us now try to understand the meaning of the term Heinrich, Peterson and Roos (1980) describe 
an accident as an event that is both unplanned and uncontrolled, in which the action or reaction of an 
object, substance, person or radiation results in personal injury or the probability thereof. Raouf (2011) 
defines an accident as any unplanned occurrence which results in injuries, fatalities, loss of produc-
tion or damage to property and assets. Haddon (1964) views an accident as an unexpected occurrence 
of physical damage to any animate or inanimate structure. According to 
Ghiselli and Brown (1948), an accident is an event that takes place with-
out foresight, and results in some type of personal injury and/or damage 
to equipment and property. Combining all these definitions, we propose 
an accident to be any unexpected occurrence where there is causation 
or probability of damage to physical objects and injury to living beings.
Causes of Accidents
Accidents do not occur without any reason; there are preceding circumstances involving humans, 
situations and machines that result in accidents. Sometimes there is an inherent risk involved in the 
nature of the job itself. The International Labour Organisation (ILO) defines risk as “a combination 
of the likelihood of an occurrence of a hazardous event and the severity of injury or damage to the 
health of people caused by this event”.
Many theories for explaining the causation of accidents have been developed, that include domino 
theory, multiple causation theory, accident proneness theory, pure chance theory and energy transfer 
theory. According to the domino theory developed by Heinrich, Peterson and Roos (1980), all ac-
cidents could be modeled with a chain of five factors. This theory was so named as the series of 
factors giving rise to an accident was compared with a row of dominoes knocking each other down 
(Figure 13.1). The sequence is as follows:
1. Ancestry and social environment, causing
2. Fault of the person, resulting inSpotlight

Petersen (1971), in his book ‘Technique of Safety Management’ , took a wider view of causes of 
accidents and proposed the ‘multiple causation model’. This model says that reasons of accidents are 
a number of contributing factors, causes and sub-causes, which combine together in a random fashion 
to cause an accident.
The factors giving rise to accidents may be divided into two categories: human factors and me-
chanical factors. 
I. Human Factors
Human factors include those causes of accidents which are related in some way to individuals and 
account for one of the most important causes of accidents. For example, it was reported that 62 per 
cent of the accidents between 1994 and 2004 in Indian Railways were caused due to failure of railway 
staff (Amitabh, n.d). The reason for occurrence of human error may be attributed to both physical and 
psychological factors (Cooper and V olard, 1978). Human errors have been differentiated by Reason 
(1990) as: active failures , that immediately precede an accident usually caused by frontline workers 
andlatent failures , that precede active failures and are usually management-related factors, e.g., poor 
supervision. According to Male (2003), human factors contribute to causation of accidents in various 
ways which include, among other aspects, designing the job and the way of managing various systems 
like training procedures, etc. Human factors are found at two levels: worker-related and management-
related.
a. Worker-Related Factors Worker-related factors are causes of 
accidents that originate from physical, psychological and behavioural 
aspects of workers. Some of the important causes are elaborated here 
as follows:
(i) Personality variables : The accident proneness theory says that 
some people are more likely to have accidents due to the presence 
of certain permanent personality variables. This theory was sup-
ported by Klumb (1995), who had observed that the majority of people never have accidents, a 
lesser percentage has one accident and a still lesser percentage experiences large number of ac-
cidents. It is the third category of people who possess the characteristics of accident-proneness.
(ii) Attitudinal problems : Presence of certain attitudes affects safety at workplace. A general 
careless attitude towards work and things, laziness, clumsiness, etc. all impact workplace safety. 
Employee attitudes have been found to be an indicator (Cox and Cox, 1991) and component 
of safety culture (Lee, 1995, cited in Correll and Andrewarth, 2000) in organisations. Several 
researchers (e.g., Barling et al., 2002; Gillen et al., 2002) have suggested that a more positive 
attitude towards safety can help prevent involvement in accidents.
(iii) Habits: Certain habits of workers may result in accidents. For example, coming drunk to work-
place may be a cause of accidents. Irritable temper and quickly getting into fights are other habits 
that may directly or indirectly lead to involvement in accidents. Life patterns may also affect 
safety at workplace. Sleeping late at night may result in sleepiness at workplace, thus threatening 
safety.Spotlight

Industrial Health and Safety 13.5
(iv) Stress: Stress is an emotional state that results from the self-per-
ceived inability of a person to bridge the gap between a desired 
state and the present state, when the outcomes are important for 
him/her. There is a direct relationship between job stress and occu-
pational accidents (Trimpop et. al., 2010). Organisations consider 
stress as related to workers’ lifestyle, personality and psychological variables, while unions find 
its roots in excessive or conflicting work demands and poor supervision (Causes and cures for 
stress still misunderstood, 1990). Work overload is supposed to be the prime cause of indus-
trial stress, which may generate a feeling of anger, fatigue, confusion and anxiety in workers 
(Goetsch, 1993). The indirect effect of stress may be on safety attitudes, as workers may deviate 
from safe work practices and are likely to commit more errors if they are under pressure to in-
crease production (Clarke and Cooper, 2004).
(v) Unsafe Acts: Unsafe acts may be understood as those human actions that arise out of errors that 
are potentially hazardous and can cause an accident. These human errors occur when workers 
deviate from the standard job procedures and hazard control processes, which may expose them 
to the risk of accidents (Joel, 1997).
b. Management-Related Factors Management-related factors include reasons of accidents 
that originate from the actions of management. In such causes management is responsible for decision 
making. As mentioned earlier, latent failures result from management actions, which may ultimately 
culminate into an accident. Some important management-related causes of accidents are explained here.
(i) Laxity in implementation of safety norms:  A casual attitude of management towards safety 
may ultimately result in accidents. Most accidents take place because small issues are either ne-
glected or overlooked. Overlooking smaller details in design of plant and equipment often leads 
to accidents. Physical layout of the workplace or work location, the condition of tools, equipment 
and materials that do not meet safety standards create unsafe conditions at work (Abdelhamid 
and Everett, 2000). Safe working is also an attitude, as already told above. Laxity or non-seri-
ousness on the part of management may result in the development of undesirable attitude among 
workers regarding safety. Stringent implementation of safety norms must be exercised and strict 
actions must be taken against workers flouting safety norms, otherwise it may convey a negative 
message to workers. The Directorate General of Factory Advisory Services and Labour Institutes 
(DGFASLI), an attached office of the Ministry of Labour & Employment, advises factories on 
various problems related to safety, health, efficiency and well-being of workers. It receives infor-
mation from time to time relating to factories covered under the provisions of the Factories Act, 
1948 from States and Union Territories. This information can be used for knowing the State-wise 
status of health and safety, and compliance level with statutory standards in factories, and for es-
timation of various trends. Statistics on the status of compliance with statutory provisions based 
on such data is given in Annexure I.
(ii) Inadequate training: Employees working on machinery of any kind and those handling hazard-
ous materials must be properly trained before they are put on job. Lack of proper training in terms 
of time or content regarding use of machines, safety equipment and gadgets is a potential threat 
and may be a precursor to accidents.
(iii) Flaws in job design: Work overload, which is a cause of workplace stress, may be a flaw of job 
design, resulting in accidents, ill health and injuries. Ergonomics need to be considered while Spotlight

occupational accidents.

designing jobs. According to the International Ergonomics Association (IEA), “Ergonomics (or 
human factors) is the scientific discipline concerned with the understanding of the interactions 
among humans and other elements of a system, and the profession that applies theoretical princi-
ples, data and methods to design in order to optimise human well-being and overall system per-
formance”. IEA further states that ergonomists contribute to the design and evaluation of tasks, 
jobs, environments and systems to make them compatible with the needs, abilities and limitations 
of people. 
(iv) Unsound recruitment policies : Selecting the right person for a job is a factor that cannot be 
ignored in maintaining workplace safety (Male, 2003). When management fails to understand 
the importance of good recruitment and selection policies, the chances of selection of a wrong 
person are high. This may aggravate the chances of human errors at work. Some of the important 
aspects to be considered in a candidate for person-job fit are physical characteristics (body size 
and shape, strength and posture), senses (vision, hearing and touch), mental abilities and work 
experience (Health and Safety Executive, 2013).
(v) Poor supervision:  Lack of proper and regular monitoring may result in problems escaping the 
attention of supervisors. Workers must be monitored if they are using safety gadgets or if they are 
complying with safety rules or not. All mechanical equipment must be checked periodically for 
their workability. Ignoring any of these aspects may be dangerous for safety.
Exhibit 13.1 Chernobyl Disaster
On 26th April 1986, a test was conducted at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Station, Ukraine, in 
former Soviet Union. During the test a sudden surge of power caused an explosion, releasing a 
cloud of radiation into the environment. Emergency actions were taken and later the damaged 
unit was completely covered in a temporary concrete structure, called the “sarcophagus,” to limit 
further release of the radioactive material. The precise causes of the accident are not clear, but 
the general belief is that the disaster was caused by both reactor design flaws and operator error.
In the aftermath, 28 out of 600 workers at the site were killed by severe radiation effects within 
the first 4 months, while 106 workers suffered from acute radiation sickness due to high radiation 
doses. About 2,00,000 workers involved in the cleanup operation in 1986 and 1987 also received 
high doses of radiation (between 1 and 100 units against the average annual radiation dose for a 
US citizen of about 0.6 unit).
As a result of the accident, inhabited areas of Belarus, the Russian Federation and Ukraine 
were contaminated with radiations. Many children and adolescents in the area drank milk con-
taminated with radioactive iodine. A number of thyroid cancer cases were detected among these 
children and a few of them even died.

Accident United States. Retrieved from ww.nrc.gov/reading-rm/doc-collections/ fact-sheets/chernobyl-
bg.html on 20/9/2014; Chernobyl Nuclear Accident. Retrieved from www.environment.about.com/od/
chernobyl/p/ chernobyl.html on 18/9/2014.)

II. Mechanical Factors
Mechanical factors may be understood as those causes of accidents that do not involve any human 
error. These include failure of machines and control systems and problems in safety gadgets.
(a) Failure of machines and control systems: Sometimes accidents occur even when no human 
fault is involved due to machine failure at some crucial juncture of work process. 
(b) Problems in safety gadgets : Faulty design or poor quality of safety gadgets like helmets, gloves, 
respirators and the like are another reason of accidents.

OCCUPATIONAL HAZARDS AND DISEASES
Occupational hazard may be defined as a risk to the health or life of an employee associated, inherent 
in the nature of an occupation or work environment. Different types of works have different types of 
risks associated with them. For example, mining and excavation work has certain unique hazards as-
sociated with it that become the cause of majority of accidents in mines. Cause-wise analysis of fatal 
accidents in coal and non-coal mines in India for the period 1996-2000 has revealed that causes like 
roof-fall, dumpers and trucks, and rope haulage in coal mines and side-fall, fall of persons, dumpers/
trucks and fall of objects in non-coal mines contribute a major share of the fatal accidents 
(www.dgfasli.nic.in ). Besides this, the environment in the underground coal mines exposes workers to 
some specific health hazards.
An occupational disease is not characterised merely by the disease 
itself, but by a combination of a disease and exposure, as well as an 
association between the two (Karjalainen, 1999). Occupational diseases 
may be seen as another type of occupational hazard. It may be defined 
as a disease occurring as a result of prolonged working in an occupa-
tion. According to the ILO (2009), these are the disease known, under 
prescribed conditions, to arise out of exposure to substances or dangerous conditions in processes, Spotlight

occupations.

In India about 10 million workers employed in mining, construction and various industries are 
exposed to silica dust. Some studies show that silicosis prevalence rates are 54.6 per cent among slate 
pencil workers and 35.2 per cent among stonecutters, while pneumoconiosis prevalence rate among coal-

to unhealthy levels of cotton dust, particles of pesticides and soil, resulting in respiratory disorders 
like asthma and a fatal disease called byssinosis (also known as brown lung). Nowadays computers 
are commonly used at workplace and it has been found that working on computers has occupational 
hazards associated with it. Prolonged use of computer can cause musculoskeletal problems, as cor-
roborated by several studies (e.g., Karlqvist et al., 2002; Jensen et al., 2002). Duration of computer 
work was found to be positively associated with neck and shoulder problems, while intensive use of 
mouse pointer has been found to be associated with hand and wrist problems. The list of notifiable

Exhibit 13.2 Noise-Induced Hearing Loss in Coal Mining
Noise-Induced Hearing Loss (NIHL) is an occupational illness in coal mining owing to high 
level of noise exposure due to the usage of heavy equipment, drilling of rocks and confined work 
environment. Barriers to reducing NIHL include: gaps in knowledge of noise dose/source relation-
ships, unavailability of effective noise controls and need for worker education and empowerment. 
A related issue is the difficulty of communication in noisy workplaces by both hearing impaired 
and normal hearing workers. The Hearing Conservation Programme aims at overcoming such 
barriers in an attempt to reduce NIHL in the mining industry.

Occupational diseases may cause permanent disablement and their cure is usually not available. 
However most of these diseases can be prevented by adopting appropriate occupational health measures. 
The ILO has its own Code of Practice that serves as a guideline for safety and health for employers, 
workers and public authorities in various sectors like construction, iron and steel industries, agriculture 
and forestry.
TRENDS IN OCCUPATIONAL DISEASES AND ACCIDENTS
Occupational health and safety is an important issue all over the world. According to estimates by the 
ILO, approximately 2.3 million deaths occur every year globally because of occupational accidents 
and work-related diseases, which means that over 6,000 workers die every day because of their work 
(www.ilo.org ). About 0.4 million people die in India every year due to work-related problems (Al-
Tuwaijri, 2008).
Certain occupational diseases occur more frequently than others. On the basis of parameters like: 
the frequency of occurrence of the illness or injury, its severity in individual cases and its potential for 
prevention, the National Institute of Occupational Safety and Health, United States of America, has 
identified certain leading occupational diseases. Of these, occupational lung disease has been found to 
be the most prevalent and includes diseases like silicosis, asbestosis, byssinosis and occupational asthma. 
Occupational cancer stands at the second number, followed by cardio-vascular diseases; disorder of 
reproduction, neurotoxicity, noise induced hearing loss, dermatological conditions and psychological 
disorders also feature in the list ( www.nihfw.org ).
Estimates by the World Health Organisation indicate that out of 11 million cases of occupational 
diseases in the world, a significant proportion of 1.9 million cases (17 per cent) comes from India and 
out of 0.7 million deaths in the world 0.12 million (17 per cent) is contributed by India ( www.nihfw.
org). The DGFASLI had reported 1,454 fatal and 30,035 non-fatal injuries in 2010, using records Exhibit 13.3 ILO Code of Practice on Safety and Health in

STATUTOR Y SAFETY MEASURES
There is no single legislation in India that addresses every aspect of occupational health and safety; in 
fact several legislations cover this issue in a fragmented manner. For mining, construction, manufactur-
ing and ports there are separate legislations that cover the health and safety issues of workers in these 
industries. The Factories Act, 1948 is a comprehensive Act that covers the health, safety and welfare of 
workers working in a factory as defined by the Act. We will talk about all such provisions in detail in 
Chapter 14. Provisions in some of the other Acts regarding health and safety of workers are covered here.
Plantations Labour Act, 1951
The Plantations Labour Act, 1951 applies to all tea, coffee, rubber and 
cinchona plantations. The objective of the Act is to regulate working 
conditions and provide for welfare of workers in plantations. Chapter III 
contains provisions for health of workers. It provides for arrangement of 
clean and wholesome drinking water (Section 8), separate latrines and 
urinals in sufficient number for males and females in every plantation (Section 9) and medical facilities 
for workers and their families (Section 10). If any accident occurs in the plantation that causes death or 
any bodily injury to a worker, by reason of which the worker is prevented from working for a period of Spotlight
Chapter III of the Plantations 
Labour Act, 1951 contains provi-
sions for health of workers.

Industrial Health and Safety 13.11
48 hours or more immediately following the accident, the employer is required to inform the authorities 
in the prescribed form (Section 32A). The Act was amended with effect from 1st June 2010 to provide 
safety and occupational healthcare to plantations workers. The Plantations Labour (Amendment) Act ,
2010 provides a new Chapter IV A to cover all aspects of safety and occupational health of workers in 
plantations. It includes provisions regarding safety m easures to be adopted in the use, handling, storage 
and transport of insecticides, chemicals and toxic substances, as given in Section 18A(1). The amended 
Act also empowers State Governments to make rules for prohibiting or restricting employment of women 
or adolescents in using or handling hazardous chemicals, provided in Section 18A(2).
Every employer shall ensure that every worker in plantation employed for handling, mixing, blend-
ing and applying insecticides, chemicals and toxic substances, is trained about the hazards involved 
in different operations in which he is engaged, the various safety measures and safe work practices to 
be adopted in emergencies arising from spillage of such insecticides chemicals and toxic substances 
and such other matters as may be prescribed by the State Government [Section 18A(4)].
Section 18A(6) provides that every employer shall maintain health record of every worker who is 
exposed to insecticides, chemicals and toxic substances which are used, handled, stored or transported 
in a plantation, and every such worker shall have access to such record.
Mines Act, 1952
The objective of the Mines Act, 1952 is to regulate the working conditions 
and safety of miners. Chapter V of the Act (sections 19 to 27) contains 
provisions for health and safety of workers. It provides for arrangement 
of clean and wholesome drinking water for workers at suitable points 
(Section 19), properly maintained urinals and latrines separately for 
males and females in the mines (Section 20), and easily accessible first-aid boxes [Section 21(1)]. 
The Act grants certain powers to the Inspectors in Section 22 to maintain and monitor safety of mine 
workers, and suitability of conditions in mines for employment. Section 22A(1) empowers inspectors 
to prohibit employment under certain situations where the employer has failed to comply with the 
provisions relating to safety. Section 23 lays down the provision for notice to be given by the owner, 
agent or manager of a mine of the occurrence of an accident, in a prescribed manner and place. The 
Central Government is empowered to appoint a court of enquiry in case of accidents (Section 24). 
Section 25 mandates notification by the owner, agent or manager of a mine if any person employed 
in the mine contracts any notified disease. The Central Government, as per Section 26, has the power 
to direct investigation of causes of notified disease(s) that have been or suspected to have been con-
tracted in a mine.
The Shops and Establishments Acts
The Shops and Establishments Act is a State-enactment. Each State has 
framed its own rules for the Act. The main objective these State-level 
legislations is to provide statutory obligation and rights to employees 
and employers in the unorganised sector of employment, i.e., shops and 
establishments, and to maintain the working conditions of employees in ‘shops’ and ‘establishments’ as 
defined in the Act. There are provisions for maintaining health of workers in these Acts. For example, 
Chapter VIII of the Bombay Shops and Establishments Act, 1948 provides for health and safety of 
employees by way of cleanliness, ventilation, lighting, precautions against fire and first-aid in sections 
39, 40, 41, 42 and 42A respectively.Spotlight
The objective of the Mines Act, 
1952 is to regulate the working 
conditions and safety of miners.
