16.12 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
RECENT INITIATIVES
The Ministry of Labour & Employment has amended Paragraph 14 of Schedule I and Paragraph 17 
of Schedule I(A) of the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Central Rules, 1946 in compliance 
with the directions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court to include ‘sexual harassment’ as misconduct, that 
includes such unwelcome sexual determined behaviour (whether directly or by implication), such as 
physical contact and advances; or demand or request for sexual favours; or sexually coloured remarks; 
or showing pornography; or any other unwelcome physical, verbal or non-verbal conduct of sexual 
nature [vide GSR 25(E), dated 19th January 2006 (w.e.f. 19.1.2006)]. Further, the same amendments 
provide that the Complaints Committee established in each establishment for inquiring into a com-
plaint of sexual harassment shall be deemed to be the inquiring authority appointed by the employer 
for the purpose of these rules. The Act has also been amended to make the guidelines applicable to 
the employees in the private sector.
SUMMAR Y
rThe Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 is designed primarily to avoid friction 
and tension between employers and workmen employed in an industry. Its principal function is 
to settle and clarify many terms and conditions of employment over which disputes normally 
arise. It also protects workers from arbitrary actions by employers.
rAs per Section 2(c), a Certifying Officer is a Labour Commissioner or a Regional Labour Com-
missioner; Section 2(g) defines standing orders as rules relating to matters set out in the Schedule.
rSection 3(1) prescribes that the employer shall submit to the Certifying Officer 5 copies of the 
draft standing orders proposed by him for adoption in his industrial establishment within 6 months 
from the date on which this Act becomes applicable to the establishment. 
rOn receiving the draft standing orders, as per Section 5(1), the Certifying Officer shall forward 
a copy thereof to the trade union, if any, or where there is no such trade union, to the workmen 
in such manner as may be prescribed, together with a notice in the prescribed form requiring 
objections, if any, which the workmen may desire to make to the draft standing orders to be 
submitted to him within 15 days from the receipt of the notice.
rAccording to Section 6(1), any employer, workmen, trade union or other prescribed representa-
tives of the workmen aggrieved by the order of the Certifying Officer may, within 30 days from 
the date on which copies are sent under Section 5(3), appeal to the appellate authority.
rStanding orders finally certified under this Act shall not, except on agreement between the em-
ployer and the workmen or a trade union or other representative body of the workmen, be liable 
to modification until the expiry of 6 months from the date on which the standing orders or the 
last modifications thereof came into operation, as provided in Section 10(1).
rSection 13(1) provides that an employer who fails to submit draft standing orders as required 
by Section 3, or who modifies his standing orders otherwise than in accordance with Section 
10, shall be punishable with fine which may extend to `5,000.
rThe Schedule contains matters to be provided in standing orders under this Act, including 
classification of workmen (e.g., whether permanent, temporary, apprentices, probationers, or 
badlis ), manner of intimating to workmen periods and hours of work, holidays, pay-days and 
wage rates, shift working, etc.

C ASE
      TUDY
CASE I
The respondent company in this case had applied to the Industrial Tribunal under Section 33 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 for permission to dismiss 27 of its employees. Its contention was that 
there was an illegal strike on 11th November 1953 of the workers of the company, that these 27 em-
ployees had participated in the illegal strike, and that they had also refused to obey lawful orders. It 
was further the contention of the respondent company that a proper inquiry as required by the standing 
orders had been held, that, the charge of misconduct with regard to these two acts had been established 
and therefore under the standing orders the company was entitled to inflict the penalty of dismissal 
upon these 27 workers.
The Industrial Court granted permission with regard to 3 out of the 27 employees and refused per-
mission involving the rest 24. The reason that induced the Industrial Tribunal to come to this conclu-
sion was that no translation in Marathi of the standing orders had been posted on special boards and 
therefore the 27 employees, who did not know English, had no notice of the standing orders, which 
were thus not binding upon those 24 employees and no proper inquiry could be deemed to have been 
held as required by the standing orders. With respect to the other 3 employees, as they knew English, 
and a copy of the standing orders having been posted on the notice board, the Tribunal took the view 
that the same were binding on those 3 employees and gave the necessary permission to the respondent 
company.
There was an appeal from the decision of the Certifying Officer certifying the standing orders and 
the copies of the Appellate Court’s decision were forwarded to the trade unions concerned and also 
IR&LL_Ch_16.indd   14 1/23/2008   12:26:00 PM

The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 16.15
to the employer on 30th September 1953. Therefore the standing orders came into operation on 8th
October 1953.
Questions
1. Which of the sections of the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 are relevant in 
this case?
2. Marathi being the language understood by the majority of the second respondent company’s 
workmen, do you think that the workmen affected are not bound by the provisions of the Stand-
ing Orders?
3. The illegal strike having taken place on 11th November 1953, do you think that the penalty in-
flicted upon the employees was a penalty permitted under the Standing Orders to the employer?
(Adapted from: Ismail Papamia and Others vs. Labour Appellate Tribunal (A) (AIR 1956 Bom 584) www.
indiankanoon.org/doc/1468795/ accessed on 6/3/2014.)
CASE II
The three petitioners in this case are employees of the Government Training Centre, a State Govern-
ment establishment, and have questioned the legality of the order by which the subsistence allowance 
paid during the period of suspension is sought to be recovered from the salary of the petitioner.
Departmental enquiries on certain charges were instituted against the petitioners, who were found 
guilty of the charges. Punishment by way of reduction of their pay was imposed by the orders dated 
19th August 1987.
As far as the validity of the order imposing the penalty is concerned, the petitioners have presented 
separate writ petitions seeking the quashing of that portion of the order denying subsistence allow-
ance. As the condition imposed in all the three orders is similar, it is sufficient to extract the relevant 
portion in one of the orders, as follows:
“Since all the charges framed in the charge sheet dated 5th September 1985 have been proved against 
you and you are found guilty of the said charges, you are deemed to be absent from duty for the period 
of suspension and shall not be entitled to any remuneration for the said period. Hence the subsistence 
allowance paid for the period 5th September 1985 till date of reinstatement will be recovered from 
your salary with effect from September 1987 in suitable instalments. You are hereby reinstated into 
service with effect from 1st September 1987.”
The question therefore is whether the direction to recover subsistence allowance paid during the 
period of suspension is valid or not?
In support of the legality of the action, the respondent relied upon the certified standing order of 
the respondent, which reads as follows: 
If, on the conclusion of the enquiry, the employee has been found to be guilty of any or all the 
charges framed against him, the employee shall be deemed to be absent from duty for the period of 
suspension and shall not be entitled to any remuneration for such period, and the order of punish-
ment shall take effect from the date of suspension. If, however, the employee is found not guilty of 
any of the charges framed against him he shall be deemed to have been on duty during the period of 
suspension and shall be entitled to the same remuneration as he would have received if he had not 
been placed under suspension, after deducting the subsistence allowance paid to him for such period.
The learned counsel for the petitioners, however, contended that the real meaning of the standing 
order was that in a case in which the disciplinary proceedings instituted against the suspended employee, 
IR&LL_Ch_16.indd   15 1/23/2008   12:26:00 PM

16.16 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
ends in his exoneration, he would become entitled to full remuneration and in the case where it ends 
in punishment, he would not be entitled to the same, and standing order does not mean that even the 
subsistence allowance paid should be recovered.
(Adapted from: R. Govendaraj and Others vs. Government Tool Room and Training Centre (ILR 1989 KAR 
1864) www.indiankanoon.org/doc/343511/ accessed on 6/3/2014.)

2. Do you think that subsistence allowance paid during the period of suspension can be recovered 
from salary?

The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961
An Act to regulate the employment of women in certain establishments for certain period before and 
after child-birth and to provide for maternity benefit and certain other benefits.
Desired Knowledge Competencies
 cTo comprehend the concept of maternity benefit and evolution of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961.
 cTo discuss the scope and cove rage of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 and of the various definitions 
given under the Act.
 cTo develop clarity of concepts like miscarriage, medical termination of pregnancy, medical bonus 
and nursing break, as laid down in the Act.
INTR ODUCTION
Motherhood and childhood are entitled to special care and assistance. All children whether born in, 
or out of, wedlock, shall enjoy the same social protection.
Article 25(2), Universal Declaration of Human Rights, 1948
Motherhood is a very special and unique experience to a woman, which brings with itself abundant 
joy and marks the beginning of a new journey in a woman’s life; however, this journey also entails 
several compromises. In the early days of wage labour system, women who would bear a child were 
not provided with any relief at work. They were required to work for long hours and thus bear heavy 
physical strains (Sinha, Sinha and Shekhar, 2006). In many instances employers would even terminate 
the services of women workers if the productivity of these workers was found to be affected due to 
maternity. This was a dubious condition for women workers: either they had to strain themselves to 
safeguard their job and thus jeopardise their own health and the health of their newborns, or forego 
their employment on account of maternity.
It was thus perceived largely that an employer must be considerate and sympathetic towards women 
workers, and a legislation that must keep in perspective the physical difficulties a working woman 
would face in performing her duties during pre- and post-natal periods was also needed. The Mater-
nity Benefit Act, 1961 is an example of the attempts by the Government of India to move legislations 
IR&LL_Ch_17.indd   1 1/1/2008   4:51:42 AM

17.2 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
to ensure social security of women by allowing them to perform their 
“social function of child bearing” (Sinha, Sinha and Shekhar, 2006, 
p. 444), undeterred by the fear of punitive measures for absence during 
pre- and/or post-natal period(s). It is a Central legislation that addresses 
the protection of employment of a working woman and her need for leave 
during pregnancy and after childbirth.
BACKDR OP OF THE MATERNITY BENEFIT ACT , 1961
The history of working women in India reveals that after the first Factories Act in 1881, only a few 
‘modern’ sectors like tea plantations had particular need for women workers (Sen, n.d.). It was a 
common practice to consider women workers as ‘special’, mainly because they also had to perform 
their social role of a wife and a mother. Legislations were sought to regulate the condition of women 
actually engaged in factory work, covering aspects like hours of work, periods of rest, prohibition of 
night work and handling of machinery.
The issue of maternity benefit acquired worldwide attention in the First Maternity Protection Confer-
ence convened in 1919 by the International Labour Organisation (ILO). The resolution of compulsory 
maternity leave, non-termination of service and other benefits for women industrial workers during 
pregnancy and immediately after childbirth passed at the Conference was however turned down by the 
Government of India on the ground that such a law would not be workable in the country.
It would be worthwhile to mention here the name of N. M. Joshi, who had introduced the Maternity 
Benefit Bill in the Legislative Assembly in 1924. The Bill aimed at prohibiting the employment of 
women in factories, mines and tea plantations in the period immediately before and after childbirth. 
However, the Assembly rejected the Bill.
In spite of long opposition from mill owners and other employers, the first maternity benefit legisla-
tion, known as the Bombay Maternity Benefit Act of 1929, was passed in Maharashtra and this was 
followed by the Madhya Pradesh Maternity Benefit Act of 1930. As a result of the Royal Commission’s 
recommendation on the subject, several State-level legislations for maternity benefit were passed in 
Madras, Uttar Pradesh, Bengal, Punjab and Assam. However, these legislations varied from each other 
as regards their scope, qualifying conditions, etc. and a need was perceived for a central legislation for 
maternity benefit. Thus the Mines Maternity Benefit Act, 1941, enforced in December 1942, came up 
as the first Central enactment extending maternity benefits to women employed in mines. The Bengal 
Maternity Benefits (Tea Estates) Bill, 1941 was introduced by the Bengal 
Government with a view to regularising maternity benefits for women 
workers in tea factories and plantations. This was followed by the Employ-
ees’ State Insurance Act, 1948 and the Plantations Labour Act, 1951. The 
report given by the Labour Investigation Committee (1946) appointed by 
the Government of India expressed dissatisfaction regarding the enforce-
ment of the State-level Acts. Meanwhile, the Constitution of India was 
adopted on 27th January 1950. Part IV of the Constitution mentions the 
Directive Principles of State Policy. Article 39 provides, inter alia , that the 
State shall, in particular, direct its policy towards securing that the citizens, 
men and women equally, have the right to an adequate means of liveli-
hood; and that the health and strength of workers, men and women, and 
the tender age of children are not abused and that citizens are not forced 
by economic necessity to enter avocations unsuited to their age or strength;Spotlight

The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 17.3
Keeping in perspective the philosophy of  ILO and understanding that woman workers need legisla-
tion towards maternity benefit, care for woman and maternity relief was recognised by the Constitution 
of India under Article 42, which provides that the State shall make provisions for securing just and 
humane conditions of work and for maternity relief. Subsequently, the Central Maternity Benefit Act 
was passed in 1961, replacing the earlier Central and State legislations.
Meanwhile the General Conference of the International Labour Organisation convened at Geneva 
by the Governing Body of the International Labour Office, and having met in its thirty-fifth Session 
on 4th June 1952, adopted Convention No. 103 that guaranteed maternity protection with effect from 
7th September 1955 ( www.ilo.org ).
Let us highlight some of the relevant excerpts from the Convention here.
Article 2
For the purpose of this Convention, the term woman means any female person, irrespective of age, 
nationality, race or creed, whether married or unmarried, and the term child means any child whether 
born of marriage or not.
Article 3
A woman to whom this Convention applies shall, on the production of a medical certificate stating 
the presumed date of her confinement, be entitled to a period of maternity leave.
The period of maternity leave shall be at least twelve weeks, and shall include a period of com-
pulsory leave after confinement.
Article 4
While absent from work on maternity leave in accordance with the provisions of Article 3, the woman 
shall be entitled to receive cash and medical benefits.
The rates of cash benefit shall be fixed by national laws or regulations so as to ensure benefits 
sufficient for the full and healthy maintenance of herself and her child in accordance with a suitable 
standard of living.
Medical benefits shall include pre-natal, confinement and post-natal care by qualified midwives 
or medical practitioners as well as hospitalisation care where necessary; freedom of choice of doctor 
and freedom of choice between a public and private hospital shall be respected.
The Convention No. 103 had worldwide implications and the guarantee of maternity protection 
with effect from 7th September 1955 became a possible reality in India when the Government of India 
passed the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961, eleven years after the adoption of the Constitution of India. 
The Act was eventually extended to all States by the end of the year 1972.
“Women do two third of the world’s work, receive ten percent of the world’s income, and own one 
percent of the means of production” (Robbins, 1999, p. 354). Not only at global level, but in India 
also women are making strides by their increasing participation in workforce. Times have changed 
since the first Central legislation on maternity benefit was passed, and so has the scenario of working 
women in India. Gone are the days when women used to be restricted at work due to their physical 
limitations and would also be unable to uphold their own interests. They are now much more educated 
and well aware of their rights. As such this Act,  though passed in 1961, is finding increasing relevance 
in modern times, and this is why the Government keeps on amending the Act to make provisions for 
social security of the new age woman. The Act has been amended several times since 1961, the latest 
being the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2008. Following is the list of Amending Acts:
1. The Central Labour Laws (Extension to Jammu and Kashmir) Act, 1970
2. The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 1972
3. The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 1973

ABOUT THE ACT
Short Title, Extent and Commencement (Section 1)
1. This Act may be called the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961. 
2. It extends to the whole of India.
   The Act has been extended to Pondicherry by Regulation 7 of 1963, Section 3 and Schedule I 
and Goa, Daman and Diu by Regulation 11 of 1963, Section 3 and Schedule.
   The words “except the State of Jammu and Kashmir” have been omitted by the Act 51 of 
1970, Section 2 and Schedule .
3. It shall come into force on such date as may be notified in this behalf in the Official Gazette—
(a) in relation to mines and to any other establishment wherein persons are employed for the 
exhibition of equestrian, acrobatic and other performances, by the Central Government; and .
(b) in relation to other establishments in a State, by the State Government.
Application of Act (Section 2)
1. It applies, in the first instance, —
(a) to every establishment being a factory, mine or plantation including any such establishment 
belonging to Government and to every establishment wherein persons are employed for the 
exhibition of equestrian, acrobatic and other performances;
(b) to every shop or establishment within the meaning of any law for the time being in force in 
relation to shops and establishments in a State, in which 10 or more persons are employed, 
or were employed, on any day of the preceding 12 months .
   Provided that the State Government may, with the approval of the Central Government, after 
giving not less than 2 months’ notice of its intention of so doing, by notification in the Official 
Gazette ,declare that all or any of the provisions of this Act shall apply also to any other establish-
ment or class of establishments, industrial, commercial, agricultural or otherwise.
2.Save as otherwise provided in sections 5A and 5B, nothing contained in this Act shall apply to any 
factory or other establishment  to which the provisions of the Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948 
apply for the time being.
Definitions (Section 3)
In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires—
Appropriate Government [Section 3(a)] Appropriate Government means, in relation to an 
establishment being a mine, or an establishment where persons are employed for the exhibition of 
equestrian, acrobatic and other performances, the Central Government and in relation to any other 
establishment, the State Government;
Child [Section 3(b)] Child includes a still-born child;

In Parjinder Kaur, wife of Shri Bhupinder Singh, R/o Quarter No.31, Maharaj Aggarsain Medical College, 
Agroha District Hisar, Haryana vs. State of Haryana, through its Financial Commissioner and Principal Sec-
retary to Government of Haryana, Health Department, Har yana, and Others [Civil Writ Petition No. 13301 of 
2011 (0&M)] , the petitioner, who was an employee as a Staff Nurse in respondent’s Medical College, had a 
grievance that the benefit of maternity leave had not been given to her. She had applied for maternity leave 
on 30th May 2011 before she had actually delivered the child on 10th May 2011, but the same was denied 
to her and she was compelled to take casual leave instead of maternity leave which she was entitled to.
 On behalf of the College, the contention raised is that the representation said to have been made itself 
is not available with the records and an application for maternity leave which the petitioner had given, had 
been taken back by her for whatever reasons. It is also to be considered here whether a medical college 
should be excluded from an establishment or not.
 The first part of Section 2 of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 (referred to hereafter as Act) relates to 
factory, mine or plantation and includes any establishment belonging to government employees for exhibi-
tion of equestrian, acrobatic and other performances. Medical College does not fall within the scheme of 
things under the first part. The second part relates to any shop or establishment and the issue here is 
whether the College could be stated to fall within any such establishment. The proviso to Section 2(1) of 
the Act enables the State Government with the approval of the Central Government to declare that all or 
any of the provisions of the Act shall apply also to any other establishment or class of establishments. No 
such notification extending the application to the houseman of medical colleges or to doctors employed in 
hospitals and medical colleges being shown, it was held that the Act does not apply to the petitioner and 
that she is not entitled to maternity benefit in the manner sought for.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/117384487/ accessed on 3/9/2014.)

CASE COR
NERIn Municipal Corporation of Delhi vs. Female Workers (Muster Roll) and Another (2000 (2) SCR 171), the 
female workers (muster roll) engaged by the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (hereafter referred to as ‘the Cor-
poration’) had raised a demand for grant of maternity leave which was made available only to regular female 
workers. The same was denied to them on the ground that their services were not regularised and therefore 
they were not entitled to any maternity leave. Their case was espoused by the Delhi Municipal Workers Union 
(hereafter referred to as ‘the Union’) and consequently the following question was referred by the Secretary 
(Labour), Delhi Administration to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication: Whether female workers working 
on muster roll should be given any maternity benefit? If so, what directions are necessary in this regard?
 The Union filed a statement of claim in which it was stated that the Corporation employs a large number 
of persons including female workers on muster roll and they are made to work in that capacity for years 
together, although they are recruited against the work of perennial nature. It was further stated that the nature 
of duties and responsibilities performed and undertaken by the employees on muster roll are the same as 
those of regular employees. It was also argued that the women employed on muster roll have been work-
ing with the Municipal Corporation of Delhi for years together; they have to work very hard in construction 
projects and maintenance of roads, including the work of digging trenches, etc., even during the period of 
mature pregnancy or soon after the delivery of child. It was pleaded that the female workers required the 
same maternity benefits as were enjoyed by regular female workers under the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 
(referred to as “Act” hereafter).
 The Corporation pleaded that the provisions under the Act or Central Civil Services (Leave) Rules were 
not applicable to the female workers engaged on muster roll as they were all engaged on daily wages. It 
was also put up that they were not entitled to any benefit under the Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948. 
Hence the Corporation contended that the demand of the female workers (muster roll) for grant of maternity 
leave as liable to be rejected.
 The Tribunal, however, allowed the claim of the female workers and directed the Corporation to extend the 
benefits under the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 to muster roll female workers who were in continuous service 
of the Corporation for three years or more.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/808569/ accessed on 4/9/2014.)

CASE COR
NERIn C. Vidya Murthy (Smt.) vs. Bangalore Metro Rail Corporation Ltd. (2012 LLR 602) , the petitioner was offered 
the post of Manager (Finance) purely on contract basis for a period of 3 years. The petitioner joined duty in 
the respondent-Corporation on 31st August 2007. On becoming pregnant around June 2008, she absented 
from duty for 106 days between 27th June 2008 and 10th November 2008 on different dates, and worked for 
53 days only. On 6th December 2008 the petitioner applied for maternity leave of 180 days, providing proof of 
her expected date of delivery as 21st March 2009, and the same was refused by the respondent. Her services 
were terminated by giving one month’s notice pay on 23rd March 2009 as per the terms and conditions of 
her appointment. It was appealed by the petitioner that the action of the respondent in not granting maternity 
leave as well as regularising the period of absence on different dates (mentioned above) as leave without 
allowance is patently illegal and in violation of the mandatory provisions of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961.
 Keeping in perspective Article 42 of the Constitution, the beneficent rule of construction which would 
enable a woman employee not only to subsist, but also to make up her dissipated energy, nurse her 
child, preserve her efficiency as an employee and maintain her previous efficiency, the Court directed 
the respondent to pay the petitioner, within a period of one month from the date of verdict, the monetary 
benefits on account of maternity, from the terms of appointment, for the period from 14th December 2008 
to 12th March 2009, and thereafter for a period of one month, being the notice period, commencing from 
13th March 2009, i.e., up to 12th April 2009.

CASE COR
NERInB. Shah vs. Presiding Officer, Labour Court Coimbatore & Others (1978 AIR 12), the respondent 
working in “Mount Stuart Estate” belonging to the appellant was allowed leave of absence on maternity 
leave. After her delivery, the appellant made a payment to her, on account of maternity benefit, an 
amount equivalent to what she would have earned on the basis of her average daily wages in 72 working 
days, falling within 12 weeks of the maternity period and excluding 12 Sundays being wageless holidays 
which fell during the period of the respondent’s actual absence immediately preceding and including the 
day of her delivery and the 6 weeks immediately following that day. The respondent moved the Labour 
Court, Coimbatore, on being refused the claim for the benefit of the entire period of 12 weeks (i.e., for 
84 days) on the plea that a week consisted of 7 days. The Court allowed the said claim by its order 
dated 26th February 1969; thereafter the appellant moved the High Court challenging the decision of the 
Labour Court. The single Judge of the High Court allowed the petition, holding that 12 weeks for which 
maternity benefit is provided for in sub-section (3) of Section 5 of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 must 
be taken to mean 12 weeks of work and the computation of the benefit had to be made with reference 
to the actual days on which the woman would have worked but for her inability.
 Aggrieved by this decision, the respondent filed an appeal, dismissing which, the Court held that 
though the Act does not contain any definition of the word “week”, it has to be understood in its ordinary 
dictionary meaning. In the context of sub-sections (1) and (3) of Section 5 of the Act, the term has to be 
taken to signify a cycle of 7 days including Sundays. By using the words, namely, “for the period of her 
actual absence immediately preceding and including the day of her delivery and for the 6 weeks imme-
diately following that day”, the Legislature intended that computation of maternity benefit is to be made 
for the entire period of the woman worker’s actual absence, that is, for all the days including Sundays 
which may be wageless holidays falling within that period and not only for the intermittent period of 6 
days, thereby excluding Sundays falling within that period. The word “period” occurring in Section 5(1) of 
the Act emphasises the continuous running of time and recurrence of 7 days. It is also in conformity with 
paragraphs 1 and 2 of Article 4 of Convention No. 103 of the Maternity Protection Convention (Revised) 
1952 adopted by the General Conference of the ILO.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/450185/ accessed on 1/9/2014.)

17.10 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Continuance of Payment of Maternity Benefit in Certain Cases (Section 5A)
Every woman entitled to the payment of maternity benefit under this Act shall, notwithstanding the 
application of the Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948,  to the factory or other establishment in which 
she is employed, continue to be so entitled until she becomes qualified to claim maternity benefit 
under Section 50 of that Act.
Payment of Maternity Benefit in Certain Cases (Section 5B)
Every woman–
(a) who is employed in a factory or other establishment to which the provisions of the Employees’ 
State Insurance Act, 1948 apply;
(b) whose wages (excluding remuneration for overtime work) for a month exceed the amount speci-
fied in sub-clause (b) of clause (9) of Section 2 of that Act; and
(c) who fulfils the conditions specified in sub-section (2) of Section 5,
shall be entitled to the payment of maternity benefit under this Act.
Notice of Claim for Maternity Benefit and Payment thereof (Section 6)
1. Any woman employed in an establishment and entitled to maternity benefit under the provisions 
of this Act may give notice in writing in such form as may be prescribed, to her employer, stating 
that her maternity benefit and any other amount to which she may be entitled under this Act may 
be paid to her or to such person as she may nominate in the notice and that she will not work in 
any establishment during the period for which she receives maternity benefit.
2. In the case of a woman who is pregnant, such notice shall state the date from which she will be 
absent from work, not being a date earlier than 6 weeks from the date of her expected delivery.
3. Any woman who has not given the notice when she was pregnant may give such notice as soon 
as possible after the delivery.
4. On receipt of the notice, the employer shall permit such woman to absent herself from the estab-
lishment during the period for which she receives the maternity benefit.
5. The amount of maternity benefit for the period preceding the date of her expected delivery shall 
be paid in advance by the employer to the woman on production of such proof as may be pre-
scribed that the woman is pregnant, and the amount due for the subsequent period shall be paid 
by the employer to the woman within 48 hours of production of such proof as may be prescribed 
that the woman has been delivered of child.
6. The failure to give notice under this section shall not disentitle a woman to maternity benefit or 
any other amount under this Act if she is otherwise entitled to such benefit or amount and in any 
such case an Inspector may either of his own motion or on an application made to him by the 
woman, order the payment of such benefit or amount within such period as may be specified in 
the order.
Payment of Maternity Benefit in Case of Death of a Woman (Section 7)
If a woman is entitled to maternity benefit or any other amount under this Act, dies before receiving 
such maternity benefit or amount, or where the employer is liable for maternity benefit under the second 
proviso to sub-section (3) of Section 5, the employer shall pay such benefit or amount to the person

Payment of Medical Bonus (Section 8)
Every woman entitled to maternity benefit under this Act shall also be 
entitled to receive from her employer a medical bonus of `1,000, if no 
pre-natal confinement and post-natal care is provided for by the employer 
free of charge.

Leave for Miscarriage, etc (Section 9)
In case of miscarriage or medical termination of pregnancy, a woman shall, on production of such 
proof as may be prescribed, be entitled to leave with wages at the rate of maternity benefit for a pe-
riod of 6 weeks immediately following the day of her miscarriage or, as the case may be, her medical 
termination of pregnancy.
Leave with Wages for Tubectomy Operation (Section 9A)
In case of tubectomy operation, a woman shall, on production of such proof as may be prescribed, 
be entitled to leave with wages at the rate of maternity benefit for a period of 2 weeks immediately 
following the day of her tubectomy operation.
Leave for Illness Arising out of Pregnancy, Delivery, Premature Birth

Operation (Section 10)

tubectomy operation shall, on production of such proof as may be pre-
scribed, be entitled in addition to the period of absence allowed to her 
under Section 6, or, as the case may be, under Section 9, to leave with 
wages at the rate of maternity benefit for a maximum period of 1 month.
Nursing Breaks (Section 11)

shall, in addition to the interval for rest allowed to her, be allowed in the 
course of her daily work 2 breaks of prescribed duration for nursing the child until the child attains

17.12 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Dismissal during Absence of Pregnancy (Section 12)
1. Where a woman absents herself from work in accordance with the provisions of this Act, it shall 
be unlawful for her employer to discharge or dismiss her during or on account of such absence 
or to give notice of discharge or dismissal on such a day that the notice will expire during such 
absence, or to vary to her disadvantage any of the conditions of her service.
2. (a)  The discharge or dismissal of a woman at any time during her pregnancy, if the woman for 
such discharge of dismissal would have been entitled to maternity benefit or medical bonus 
referred to in Section 8, shall not have the effect of depriving her of the maternity benefit or 
medical bonus:
      Provided that where the dismissal is for any prescribed gross misconduct, the employer 
may, by order in writing communicated to the woman, deprive her of the maternity benefit or 
medical bonus or both.
  (b)  Any woman deprived of maternity benefit or medical bonus, or both, or discharged or dis-
missed during or on account of her absence from work in accordance with the provisions of 
this Act, may, within 60 days from the date on which the order of such deprivation is com-
municated to her, appeal to such authority as may be prescribed, and the decision of that 
authority on such appeal, whether the woman should or should not be deprived of maternity 
benefit or medical bonus or both, or discharged or dismissed shall be final.
  (c)  Nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect the provisions contained in sub-section (1).
No Deduction of Wages in Certain Cases (Section 13)
No deduction from the normal and usual daily wages of a woman entitled to maternity benefit under 
the provisions of this Act shall be made by reason only of–
(a) the nature of work assigned to her by virtue of the provisions contained in sub-section (3) of Sec-
tion 4; or
(b) breaks for nursing the child allowed to her under the provisions of Section 11.
Appointment of Inspectors (Section 14)
The appropriate Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint such officers as it 
thinks fit to be Inspectors for the purposes of this Act and may define the local limits of the jurisdic-
tion within which they shall exercise their functions under this Act.
Powers and Duties of Inspectors (Section 15)
An Inspector may, subject to such restrictions or conditions as may be prescribed, exercise all or any 
of the following powers, namely: 
(a) enter at all reasonable times with such assistants, if any, being persons in the service of the 
Government or any local or other public authority, as he thinks fit, any premises or place where 
women are employed or work is given to them in an establishment, for the purposes of examining 
any registers, records and notices required to be kept or exhibited by or under this Act and require 
their production for inspection;
(b) examine any person whom he finds in any premises or place and who, he has reasonable cause to 
believe, is employed in the establishment:
Provided that no person shall be compelled under this section to answer any question or give any 
evidence tending to incriminate himself;

17.14 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Penalty for Contravention of Act by Employer (Section 21)
1. If any employer fails to pay any amount of maternity benefit to a woman entitled under this Act 
or discharges or dismisses such woman during or on account of her absence from work in accor-
dance with the provisions of this Act, he shall be punishable with imprisonment which shall not 
be less than 3 months but which may extend to 1 year and with fine which shall not be less than 
`2,000 but which may extend to `5,000:
   Provided that the court may, for sufficient reasons to be recorded in writing, impose a sentence 
of imprisonment for a lesser term or fine only in lieu of imprisonment.
2. If any employer contravenes the provisions of this Act or the rules made thereunder, he shall, if 
no other penalty is elsewhere provided by or under this Act for such contravention, be punishable 
with imprisonment which may extend to 1 year, or with fine which may extend to `5,000, or with 
both:
   Provided that where the contravention is of any provision regarding maternity benefit or re-
garding payment of any other amount and such maternity benefit or amount has not already been 
recovered, the court shall, in addition, recover such maternity benefit or amount as if it were a 
fine, and pay the same to the person entitled thereto.
Penalty for Obstructing Inspector (Section 22)
Whoever fails to produce on demand by the Inspector any register or document in his custody kept in 
pursuance of this Act or the rules made thereunder or conceals or prevents any person from appearing 
before or being examined by an Inspector, shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend 
to 1 year, or with fine which may extend to `5,000, or with both.
Cognizance of Offences (Section 23)
1. Any aggrieved woman, an office-bearer of a trade union registered under the Trade Unions Act, 
1926 of which such woman is a member or a voluntary organisation registered under the Societ-
ies Registration Act, 1860 or an Inspector, may file a complaint regarding the commission of an 
offence under this Act in any court of competent jurisdiction and no such complaint shall be filed 
after the expiry of 1 year from the date on which the offence is alleged to have been committed.
2. No court inferior to that of a Metropolitan Magistrate or a Magistrate of the first class shall try 
any offence under this Act.
Protection of Action Taken in Good Faith (Section 24)
No suit, prosecution or other legal proceeding shall lie against any person for anything which is in good 
faith done or intended to be done in pursuance of this Act or of any rule or order made thereunder.
Power of Central Government to Give Directions (Section 25)
The Central Government may give such directions as it may deem necessary to a State Government 
regarding the carrying into execution the provisions of this Act and the State Government shall comply 
with such directions.

Power to Exempt Establishments (Section 26)
If the appropriate Government is satisfied that having regard to an establishment or a class of establish-

Effect of Laws and Agreements Inconsistent with this Act (Section 27)
1. The provisions of this Act shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith con-

made before or after the coming into force of this Act:
   Provided that where under any such award, agreement, contract of service or otherwise, a

to which she would be entitled under this Act, the woman shall continue to be entitled to the 
more favourable benefits in respect of that matter, notwithstanding that she is entitled to receive 
benefits in respect of other matters under this Act.
2. Nothing contained in this Act shall be construed to preclude a woman from entering into an 
agreement with her employer for granting her rights or privileges in respect of any matter which 
are more favourable to her than those to which she would be entitled under this Act.

(j) the form and manner in which complaints may be made to Inspectors under sub-section (1)

(k) any other matter which is to be, or may be, prescribed.

Repeal (Section 30)
On the application of this Act–
(i) to mines, the Mines Maternity Benefit Act, 1941; and 
(ii) to factories situate in the Union Territory of Delhi, the Bombay Maternity Benefit Act, 1929, as 
in force in that territory, shall stand repealed.
ADMINISTRATION OF THE ACT
For organisations where the Central Government is the appropriate Government, the Maternity Benefit 
Act, 1961 is enforced through the Central Industrial Relation Machinery (CIRM), an attached office of 
the Ministry of Labour & Employment. This office is also known as the Chief Labour Commissioner 
(Central) Organisation, and is headed by the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central).
Summary
●The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 ensures social security of working women by allowing them 
to perform their social obligation of child bearing, undeterred by the fear of punitive measures 
for absence during pre- and/or post-natal period(s).
●Maternity benefit legislations prior to the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 include the Bombay Ma-
ternity Benefit Act, 1929, the Madhya Pradesh Maternity Benefit Act, 1930, other State-level 
legislations, the Mines Maternity Benefit Act, 1941, the Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948 
and the Plantations Labour Act, 1951.
●Section 3(ha) defines medical termination of pregnancy as the termination of pregnancy permis-
sible under the provisions of Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971 .
●Miscarriage as per Section 3(j) means expulsion of the contents of a pregnant uterus at any 
period prior to or during the 26th week of pregnancy, but does not include any miscarriage, the 
causing of which is punishable under the Indian Penal Code.

●According to Section 4(1), no employer shall knowingly employ a woman in any establishment

      TUDY
CASE STUDY-I
The petitioner in this case is a Block Resources Teacher Educator in Mathematics in Thoothukudi 
District, who had her second delivery during the period between 16th October 2006 and 11th January 
2007. She was not given maternity benefit for the aforesaid period, stating that during the first labour, 
she had given birth to twins and therefore, by the present delivery, she had given birth to a third child. 
As such, by the order of the Government in G. O. Ms. No. 237, School Education Department, dated 
29th June 1993, she will not be paid wages for her leave.
(Adapted from: J. Sharmila vs. The Secretary to Government on 19 October, 2010, www.indiankanoon.org/
doc/1925964/ accessed on 4/9/2014.)
Questions
1. Analyse whether the order refusing to grant maternity leave to the petitioner for the birth of her 
third child in the second delivery was legally justified or not.
2. What logic can the petitioner put up in defence?
3. Is maternity leave confined only to the second delivery and not based on the third child norm?
CASE STUDY-II
In this case the petitioner, a qualified architect, was initially offered contractual appointment for a 
period of 6 months on 8th October 1997 by the respondents (hereafter referred to as “RITES’). She 
had continued in the employment of RITES subsequent to her contract being renewed after the expiry 
of the 6 months period. The petitioner has questioned the impugned order dated 13th December 2000 
which states that the contractual engagement ceased from 16th October 2000 and that she was no longer 
in the rolls of the organisation after that date. The claim in the petition was confined to the release of 
maternity leave benefits, which was also declined.
The petitioner claimed that her services were continued and she was working uninterruptedly till 
she applied for maternity leave on 15th October 2000. It is averred by that application RITES was 
intimated that the petitioner was proceeding on maternity leave from 11th November 2000 onwards 
till further notice, after which she delivered a baby on 5th December 2000. The petitioner has further 
mentioned that RITES did not reply to this notice and by the impugned order, referred to the last let-
ter dated 23th May 2000, and stated that the period of her engagement was to come to an end upon 
expiry of 6 months. The petitioner made representations on 10th November 2001 and 24th December 
2001, inter alia , for release of maternity benefits. RITES however did not accept the request. Hence 
she approached this Court for appropriate directions.
IR&LL_Ch_17.indd   19 1/1/2008   4:51:44 AM

17.20 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
The respondents in their counter affidavit have denied the claim. They claimed that the petitioner 
was engaged on purely contractual basis and that her period of engagement came to an end on 16th
October 2000. They have further denied the receipt of letter dated 15th October 2000 and have even 
alleged that the letter was given to RITES on 17th November 2000. The respondents have also placed 
on record copies of letters written on 21th June 2000, 17th July 2000, 4th August 2000 and 19th October 
2000, by which the petitioner sought medical leave. It is further alleged that the petitioner accepted 
her termination as evidenced by a duly filled Form No. 19, which was an application for release of 
provident fund and other dues, furnished to the respondent RITES under cover of a letter dated 11th
September 2001, and that the petitioner had collected all her dues on 7th December 2001 from RITES. 
The record shows that the petitioner continued in employment till 11th November 2000, as per RITES 
itself.
The pleadings in this case show that apparently the contract was for spells of 6 months. As is 
evident from an examination of the last contract/order dated 23th May 2000, the RITES was issuing 
contracts/appointment letters for fresh periods after the expiry of the previous period(s). For instance, 
the order dated 23th May 2000 states that the term of employment is 6 months from 17th April 2000 
to 16th October 2000. The last order, extending the contract of appointment by 6 months, was issued 
on May, 2000; the previous period had expired on 17th April 2000. Hence, the period commenced on 
17th April 2000, and continued till 16th October 2000. Further, the petitioner continued to report for 
duties after 16th October 2000, though the period of contractual appointment came to an end on 16th
October 2000. The letter seeking leave does indicate that the petitioner would be on leave after 11th
November 2000. RITES does not dispute the existence of this letter; it only alleges that the letter in 
fact was given on 17th November 2000.
(Adapted from: Mrs. Bharti Gupta vs. Rail India Technical and Economic Services (2005 (84) DRJ 53) 
www.indiankanoon.org/doc/1796719/ accessed on 3/9/2014.)

18
The Minimum Wages Act, 1948
An Act to provide for fixing minimum rates of wages in certain employments.
Desired Knowledge Competencies
cTo discuss the notions of fair wage, minimum wage and living wage and the evolution of the legisla-
tion on minimum wages in India.
cTo become familiar with the scope and cove rage of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 and of the various 
definitions given under the Act.
cTo comprehend issues like fixing of minimum wage, minimum wage for overtime work, etc.
CONCEPT OF FIXATION OF WAGE
Wage to a worker is a means of livelihood; for an employer, it is an expense. If we consider an economy 
to comprise only two agents, i.e., firms and households, we can easily visualise an exchange process 
between them. Physical (or intellectual) labour is supplied by the household to the firm, in return of 
which, firm pays wage/salary to the household. This process of exchange in reality becomes a process 
of bargaining between these agents, where workers try to get high wages but employers want to pay 
less to reduce their cost. Workers often seek the intervention of unions in such bargaining. On the 
other hand, employers bargain with workers to ensure greater contribution to production. The level of 
wages employers offer to workers is one of the basic determinants in this process.
The next issue is how much wage should paid to workers in lieu of the work done? In other words, 
we are referring to the adequacy of wages (which is actually the issue of fair wages). Let us discuss 
the relevance of fair wages here. The very purpose of seeking employment is to sell labour for earn-
ing wages; in return that would enable a worker to achieve a decent standard of living. The primary 
expectation out of earning wage is both to fulfill one’s basic needs and to feel reassured that he/she 
receives a fair return for the work done. The onus lies on both the society and the State to ensure such 
a wage is paid to every worker to help prevent starvation and poverty, and also ensure that at least the 
basic needs of every worker with a standard family size are met.
Fundamental rules of economics propose that the level of wage is determined by the demand for 
and supply of labour. Interestingly, the labour market is characterised by the dual-existence of a highly 
IR&LL_Ch_18.indd   1 1/1/2008   4:51:57 AM

18.2 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
skilled segment commanding high wage rate and a low-skilled segment having low wage rate. The 
reason, again, can be explained by economics—the former has a demand for labour that exceeds its 
supply, while the latter segment has supply of labour in excess of demand. This is one of the primary 
reasons behind diversity in wage-levels across skill-sets and industries, especially in India. As the 
demand for skilled labour would increase, the already existing wage differential between skilled and 
unskilled labour would rise. Most of the studies of wage differentials in India, comment Sarkar and 
Mehta (2010), indicate that the labour market generates differences in wage rate and earnings that are 
based on geographical locations, level of education, industry, social group and gender. Considering the 
sectors of the Indian economy, we can find wide disparities in wages across organised and unorganised 
sectors as well. Such disparities are found across rural and urban areas, with urban workers earning 
more wages than their rural counterparts.
Occupation-wise, non-agricultural wage rate has been historically higher than agricultural wage rate 
in India. In spite of more and more women joining the labour force, wages paid to women workers are 
usually lesser than men. Significant gaps in the earnings of men and women still exist; in fact, 2008-
2009 figures reveal that wages/salaries per man day worked for directly employed women workers (at 
`131.23) was nearly half of that of their male counterparts (at `258.04) (Statistical Profile on Women 
Labour, 2009-2011). Ownership pattern of industrial enterprises also dictates differences in wages, 
with the public sector usually offering better fringe benefits than the private sector. 
Let us now explore the role of government in fixing the level of wage, which is usually a two-
pronged situation. While increased wages would lead to improved standard of living for the masses, it 
would put pressure on employers due to a higher wage bill. Not to forget that such increase in wage 
bill would be passed on ultimately to consumers by way of higher price to be paid for goods/services. 
The situation becomes more difficult if the government also has to ensure uniformity in wage-levels 
across different sectors of the economy.
BACKDR OP OF THE MINIMUM WAGES ACT , 1948 
The issue of discrepancies in wage levels across the nation has always been of paramount concern to 
the Government of India. Article 39 of the Constitution of India holds that the State shall, in particu-
lar, direct its policy towards securing that the citizens, men and women equally, have the right to an 
adequate means of livelihood, and that there is equal pay for equal work for both men and women. 
Article 43 states that the State shall endeavour to secure, by suitable legislation or economic organi-
sation or in any other way, to all workers, agricultural, industrial or otherwise, work, a living wage, 
conditions of work ensuring a decent standard of life, and full enjoyment of leisure and social and 
cultural opportunities.
The beginning of the 19th century had marked the onset of a perceived need for fixing a minimum 
rate of wages. In its report submitted in 1931, the Royal Commission on Labour had recommended 
investigations pertaining to fixation of minimum wage rates in certain small industries and establish-
ment of machinery towards this end. A large number of committees were set up thereafter from time 
to time to address this issue. The most notable of these were the Cawnpore Labour Enquiry Committee 
and the Bombay Textile Labour Enquiry Committee (both in 1937), the Bihar Labour Enquiry Com-
mittee (in 1938), the C.P. and Berar Textile Labour Enquiry Committee and the U.P. Labour Enquiry 
Committee (both in 1946) set up by the respective provincial governments (Sinha, Sinha and Shekhar, 
2006). Investigations made by such committees on the wage levels of workers across industries revealed 
disparities and fixation of minimum wages was recommended.
IR&LL_Ch_18.indd   2 1/1/2008   4:51:57 AM

The Minimum Wages Act, 1948 18.3
Post-Independence, the first notable development in fixation of a minimum wage rate was the 
formation of a tripartite committee named as the Committee on Fair Wages in the year 1946, to provide 
guidelines for wage structures in the country. The report of the Committee published in 1948 was a 
major landmark in the formulation of wage policies. The Committee prescribed clarification of the 
various concepts of wages (like fair wage, living wage and subsistence wage), standardisation of 
wages in the organised sector and enactment of a minimum wage legislation. The concepts of wages 
laid down in the report are as follows:
rMinimum wage: Minimum wage was proposed to be paid for the 
bare subsistence of a worker and should ideally include enough for 
the efficiency, health and working capability of the worker. For this 
purpose, the minimum wage must also provide for some measure 
of education, medical requirements and amenities. The Committee 
on Fair Wages emphasised that an industry had no right to exist 
unless this minimum level of wages was paid.
rFair wage:  Such wage was proposed to be above the minimum wage level, aiming at living 
wage level. The actual wage in an industry or organisation should be determined by factors 
like the capacity of an employer to pay, the position of an industry in the economy, per capita 
income, etc. The Committee recommended that fair wage should be related with the productivity 
of labour. Since the prevailing level of wages in India was unable to maintain the workers on 
subsistence plus standard, it was essential that workers must be first assured a living wage, and 
only after this, wages should be related to productivity. The Committee further suggested that 
fair wage should be related with the prevailing rates of wages.
rLiving wage: Living wage was the concept of an ideal wage; it represented the highest level of 
wage which could enable a male earner of a family to provide for himself and his family not 
only the bare necessities of food, clothing and shelter, but also a measure of comfort, education 
for his children, protection against ill-health, essential social needs and insurance against more 
important misfortunes, including old age.
Let us quickly analyse the implications of these concepts here. As per the Committee, industrial 
wages paid out must have a floor-level, namely subsistence wage, below which no industry must pay 
any worker. It is thus implied that this subsistence wage represents the absolute minimum wage to 
be paid to workers. This apart, the concept of living wage was introduced in lines with an ideal wage 
rate. The Committee was of the opinion that when such a wage is to be determined, the considerations 
of national income and capacity to pay of the industry concerned must also be taken into account. 
Living wage had to be the ultimate goal or target and a benchmark that all workers and their repre-
sentative unions should attain. Next arises the question: what should the minimum wage be? Should 
it be subsistence wage, which may enable a worker to stay alive and maintain his working capacity; 
or should it be a living wage, which may also provide for the maintenance of health and efficiency, 
measures of economic comfort and insurance against unforeseen exigencies; or should it be a fair 
wage, lying somewhere between the levels of subsistence and living wages? It must be noted here 
that “minimum” is essentially a relative term and minimum wages may have different meanings in 
different countries, according to their level of social and economic development. Further, it needs to 
be considered whether there should be a national system of minimum wages providing for a uniform 
level of wage for all workers, but for regional variations, or a system of fixing different minimum 
wage rates for different sectors or industries.
Incidentally, the Committee on Fair Wages did not actually prescribe any actual wage rate to be fol-
lowed uniformly across industries principally due to the large scale disparities in them. This provided Spotlight

bare subsistence of a worker. 
Fair wage  aims at the living wage 
level. Living wage is the concept 
of an ideal wage.

18.4 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
industries with enough flexibility to work on determining wage levels on the basis of various param-
eters, including capacity to pay. On the whole, the Committee provided the much needed momentum 
to initiate fixation of a minimum level of wage through the legislative machinery.
The issue of a minimum level of wages and the establishment of a machinery for the fixation of 
such a level has been of concern to the International Labour Organisation (ILO) as well, which has 
come up with several Conventions and Recommendations to this effect. The Minimum Wage Fixing 
Machinery Convention, 1928 (Convention No. 26) provided for the creation of wage-fixing machinery 
in certain trades. The Convention required consultation with representatives of employers and workers 
before such machinery is applied in a trade and hence imposed an obligation on the ratifying countries 
to associate both employers and workers in the working of the machinery. Such a machinery was also 
recommended to conduct investigation into the conditions relevant to the specific trades under the pur-
view of the Recommendation. Further, the Convention laid down the mandate of minimum wages fixed 
by the machinery to be binding on both employers and workers. India ratified the Convention in 1955, 
after the enactment of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948. Both the Convention and Recommendation of 
1928 were restricted to the non-agriculture sectors of employment. Hence the ILO Conference, in its 
34th Session in the year 1957, adopted the Minimum Wage Fixing Machinery (Agriculture) Convention 
and the Minimum Wage Fixing Machinery Recommendation for agricultural employments. This was 
followed by the adoption of the Minimum Wage Fixing Machinery Convention in 1970.
The question of the fixation of minimum rates of wages in India was considered by the Standing
Labour Committee and the 5th Session of the Indian Labour Conference in 1943, on recommendation 
of which, a Labour Investigation Committee was appointed in the same year to investigate into the 
question of wages and other matters like housing, social conditions and employment. The issue drew 
the attention of the Standing Labour Committee and the 6th and 7thsessions of the Indian Labour 
Conference again in 1944 and 1945 respectively. A draft bill was considered by the Indian Labour 
Conference in 1945. The 8th meeting of the Standing Labour Committee in the year 1946 recom-
mended enactment of a separate legislation for the unorganised sector, including working hours, 
minimum wages and paid holidays. In light of these recommendations, the Government of India in-
troduced the Minimum Wages Bill in the Central Legislative Assembly in 1946, which was passed on 
9thFebruary 1948. The Act came into force from 15thMarch the same year. 
The sole purpose of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 is to prevent 
exploitation of labour and it provides for fixation and/or periodic revi-
sion of minimum wages in employments where labour is vulnerable to 
exploitation. The Act has been amended several times since its enactment 
in 1948. Following is the list of amending acts and adaptation orders:
1. The Adaptation of Laws Order, 1950
2. The Minimum Wages (Amendment) Act, 1950
3. The Part B States (Laws) Act, 1951
4. The Minimum Wages (Amendment) Act, 1951
5. The Minimum Wages (Amendment) Act, 1954
6. The Minimum Wages (Amendment) Act, 1957
7. The Minimum Wages (Amendment) Act, 1961
8. The Central Labour Laws (Extension to Jammu and Kashmir) Act, 1970
9. The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986
10. The Delegated Legislation Provisions (Amendment) Act, 2004Spotlight

The Minimum Wages Act, 1948 18.5
ABOUT THE ACT
Short Title and Extent (Section 1)
1. This Act may be called the Minimum Wages Act, 1948.
2. It extends to the whole of India
This Act has been extended to Dadra and Nagar Haveli, Pondicherry, Laccadive, Minicoy and 
Amindivi Islands and Union Territory of Goa, Daman and Diu.
Interpretation (Section 2)
In this Act, unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context:
Adolescent [Section 2(a)] Adolescent means a person who has completed his fourteenth year 
of age but has not completed his eighteenth year;
Adult [Section 2(aa)] Adult means a person who has completed his eighteenth year of age;
Appropriate Government [Section 2(b)] Appropriate Government means,—
(i) in relation to any scheduled employment carried on by or under the authority of the Central 
Government, or a railway administration, or in relation to a mine, oilfield or major port, or any 
corporation established by a Central Act, the Central Government, and
(ii) in relation to any other scheduled employment, the State Government;
Child [Section 2(bb)] Child means a person who has not completed his fourteenth year of age;
Competent authority [Section 2(c)] Competent authority means the authority appointed by 
the appropriate Government by notification in its Official Gazette to ascertain from time to time the 
cost of living index number applicable to the employees employed in the scheduled employments 
specified in such notification;
Cost of living index number [Section 2(d)] Cost of living index number, in relation to 
employees in any scheduled employment in respect of which minimum rates of wages have been fixed, 
means the index number ascertained and declared by the competent authority by notification in the 
Official Gazette to be the cost of living index number applicable to employees in such employment;
In Mangalore Ganesh Beedi and Allied Industries vs. State of Karnataka and Others  [(2003) IIILLJ 
861 Kant] it has been mentioned that consumer price index numbers are also known as cost of living 
index numbers, which are generally intended to represent the average change over time in the prices 
paid by the ultimate consumer of a specified basket of goods and services. The need for constructing 
these numbers arises mainly because of the fact general index numbers fail to give an exact idea of 
the effect of change in the general price level on the cost of living of different classes of people, since 
a given change in prices affect different classes in different manners. 
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/1971257/ accessed on 12/4/2014.)

CASE COR
NERInChampak Lal H. Thakkar and Others vs. State of Gujarat and Another (1980 AIR 1889), the defence 
of the appellants was on the plea that different types of industries are covered by the Minimum Wages 
Act, 1948 (or Act) but the company does not run any such industry, and is therefore not liable for any 
contravention of the Act or the rules framed thereunder. According to the prosecution, the factory run by 
the company is an oil mill, an industry which is certainly covered by the Act. However, the company is 
running a mill which manufactures vanaspati and vanaspati is not oil, but is vegetable ghee. Oil extrac-
tion is undoubtedly a major operation carried on by the company, but that operation is incidental to the 
preparation of vanaspati. Vanaspati is manufactured by subjecting oil to the processes of neutralisation, 
bleaching, deodorisation, hardening, hydrogenation, etc., and is a product quite different from oil. In spite 
of the sale of oil, therefore, the company remains a vanaspati manufacturer and cannot be considered 
to be running an oil mill.
 The Court was of the view that oil will remain oil if it retains its essential properties, and merely 
because it has been subjected to certain processes would not convert it into a different substance. In 
other words, although certain additions have been made to and operations carried out on oil, it will still 
be classified as oil unless its essential characteristics have undergone change. No doubt, the word ‘oil’ 
is not defined in the Act. Taking the dictionary meaning for interpreting the term ‘oil mill’, in this case it 
is clear that hydrogenated vegetable oil falls within the said term. The various processes to which oil is 
subjected for being converted into vanaspati leave its basic characteristics untouched, that is, it remains 
a cooling medium with vegetable fat as its main ingredient. Thus vanaspati must be regarded as an oil for 
the purpose of Item 5 in Part-I of the Schedule to the Act, and employment in a vanaspati manufacturing 
concern is a scheduled employment within the scope of Section 2(g) of the Act.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/1480973/ accessed on 9/4/2014.)

an ex-employee. It was held that a person who is not in the actual employment of the employer at the 
time of making an application under Section 20(2) of the Act, was not entitled to seek relief.

CASE COR
NERIn Tamil Nadu Spinning Mills Association vs. The State of Tamil Nadu (W.P.Nos. 28741, 28749, 28782, 
28783 and 28805 of 2008), the State Textile Workers Federation made a representation in February 2006 
through the Centre of Indian Trade Unions (CITU), to the Government of Tamil Nadu, alleging that the 
textile mills in Tamil Nadu were indulging in an exploitative practice of engaging adolescent girls under a 
scheme known as “Thirumagal Thirumana Thittam”, and that the same amounted to forced labour. The 
Chief Inspector of Factories sent a report in February 2007 to the Government, stating that a camp coolie 
scheme was prevalent in these mills and young girls above the age of 15 years were being engaged 
under this scheme for 3 years as apprentices. The Government took into consideration various factors 
like the existing low wages paid to apprentices, the rapid changes in the consumer price index adversely 
affecting the living conditions of workers, representations made by various trade unions regarding the 
plight of apprentices, notice issued by the National Human Rights Commission in this issue, and the 
direction by the Division Bench of the Honourable Madras High Court to the authorities to take steps to 
ensure that these apprentices receive wages as per the Minimum Wages Act, 1948. Accordingly, the 
Government issued a draft notification dated 16th May 2008, proposing to fix the minimum rate of wages 
payable to these apprentices at `110/- per day, apart from Dearness Allowance. 
 However, the Southern India Mills Association, the South India Small Spinners Association, the Tamil 
Nadu Spinning Mills Association, the Employers’ Federation of South India, around 302 mills, and some 
other trade unions sent objections and suggestions to this draft notification. One of the contentions of the 
petitioners was that the power to fix minimum rate of wages under Section 3(1)(a) of the Act does not 
extend to apprentices, but is limited only to employees. They argued that apprentices are not “employees 
employed in an employment” and hence the State Government has no power to fix the minimum rate of 
wages for apprentices in an employment specified in the Schedule.
 It was held by the Court that to secure living wages to labour is one of the Directive Principles of State 
Policy embodied in Article 43 of the Constitution. The challenge to the vires of Section 3(3)(a)(iii) was 
not validated on any well accepted principles on which such challenges are possible.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/1102952/ accessed on 8/4/2014.)

18.10  Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
 (iii) an all-inclusive rate allowing for the basic rate, the cost of living allowance and the cash 
value of the concessions, if any.
 2. The cost of living allowance and the cash value of the concessions in respect of supplies of es-
sential commodities at concession rates shall be computed by the competent authority at such 
intervals and in accordance with such directions as may be specified or given by the appropriate

It has been mentioned in Mangalore Ganesh Beedi and Allied Industries vs. State of Karnataka and 
Others  [(2003) IIILLJ 861 Kant] that the concept of “cost of living allowance” is popularly known 
as Dearness Allowance (DA). The Act makes no specific mention of the term “dearness allowance”, 
but it refers to an allowance paid on the rise of cost of living. Further, Variable Dearness Allowance 
(VDA) is very much a part and parcel of wages. Once the rates of minimum wages are prescribed 
under the Act, whether as all-inclusive under Section 4(1)(iii) or by combining basic plus DA under 
Section 4(1)(i), they are not amenable to split up.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/1971257/ accessed on 12/4/2014.)
Procedure for Fixing and Revising Minimum Wages (Section 5)
 1. In fixing minimum rates of wages in respect of any scheduled employment for the first time under 
this Act or in revising minimum rates of wages so fixed, the appropriate Government shall either:
 (a) appoint as many committees and sub-committees as it considers necessary to hold enquiries 
and advise it in respect of such fixation or revision, as the case maybe, or
 (b) by notification in the Official Gazette, publish its proposals for the information of persons 
likely to be affected thereby and specify a date, not less than 2 months from the date of the 
notification, on which the proposals will be taken into consideration.
CASE COR
NERInKarnataka Film Chamber of Commerce vs. State of Karnataka [(1987) ILLJ 182 Kant], it has been 
mentioned that Section 4 of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 (referred to hereafter as the Act) indicates 
that basic wage is an integral part of minimum wage, which may consist of a basic rate of wages and 
a special allowance at a rate to be adjusted at such intervals and in such manner as the appropriate 
Government may direct. When the question of neutralisation of the cost of living arises by payment of 
Dearness Allowance, it necessarily follows that the Court should keep in view whether there had been 
an increase or decrease in the basic wage in a particular industry over a given period of time for the 
purpose of determining whether the neutralisation factor adopted by the State Government exceeds 100 
per cent or 200 per cent or 300 per cent in a given situation.
 In its attempt to define “dearness allowance”, the DA Commission has referred to it as “a device to 
protect, to a greater or lesser extent, the real income of wage earners and salaried employees from the 
effects of rise in prices”. Hence DA is a wider concept and is intended to neutralise the erosion of the 
real income of wage earners. Further, the Commission was of the opinion that DA should protect wage-
earners at, or a little above, the subsistence level. It is hence clear that the payment of DA would arise 
only if the basic wage fixed for a particular category of workmen fell short of the minimum wage which 
the State Government has to fix, taking into consideration the needs of a worker’s family consisting of 
3 consumption units.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/1000631/ accessed on 10/4/2014.)

to advise and not to take a decision. It is open to the Advisory Board to devise its own procedure for 
obtaining information necessary for the purpose of discharging its advisory duty.

CASE COR
NERIn State of Andhra Pradesh vs. Narayana Velur Beedi Manufacturing Factory and  Others (1973 SCR (3) 
755), the appellant-Government had passed an order revising minimum wages in the beedi  industry based 
on the recommendation of a committee of 6 members consisting of persons representing employers and 
employees and the Chief inspector and Deputy Chief Inspector of Factories. Section 9 of the Minimum 
Wages Act, 1948 requires that the Committee shall consist of an equal number of representatives of 
employer and employees, and of independent persons not exceeding one-third of its total number.
 On the question whether the 2 Government officials could be regarded as independent persons, it 
was held that the mere fact that these 2 officials happened to be Government officials or Government 
servants will not divest them of the character of independent persons. It was further held by the Court 
that the language of Section 9 does not contain any indication that persons in the employment of the 
Government would be excluded from the category of ‘independent persons’. These words have essentially 
been employed in contra-distinction to representatives of employers and employees. In other words, 
apart from the representatives of employers and employees in the committee, there should be persons 
who should be independent of them.

1. In regard to any scheduled employment minimum rates of wages 
in respect of which have been fixed under this Act, the appropriate 
Government may:
(a) fix the number of hours of work which shall constitute a nor-

hours of duty of the employee, or if there be no daily hours of duty as such for the employee, the 
hours of duty, normally include periods of inaction during which the employee may be on duty 
but is not called upon to display either physical activity or sustained attention.

18.14 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Wages of Worker who Works for Less than Normal Working Day (Section 15)
If an employee whose minimum rate of wages has been fixed under this Act by the day works on any 
day on which he was employed for a period less than the requisite number of hours constituting a 
normal working day, he shall, save as otherwise hereinafter provided, be entitled to receive wages in 
respect of work done by him on that day as if he had worked for a full normal working day:
Provided, however, that he shall not be entitled to receive wages for a full normal working day:
(i) in any case where his failure to work is caused by his unwillingness to work and not by the omis-
sion of the employer to provide him with work, and
(ii) in such other cases and circumstances as may be prescribed.
Wages for Two or more Classes of Work (Section 16)
Where an employee does 2 or more classes of work to each of which a different minimum rate of wages 
is applicable, the employer shall pay to such employee in respect of the time respectively occupied in 
each such class of work, wages at not less than the minimum rate in force in respect of each such class.
Minimum Time Rate Wages for Piece Work (Section 17)
Where an employee is employed on piece work for which minimum time rate and not a minimum 
piece rate has been fixed under this Act, the employer shall pay to such employee wages at not less 
than the minimum time rate.
Maintenance of Registers and Records (Section 18)
1. Every employer shall maintain such registers and records giving such particulars of employees 
employed by him, the work performed by them, the wages paid to them, the receipts given by 
them and such other particulars and in such form as may be prescribed.
2. Every employer shall keep exhibited, in such manner as may be prescribed, in the factory, work-
shop or place where the employees in the scheduled employment may be employed, or in the case 
of out-workers, in such factory, workshop or place as may be used for giving out-work to them, 
notices in the prescribed form containing prescribed particulars.
3. The appropriate Government may, by rules made under this Act, provide for the issue of wage 
books or wage slips to employees employed in any scheduled employment in respect of which 
minimum rates of wages have been fixed and prescribe the manner in which entries shall be made 
and authenticated in such wage books or wage slips by the employer or his agent.

General Provision for Punishment of Other Offences (Section 22A)
Any employer who contravenes any provision of this Act or of any rule or order made thereunder

Cognizance of Offences (Section 22B)
1. No Court shall take cognizance of a complaint against any person for an offence:
