The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 20.7
CASE COR
NERInJeevanlal (1929) Ltd. and Others vs. Controlling Authority [(1982) ILLJ 86 (Mad)], the employees 
concerned had reached the age of superannuation, which was 58 years well before the Payment of 
Gratuity Act, 1972 (or, the Act) came into force. They were, however, re-employed on a yearly basis, 
and eventually their employment came to an end on 31st December 1972 or 31st December 1973, as the 
case may be. Having regard to this factor, the employees claimed that they were entitled to payment of 
gratuity according to the terms of the Act. However the management contended that their employment 
had come to a termination on their reaching the age of superannuation long before the Act came into 
force; as such, they will be entitled to get gratuity only in accordance with the terms of the scheme or 
award which was in force earlier.
 It was finally decided that an employee who is re-employed without any break in service will be eligible 
for gratuity, and he cannot be denied gratuity simply on the ground of change in employment.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/1399016/ accessed on 11/6/2014.)
employee subsists, and the new employer cannot escape from the liability of payment of gratuity to 
the employee. As per Travancore Plywood Industries Pvt. Ltd. vs. Regional Joint Labour Commis-
sioner [(1996) II LLJ 85 (Ker)], refusal of employee to surrender land belonging to the employer is 
not a ground to withhold gratuity.
Controlling Authority (Section 3)
The Appropriate Government may, by notification, appoint any officer to be a controlling authority, 
who shall be responsible for the administration of this Act and different authorities may be appointed 
for different areas.
Payment of Gratuity (Section 4)
 1. Gratuity shall be payable to an employee on the termination of his employment after he has 
rendered continuous service for not less than 5 years,-
 (a) on his superannuation, or
 (b) on his retirement or resignation, or
 (c) on his death or disablement due to accident or disease:
   Provided that the completion of continuous service of 5 years shall not be necessary where the 
termination of the employment of any employee is due to death or disablement:
   Provided further that in the case of death of the employee, gratuity payable to him shall be 
paid to his nominee or, if no nomination has been made, to his heirs, and where any such nomi-
nees or heirs is a minor, the share of such minor, shall be deposited with the controlling authority 
who shall invest the same for the benefit of such minor in such bank or other financial institution, 
as may be prescribed, until such minor attains majority.
Explanation For the purposes of this section, disablement means such disablement as 
incapacitates an employee for the work which he was capable of performing before the accident 
or disease resulting in such disablement.
IR&LL_Ch_20.indd   7 1/1/2008   4:52:24 AM

20.8 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
2. For every completed year of service or part thereof in excess of 6 months, the employer shall pay 
gratuity to an employee at the rate of 15 days’ wages based on the rate of wages last drawn by the 
employee concerned: 
   Provided that in the case of a piece-rated employee, daily wages shall be computed on the 
average of the total wages received by him for a period of 3 months immediately preceding the 
termination of his employment, and, for this purpose, the wages paid for any overtime work shall 
not be taken into account: 
   Provided further that in the case of an employee who is employed in a seasonal establishment 
and who is not so employed throughout the year, the employer shall pay the gratuity at the rate of 
7 days’ wages for each season. 
Explanation In the case of a monthly rated employee, the 15 days’ wages shall be calculated 
by dividing the monthly rate of wages last drawn by him by 26 and multiplying the quotient by 
15.
3. The amount of gratuity payable to an employee shall not exceed 
`10 lakh.
4. For the purpose of computing the gratuity payable to an employ-
ee who is employed, after his disablement, on reduced wages, his 
wages for the period preceding his disablement shall be taken to be 
the wages received by him during that period, and his wages for the 
period subsequent to his disablement shall be taken to be the wages 
as so reduced.
5. Nothing in this section shall affect the right of an employee to receive better terms of gratuity 
under any award or agreement or contract with the employer.
6. Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1),-
(a) the gratuity of an employee, whose services have been terminated for any act, willful omis-
sion or negligence causing any damage or loss to, or destruction of, property belonging to 
the employer shall be forfeited to the extent of the damage or loss so caused;
(b) the gratuity payable to an employee may be wholly or partially forfeited-
(i) if the services of such employee have been terminated for his riotous or disorderly con-
duct or any other act of violence on his part, or
(ii) if the services of such employee have been terminated for any act which constitutes an 
offence involving moral turpitude, provided that such offence is committed by him in 
the course of his employment.

The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 20.9
Compulsory Insurance (Section 4A) 
1. With effect from such date as may be notified by the appropriate Government in this behalf, every 
employer, other than an employer or an establishment belonging to, or under the control of, the 
Central Government or a State Government, shall, subject to the provisions of sub-section (2), 
obtain an insurance in the manner prescribed, for his liability for payment towards the gratuity 
under this Act, from the Life Insurance Corporation of India established under the Life Insurance 
Corporation of India Act, 1956 or any other prescribed insurer.
   Provided that different dates may be appointed for different establishments or class of estab-
lishments or for different areas. 
2. The appropriate Government may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, exempt every 
employer who had already established an approved gratuity fund in respect of his employees and 
who desires to continue such arrangement, and every employer employing five hundred or more 
persons who establishes an approved gratuity fund in the manner prescribed from the provisions 
of sub-section (1).

Recovery of Gratuity (Section 8)
If the amount of gratuity payable under this Act is not paid by the employer, within the prescribed 
time, to the person entitled thereto, the controlling authority shall, on an application made to it in this 
behalf by the aggrieved person, issue a certificate for that amount to the Collector who shall recover 
the same, together with compound interest thereon at such rate as the Central Government may, by 
notification, specify, from the date of expiry of the prescribed time as arrears of land revenue and pay

Provided further that the amount of interest payable under this section shall, in no case exceed the 
amount of gratuity payable under this Act.
An aggrieved person make an application made to the controlling authority in duplicate in Form 
T. The Collector shall recover the same, together with compound interest thereon at the rate of 9 per 
cent (with effect from 1st October 1987) from the date of expiry of the prescribed time and pay the 
same to the person entitled to it. 
Mode of Payment of Gratuity 
The amount of gratuity payable under the Act is to be paid in cash, or if 
so desired by the payee, in the form of demand draft or bank cheque to 
the employee or nominee, or legal heir, as the case may be. If the amount 
of gratuity is less than `1,000, then such payment may be made by postal 
money order, if the employee or nominee or legal heir so desires. The 
commission on the postal money order may be deducted from the amount 
of gratuity payable.
The employer must also intimate the controlling authority of that area about the details of such 
payment. If the nominee or legal heir is a minor, the controlling authority shall invest the amount of 
gratuity deposited with him for the benefit of such minor in a term deposit with the State Bank of 
India, or any of its subsidiaries, or any nationalised bank.

Exemption of Employer from Liability in Certain Cases (Section 10)
Where an employer is charged with an offence punishable under this Act, he shall be entitled, upon 
complaint duly made by him and on giving to the complainant not less than 3 clear days’ notice in 
writing of his intention to do so, to have any other person whom he charges as the actual offender 
brought before the court at the time appointed for hearing the charge; and if, after the commission of 
the offence has been proved, the employer proves to the satisfaction of the court-
(a) that he has used due diligence to enforce the execution of this Act, and
(b) that the said other person committed the offence in question without his knowledge, consent or 
connivance, that other person shall be convicted of the offence and shall be liable to the like pun-
ishment as if he were the employer and the employer shall be discharged from any liability under 
this Act in respect of such offence: 
Provided that in seeking to prove as aforesaid, the employer may be examined on oath and his 
evidence and that of any witness whom he calls in his support shall be subject to cross-examination 
on behalf of the person he charges as the actual offender and by the prosecutor: 
Provided further that, if the person charged as the actual offender by the employer cannot be brought 
before the court at the time appointed for hearing the charge, the court shall adjourn the hearing from 
time to time for a period not exceeding 3 months and if by the end of the said period the person 
charged as the actual offender cannot still be brought before the court, the court shall proceed to hear 
the charge against the employer and shall, if the offence be proved, convict the employer.
Cognizance of Offences (Section 11)
1. No court shall take cognizance of any offence punishable under this Act save on a complaint 
made by or under the authority of the appropriate Government: 
   Provided that where the amount of gratuity has not been paid, or recovered, within 6 months 
from the expiry of the prescribed time, the appropriate Government shall authorise the control-
ling authority to make a complaint against the employer, where-upon the controlling authority 
shall within 15 days from the date of such authorisation, make such complaint to a magistrate 
having jurisdiction to try the offence.
2. No court inferior to that of a Metropolitan Magistrate or a Judicial Magistrate of the first class 
shall try any offence punishable under this Act.
Protection of Action Taken in Good Faith (Section 12)
No suit or other legal proceeding shall lie against the controlling authority or any other person in 
respect of anything which is in good faith done or intended to be done under this Act or any rule or 
order made thereunder.

Protection of Gratuity (Section 13)
No gratuity payable under this Act and no gratuity payable to an employee employed in any establish-
ment, factory, mine, oilfield, plantation, port, railway company or shop exempted under Section 5 shall 
be liable to attachment in execution of any decree or order of any civil, revenue or criminal court.
Act to Override other Enactments, etc. (Section 14)
The provisions of this Act or any rule made thereunder shall have effect notwithstanding anything 
inconsistent therewith contained in any enactment other than this Act or in any instrument or contract 
having effect by virtue of any enactment other than this Act.
Power to Make Rules (Section 15)
1. The appropriate Government may, by notification, make rules for the purpose of carrying out the 
provisions of this Act.
2. Every rule made by the Central Government under this Act shall be laid, as soon as may be after it 
is made, before each House of Parliament while it is in session, for a total period of 30 days which 
may be comprised in 1 session or in 2 or more successive sessions, and if, before the expiry of 
the session immediately following the session or the successive sessions aforesaid, both Houses 
agree in making any modification in the rule or both Houses agree that the rule should not be 
made, the rule shall, thereafter, have effect only in such modified form or be of no effect, as the 
case may be; so, however, that any such modification or annulment shall be without prejudice to 
the validity of anything previously done under that rule.
TAX EXEMPTION OF GRATUITY RECEIVED
As per Section 10(10) of the Income-tax Act, employees have been divided into 3 categories in context 
of tax exemption of gratuity received:
i. Employees of Central or State Government and local bodies:  Gratuity received by such em-
ployees is fully exempted without any limit.
ii. Employees covered under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972:  Amount as per the Payment of 
Gratuity Act, 1972 is fully exempted.
iii. Other employees:  For other employees, the earlier limit was 3.5 lakhs as per the Income-tax Act. 
Many Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) not covered under the Central or State Government 
have started paying gratuity as per the Sixth Pay Commission, up to a maximum of 10 lakhs. In 
case of such employees, the amount in excess of 3.5 lakhs is taxable. 
The Government has enhanced the exemption limit for PSU employees retired after 24th May 2010. 
The increased limit is also available for claiming income tax exemption for employees of private sector 
establishments, who receive gratuity as per Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972.
(Adapted from: www.sriramconsultancyservices.com accessed on 10/6/2014.)

Summary
rThe Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 is an enactment towards social security that applies to every 
factory, mine, oilfield, plantation, port, railway company, and shop or other establishment in 
which 10 or more persons are employed.
rThe benefits of the Act are available not only to employees regardless of their wages, but also 
to people working in managerial or administrative capacity.
rSection 2(A) of the Act defines the term “continuous service” to mean uninterrupted service that 
includes service which is interrupted, among others, by leave or cessation of work, not due to any 
fault of the employee concerned. Completed year of service means continuous service for 1 year.
rGratuity is payable to an employee covered under the Act on termination of his employment 
after having rendered continuous service for not less than 5 years at the time of superannuation; 
or on his retirement or resignation; or on his death or disablement due to accident or disease.
rFor every completed year of service or part thereof, in excess of 6 months, the employer has 
to pay gratuity to an employee at the rate of 15 days’ wages, based on the rate of wages he has 
last drawn; for an employee in a seasonal establishment gratuity is paid at the rate of 7 days’ 
wages for each season.
rAs per Section 4(6)(a), the amount of gratuity payable to an employee whose services have 
been terminated for any act, willful omission or negligence, causing any damage or loss to, or 
destruction of, property belonging to the employer shall be forfeited to the extent of the damage 
or loss so caused.
rUnder normal circumstances gratuity is payable to an employee when his services are terminated 
during his lifetime; however, the said amount is paid to his successors on the unfortunate event 
of his death, for which the Act has a provision for nomination.
rAn employer must arrange to pay the amount of gratuity within 30 days from the date it 
becomes due.

C ASE
      TUDY
CASE STUDY-I
The respondent in this case was a workman in the service of the appellant, Bharath Gold Mines. 
Disciplinary proceedings were instituted against him on the charge that he had committed theft of gold 
worth `15,561.00 in the course of his employment with the appellant. In the inquiry he was found 
guilty of the charge. The Disciplinary Authority accepted the findings and imposed the penalty of 
dismissal from service against the respondent w.e.f. 18th August 1981, forfeiting all rights and privileges 
accrued to him, including gratuity, from the 26 years of service which he had put in before the date 
of termination of his service. The order of dismissal has not been challenged by the respondent in any 
proceeding and consequently it has become final. 
(Adapted from: Bharath Gold Mines Ltd. vs. Regional Labour Commissioner [(1994) III LLJ 54 Kant] www.
indiankanoon.org/doc/732409 accessed on 10/7/2014.)
Review Questions
1. On what ground do you think gratuity of this workman has been forfeited?
2. Given the circumstance that no show cause notice was issued to the respondent, would forfeiting 
of the gratuity amount be wrong?
3. On what basis can the workman appeal for payment of the gratuity amount?
CASE STUDY-II
While calculating gratuity, the petitioner-employee claimed that an equivalent money for free supply of 
food should form a part and be added to the cash salary paid to him to form total wages for computing 
the amount of gratuity payable to him. The respondent-company argued that the definition of wages 
in the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 refers only to the amount paid in cash and shall not include the 
food allowance or amount equivalent to the food or tiffin given along with wages as conditions of 
employment. The petitioner’s claim was rejected on the plea that merely an amenity could not form a 
part of and be added to the cash salary paid to him to form his total wages for computing the amount 
of gratuity payable to him. 
(Adapted from: N. Sivadasan vs. Appellate Authority under Payment of Gratuity Act, Madras & Others  [(1992)
IILLJ 794 Mad.] www.indiankanoon.org/doc/449861 accessed on 12/7/2014)
Review Questions
1. Do you think the employee in this case is correct in claiming for free supply of food by the em-
ployer in computation of gratuity?
2. Following Section 2(s) of the Act, wages does not include any bonus, commission, house rent 
allowance, overtime wages and any other allowance. Do you think value of food provided to the 
employee should be a part of wage?
3. Can you link this with any of the other labour legislations you have come across?

The Payment of Wages Act, 1936
An Act to regulate the payment of wages to certain classes of employed persons.
Desired Knowledge Competencies
cTo gauge the importance of payment of wages and the evolution of the legislation on payment of 
wages in India.
cTo discuss the scope and cover age of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 and of the various definitions 
given under the Act.
cTo comprehend issues like fixation of wage-periods, time of payment of wages and authorised 
deductions from wages. 
CONCEPT OF WAGE AND PA YMENT OF WAGES 
Wages refer to the total pay package an employee receives from his/her employer on a periodic basis 
in return of the physical labour supplied to the firm. A robust and fair wage structure is instrumental 
for attracting and retaining employees. The following factors must be taken into consideration by any 
organisation while determining wage rates: its own bargaining capacity and that of its employees; 
its financial capacity to pay higher wages; the on-going wage rate for similar type of work in the 
market (i.e., level of competition) as well as the prevailing condition of the economy; requirement of 
specialised skills and training in a job; nature and type of work done by the workers (e.g., hazardous 
jobs demanding higher wage rates); and productivity of workers (e.g., workers who are more efficient 
and experienced should get higher wages).
(Adapted from: www.business.gov.in accessed on 4/6/2014.)
 Given the above considerations, there can be 3 important methods of 
wage payment, namely:
rTime-rate system:  This is one of the simplest and oldest methods

form of time-rate and piece-rate systems for wage payment. Under this method, workers get 
additional wages on the basis of their efficiency, in addition to the minimum guaranteed wages. 
Incentive wage rate rises or falls with increase or decrease in the quantity of production.
We have already discussed in Chapter 18 about the Committee on Fair Wages as a major landmark 
in the history of formulation of wage policy in India. The recommendations of the Committee have 
been instrumental in formulation of the concepts of living wage, minimum wage and fair wage, besides 
laying down the guidelines for wage fixation. In this chapter we would be focusing on the Payment 
of Wages Act, 1936 as the key legislation enacted to regulate payment of wages to workers employed 
in industries and to ensure speedy and effective remedies against illegal deductions and/or unjustified 
delays in such payments.
BACKDR OP OF THE PA YMENT OF WAGES ACT , 1936 
It may be little known to large number of people in modern times that the concept of fair wages paid 
at regular intervals with commonly known and acceptable deductions was unthinkable at the begin-
ning of the 20th century. Industrialisation in India had created enormous employment opportunities 
but industrialists used it as a tool for undue exploitation of workers by not paying their due in return 
of work done; hence the issue of payment of wages brought forth new challenges to authorities. As a 
general practice wages were not paid at regular intervals, and delay in payment was routine. Further, 
wages paid were not uniform across industries. Deductions were made from wages at the discretion 
of employers without any justification; various kinds of fines were also imposed on workers. In fact, 
employers had the sole authority to decide and execute the mode and manner of all such payments. 
Workers were thus subjected to severe exploitation. An urgent need for legislation to protect the rights 
of workers in matters of wages and compensation was hence perceived.
The anomalies in payment of wages were first addressed in 1925 by way of a private member’s 
bill called the “Weekly Payment Bill”, which suggested the need for legislation for payment of 
wages. The Bill was however withdrawn on assurance by the government that remedial measures 
would be initiated towards regularisation of payment of wages. In fact, in the year 1926, the govern-
ment wrote to local governments to ascertain the delays in the payment of wages to the persons em-
ployed in industry and the practice of imposing fines on them. Investigations revealed the existence 
of abuses in both directions and the findings were placed before the Royal Commission on Labour 
which was appointed in 1929. The report of the C ommission recommended the necessity of legislation 
to address all these problems related to payment of wages. Following such recommendations, the 
government re-examined the matter and in February 1933 the Payment of Wages Bill was introduced 
in the Legislative Assembly, though it lapsed eventually. This was followed by the Payment of Wages 
Bill, 1935, based upon the same principles as the Bill of 1933 but thoroughly revised, and was intro-
duced in the Legislative Assembly on 15th February 1935. Having been passed by the Legislative Spotlight

piece-rate systems

Assembly, the Payment of Wages Bill, 1935 received its assent on 23rd April 1936, and it came on the

The Payment of Wages Act, 1936 was introduced for the broad purpose 
of safeguarding wages of workers under certain conditions laid down in 
the Act. The specific objectives of the Act are:
rregulation of payment of wages and imposition of fines and deduc-
tions from wages, and 
relimination of all malpractices by laying down wage-periods and 
time and mode of payment of wages.
The Act therefore ensures payment of wages in a particular form at regular intervals, without 
unauthorised deductions. It has been amended several times according to the needs of the situation.

ABOUT THE ACT
Short Title, Extent, Commencement and Application (Section 1)
1. This Act may be called the Payment of Wages Act, 1936.
2.It extends to the whole of India. 
3. It shall come into force on such date as the Central Government may, by notification in the Of-
ficial Gazette, appoint.
4. It applies in the first instance to the payment of wages to persons employed in any factory, to 
persons employed (otherwise than in a factory) upon any railway by a railway administration or, 
either directly or through a sub-contractor, by a person fulfilling a contract with a railway admin-
istration, and to persons employed in an industrial or other establishment specified in sub-clauses 
(a) to (g) of clause (ii) of Section 2.
5. The appropriate Government may, after giving 3 months’ notice of its intention of so doing, by 
notification in the Official Gazette, extend the provisions of this Act or any of them to the pay-
ment of wages to any class of persons employed in any establishment or class of establishments 
specified by the appropriate Government under sub-clause (h) of clause (ii) of Section 2.Spotlight

CASE COR
NERIn K.L. Garg vs. New India Assurance Co. Ltd. and Others [(1991) (62) FLR 869] the petitioner had 
submitted that the respondent, New India Assurance Co. Ltd. was an “industry”, with reference to the 
definition of “industrial or other establishment” in the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 (referred to as the 
Act now onwards); therefore, it was submitted further that the provisions of the Act were applicable 
to the petitioner. On the other hand, the respondent pleaded that the definition of “industrial or other 
establishment” in the Act does not include insurance companies and, therefore, the Act, as such, was not 
applicable to them. It was further submitted that in the said definition in clause (h), it has been provided 
that an industrial or other establishment shall mean any other establishment or class of establishments 
which the Central Government or the State Government may specify by notification in the Official Gazette. 
However, no such notification has been issued by either the Central Government or the State Govern-
ment in this behalf. Hence the learned authority had wrongly relied on the said notification to come to 
the conclusion that the insurance business was an industry under the Act.

InMd. Qasim Larry, Factory Manager, Sasamusa Sugar Works vs. Muhammad Samsuddin and 
Another  [(1964) AIR 1699], it was pointed out that the amendment in the payment of Wages Act, 
1936 in 1958 expressly provides by Section 2(vi)(a) that any remuneration payable under any award 
or settlement between the parties or order of a Court, would be included in the main definition of 
wages under Section 2(vi). When an award is made and it prescribes a new wage structure, in law 
the old contractual wage structure becomes inoperative and is replaced by the one prescribed by the 
award. In other words, the latter wage structure must be deemed to be a contract between the parties, 
because that, in substance, is the effect of industrial adjudication. When industrial disputes are decided 
by industrial adjudication and awards are made, such awards replace contractual terms in respect of 
matters covered by them and are substituted for them.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/435033/ accessed on 10/6/2014.)
In Balaram Abaji Patil vs. M.C. Ragojiwalla [(1960) IILLJ 491 Bom], it was held by the Court that 
all remuneration would be “wages” if such remuneration satisfies two conditions; first: it should be 
payable to “a person employed in respect of his employment or of work done in such employment”, 
and second: it should be payable “if the terms of the contract of employment, express or implied, 
were fulfilled”. The definition of “wages” given in Section 2(h) of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 is 
identical with that in Section 2(vi) of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936. Under the Minimum Wages 
Act, 1948, minimum wages are undoubtedly “wages” and in view of the identity of the definition 
of the term “wages” in both the Acts, it must follow that minimum wages are also wages under the 
Payment of Wages Act, 1936.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/1736060/ accessed on 12/6/2014.)

CASE COR
NERIn Cominco Binani Zinc Ltd. vs. Pappachan  [(1989) ILLJ 452 Ker], the petitioner-company is having 
more than 250 workers on its rolls, and as per Section 46 of the Factories Act, 1948, the company had 
to provide and maintain a canteen for its employees. The right to conduct the canteen was being given 
on contract to others from time to time, and at no point of time had the company run the canteen by 
itself. The contractors who took up the responsibility of running the canteen were engaging their own 
workmen, who were paid by the contractors. 
 As per the Industrial Tribunal, the mere fact that the petitioner had the responsibility to provide and 
maintain a canteen under Section 46 of the Factories Act, 1948 cannot make it the ultimate employer of 
the workers engaged in the canteen for all purposes. When the management has entrusted the respon-
sibility of running the canteen with a contractor, then the workmen employed and paid by such contractor 
cannot be treated as workmen of the management. There is no employer-employee relationship between 
the management and such workmen. All claims of these workmen are to be met by the contractor, who 
would be the employer in this case.
 However, it was held that even in a case where the canteen is run by the contractor, the management 
of the factory cannot absolve itself from the liability to pay wages to the workers engaged in the canteen. 
The principal-employer’s liability to pay wages is recognised in Section 21(4) of the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970, by which, if the contractor fails to pay the wages the petitioner 
shall be bound to pay the same.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/1387153/ accessed on 15/6/2014.)

CASE COR
NERIn General Manager, Northern Railway , New Delhi  vs. Sajjan Raj and Another  (AIR (1957) Raj 78), it 
has been pointed out that there is a seeming contradiction between Section 2(vi) and Section 6 of the 
Payment of Wages Act, 1936 (or, “the Act”). It was further held that perhaps the definition of wages 
was left wide by the framers of the Act to cover remuneration which was paid in kind by employers to 
employees before the enforcement of the Act, so that it may be possible to convert the same into cash 
and include it in wages afterwards. Sections 6, 20 and 23 read together clearly exclude payments in kind 
from “wages” which can be paid only in current coin or currency notes after the enforcement of the Act.
 If Section 6 of the Act envisages that payment in kind, according to earlier practice or agreement 
made before the Act, could be converted into cash according to its value before payment, the Court held 
that this could be done by a subsequent agreement between an employer and his employees. In such a 
case, there would be no contravention of Section 6 of the Act and Section 23 would not apply unless the 
contract or agreement expressly forbids such conversion into cash. Anything agreed to be paid in kind in 
circumstances contemplated by the definition of “wages” is covered by the expression “capable of being 
so expressed”, which implies, capable of being expressed in terms of money but, as required by Section 
6, it has to be converted into money according to its value and then paid in coins or currency notes.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/1708747/ accessed on 14/6/2014.)

Fines (Section 8) 
1. No fine shall be imposed on any employed person save in respect of such acts and omissions 
on his part as the employer, with the previous approval of the appropriate Government or of the 
prescribed authority, may have specified by notice under sub-section (2).
2. A notice specifying such acts and omissions shall be exhibited in the prescribed manner on the 
premises in which the employment is carried on or in the case of person employed upon a railway 
(otherwise than in a factory), at the prescribed place or places.
3. No fine shall be imposed on any employed person until he has been given an opportunity of 
showing cause against the fine, or otherwise than in accordance with such procedure as may be 
prescribed for the imposition of fines.
4. The total amount of fine which may be imposed in any 1 wage-period on any employed person 
shall not exceed an amount equal to 3 per cent of the wages payable to him in respect of that 
wage-period.
5. No fine shall be imposed on any employed person who is under the 
age of 15 years.
6. No fine imposed on any employed person shall be recovered from 
him by instalments or after the expiry of 90 days from the day on 
which it was imposed.
7. Every fine shall be deemed to have been imposed on the day of the act or omission in respect of 
which it was imposed.
8. All fines and all realisations thereof shall be recorded in a register to be kept by the person re-
sponsible for the payment of wages under Section 3 in such form as may be prescribed; and all 
such realisations shall be applied only to such purposes beneficial to the persons employed in the 
factory or establishment as are approved by the prescribed authority.
Explanation When the persons employed upon or in any railway, factory or industrial or other

21.12 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Deductions for Absence from Duty (Section 9) 
1. Deductions may be made under clause (b) of sub-section (2) of Section 7 only on account of the 
absence of an employed person from the place or places where, by the terms of his employment, 
he is required to work, such absence being for the whole or any part of the period during which 
he is so required to work.
2. The amount of such deduction shall in no case bear to the wages payable to the employed person 
in respect of the wage-period for which the deduction is made a larger proportion than the period 
for which he was absent bears to the total period, within such wage-period, during which by the 
terms of his employment, he was required to work:
   Provided that, subject to any rules made in this behalf by the appropriate Government, if 10 
or more employed persons acting in concert absent themselves without due notice (that is to say 
without giving the notice which is required under the terms of their contracts of employment) and 
without reasonable cause, such deduction from any such person may include such amount not 
exceeding his wages for 8 days as may be any such terms be due to the employer in lieu of due 
notice.
Explanation For the purposes of this section, an employed person shall be deemed to be absent from 
the place where he is required to work if, although present in such place, he refuses, in pursuance of a 
stay-in strike or for any other cause which is not reasonable in the circumstances, to carry out his work.
Deductions for Damage or Loss (Section 10) 
1. A deduction under clause (c) or clause (o) of sub-section (2) of Section 7 shall not exceed the 
amount of the damage or loss caused to the employer by the neglect or default of the employed 
person.
1A. A deduction shall not be made under clause (c) or clause (m) or clause (n) or clause (o) of sub-
section (2) of Section 7 until the employed person has been given an opportunity of showing 
cause against the deduction, or otherwise than in accordance with such procedure as may be 
prescribed for the making of such deductions.
2. All such deductions and all realisations thereof shall be recorded in a register to be kept by the 
person responsible for the payment of wages under Section 3 in such form as may be prescribed.
Deductions for Services Rendered (Section 11)
A deduction under clause (d) or clause (e) of sub-section (2) of Section 7 shall not be made from 
the wages of an employed person, unless the house-accommodation amenity or service has been ac-
cepted by him, as a term of employment or otherwise, and such deduction shall not exceed an amount 
equivalent to the value of the house-accommodation amenity or service supplied and, in the case of 
a deduction under the said clause (e), shall be subject to such conditions as the appropriate Govern-
ment may impose.
Deductions for Re covery of Adv ances (Section 12)
Deductions under clause (f) of sub-section (2) of Section 7 shall be subject to the following condi-

CASE COR
NERInA. V. D’ Costa, Divisional Engineer, G.I.P . Railway vs. B.C. Patel and Another  [(1955) AIR SC 412], 
the respondent was employed as a carpenter on daily wages basis with the Railway Administration. 
The Railway Administration had introduced a scheme which created a cadre of skilled labourers on the 
scale of monthly-rated pay and admitted only those persons to it who would pass a test. The respondent 
could not pass the test and continued to serve as an employee on daily wages. He subsequently filed 
an application under Section 15(2) of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 (now onwards referred to as 
“the Act”) before the Authority under the Act to recover the additional amount of wages that would have 
become payable to him had he been taken on the cadre of monthly-rated employee. 
 The Supreme Court held that “If the parties entered into the contract of service, say by correspondence 
and the contract is to be determined with reference to the letters that passed between them, it may be 
open to the Authority to decide the controversy and find-out what the terms of contract with reference 
to these letters were. But if an employee were to say that his wages were `100 per month, which he 
actually received as and when they fall due, but that he would be entitled to higher wages, if his claims 
to be placed on the higher wages scheme had been recognised and given effect to, that would not, in 
our opinion, be a matter within the ambit of jurisdiction.”
 In other words, the Authority has the jurisdiction to decide what actually the terms of the contract 
between the parties were, that is, to determine the actual wages; but the Authority has no jurisdiction to 
determine the question of potential wages.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/924929/ accessed on 14/6/2014.)

section (2) of Section 15, or against a direction made under sub-section (3) or sub-section 
(4) of that section may be preferred, within 30 days of the date on which the order or direction

District Court–
(a) by the employer or other person responsible for the payment of wages under Section 3, if 
the total sum directed to be paid by way of wages and compensation exceeds `300 or such 
direction has the effect of imposing on the employer or the other person a financial liability 
exceeding `1,000, or
(b) by an employed person or any legal practitioner or any official of a registered trade union

made under sub-section (2) of Section 15, or a direction made under sub-section (3) or sub-
section (4) of that section shall be final.
3. Where an employer prefers an appeal under this section, the authority against whose decision the 
appeal has been preferred may, and if so directed by the court referred to in sub-section (1) shall, 
pending the decision of the appeal, withhold payment of any sum in deposit with it.
4. The court referred to in sub-section (1) may, if it thinks fit, submit any question of law for the 
decision of the High Court and, if it so does, shall decide the question in conformity with such 
decision.

21.20  Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
CASE COR
NERInMining Engineer (Vig.) vs. Akhlesh Kumar Sharma and Another  [(2006) IIILLJ 992 Raj], it has been 
stated that while Section 20 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 (or the Act) is only in regard to penalty 
for various offences under different sections of the Act, Section 21 further provides for procedure in 
trial of offences. Under the procedure as provided under Section 21, it is only a Court which can make 
cognizance of the offence and impose penalty as provided under Section 20. The Authority under the 
Act has been defined under Section 15 of the Act itself. However, the Payment of Wages Authority, 
Bharatpur (the Authority in the present case), cannot be treated as the Court as referred to under Section 
21. The Authority could only grant sanction to the concerned workman for prosecution of the defaulting 
employer; it could not have imposed penalty on its own.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/31322/ accessed on 14/6/2014.)
Bar of Suits (Section 22)
No Court shall entertain any suit for the recovery of wages or of any deduction from wages in so far 
as the sum so claimed:
 (a) forms the subject of an application under Section 15 which has been presented by the plaintiff 
and which is pending before the authority appointed under that section or of an appeal under Sec-
tion 17; or
 (b) has formed the subject of a direction under Section 15 in favour of the plaintiff; or
 (c) has been adjudged, in any proceeding under Section 15, not to be owed to the plaintiff; or
 (d) could have been recovered by an application under Section 15.
Protection of Action Taken in Good Faith (Section 22A)
No suit, prosecution or other legal proceeding shall lie against the Government or any officer of the 
Government for anything which is in good faith done or intended to be done under this Act.
Contracting out (Section 23)
Any contract or agreement, whether made before or after the commencement of this Act, whereby 
an employed person relinquishes any right conferred by this Act shall be null and void in so far as it 
purports to deprive him of such right.
Delegation of Powers (Section 24)
The appropriate Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, direct that any power exer-
cisable by it under this Act shall, in relation to such matters and subject to such conditions, if any, as 
may be specified in the direction, be exercisable:
 (a) where the appropriate Government is the Central Government, by such officer or authority sub-
ordinate to the Central Government or by the State Government or by such officer or authority 
subordinate to the State Government, as may be specified in the notification;
 (b) where the appropriate Government is a State Government, by such officer or authority subordi-
nate to the State Government as may be specified in the notification.

(i) prescribe the extent to which advances may be made and the instalments by which they may 
be recovered with reference to clause (b) of Section 12;
(ia) prescribe the extent to which loans may be granted and the rate of interest payable thereon 
with reference to Section 12A;
(ib) prescribe the powers of Inspectors for the purposes of this Act;
(j) regulate the scales of costs which may be allowed in proceedings under this Act;
(k) prescribe the amount of court-fees payable in respect of any proceedings under this Act; 
(l) prescribe the abstracts to be contained in the notices required by Section 25; 
(la) prescribe the form and manner in which nominations may be made for the purposes of 
sub-section (1) of Section 25A, the cancellation or variation of any such nomination, or the 
making of any fresh nomination in the event of the nominee predeceasing the person making 
nomination, and other matters connected with such nominations;
(lb) specify the authority with whom amounts required to be deposited under clause (b) of sub-
section (1) of Section 25A shall be deposited, and the manner in which such authority shall 
deal with the amounts deposited with it under that clause;
(m) provide for any other matter which is to be or may be prescribed.
4. In making any rule under this section the State Government may provide that a contravention of 
the rule shall be punishable with fine which shall not be less than `750 but which may extend to 
`1,500.
5. All rules made under this section shall be subject to the condition of previous publication, and the 
date to be specified under clause (3) of Section 23 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, shall not be 
less than 3 months from the date on which the draft of the proposed rules was published.
6. Every rule made by the Central Government under this section shall be laid, as soon as may 
be after it is made, before each House of Parliament while it is in session for a total period of 
30 days which may be comprised in 1 session or in 2 or more successive sessions, and if, before 
the expiry of the session immediately following the session or the successive sessions aforesaid, 
both Houses agree in making any modification in the rule, or both Houses agree that the rule 
should not be made, the rule shall thereafter have effect only in such modified form or be of no 
effect, as the case may be; so, however, that any such modification or annulment shall be without 
prejudice to the validity of anything previously done under that rule.
7. All rules made under this section by the State Government shall, as soon as possible after they are 
made, be laid before the State Legislature.

The Payment of Wages Act, 1936 21.23
RECENT INITIATIVES 
The wage ceiling under the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 was fixed at `1,600 per month in the year 
1982. With a view to enhance the wage ceiling to `6,500 per month for applicability of the Act, to 
empower the Central Government to further increase the ceiling in future by way of notification, and 
to enhance the penal provisions, etc., the Payment of Wages (Amendment) Act, 2005 was notified 
on 6th September 2005 as Act 41 of 2005 by the Ministry of Law and Justice. It was made effective 
from 9th November 2005.
Further, exercising the powers conferred by sub-section (6) of Section 1 of the Act, the Central 
Government, on the basis of the figures of the Consumer Expenditure Survey published by the 
National Sample Survey Office, has enhanced the wage ceiling further to `10,000 per month (Ministry 
of Labour & Employment, 2011).
Summary 
rWages refer to the total pay package an employee receives from his/her employer on a periodic 
basis in return of the physical labour supplied to the firm. The important methods of wage pay-
ment are: time-rate system, piece-rate system, and incentive wage plan.
rWith the onset of industrialisation in India, industrialists were found to be unduly exploiting 
workers by not paying their due in return of their labour. The Payment of Wages Act, 1936 was 
introduced for the broad purpose of safeguarding the wages of workers under certain conditions 
laid down in the Act. The Act ensures payment of wages in a particular form at regular intervals, 
without unauthorised deductions.
rOn the basis of the figures of the Consumer Expenditure Survey published by NSSO, the Central 
Government has enhanced the wage ceiling to `10,000 per month.
rSection 2(vi) defines wages as all remuneration (whether by way of salary, allowances or other-
wise) expressed in terms of money or capable of being so expressed which would, if the terms 
of employment, express or implied, were fulfilled, be payable to a person employed in respect 
of his employment or of work done in such employment.
rSection 3 mandates every employer to pay wages required to be paid under this Act to persons 
employed by him and even in case the contractor or the person designated by him fails to make 
such payment.
rAs per Section 5(1), the wages of every person employed upon or in any railway, factory or 
industrial, or other establishment upon or in which less than 1,000 persons are employed, shall 
be paid before the expiry of the seventh day, and in any other railway, factory or industrial or 
other establishment, wages shall be paid before the expiry of the tenth day, after the last day of 
the wage-period.
rSection 7 lays down the deductions which may be made from wages.
rAccording to Section 8(1), no fine shall be imposed on any employed person save in respect of 
such acts and omissions on his part as the employer, with the previous approval of the appropriate 
Government or of the prescribed authority, may have specified by notice under sub-section (2). 
The total amount of fine which may be imposed in any wage-period on any employed person 
shall not exceed an amount equal to 3 per cent of the wages payable to him in respect of that 
wage-period, as provided in Section 8(4).
rSection 15 provides for claims arising out of deductions from wages or delay in payment of 
wages and penalty for malicious and vexation claims.

rAs per Section 16(1), employed persons are said to belong to the same unpaid group if they are 
borne on the same establishment and if deductions have been made from their wages in contra-
vention of this Act for the same cause and during the same wage-period(s) or if their wages for 
the same wage-period(s) have remained unpaid after the day fixed by Section 5.
rWhoever responsible for the payment of wages to an employed person, as laid down in Section

CASE STUDY–I
The appellant is a nationalised bank and two of the respondents are its employees. The other two are 
the trade unions representing the Bank’s employees. In furtherance of certain demands for wage revi-
sion made by the employees in June 1977 the All the India Bank Employees’ Association gave a call 
for an all-India strike on certain days. The Bank issued a circular dated 23rd September 1977 to its 
managers and agents directing them to deduct the wages of such of the employees who participated 
in the strike on the principle of ‘no work no pay’. There was a 4-hour strike on 25th December 1977. 
The Bank issued an administrative circular dated 27th December 1977 to its managers and agents that 
such employees who participated in the 4-hour strike would be committing a breach of their contract 
of service and would not draw salary for the entire day.
IR&LL_Ch_21.indd   25 1/1/2008   4:52:48 AM

21.26 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
The employees struck work for 4 hours on 29th December 1977. On 16th January 1978 the Bank 
issued a circular to its managers and agents directing them to deduct the full day’s wages of such em-
ployees who had participated in the 4-hour strike. The respondents filed a writ petition for rescinding 
that circular. The petition was allowed. Hence the present appeal was made by the Bank.
(Adapted from: The Bank of India, Bombay and Another vs. T.S. Kelawala, Bombay and Others [(1990) 
SCR(3)214) www.indiankanoon.org/doc/398653/ accessed on 13/6/2014.)
Review Questions
1. Was it permissible for the Bank, by means of the impugned administrative circular, to deduct a 
full day’s wages (or even a part thereof) of the employees who participated in the 4-hour strike 
on 29th December 1977?
2. Given that strikes are recognised as a legitimate form of protest for workers, do you think that the 
bank is justified in suppressing such a legitimate mode of protest by an administrative circular?
3. Which all sections of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 are relevant in this case?
CASE STUDY–II
The State Electricity Board had revoked the license of a company and taken over the undertaking. 
The first respondent, who was the director of the company, served notices on the employees that their 
services would not be required. Thereupon, the appellant filed an application under Section 15(2) of 
the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 (hereby “the Act”), on behalf of the employees, for recovering wages 
for the notice month and retrenchment compensation under Section 25FF of the Industrial Disputes 
Act, 1947. The first respondent contested the claim as well as the jurisdiction of the authority under the 
Payment of Wages Act to deal with the application on the ground that he was not the person responsible 
for payment of compensation and that the right of the workmen was defeated by reason of the proviso 
to Section 25FF of the Industrial Disputes Act, because there was no interruption in their employment 
and the new employer (the Electricity Board) was responsible for payment of the compensation. In 
response the Authority held against the first respondent, who then filed a writ petition in the High 
Court and the High Court held that Section 15 of the Act did not apply and that the proper forum for 
such an application was the Labour Court under Section 33C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
Note: The 3 sections, namely Section 25F introduced into the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 by 
Act 43 of 1951 and sections 25FF and 25FFF incorporated by Act 18 of 1957, involve termination of 
service in consequence of retrenchment, transfer and closure respectively. In sections 25FF and 25FFF, 
notice and compensation have been provided for “in accordance with the provisions of Section 25F”. 
These words are used only as a measure of compensation and not for laying down any time within 
which the employer must pay compensation. 
(Adapted from: Payment of Wages Inspector vs. Surajmal Mehta and Another (1969 SCR (3) 1051) 
www.indiankanoon.org/doc/1757386/ accessed on 14/6/2014.)
Review Questions
1. Referring to compensation payable under Section 25FF of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, 
justify if it can fall under the amended definition of wages in the Payment of Wages Act, 1936.
2. Do you think that the authority under Section 15 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 had jurisdic-
tion to entertain the application?
3. Which all sections of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 are relevant in this case?

CONCEPT AND RELEVANCE OF TRADE UNIONS
Management and workers are the two indispensible components of organ-
ised industrial world, and prosperity of industry is contingent upon their 
joint contribution. Whenever the conditions at work create divergence of 
interest between these two components, the natural outcome is conflict. 
It is here that trade unions play a significant role by bridging the notional 
and functional gap between the interests of management and workers and 
by maintaining cordial relations between them.
Unions are a legitimate system to organise workers and to voice their rights and grievances. Union 
representation and collective bargaining are the keys to the growth of a stable workforce through which 
workers are able to gain a more equitable share of the wealth that they create; they are also able to 
improve their working conditions and gain job security. Protection of basic worker and human rights in 
industrial settings thus necessitates unionisation, so that the working population can reap the benefits 
from economic growth (Ghosh and Geetika, 2007).Reflection

22.2 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
BACKDR OP OF THE TRADE UNIONS ACT , 1926
The concept of trade unions and the emergence of trade unionism in India has already been discussed 
in Chapter 3. Let us now touch briefly upon the historical backdrop of the Trade Unions Act, 1926.
The main protagonist in the movement for trade union legislation was N. M. Joshi, who was the 
founder of the All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) and the then General Secretary of the AITUC. 
In March 1921, Joshi moved a resolution in the Central Legislative Assembly with the recommenda-
tion that the government should introduce a legislation towards protection of trade unions. However, 
the very idea of such a legislative measure faced severe opposition from employers and it took the 
government 5 long years to pass the Indian Trade Unions Act. The Indian Trade Unions Bill, 1925, 
passed by the Legislature, received assent on 25th March 1926, though it came into force only on and 
from 1st June 1927, as the Indian Trade Unions Act, 1926.
The Trade Unions Act, 1926 is a legislation that has provisions for 
registration of trade unions, their rights, liabilities and responsibilities. It 
gives corporate status to a registered trade union, with a common seal and 
having perpetual succession. The Act gives guidelines on the utilisation 
of funds of registered unions as well. Further, as per the Act, the Societ-
ies Registration Act, 1860, the Co-operative Societies Act, 1912 and the 
Companies Act, 1956 shall not apply to any registered trade union, and the registration of any union 
under any such Act shall be void.
The Trade Unions Act, 1926 has undergone several amendments ever since it has been passed. 
In 1929 it was amended to make provisions for the procedure of appeal against the decision of the 
Registrar to refuse to register a trade union or to withdraw registration of a union. The Royal Com-
mission on Labour (1929) examined the working of the Act and made the following recommendations:
(i) The Act was to be re-examined within 3 years. Further, the limitations imposed upon the activi-
ties of trade unions and their office-bearers were to be reconsidered, so as to ensure that under no 
circumstances shall a bona fide  trade union be prevented from registration.
(ii) The accounts of trade unions would be audited by government officials free of charge.
(iii) Minimum two-thirds of the members of the executive of a trade union should be persons who are 
actually engaged or employed in the industry to which the union belongs.
(iv) No union shall be deprived of initiating and carrying out cooperative societies. 
Among the above recommendations made by the Commission, the government reserved the first 
one, while it did not consider the legislation necessary as regards the second recommendation.
As we have mentioned earlier, the Trade Unions Act, 1926 provides for registration of a trade 
union subject to fulfilment of specific requirements. However, the original Act did not provide for 
any obligation on the part of an employer to recognise or deal with a union, even if it was registered 
either in spirit or in letter. The Act was again amended in the year 1947. The Amendment provided for 
recognition of trade unions by employers; it was laid down that recognition would be granted if the 
union applying for recognition was representative of all the workers in the establishment or industry 
concerned, though it did not have any provision for inspection of books of trade unions by the Registrar. 
However, the Indian Trade Unions (Amendment) Act, 1947 was neither notified, nor brought into force.
Issues related to amending the Indian Trade Unions Act, 1926 were discussed in the 11th Session 
of the Standing Labour Committee in January 1949, on the basis of which, the Trade Unions Bill was 
introduced in the Parliament in February 1950. However the Bill lapsed with the dissolution of the 
Parliament. Minor amendments were made to the original Act in 1960 and the word “Indian” was deleted
from the Act by the Amendment Act of 1964. This was followed by the Trade Unions (Amendment) Spotlight

CHAPTER I: PRELIMINAR Y 
Short Title, Extent and Commencement (Section 1)
1. This Act may be called the Trade Unions Act, 1926.
2. It extends to the whole of India.
  This Act has been extended to Goa, Daman and Diu, to Pondicherry, and to Laccadive, Minicoy 
and Amindivi Islands. It has been amended in Madhya Pradesh and in Maharashtra.
3. It shall come into force on such date as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official 
Gazette, appoint.
Definitions (Section 2)
In this Act “the appropriate Government” means, in relation to Trade Unions whose objects are not 
confined to one State, the Central Government, and in relation to other Trade Unions, the State Gov-
ernment, and unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context,-
Executive [Section 2(a)] Executive means the body, by whatever name called, to which the 
management of the affairs of a Trade Union is entrusted;
Office-bearer [Section 2(b)] Office-bearer, in the case of a Trade Union, includes any member 
of the executive thereof, but does not include an auditor;
Prescribed [Section 2(c)] Prescribed means prescribed by regulations made under this Act;
Registered office [Section 2(d)] Registered office means that office of a Trade Union which 
is registered under this Act as the head office thereof;

Provisions to be Contained in the Rules of a Trade Union (Section 6)
A Trade Union shall not be entitled to registration under this Act, unless the executive thereof is con-
stituted in accordance with the provisions of this Act, and the rules thereof provide for the following 
matters, namely:
(a) the name of the Trade Union;
(b) the whole of the objects for which the Trade Union has been established;
(c) the whole of the purposes for which the general funds of the Trade Union shall be applicable, all

Power to Call for Further Particulars and to Require Alterations of Names
(Section 7)
1. The Registrar may call for further information for the purpose of satisfying himself that any

in such form as may be prescribed, the particulars relating to the Trade Union contained in the state-

The Registrar, on registering a Trade Union under Section 8, shall issue a certificate of registration in 
the prescribed form which shall be conclusive evidence that the Trade Union has been duly registered 
under this Act.

22.8 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Minimum Requirement about Membership of a Trade Union (Section 9A)
A registered Trade Union of workmen shall at all times continue to have 
not less than 10 per cent or 100 of the workmen, whichever is less, subject 
to a minimum of 7, engaged or employed in an establishment or industry 
with which it is connected, as its members.
Cancellation of Registration (Section 10)
A certificate of registration of a Trade Union may be withdrawn or cancelled by the Registrar–
(a) on the application of the Trade Union to be verified in such manner as may be prescribed, or
(b) if the Registrar is satisfied that the certificate has been obtained by fraud or mistake, or that the 
Trade Union has ceased to exist or has wilfully and after notice from the Registrar contravened 
any provision of this Act or allowed any rule to continue in force which is inconsistent with any 
such provision, or has rescinded any rule providing for any matter provision for which is required 
by Section 6;
(c) If the Registrar is satisfied that a registered Trade Union of workmen ceases to have the requisite 
number of members.
Provided that not less than 2 months’ previous notice in writing specifying the ground on which it 
is proposed to withdraw or cancel the certificate shall be given by the Registrar to the Trade Union 
before the certificate is withdrawn or cancelled otherwise than on the application of the Trade Union.
Appeal (Section 11)
1. Any person aggrieved by any refusal of the Registrar to register a Trade Union or by the with-
drawal or cancellation of a certificate of registration may, within such period as may be pre-
scribed, appeal–
(a) where the head office of the Trade Union is situated within the limits of a Presidency town, 
to the High Court, or
(aa) where the head office is situated in an area, falling within the jurisdiction of a Labour Court 
or an Industrial Tribunal, to that Court or Tribunal, as the case may be;
(b) where the head office is situated in any other area, to such Court, not inferior to the Court 
of an additional or assistant Judge of a principal Civil Court of original jurisdiction, as the 
appropriate Government may appoint in this behalf for that area.
2. The appellate Court may dismiss the appeal, or pass an order directing the Registrar to register 
the Union and to issue a certificate of registration under the provisions of Section 9 or setting 
aside the order for withdrawal or cancellation of the certificate, as the case may be, and the Reg-
istrar shall comply with such order.
3. For the purpose of an appeal under sub-section (1) an appellate Court shall, so far as may be, fol-
low the same procedure and have the same power as it follows and has when trying a suit under 
the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and may direct by whom the whole or any part of the costs of 
the appeal shall be paid, and such costs shall be recovered as if they had been awarded in a suit 
under the said Code.
4. In the event of the dismissal of an appeal by any Court appointed under clause (b) of sub-section 
(1), the person aggrieved shall have a right of appeal to the High Court, and the High Court shall, 
for the purpose of such appeal, have all the powers of an appellate Court under sub-sections 
(2) and (3), and the provisions of those sub-sections shall apply accordingly.Spotlight

The Trade Unions Act, 1926 22.9
CASE COR
NERInRangaswami and Another vs. Registrar of Trade Unions and Another [(1961) ILLJ 599 (Mad)], a peti-
tion was made under Section 11 of the Trade Unions Act, 1926 (referred hereafter as “the Act”), seeking 
to set aside the order of the Registrar of Trade Unions, Madras (now Chennai) refusing to register the 
union of employees of the Madras Raj Bhavan as a trade union under the Act.
 In the Raj Bhavan at Guindy, a number of persons are employed in various capacities such as 
household, staff, peons, chauffeurs, tailors, carpenter s, maistries, gardeners, sweepers, etc. Maistries and 
gardeners are employed at the Raj Bhavan at Ootacamund; they are employed for doing domestic and 
other services, maintenance of the Governor’s household, and to attend to the needs of the Governor, 
the members of his family, staff and State guests. Their service is not pensionable but they are entitled 
to gratuity at certain rates. With the object of securing better service conditions and to facilitate collec-
tive bargaining with the employer, the employees formed themselves into a union called the Madras Raj 
Bhavan Workers’ Union, and 7 of the employees applied to the Registrar of Trade Unions, Madras for 
registration of their union under the Trade Unions Act, 1926. The applicants did not however claim before 
the Registrar that the employees were engaged in either trade or an industry; the claim was that their 
services could not be held to be purely domestic services and that their union would hence be entitled 
to the benefits of registration under the Act. 
 The Registrar was of the view that before a union can be registered, the members thereof must be 
connected with a trade or industry or business of an employer, and that condition not being fulfilled in 
this case, the employees could not be held to be workmen within the meaning of the Act to entitle them 
to the registration; the application for registration was hence rejected.
 The Court held that the services rendered by these employees to the State guests are personal in 
nature, indirectly to the employer, and would not be indicative of any co-operation between the employer 
and the employees for the purpose of a trade or business. Further, the occasional sale of unserviceable 
articles and garden products are incidents of the ordinary administration of Government property, and 
would not amount to a trade or business. The union of such workers would hence not come within the 
scope of the Act, so as to entitle it to registration. The order of the Register of Trade Unions rejecting 
the application of the petitioner was hence considered to be correct.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/1314449/ accessed on 16/8/2014.)
Registered Office (Section 12)
All communications and notices to a registered Trade Union may be addressed to its registered office. 
Notice of any change in the address of the head office shall be given within 14 days of such change 
to the Registrar in writing, and the changed address shall be recorded in the register referred to in 
Section 8.
Incorporation of Registered Trade Unions (Section 13)
Every registered Trade Union shall be a body corporate by the name under which it is registered, and 
shall have perpetual succession and a common seal with power to acquire and hold both movable and 
immovable property and to contract, and shall by the said name sue and be sued.

22.10  Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
CASE COR
NERInState Bank of Travancore Employees Union vs. Wealth-Tax Officer [(1984) 8 ITD 529 (Mad)], the 
point for determination is whether the assessee, State Bank of Travancore Employees Union, a trade 
union registered under the (Indian) Trade Unions Act, 1926 (hereafter “the Act”), is liable to wealth-tax 
(in context of the Wealth-tax Act, 1957) in the status of an individual.
 The representative of the assessee pointed out that Section 13 of the Act states that every registered 
trade union shall be a body corporate. According to him, a body corporate is not an assessable entity 
under the Act; in fact, the expression “body corporate” is wider in context than the expression “company” 
and a body corporate is distinct and apart from the members constituting it. In his submission, all body 
corporates are not individuals and holding of assets by a body corporate cannot be equated to holding 
of assets by an individual. Artificial persons are not contemplated to be included in the term “individual”, 
and only normal human beings are to be included in the expression “individual” for the purpose of charge 
to wealth-tax. It was also pointed out that the assessee-trade union has not been declared by the Board 
as a company for the purpose of the Act. 
 The Court however pointed out the authorities of both the High Courts and the Supreme Court affirm-
ing and reaffirming the proposition that the term ‘individual’ is not confined in its meaning or connotation 
to a natural human being, but includes every entity, such as a body corporate, not only for purposes 
of income-tax, but also for assessment under the Wealth-tax Act, 1957. The status of the assessee 
can only be “individual” and it clearly follows, therefore, that the assessee-trade union, which is a body 
corporate having independent legal existence and personality, is chargeable to wealth-tax in the status 
of “individual”. The Court therefore rejected the objection of the assessee.
(Adapted from: www.indiankanoon.org/doc/369494/ accessed on 15/8/2014.)
Certain Acts Not to Apply to Registered Trade Unions (Section 14)
The following Acts, namely:
 (a) The Societies Registration Act, 1860;
 (b) The Co-operative Societies Act, 1912; 
 (c) The Companies Act, 1956,
shall not apply to any registered Trade Union, and the registration of any such Trade Union under any 
such Act shall be void.

Objects on which General Funds May be Spent (Section 15)
The general funds of a registered Trade Union shall not be spent on any other objects than the fol-
lowing, namely:
 (a) the payment of salaries, allowances and expenses to office-bearers of the Trade Union;
 (b) the payment of expenses for the administration of the Trade Union, including audit of the 
accounts of the general funds of the Trade Union;

(c) the prosecution or defence of any legal proceeding to which the Trade Union or any member

protecting any rights of the Trade Union as such or any rights arising out of the relations of any

(d) the conduct of trade disputes on behalf of the Trade Union or any member thereof;

Criminal Conspiracy in Trade Disputes (Section 17)
No office-bearer or member of a registered Trade Union shall be liable to punishment under sub-section 
(2) of Section 120B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, in respect of any agreement made between the 
members for the purpose of furthering any such object of the Trade Union as is specified in Section 
15, unless the agreement is an agreement to commit an offence. 
Immunity from Civil Suit in Certain Cases (Section 18)
1. No suit or other legal proceeding shall be maintainable in any Civil Court against any registered 
Trade Union or any office-bearer or member thereof in respect of any act done in contemplation 
or furtherance of a trade dispute to which a member of the Trade Union is a party on the ground 
only that such act induces some other person to break a contract of employment, or that it is in 
interference with the trade, business or employment of some other person or with the right of 
some other person to dispose of his capital or of his labour as he wills.
2. A registered Trade Union shall not be liable in any suit or other legal proceeding in any Civil 
Court in respect of any tortious act done in contemplation or furtherance of a trade dispute by 
an agent of the Trade Union if it is proved that such person acted without the knowledge of, or 
contrary to express instructions given by, the executive of the Trade Union.
Enforceability of Agreements (Section 19)
Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, an agreement between 
the members of a registered Trade Union shall not be void or voidable merely by reason of the fact 
that any of the objects of the agreement are in restraint of trade:
Provided that nothing in this section shall enable any Civil Court to entertain any legal proceeding 
instituted for the express purpose of enforcing or recovering damages for the breach of any agreement 
concerning the conditions on which any members of a Trade Union shall or shall not sell their goods, 
transact business, work, employ or be employed.
Right to Inspect Books of Trade Union (Section 20)
The account books of a registered Trade Union and the list of members thereof shall be open to in-
spection by an office-bearer or member of the Trade Union at such times as may be provided for in 
the rules of the Trade Union.

a registered Trade Union subject to any rules of the Trade Union to the Spotlight

22.14 Industrial Relations and Labour Laws
Amalgamation of Trade Unions (Section 24)
Any 2 or more registered Trade Unions may become amalgamated together as 1 Trade Union with or 
without dissolution or division of the funds of such Trade Unions or either or any of them, provided 
that the votes of at least one-half of the members of each or every such Trade Union entitled to vote 
are recorded, and that at least 60 per cent of the votes recorded are in favour of the proposal.
As laid down in Rattan Kumar Dey vs. Union of India [(1991) 63 FLR 463 (Gau)], a trade union 
and its office-bearers do not lose their identity on merger.
Notice of Change of Name or Amalgamation (Section 25) 
1. Notice in writing of every change of name and of every amalgamation signed, in the case of a 
change of name, by the Secretary and by 7 members of the Trade Union changing its name, and, 
in the case of an amalgamation, by the Secretary and by 7 members of each and every Trade 
Union which is a party thereto, shall be sent to the Registrar, and where the head office of the 
amalgamated Trade Union is situated in a different State, to the Registrar of such State.
2. If the proposed name is identical with that by which any other existing Trade Union has been 
registered or, in the opinion of the Registrar, so nearly resembles such name as to be likely to 
deceive the public or the members of either Trade Union, the Registrar shall refuse to register the 
change of name.
3. Save as provided in sub-section (2), the Registrar shall, if he is satisfied that the provisions of this 
Act in respect of change of name have been complied with, register the change of name in the 
register referred to in Section 8, and the change of name shall have effect from the date of such 
registration.
4. The Registrar of the State in which the head office of the amalgamated Trade Union is situated 
shall, if he is satisfied that the provisions of this Act in respect of amalgamation have been com-
plied with and that the Trade Union formed thereby is entitled to registration under Section 6, 
register the Trade Union in the manner provided in Section 8, and the amalgamation shall have 
effect from the date of such registration. 
Effects of Change of Name and of Amalgamation (Section 26)
1. The change in the name of a registered Trade Union shall not affect any rights or obligations of 
the Trade Union or render defective any legal proceeding by or against the Trade Union, and any 
legal proceeding which might have been continued or commenced by or against it by its former 
name may be continued or commenced by or against it by its new name.
2. An amalgamation of 2 or more registered Trade Unions shall not prejudice any right of any of 
such Trade Unions or any right of a creditor of any of them. 
Dissolution (Section 27)
1. When a registered Trade Union is dissolved, notice of the dissolu-
tion signed by 7 members and by the Secretary of the Trade Union 
shall, within 14 days of the dissolution be sent to the Registrar, and 
shall be registered by him if he is satisfied that the dissolution has 
been effected in accordance with the rules of the Trade Union, and 
the dissolution shall have effect from the date of such registration.Spotlight

Returns (Section 28)
1. There shall be sent annually to the Registrar, on or before such date as may be prescribed, a 
general statement, audited in the prescribed manner, of all receipts and expenditure of every 
registered Trade Union during the year ending on the 31st day of December next preceding such 
prescribed date, and of the assets and liabilities of the Trade Union existing on such 31st day of 
December. The statement shall be prepared in such form and shall comprise such particulars as 
may be prescribed.
2. Together with the general statement there shall be sent to the Registrar a statement showing all 
changes of office-bearers made by the Trade Union during the year to which the general state-
ment refers, together also with a copy of the rules of the Trade Union corrected up to the date of 
the despatch thereof to the Registrar.
3. A copy of every alteration made in the rules of a registered Trade Union shall be sent to the Reg-
istrar within 15 days of the making of the alteration.
4. For the purpose of examining the documents referred to in sub-sections (1), (2) and (3), the Reg-
istrar, or any officer authorised by him, by general or special order, may at all reasonable times 
inspect the certificate of registration, account books, registers, and other documents, relating to 
a Trade Union, at its registered office or may require their production at such place as he may 
specify in this behalf, but no such place shall be at a distance of more than 10 miles from the 
registered office of a Trade Union.
InRashtriya Mukund Employees’ Union vs. Mukund Iron and Steel Works Ltd . [(1995) IIILLJ 200 
(Bom)], registration of the union was cancelled on account of failing to send an annual return in ac-
cordance with the provisions contained in Section 28 of the Trade Unions Act, 1926. It was held that 
the order of cancellation of the registration of a trade union cannot be withdrawn or revoked by the 
Registrar; the only remedy is to go in for appeal or apply for re-registration.
